enheduanna-named-author-2285bce.summary: Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon of Akkad, serves as high priestess of moon god Nanna at Ur around 2285 BCE. A calcite disk from Ur carries her name and image, and later copies of Sumerian hymns, above all Inanna's Exaltation (Nin-me-šara) and a cycle of temple hymns, name her as speaker and composer. Hallo and van Dijk's 1968 edition presented her as history's first author known by name. Her poems describe exile from office during a revolt and appeal to Inanna for restoration. Helle's 2023 translation gathers her corpus and reviews authorship questions for a general readership.

sources.title: Hallo, W. W. and van Dijk, J. J. A., The Exaltation of Inanna, Yale Near Eastern Researches 3 (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1968)
sources.author: Hallo, William W.; van Dijk, J. J. A.
sources.confirms: Edits Nin-me-šara and argues for Enheduanna as its author, the first named author in world literature.

sources.title: Helle, S., Enheduana: The Complete Poems of the World's First Author (New Haven: Yale University Press, 2023)
sources.author: Helle, Sophus
sources.confirms: Translates the attributed corpus and reviews the authorship debate.
sources.qualifies: Notes that all manuscripts are Old Babylonian copies and that some Sumerologists doubt the attribution.

sources.title: ETCSL, 'The exaltation of Inana (Inana B)' (t.4.07.2)
sources.author: Black, Jeremy et al. (eds)
sources.confirms: Composite text and translation in which the speaker names herself as Enheduanna.

sources.title: Penn Museum, 'Disk of Enheduanna', object CBS 16665
sources.author: Penn Museum
sources.confirms: Catalogue record of the alabaster disk from Ur naming Enheduanna as wife of Nanna and daughter of Sargon.

enheduanna-named-author-2285bce.verification_note: Her office and existence are contemporary; authorship of the hymns rests on later copies and is debated.
enheduanna-named-author-2285bce.detail: Scholarly caution matters: surviving manuscripts of her hymns are Old Babylonian school copies written some 500 years after her life, and Civil, Black and others have asked whether later scribes attributed these works to her. Her existence and office are secure from contemporary objects: her disk, seals of her servants and a votive inscription. Dating by Sargonic king lists follows middle chronology.

picture.alt: Alabaster disc of Enheduanna from Ur showing the priestess at a libation, Penn Museum.

enheduanna-named-author-2285bce.dating_note: Textual dates for Mesopotamian kings depend on a chosen chronology; middle chronology figures are given here, short chronology runs about 64 years later. Sargon's accession c. 2334 BCE (middle) or c. 2270 BCE (short).

austronesian-voyaging-philippines-2200bc.summary: Around 2200 BCE, Neolithic communities from Taiwan cross the Luzon Strait to the northern Philippines, bringing red-slipped pottery, polished stone adzes, rice and ornaments of Taiwan nephrite, and within a millennium their descendants' languages and material culture spread through Island Southeast Asia to the Bismarcks, where Lapita forms. Electron microprobe analysis traces nephrite artefacts across Southeast Asia to a single source at Fengtian in eastern Taiwan, documenting exchange from 3000 BCE onward. Archaeological, linguistic and genetic evidence charts this expansion, which carried Austronesian languages from Madagascar to Easter Island.

sources.title: Hung, H.-c. et al., 'Ancient jades map 3,000 years of prehistoric exchange in Southeast Asia', PNAS 104.50 (2007), 19745-19750
sources.author: Hung, Hsiao-chun; Iizuka, Yoshiyuki; Bellwood, Peter et al.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Traces nephrite artefacts across Southeast Asia to a Taiwan source from 3000 BCE.

sources.title: Bellwood, P., First Islanders: Prehistory and Human Migration in Island Southeast Asia (Hoboken: Wiley Blackwell, 2017)
sources.author: Bellwood, Peter
sources.confirms: Synthesises the Austronesian expansion from Taiwan c. 2200 BCE onward.

austronesian-voyaging-philippines-2200bc.verification_note: Dates are secure; the Out of Taiwan model's weight relative to local developments is debated.
austronesian-voyaging-philippines-2200bc.detail: Peter Bellwood's 'Out of Taiwan' model credits migrants from Taiwan; alternative models stress indigenous Island Southeast Asian contributions and genetic mixing, and Lapita populations show both Asian and Papuan ancestry. Sailing technology at this stage is inferred; no boats survive. Dates come from radiocarbon on shell and charcoal at Batanes and Cagayan sites. Red-slipped pottery with stamped circles links Taiwan, Batanes, Luzon and later Lapita wares, a ceramic thread across 5,000 km.

picture.alt: Map of Austronesian expansion with hypothetical greatest extent after Blench 2009.
picture.credit: BlankMap-World-162E.svg: Lokal_Profil derivative work: Milenioscuro (talk) derivative work: Obsidian Soul], via Wikimedia Commons

austronesian-voyaging-philippines-2200bc.dating_note: Earliest Neolithic in Batanes and northern Luzon c. 2200-2000 BCE by radiocarbon.

domestic-horse-dom2-steppe-2200bce.summary: A 2021 analysis of 273 ancient horse genomes identified lower Volga-Don steppes as homeland of a lineage (DOM2) ancestral to all modern domestic horses. This population expanded after about 2200 BCE, replacing local horse populations across Eurasia within a few centuries and carrying variants associated with docility and a stronger back. Earlier horse keeping at Botai (c. 3500 BCE) left no descendants among modern horses. A 2023 examination of skeletal markers in Yamnaya individuals (c. 3000-2500 BCE) found pathologies consistent with habitual riding, so riding may predate DOM2 expansion. Spoked-wheel chariots spread alongside DOM2 horses.

sources.title: Librado, P. et al., 'The origins and spread of domestic horses from the Western Eurasian steppes', Nature 598 (2021), 634-640
sources.author: Librado, Pablo; Orlando, Ludovic et al.
sources.confirms: Identifies the Volga-Don origin of modern domestic horses and their expansion after c. 2200 BCE.

sources.title: Trautmann, M. et al., 'First bioanthropological evidence for Yamnaya horsemanship', Science Advances 9.9 (2023)
sources.author: Trautmann, Martin et al.
sources.confirms: Reports skeletal markers of riding in Yamnaya individuals dated 3021-2501 BCE.
sources.qualifies: Suggests riding began before the DOM2 expansion, among Yamnaya herders.

domestic-horse-dom2-steppe-2200bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Librado 2021 and Trautmann 2023.
domestic-horse-dom2-steppe-2200bce.detail: Horse riding's origins remain difficult to prove from bones alone; bits and bridles rarely survive. This genomic turnover coincides with Sintashta chariotry and with movement of steppe populations. Horses did not reach China in domestic form until Shang times. Selection for a back variant (GSDMC) and a docility gene (ZFPM1) in DOM2 horses points to breeding for rideability and traction rather than for meat or milk.

picture.alt: Herd of Przewalski's horses, modern wild horses shown for illustration; not DOM2 domestic horses.

domestic-horse-dom2-steppe-2200bce.dating_note: Genomic expansion dated c. 2200-2000 BCE from directly dated specimens; Yamnaya riding evidence 3000-2500 BCE.

four-point-two-kiloyear-event-2200bce.summary: Palaeoclimate records from Mesopotamia, Red Sea sediments, Indian lakes, Chinese caves and elsewhere register an abrupt shift to drier conditions around 2200 BCE lasting one to three centuries. Harvey Weiss tied abandonment of Tell Leilan on Syria's Habur plains and Akkadian imperial collapse to this aridification in 1993, and later added evidence from Egypt's First Intermediate Period, Indus deurbanisation and Chinese Longshan decline. This event marks formal start of Holocene's Meghalayan stage, ratified in 2018. Historians stress political and economic factors instead, and some records show no clear signal.

sources.title: Weiss, H. et al., 'The Genesis and Collapse of Third Millennium North Mesopotamian Civilization', Science 261.5124 (1993), 995-1004
sources.author: Weiss, Harvey; Courty, Marie-Agnès; Wetterstrom, Wilma et al.
sources.confirms: Links Tell Leilan abandonment and Akkadian collapse to abrupt aridification at 2200 BCE.

sources.title: Weiss, H., '4.2 ka BP Megadrought and the Akkadian Collapse', in H. Weiss (ed.), Megadrought and Collapse: From Early Agriculture to Angkor (New York: Oxford University Press, 2017), 93-160
sources.author: Weiss, Harvey (ed.)
sources.confirms: Compiles 4.2 ka BP evidence across regions and its archaeological correlates.

sources.title: Dixit, Y., Hodell, D. A. and Petrie, C. A., 'Abrupt weakening of the summer monsoon in northwest India ~4100 yr ago', Geology 42.4 (2014), 339-342
sources.author: Dixit, Yama; Hodell, David A.; Petrie, Cameron A.
sources.confirms: Monsoon weakening c. 2100 BCE in north-west India.
sources.qualifies: Notes dating uncertainty in both climate and archaeological records.

four-point-two-kiloyear-event-2200bce.verification_note: Climate event is well documented; its causal role in political collapses is contested.
four-point-two-kiloyear-event-2200bce.detail: An Indian lake record places monsoon weakening at 2100 BCE, and a separate drought followed around 1200 BCE. Critics argue that global synchronicity is overstated and that dating uncertainties of a century or more blur correlations with historical collapses. Records of this horizon in the Americas and Australia show regional variation. Some scholars question whether a single global event occurred at all, noting that records show drying in some regions and wetter conditions in others.

picture.alt: View of Tell Leilan, northeast Syria, abandoned around 2200 BCE.

four-point-two-kiloyear-event-2200bce.dating_note: Climate proxies date the event c. 2250-1900 BCE with regional variation; links to specific collapses are debated.

laws-of-ur-nammu-2100bce.summary: A Sumerian law collection attributed in its prologue to Ur-Nammu, founder of the Third Dynasty of Ur (c. 2112-2095 BCE), survives in Old Babylonian copies from Nippur, Ur and Sippar. About forty provisions set compensation in silver for injuries, regulate marriage, divorce, slavery, false witness and agricultural damage, and the prologue claims standardisation of weights and measures. Roth's edition notes some scholars assign the text to Shulgi, his son. Compensation in silver rather than retaliation distinguishes it from later Hammurabi provisions. It predates Hammurabi's stele by three centuries.

sources.title: Roth, M. T., Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor, 2nd edn, Writings from the Ancient World 6 (Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1997)
sources.author: Roth, Martha T.
sources.confirms: Edits and translates the Laws of Ur-Nammu with discussion of attribution to Ur-Nammu or Shulgi.

sources.title: Kramer, S. N., 'Ur-Nammu Law Code', Orientalia 23 (1954), 40-51
sources.author: Kramer, Samuel Noah
sources.confirms: First publication and translation of the Istanbul tablet.

sources.title: Klein, J., The Royal Hymns of Shulgi King of Ur: Man's Quest for Immortal Fame, Transactions of the American Philosophical Society 71.7 (Philadelphia: American Philosophical Society, 1981)
sources.author: Klein, Jacob
sources.confirms: Context for Shulgi's reign and claims of justice and standardisation in royal hymns.

laws-of-ur-nammu-2100bce.verification_note: Author king uncertain between Ur-Nammu and Shulgi.
laws-of-ur-nammu-2100bce.detail: Law collections in this tradition (Ur-Nammu, Lipit-Ishtar, Eshnunna, Hammurabi) share casuistic form: 'if a man ... then'. Whether they were applied in courts or served as royal self-presentation and scribal training is debated; contemporary trial records rarely cite them. Middle chronology dates are given; short chronology lowers them by about 64 years. Provisions cover bodily injury with graded silver payments: a severed foot costs ten shekels, a broken bone one mina, a cut-off nose two-thirds of a mina.

picture.alt: Cuneiform tablet of the Laws of Ur-Nammu, Istanbul Archaeology Museums.
picture.credit: Istanbul Archaeology Museums, via Wikimedia Commons

laws-of-ur-nammu-2100bce.dating_note: Textual dates for Mesopotamian kings depend on a chosen chronology; middle chronology figures are given here, short chronology runs about 64 years later. Ur-Nammu 2112-2095 BCE (middle), 2048-2031 BCE (short); attribution to Shulgi is possible.

taosi-observatory-2100bce.summary: At Taosi in Shanxi, a walled settlement of about 280 hectares dated c. 2300-1900 BCE, excavators found a semicircular rammed-earth platform with foundations for about a dozen pillars; from an observation point, sunrise over Mount Taer appears in successive slots through the year, with slots matching winter and summer solstices. Sun Xiaochun's account and simulations support use as a horizon calendar. Taosi also yielded a lacquered pole interpreted as a gnomon, early bronze objects, a large cemetery with elite tombs holding crocodile-skin drums and chime stones, and two brush-written characters on a pot sherd.

sources.title: Sun, X., 'Taosi Observatory', in C. L. N. Ruggles (ed.), Handbook of Archaeoastronomy and Ethnoastronomy (New York: Springer, 2015), 2095-2104
sources.author: Sun, Xiaochun
sources.confirms: Describes the pillar arc, sightline observations and dating c. 2100 BCE.

sources.title: Liu, L. and Chen, X., The Archaeology of China (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2012)
sources.author: Liu, Li; Chen, Xingcan
sources.confirms: Summarises Taosi's walls, cemetery and the observatory structure.

sources.title: Pankenier, D. W., Astrology and Cosmology in Early China: Conforming Earth to Heaven (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2013)
sources.author: Pankenier, David W.
sources.confirms: Discusses Taosi in relation to early Chinese astronomical practice.

taosi-observatory-2100bce.verification_note: Structure and date are secure; astronomical function is inferred.
taosi-observatory-2100bce.detail: The observatory interpretation is accepted by many Chinese archaeologists but relies on reconstruction, since only pillar bases survive. Taosi's size and stratified cemetery make it a candidate for the legendary capital of Yao in later texts; such identifications remain speculative. It precedes Erlitou by several centuries. Elite tombs at Taosi held painted pottery, jade axes and lacquered wood, while ordinary burials had nothing, an early case of sharp status difference in Chinese prehistory.

picture.alt: Painted pottery plate with dragon design from the Taosi site, Shanxi, Capital Museum, Beijing.
picture.credit: Fo Guang Shan 佛光山, via Wikimedia Commons

taosi-observatory-2100bce.dating_note: Taosi middle period c. 2100-2000 BCE by radiocarbon; observatory function is an interpretation.

debate-hoe-and-plough-2000bce.summary: A Sumerian school composition, Debate between Hoe and Plough, copied around 2000-1700 BCE, stages a verbal contest in which aristocratic Plough boasts of royal festivals and large fields, and humble Hoe answers that it works all year, digs canals, builds houses and city walls and serves poor people; Enlil awards victory to Hoe. It belongs to a genre of disputations (Summer and Winter, Sheep and Grain, Silver and Copper) used in scribal training. Vanstiphout's translation in Context of Scripture presents it as reflection on technology and labour, weighing Plough's need for oxen against Hoe's versatility.

sources.title: Vanstiphout, H. L. J., 'The Disputation between the Hoe and the Plow', in W. W. Hallo and K. L. Younger (eds), The Context of Scripture, vol. 1 (Leiden: Brill, 1997), 578-581
sources.author: Vanstiphout, Herman L. J. (trans.)
sources.confirms: Scholarly translation with introduction to the disputation genre and date of copies.

sources.title: ETCSL, 'The debate between Hoe and Plough' (t.5.3.1)
sources.author: Black, Jeremy et al. (eds)
sources.confirms: Composite text and translation with manuscript list.

sources.title: Robson, E., 'The Tablet House: A Scribal School in Old Babylonian Nippur', Revue d'assyriologie 95 (2001), 39-66
sources.author: Robson, Eleanor
sources.confirms: Places disputations within the Old Babylonian school curriculum.

debate-hoe-and-plough-2000bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Vanstiphout 1997 and Black 2006.
debate-hoe-and-plough-2000bce.detail: Seeder ploughs, with a funnel dropping seed into each furrow, appear on Mesopotamian seals and in a farmer's almanac text. Disputations give rare evidence of how a literate society argued about tools, status and work, two centuries before Egypt's Satire of the Trades took a different view. Vanstiphout notes that disputations end with a divine verdict, so school texts also taught that technical merit was judged by authority rather than by argument alone.

picture.alt: Mesopotamian serpentine cylinder seal with a ploughing scene, British Museum 129478.

debate-hoe-and-plough-2000bce.dating_note: Copies are Old Babylonian (c. 1800-1700 BCE); composition is conventionally placed in Ur III or early Isin period, c. 2100-1900 BCE.

sintashta-chariot-spoked-wheel-2000bce.summary: Sintashta-Petrovka graves east of Ural mountains, around 2000 BCE, contain two-wheeled vehicles set in wheel slots, paired horse sacrifices and disc-shaped antler cheekpieces. Wheel impressions show spokes, our earliest evidence anywhere for light spoked wheels. Lindner's 2020 Bayesian modelling of radiocarbon dates from Kamennyj Ambar-5 places these vehicles no later than any Near Eastern proto-chariot, and Chechushkov and Epimakhov's survey of 28 burials examines their construction and social role. Anthony's synthesis connects chariots to steppe horse breeding and bronze weaponry. Within two centuries, chariots appear in Anatolia, Syria and Egypt and by 1200 BCE in Shang China.

sources.title: Lindner, S., 'Chariots in the Eurasian Steppe: a Bayesian approach to the emergence of horse-drawn transport in the early second millennium BC', Antiquity 94.374 (2020), 361-380
sources.author: Lindner, Stephan
sources.confirms: Bayesian radiocarbon modelling dates Sintashta chariots to c. 2050-1900 BCE, no later than Near Eastern proto-chariots.

sources.title: Chechushkov, I. V. and Epimakhov, A. V., 'Eurasian Steppe Chariots and Social Complexity During the Bronze Age', Journal of World Prehistory 31 (2018), 435-483
sources.author: Chechushkov, Igor V.; Epimakhov, Andrey V.
sources.confirms: Catalogues steppe chariot burials and discusses construction and function.

sources.title: Anthony, D. W., The Horse, the Wheel, and Language (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2007)
sources.author: Anthony, David W.
sources.confirms: Synthesises Sintashta chariots, horse use and metallurgy.

sintashta-chariot-spoked-wheel-2000bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Lindner 2020 and Chechushkov 2018.
sintashta-chariot-spoked-wheel-2000bce.detail: Whether Sintashta vehicles were true war chariots or lighter ceremonial carts is debated; their wheel gauge is narrow. Composite bows, made of wood, horn and sinew, appear in steppe and Near Eastern contexts in these same centuries and pair with chariots in Egyptian New Kingdom warfare. Sintashta sites also show intensive copper smelting in fortified settlements such as Arkaim. Cheekpieces with spikes gave precise control of paired horses, and bone and antler examples spread from Urals to Mycenae within two centuries along with chariot imagery.

picture.alt: Line drawings of Sintashta culture pots and bone cheekpieces for chariot horses from graves 11, 12 and 30 at the Sintashta cemetery.
picture.credit: Lindner, S. (2020). Chariots in the Eurasian Steppe: A Bayesian approach to the emergence of horse-drawn transport in the early second millennium BC. Antiquity, 94(374), 361-380. doi:10.15184/aqy.2020.37, via Wikimedia Commons

sintashta-chariot-spoked-wheel-2000bce.dating_note: Bayesian model c. 2050-1900 BCE (Lindner 2020); older conventional date c. 2000 BCE.

sub-saharan-early-iron-lejja-oboui-2000b.summary: Étienne Zangato and Augustin Holl date smelting and forging sites at Oboui and Gbabiri in Central African Republic to about 3000-2500 BCE by radiocarbon; Pamela Eze-Uzomaka reports slag deposits at Lejja in south-eastern Nigeria with dates around 2000 BCE, which would place sub-Saharan iron working earlier than anywhere in Eurasia. Chirikure, Craddock and Eggert question sample association, old wood and stratigraphic integrity, and David Killick treats dates before about 1000 BCE as unproven. Secure iron working in West Africa, at Nok and in Niger's Termit massif, begins around 1000-800 BCE.

sources.title: Zangato, É. and Holl, A. F. C., 'On the Iron Front: New Evidence from North-Central Africa', Journal of African Archaeology 8.1 (2010), 7-23
sources.author: Zangato, Étienne; Holl, Augustin F. C.
sources.confirms: Reports iron production at Oboui and Gbabiri with dates of 3000-2500 BCE.

sources.title: Killick, D., 'Invention and Innovation in African Iron-smelting Technologies', Cambridge Archaeological Journal 25.1 (2015), 307-319
sources.author: Killick, David
sources.confirms: Reviews African smelting and treats very early dates as unconfirmed.
sources.qualifies: Does not accept dates before c. 1000 BCE as secure.

sources.title: Alpern, S. B., 'Did They or Didn't They Invent It? Iron in Sub-Saharan Africa', History in Africa 32 (2005), 41-94
sources.author: Alpern, Stanley B.
sources.confirms: Surveys the independent invention versus diffusion debate and early dates.

sources.title: Eze-Uzomaka, P. et al., 'Lejja archaeological site, Southeastern Nigeria and its potential for archaeological science research', Heritage Science 12 (2024)
sources.author: Eze-Uzomaka, Pamela et al.
sources.confirms: Describes Lejja's slag landscape and plans for secure dating.

sources.title: Chirikure, S., 'On Evidence, Ideas and Fantasy: The Origins of Iron in Sub-Saharan Africa', Journal of African Archaeology 8.1 (2010), 25-28
sources.author: Chirikure, Shadreck
sources.confirms: Critiques the Oboui dates on methodological grounds.

sub-saharan-early-iron-lejja-oboui-2000b.verification_note: Claim is published but widely disputed; recorded here as a dispute, not as an accepted date.
sub-saharan-early-iron-lejja-oboui-2000b.detail: These dates bear on whether iron metallurgy was invented independently in Africa, a view resting on distinctive bloomery furnaces and lack of a preceding copper age, or diffused from Carthage or Nubia. New excavations at Lejja in 2024 aim to resolve dating with controlled samples. Charcoal from termite-disturbed tropical soils and long-lived hardwoods can be far older than smelting events it is taken to date.

picture.alt: Iron slag blocks at Lejja, Nsukka area, Nigeria.
picture.credit: Lejja Iron Slags, via Wikimedia Commons
picture.changes: re-encoded as JPEG at source size 708x512; source smaller than 1200px

sub-saharan-early-iron-lejja-oboui-2000b.dating_note: Claimed dates c. 3000-2000 BCE rest on charcoal of uncertain association; most specialists accept iron in West Africa only from c. 1000-800 BCE.

barra-pottery-soconusco-1900bce.summary: Along Chiapas' Pacific coast, Barra-phase villagers produce thin-walled, well-fired tecomates (neckless jars) and bowls with fluted, incised and red-slipped surfaces, imitating gourd forms, from about 1900 BCE. Radiocarbon chronology for Soconusco places Barra at about 1900-1700 BCE, earlier than any other Mesoamerican pottery. John Clark and Michael Blake read these decorated serving vessels as wares for competitive feasting by aspiring leaders rather than for cooking staples, since maize was then a minor crop. Pottery had appeared earlier in South America, at sites in Colombia and Ecuador, around 3500-3000 BCE.

sources.title: Blake, M., Clark, J. E., Voorhies, B. et al., 'Radiocarbon Chronology for the Late Archaic and Formative Periods on the Pacific Coast of Southeastern Mesoamerica', Ancient Mesoamerica 6 (1995), 161-183
sources.author: Blake, Michael; Clark, John E.; Voorhies, Barbara et al.
sources.confirms: Dates the Barra phase c. 1900-1700 BCE (calibrated) as earliest Mesoamerican pottery.

sources.title: Clark, J. E. and Gosser, D., 'Reinventing Mesoamerica's First Pottery', in W. K. Barnett and J. W. Hoopes (eds), The Emergence of Pottery: Technology and Innovation in Ancient Societies (Washington: Smithsonian Institution Press, 1995), 209-221
sources.author: Clark, John E.; Gosser, Dennis
sources.confirms: Interprets Barra vessels as serving wares for social display.

sources.title: Lesure, R. G. (ed.), Settlement and Subsistence in Early Formative Soconusco (Los Angeles: Cotsen Institute, 2011)
sources.author: Lesure, Richard G. (ed.)
sources.confirms: Reports Early Formative Soconusco villages and chronology.

barra-pottery-soconusco-1900bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Blake 1995 and Clark 1995.
barra-pottery-soconusco-1900bce.detail: Barra ceramics appear with sedentary villages and Mesoamerica's earliest ballcourt at Paso de la Amada (c. 1650 BCE). Mesoamerican pottery traditions developed from here through Locona and Ocós phases into Olmec-period wares. Dates have been revised with calibration and may yet shift. Tecomates mimic gourds in shape and surface, which suggests pottery copied older containers before developing its own forms.

picture.alt: Olmec-period tecomate (neckless bowl), Metropolitan Museum of Art 1978.309.3; a later example of the form.
picture.credit: This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art. See the Image and Dat

dhar-tichitt-stone-villages-1900bce.summary: On Tichitt and Walata escarpments of south-eastern Mauritania, pastoral communities build hundreds of dry-stone compounds and villages between about 1900 and 400 BCE, with walled enclosures, granaries and livestock pens, some settlements covering tens of hectares. Holl's 2009 synthesis dates domesticated pearl millet impressions in pottery across Tichitt's sequence and reconstructs a seasonal round of cattle herding and cultivation. MacDonald's Cambridge World History chapter treats Tichitt as West Africa's earliest complex Sahelian society and a precursor to later Niger valley polities such as Dia and Jenne-jeno.

sources.title: Holl, A. F. C., 'Coping with uncertainty: Neolithic life in the Dhar Tichitt-Walata, Mauritania (ca. 4000-2300 BP)', Comptes Rendus Geoscience 341.8-9 (2009), 703-712
sources.author: Holl, Augustin F. C.
sources.confirms: Reconstructs Tichitt settlement, millet cultivation and chronology c. 4000-2300 BP.

sources.title: MacDonald, K. C., 'The Tichitt tradition in the West African Sahel', in G. Barker and C. Goucher (eds), The Cambridge World History, vol. 2 (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2015), 499-513
sources.author: MacDonald, Kevin C.
sources.confirms: Synthesises Tichitt as the earliest complex society of the Sahel.

dhar-tichitt-stone-villages-1900bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Holl 2009 and MacDonald 2015.
dhar-tichitt-stone-villages-1900bce.detail: Rock engravings of cattle and chariots occur nearby. Increasing aridity drove abandonment around 400 BCE and migration south toward Middle Niger floodplains. Dating rests on radiocarbon series from several surveys since Munson's 1970s work. Settlement layouts show compounds grouped within village walls, with granary foundations and cattle pens, an architecture of permanence rare in Africa at this date. Compounds grouped within village walls, with granary foundations and cattle pens, show an architecture of permanence rare in Africa at this date.

picture.alt: Town of Tichitt with the Dhar Tichitt escarpment behind, Mauritania.

dhar-tichitt-stone-villages-1900bce.dating_note: Tichitt tradition c. 1900-400 BCE (c. 4000-2300 BP calibrated).

indus-urban-decline-era-1900bce.summary: Between about 1900 and 1700 BCE, Mohenjo-daro, Harappa and other large Indus cities lose population, drains and standard weights fall out of use, seals and script disappear, and settlement shifts toward Ganges-Yamuna country and Gujarat in smaller villages. Rivers in Harappan territory stabilised as aridity increased after about 3000 BCE, with monsoon-fed rivers like Ghaggar-Hakra becoming seasonal; a lake record from Haryana shows an abrupt monsoon weakening about 2100 BCE. No evidence supports invasion. Change was gradual and regional rather than a single collapse.

sources.title: Giosan, L. et al., 'Fluvial landscapes of the Harappan civilization', PNAS 109.26 (2012), E1688-E1694
sources.author: Giosan, Liviu et al.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Links Harappan decline after c. 1900 BCE to aridification and river changes.

sources.title: Dixit, Y., Hodell, D. A. and Petrie, C. A., 'Abrupt weakening of the summer monsoon in northwest India ~4100 yr ago', Geology 42.4 (2014), 339-342
sources.author: Dixit, Yama; Hodell, David A.; Petrie, Cameron A.
sources.confirms: Lake isotope record shows monsoon weakening c. 2100 BCE near Indus settlements.

sources.title: Possehl, G. L., The Indus Civilization: A Contemporary Perspective (Walnut Creek: AltaMira, 2002)
sources.author: Possehl, Gregory L.
sources.confirms: Discusses deurbanisation and eastward settlement shift.

indus-urban-decline-era-1900bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Giosan 2012 and Dixit 2014.
indus-urban-decline-era-1900bce.detail: Deurbanisation left no literate successor; Rig Veda hymns, composed later in Punjab, does not describe cities. Shifts in crops toward drought-tolerant millets and rice accompany this eastward move. Dating uses radiocarbon and ceramic phases; absolute dates for script's disappearance are approximate. Later Harappan settlements in Haryana and Uttar Pradesh adopted rice and millets, and craft traditions such as faience continued in simplified form.

picture.alt: Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro, Sindh, Pakistan.

indus-urban-decline-era-1900bce.dating_note: Late Harappan transition c. 1900-1700 BCE by radiocarbon and ceramics.

kanesh-assyrian-tin-trade-1900bce.summary: Between about 1950 and 1750 BCE, merchant families from Assur keep a trading colony at Kanesh (Kültepe) in central Anatolia. More than 23,000 cuneiform tablets from their houses record donkey caravans carrying tin from the east and woollen textiles from Babylonia, sold in Anatolia for silver and gold that returned to Assur. Larsen's synthesis shows contracts, loans with interest, partnerships, transport insurance and letters between spouses; silver served as money of account with standard weights. Tin, essential for bronze, arrived through Assur from Iranian or Central Asian sources, about two tonnes a year in attested shipments. Kanesh is the earliest commercial society documented in private records.

sources.title: Larsen, M. T., Ancient Kanesh: A Merchant Colony in Bronze Age Anatolia (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2015)
sources.author: Larsen, Mogens Trolle
sources.confirms: Synthesises the Kanesh archives: caravans, tin and textile trade, silver as money, contracts and family firms, c. 2000-1750 BCE.

sources.title: Dercksen, J. G., 'The Old Assyrian Copper Trade in Anatolia' and related studies; see Dercksen, Old Assyrian Institutions (Leiden: NINO, 2004)
sources.author: Dercksen, Jan Gerrit
sources.venue: Nederlands Instituut voor het Nabije Oosten
sources.confirms: Reconstructs institutions, prices and routes of tin, copper and textile trade.

sources.title: Barjamovic, G., Hertel, T. and Larsen, M. T., Ups and Downs at Kanesh: Chronology, History and Society in the Old Assyrian Period (Leiden: NINO, 2012)
sources.author: Barjamovic, Gojko; Hertel, Thomas; Larsen, Mogens Trolle
sources.venue: Nederlands Instituut voor het Nabije Oosten
sources.confirms: Uses eponym lists and dendrochronology to date the colony c. 1972-1718 BCE.

kanesh-assyrian-tin-trade-1900bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Larsen 2015 and Dercksen 2004.
kanesh-assyrian-tin-trade-1900bce.detail: Dercksen's studies of copper and tin trade reconstruct routes and prices; tin cost about 14 shekels of silver per mina at Assur and twice that in Anatolia. Dendrochronology of Kanesh buildings gives absolute dates independent of king lists and has supported middle-chronology placements. Interest rates of 30 percent per year and compound accounting appear in the texts. Women in Assur wove textiles for export and wrote letters chasing payment, giving an unusual record of female economic agency in an early commercial economy.

picture.alt: Old Assyrian silver debt tablet with its clay envelope from Kanesh (Kultepe), Istanbul Archaeology Museums.

kanesh-assyrian-tin-trade-1900bce.dating_note: Eponym lists plus dendrochronology date the main archive level (II) c. 1972-1836 BCE; figures assume middle chronology.

satire-of-trades-scribe-1900bce.summary: Composed in the Middle Kingdom, probably around 1900 BCE, and copied by New Kingdom schoolboys, a text now called Satire of the Trades (Instruction of Dua-Khety) has a father escort his son to scribal school while describing each manual craft in scathing terms: smiths with fingers like crocodile hide, potters caked in mud, weavers confined indoors, builders exposed on scaffolds. Scribes, by contrast, give orders and pay no tax. Lichtheim's translation and the Context of Scripture edition present it as school literature that shaped attitudes to craft and literacy. Ramesside miscellanies continue with exhortations to 'be a scribe', contrasting desk work with soldiering and farming.

sources.title: Lichtheim, M., Ancient Egyptian Literature, Volume I: The Old and Middle Kingdoms (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1973; 2006 edn)
sources.author: Lichtheim, Miriam
sources.confirms: Translates Satire of the Trades with notes on its Middle Kingdom composition and Ramesside copies.

sources.title: Lichtheim, M., Ancient Egyptian Literature, Volume II: The New Kingdom (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1976; 2006 edn)
sources.author: Lichtheim, Miriam
sources.confirms: Translates Papyrus Lansing and Chester Beatty IV passages urging the student to be a scribe.

sources.title: Hallo, W. W. and Younger, K. L. (eds), The Context of Scripture, vol. 1 (Leiden: Brill, 1997), 'Dua-Khety or The Satire on the Trades' (1.48)
sources.author: Hoch, James E. (trans.)
sources.confirms: Scholarly translation with introduction on manuscripts and date.

satire-of-trades-scribe-1900bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Lichtheim 1973 and Lichtheim 1976.
satire-of-trades-scribe-1900bce.detail: The text survives mainly in Ramesside copies (Papyrus Sallier II, Papyrus Anastasi VII and hundreds of ostraca), so its Middle Kingdom composition is inferred from language and from a mention in later lists of classic authors. It documents a hierarchy of labour in which writing confers status over making, an attitude that recurs in later bureaucratic cultures. Teachers set pupils to copy it line by line, so its contempt for manual work was absorbed with handwriting practice by generations of future officials.

picture.alt: Limestone ostracon with a copy of the Teaching of Khety (Satire of the Trades) praising the scribe's profession, Egyptian Museum Berlin.

satire-of-trades-scribe-1900bce.dating_note: Composition placed in Dynasty 12 (c. 1990-1800 BCE) on linguistic grounds; surviving copies are Ramesside, c. 1300-1100 BCE.

proto-sinaitic-alphabet-serabit-1850bce.summary: Short inscriptions carved by Semitic-speaking people at Serabit el-Khadim's turquoise mines in Sinai and on a desert road at Wadi el-Hol in Upper Egypt use about two dozen pictorial signs, each standing for a consonant. Signs borrow hieroglyphic shapes (ox head, house, water) but record Semitic words by acrophony: a sign's first consonant in a Semitic word gives its value. Darnell's team published Wadi el-Hol's graffiti in 2005 and dated them palaeographically to the late Middle Kingdom, c. 1850-1700 BCE. Goldwasser argues its inventors were illiterate Canaanite workers who saw hieroglyphs but could not read them. Every later alphabet, from Phoenician to Greek, Latin, Arabic and Devanagari-adjacent Brahmi debates aside, descends from this experiment.

sources.title: Goldwasser, O., 'Canaanites Reading Hieroglyphs: Horus is Hathor? The Invention of the Alphabet in Sinai', Ägypten und Levante 16 (2006), 121-160
sources.author: Goldwasser, Orly
sources.confirms: Argues the alphabet was invented by Canaanite workers at Serabit el-Khadim in the Middle Kingdom by reinterpreting hieroglyphic shapes acrophonically.

sources.title: Darnell, J. C., Dobbs-Allsopp, F. W., Lundberg, M. J., McCarter, P. K. and Zuckerman, B., 'Two Early Alphabetic Inscriptions from the Wadi el-Ḥôl', Annual of the American Schools of Oriental Research 59 (2005), 63-124
sources.author: Darnell, John Coleman; Dobbs-Allsopp, F. W.; Lundberg, Marilyn J.; McCarter, P. Kyle; Zuckerman, Bruce
sources.venue: Annual of the American Schools of Oriental Research
sources.confirms: Publishes the Wadi el-Hol inscriptions and dates them palaeographically to the late Middle Kingdom, c. 1850-1700 BCE.

sources.title: Hamilton, G. J., The Origins of the West Semitic Alphabet in Egyptian Scripts, CBQ Monograph Series 40 (Washington: Catholic Biblical Association, 2006)
sources.author: Hamilton, Gordon J.
sources.confirms: Derives each early alphabetic letter from a specific hieroglyphic or hieratic model and supports a Middle Kingdom origin.
sources.qualifies: Sass (1988, 2005) dates most Serabit texts to c. 1500 BCE on archaeological grounds; the question is open.

sources.title: Albright, W. F., 'The Early Alphabetic Inscriptions from Sinai and Their Decipherment', Bulletin of the American Schools of Oriental Research 110 (1948), 6-22
sources.author: Albright, William F.
sources.venue: Bulletin of the American Schools of Oriental Research
sources.confirms: Classic decipherment attempt establishing acrophonic principle and reading of b'lt.

proto-sinaitic-alphabet-serabit-1850bce.verification_note: Invention and Egyptian derivation are agreed; date and the exact mechanism of invention are disputed within a 350-year window.
proto-sinaitic-alphabet-serabit-1850bce.detail: Dating stays argued. Sass places most Proto-Sinaitic texts in New Kingdom times, around 1500 BCE, while Darnell, Goldwasser and Hamilton prefer Middle Kingdom dates. A cuneiform alphabet at Ugarit (c. 1300 BCE) with a fixed letter order shows alphabetic writing well established in the Levant by the Late Bronze Age. Readings beyond a few words, such as b'lt 'lady', remain insecure.

picture.alt: Sandstone sphinx from Serabit el-Khadim bearing a bilingual Egyptian and Proto-Sinaitic inscription, British Museum EA 41748.

proto-sinaitic-alphabet-serabit-1850bce.dating_note: Palaeographic dating c. 1850-1700 BCE (Darnell, Goldwasser, Hamilton) versus c. 1500 BCE (Sass); no stratified context fixes either.

australian-backed-artefacts-1800bce.summary: Between about 2500 and 1500 BCE, Aboriginal toolmakers across south-eastern Australia increase production of backed artefacts, small blades blunted along one edge for hafting into composite spears and knives, by an order of magnitude. Hiscock's 2002 analysis argues the proliferation responded to heightened El Niño-driven climate variability from about 4000 years ago, with standardised, reliable tools reducing risk for mobile foragers. Attenbrow, Robertson and Hiscock's 2009 radiocarbon review of Sydney-region sites confirmed the timing of peak production. Backed artefacts had existed in small numbers since the Pleistocene.

sources.title: Hiscock, P., 'Pattern and Context in the Holocene Proliferation of Backed Artifacts in Australia', Archeological Papers of the American Anthropological Association 12.1 (2002), 163-177
sources.author: Hiscock, Peter
sources.venue: Archeological Papers of the American Anthropological Association
sources.confirms: Links mid-Holocene proliferation of backed artefacts to ENSO-driven risk.

sources.title: Attenbrow, V., Robertson, G. and Hiscock, P., 'The changing abundance of backed artefacts in south-eastern Australia: a response to Holocene climate change?', Journal of Archaeological Science 36.12 (2009), 2765-2770
sources.author: Attenbrow, Val; Robertson, Gail; Hiscock, Peter
sources.confirms: Radiocarbon review of Sydney-region sites dates peak production c. 4000-3000 BP.

australian-backed-artefacts-1800bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Hiscock 2002 and Attenbrow 2009.
australian-backed-artefacts-1800bce.detail: The mid-Holocene change coincides with dingo arrival and with population growth inferred from site numbers. Interpretations in terms of climate risk compete with social explanations involving exchange and identity. Production declined after about 1000 BCE in many regions. Resin residues on backed pieces show hafting in rows along spear shafts, an insert technology that made weapons repairable from standardised parts.

picture.alt: Aboriginal Australian stone knife with steeply backed blade in a hafted handle, Wellcome Collection; ethnographic example.

australian-backed-artefacts-1800bce.dating_note: Peak production c. 4000-3000 cal BP (c. 2000-1000 BCE).

eastern-agricultural-complex-1800bce.summary: By about 1800 BCE, people in river valleys of eastern North America cultivate a set of native seed plants showing domestication traits: squash (Cucurbita pepo), sunflower, marshelder (Iva annua) and goosefoot (Chenopodium berlandieri), joined by erect knotweed and little barley. Riverton site, Illinois, held at least five domesticates together at that date, defining a crop complex that developed independently of Mesoamerican maize, which arrived in eastern woodlands only around 200 BCE. Eastern North America is one of about ten independent centres of plant domestication.

sources.title: Smith, B. D. and Yarnell, R. A., 'Initial formation of an indigenous crop complex in eastern North America at 3800 B.P.', PNAS 106.16 (2009), 6561-6566
sources.author: Smith, Bruce D.; Yarnell, Richard A.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Documents five domesticated seed plants at Riverton, Illinois, by 3800 BP.

sources.title: Smith, B. D., 'Eastern North America as an independent center of plant domestication', PNAS 103.33 (2006), 12223-12228
sources.author: Smith, Bruce D.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Reviews evidence for independent domestication of four species in eastern North America.

eastern-agricultural-complex-1800bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Smith 2009 and Smith 2006.
eastern-agricultural-complex-1800bce.detail: Domestication markers include thinner seed coats in goosefoot and enlarged seeds in sunflower and marshelder. These crops supported later Woodland societies and Hopewell mound builders before maize displaced most of them after 900 CE. Sunflower alone is still widely grown. Floodplain gardens and seasonal camps supported cultivation without full sedentism, so farming here began within a mobile foraging economy of hunters and fishers.

picture.alt: Chenopodium berlandieri (goosefoot) in flower; modern photograph of a domesticated species of the complex.

eastern-agricultural-complex-1800bce.dating_note: Riverton assemblage directly dated c. 3800 BP (c. 1800 BCE).

gajiganna-chad-basin-settlement-1800bce.summary: Around 1800 BCE, as Lake Mega-Chad retreated, Gajiganna pastoral groups settle clay plains south-west of Lake Chad in north-eastern Nigeria, leaving mounds with pottery, cattle, sheep and goat bones and fish remains. Domesticated pearl millet appears by about 1200 BCE and permanent villages with storage pits by 1000 BCE. Gajiganna documents a transition from mobile herding to sedentary farming in Sahelian country comparable to Tichitt.

sources.title: Breunig, P., Neumann, K. and Van Neer, W., 'New research on the Holocene settlement and environment of the Chad Basin in Nigeria', African Archaeological Review 13 (1996), 111-145
sources.author: Breunig, Peter; Neumann, Katharina; Van Neer, Wim
sources.confirms: Establishes the Gajiganna sequence from c. 1800 BCE with herding and later millet.

sources.title: Klee, M., Zach, B. and Stika, H.-P., 'Four thousand years of plant exploitation in the Lake Chad Basin (Nigeria), part III: plant impressions in potsherds from the Final Stone Age Gajiganna Culture', Vegetation History and Archaeobotany 13 (2004), 131-142
sources.author: Klee, Marlies; Zach, Barbara; Stika, Hans-Peter
sources.confirms: Documents pearl millet and wild plant use in Gajiganna pottery impressions.

gajiganna-chad-basin-settlement-1800bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Breunig 1996 and Klee 2004.
gajiganna-chad-basin-settlement-1800bce.detail: Chad basin occupation continues after 1000 BCE with fortified settlements such as Zilum. Pottery with rocker-stamp and cord decoration links Gajiganna to wider Saharan traditions. Climate drying is a proposed driver of both settlement and later agricultural intensification. Fish bones and shellfish in early mounds show lake and river resources sustaining herders before cultivation, with cattle as main domestic animal.

picture.alt: Satellite map of present-day Lake Chad and the extent of Holocene Lake Mega-Chad (NASA Earth Observatory).
picture.credit: Joshua Stevens, NASA Earth Observatory, via Wikimedia Commons

gajiganna-chad-basin-settlement-1800bce.dating_note: Gajiganna phase I from c. 1800 BCE; millet cultivation from c. 1200 BCE.

linear-a-minoan-writing-1800bce.summary: From about 1800 BCE palace administrators on Crete record commodities with Linear A, a syllabic script of roughly 90 signs plus logograms and a decimal numeral system with fractions, used on tablets, roundels and nodules at Hagia Triada, Phaistos, Knossos, Zakros and Chania until about 1450 BCE. Schoep's 1999 study traces its origin alongside Cretan Hieroglyphic from an earlier sealing system, and Salgarella's 2020 analysis compares its sign repertoire with the Linear B derived from it. Sign values can be read by analogy with Linear B, but the underlying Minoan language remains unidentified, so Linear A is undeciphered.

sources.title: Schoep, I., 'The Origins of Writing and Administration on Crete', Oxford Journal of Archaeology 18.3 (1999), 265-276
sources.author: Schoep, Ilse
sources.confirms: Traces Linear A and Cretan Hieroglyphic to Protopalatial administration and an earlier sealing system.

sources.title: Salgarella, E., Aegean Linear Script(s): Rethinking the Relationship between Linear A and Linear B (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2020)
sources.author: Salgarella, Ester
sources.confirms: Analyses Linear A sign repertoire, chronology and its relation to Linear B.

linear-a-minoan-writing-1800bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Schoep 1999 and Salgarella 2020.
linear-a-minoan-writing-1800bce.detail: About 1,400 Linear A documents survive, most of them short. Libation formulae on stone vessels give the longest religious texts. The Phaistos Disc, stamped with 45 distinct signs on both faces around 1700 BCE, is a separate unread script and the earliest known use of movable stamps for text. Dating follows Minoan pottery phases tied to Egyptian synchronisms. Fractions in Linear A follow a system distinct from Mesopotamian sexagesimals, with signs for halves, quarters and smaller units attached to commodity logograms.

picture.alt: Linear A clay tablet from Hagia Triada, Crete, Heraklion Archaeological Museum.

linear-a-minoan-writing-1800bce.dating_note: Earliest Linear A documents belong to Middle Minoan II (c. 1800-1700 BCE); use ends with Late Minoan IB destructions c. 1450 BCE.

mesopotamian-beer-bread-economy-1800bce.summary: Ration lists from Ur III and Old Babylonian administrations allot barley, bread and beer to workers by rank, and a Sumerian Hymn to Ninkasi, goddess of beer, preserved in Old Babylonian copies around 1800 BCE, describes brewing steps from bappir barley bread and malt through mash, filtering and a vat 'like the Tigris and Euphrates'. Damerow's 2012 study warns that the hymn's technical vocabulary is too uncertain to give a reliable recipe. Samuel's microscopy of desiccated bread and beer residues from Amarna and Deir el-Medina showed Egyptian brewers combining cooked and uncooked malt and straining before fermentation, a process distinct from bread-based brewing.

sources.title: Damerow, P., 'Sumerian Beer: The Origins of Brewing Technology in Ancient Mesopotamia', Cuneiform Digital Library Journal 2012:2
sources.author: Damerow, Peter
sources.confirms: Reviews administrative and literary evidence for brewing and cautions against reading the Ninkasi hymn as a recipe.
sources.qualifies: Argues the hymn's technical terms are too uncertain to reconstruct a process.

sources.title: Samuel, D., 'Investigation of Ancient Egyptian Baking and Brewing Methods by Correlative Microscopy', Science 273.5274 (1996), 488-490
sources.author: Samuel, Delwen
sources.confirms: Microscopy of Egyptian residues shows malt-based brewing with straining before fermentation.

sources.title: Paulette, T., 'Brewing technologies and techniques', in In the Land of Ninkasi: A History of Beer in Ancient Mesopotamia (New York: Oxford University Press, 2024), ch. 4
sources.author: Paulette, Tate
sources.confirms: Surveys brewing technologies, ingredients and institutional contexts.

sources.title: ETCSL, 'A hymn to Ninkasi (Ninkasi A)' (t.4.23.1)
sources.author: Black, Jeremy et al. (eds)
sources.confirms: Composite text and translation of the hymn.

mesopotamian-beer-bread-economy-1800bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Damerow 2012 and Samuel 1996.
mesopotamian-beer-bread-economy-1800bce.detail: Beer, drunk through straws from shared jars on seals from 3000 BCE onward, carried calories and a safer liquid than untreated water. Paulette's 2024 survey covers Mesopotamian brewing archaeology and texts. Large-scale bakeries beside Khufu's pyramid show the same bread-and-beer provisioning at Giza. Ration texts from Ur III assign about 60 litres of barley a month to adult male workers, with beer allotments graded by rank, so brewing capacity scaled with state labour.

picture.alt: Neo-Sumerian cuneiform tablet recording rations of beer, bread, oil and onions for messengers, Metropolitan Museum of Art.
picture.credit: This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art. See the Image and Dat
picture.changes: re-encoded as JPEG at source size 800x707; source smaller than 1200px

mesopotamian-beer-bread-economy-1800bce.dating_note: Hymn copies are Old Babylonian c. 1800 BCE; ration practice is documented from c. 2400 BCE onward.

plimpton-322-sexagesimal-1800bce.summary: Around 1800 BCE an Old Babylonian scribe, probably at Larsa, writes a table now called Plimpton 322: four columns and fifteen rows of sexagesimal numbers whose entries satisfy relations equivalent to right triangles with integer sides. Robson's 2001 reassessment reads it as a teacher's aid for generating reciprocal-pair problems rather than as number theory or trigonometry. Sexagesimal place-value notation, standard in Mesopotamian schools by 2000 BCE, allowed division by reciprocals and survives in our minutes, seconds and degrees. Knuth's 1972 analysis of Babylonian problem texts argued they contain procedures that read as algorithms, with stepwise operations and worked examples.

sources.title: Robson, E., 'Neither Sherlock Holmes nor Babylon: A Reassessment of Plimpton 322', Historia Mathematica 28 (2001), 167-206
sources.author: Robson, Eleanor
sources.confirms: Dates the tablet to c. 1800 BCE at Larsa and interprets it as a teacher's list of reciprocal pairs for setting problems.

sources.title: Knuth, D. E., 'Ancient Babylonian algorithms', Communications of the ACM 15.7 (1972), 671-677
sources.author: Knuth, Donald E.
sources.confirms: Reads Old Babylonian procedure texts as stepwise algorithms.

sources.title: Robson, E., Mathematics in Ancient Iraq: A Social History (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2008)
sources.author: Robson, Eleanor
sources.confirms: Surveys sexagesimal place value, school mathematics and Plimpton 322 in social context.

plimpton-322-sexagesimal-1800bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Robson 2001 and Knuth 1972.
plimpton-322-sexagesimal-1800bce.detail: The tablet is one of thousands of mathematical school texts from Nippur, Ur, Larsa and Sippar covering area, volume, inheritance division and quadratic problems. Later Neo-Babylonian astronomers inherited both the number system and the tabular habit. Claims that the tablet is an exact trigonometric table (Mansfield and Wildberger 2017) have not persuaded most historians of mathematics. Scribes solved problems with fixed procedures rather than symbolic algebra, and errors in Plimpton 322 reveal computational steps used to generate each row.

picture.alt: Old Babylonian tablet YBC 7289, obverse and reverse, with a sexagesimal approximation of the square root of two; shown in place of Plimpton 322, Yale Peabody Museum.
picture.credit: Urcia, A., Yale Peabody Museum of Natural History, http://peabody.yale.edu, http://hdl.handle.net/10079/8931zqj derivative work, user:Theodor Langhorne Franklin, via Wikimedia Commons

plimpton-322-sexagesimal-1800bce.dating_note: Palaeography and findspot place the tablet c. 1822-1762 BCE (Robson); absolute dates follow middle chronology.

code-of-hammurabi-stele-1750bce.summary: Late in his reign (c. 1792-1750 BCE, middle chronology), Hammurabi erects a 2.25 metre black diorite stele carved with a relief of Hammurabi before Shamash and about 282 casuistic laws in Akkadian, covering false accusation, theft, agriculture, debt, marriage, inheritance, assault, professional liability and wages. Penalties mix fines, mutilation and death, and vary with status of victim and offender; a builder whose house collapses on its owner is put to death. Roth's edition translates its full text. Elamites carried it off to Susa around 1150 BCE and found there in 1901; copies on tablets show it taught in schools for a millennium.

sources.title: Roth, M. T., Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor, 2nd edn (Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1997)
sources.author: Roth, Martha T.
sources.confirms: Full edition and translation of the Laws of Hammurabi with prologue and epilogue.

sources.title: Van De Mieroop, M., King Hammurabi of Babylon: A Biography (Oxford: Blackwell, 2005)
sources.author: Van De Mieroop, Marc
sources.confirms: Places the stele in Hammurabi's reign and discusses its function and chronology.

sources.title: Musée du Louvre, 'Law Code of Hammurabi, king of Babylon', Sb 8
sources.author: Musée du Louvre
sources.confirms: Museum record of the stele, its dimensions, findspot at Susa and date.

code-of-hammurabi-stele-1750bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Roth 1997 and Van De Mieroop 2005.
code-of-hammurabi-stele-1750bce.detail: Van De Mieroop reads it as royal self-presentation as 'king of justice' as much as applied statute, since court records rarely cite it. Wage and price provisions make it a source for economic history. Chronology debates shift Hammurabi's reign by about 64 years between middle (1792-1750) and short (1728-1686) systems; Mesopotamian textual dates throughout this period carry that uncertainty. Hammurabi's epilogue invites a wronged man to have its words read aloud to him, which implies public access mediated by literate readers.

picture.alt: Diorite stele of the Code of Hammurabi showing the king before the sun god Shamash, Louvre Sb 8.
picture.credit: Fred Romero from Paris, France, via Wikimedia Commons

code-of-hammurabi-stele-1750bce.dating_note: Textual dates for Mesopotamian kings depend on a chosen chronology; middle chronology figures are given here, short chronology runs about 64 years later. Hammurabi 1792-1750 BCE (middle), 1728-1686 BCE (short).

nippur-scribal-school-1740bce.summary: A small house in Nippur, called House F by its excavators, yielded about 1,400 tablets from the 1740s BCE, the years of Samsu-iluna. Robson's 2001 study reconstructed its teaching: pupils progressed from sign lists and name lists through metrological and mathematical tables, proverbs and model contracts to a canon of Sumerian literature including Gilgamesh poems and hymns, while Sumerian was no longer a spoken language. Teachers recycled tablets in a bin of clay. House F shows how a dead language, mathematics and literature were transmitted by a private household rather than a palace institution.

sources.title: Robson, E., 'The Tablet House: A Scribal School in Old Babylonian Nippur', Revue d'assyriologie et d'archéologie orientale 95.1 (2001), 39-66
sources.author: Robson, Eleanor
sources.confirms: Reconstructs curriculum and date of House F from 1,400 tablets.

sources.title: George, A. R., The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic: Introduction, Critical Edition and Cuneiform Texts (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2003)
sources.author: George, Andrew R.
sources.confirms: Edits Old Babylonian Gilgamesh tablets including school copies.

sources.title: Veldhuis, N., Elementary Education at Nippur: The Lists of Trees and Wooden Objects (PhD dissertation, Groningen, 1997)
sources.author: Veldhuis, Niek
sources.confirms: Reconstructs elementary curriculum from lexical lists.

nippur-scribal-school-1740bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Robson 2001 and George 2003.
nippur-scribal-school-1740bce.detail: School texts from Nippur, Ur, Isin and Sippar form the main corpus of Sumerian literature we possess; Enheduanna's hymns and Instructions of Shuruppak survive through such copies. George's Gilgamesh edition traces Old Babylonian school versions. Dating uses year names of Samsu-iluna, so it carries the chronology dispute. Pupils copied model letters, contracts and lists of professions, gaining practical skills alongside literary prestige; most graduates became administrators rather than poets.

picture.alt: Old Babylonian school tablet with a teacher's model proverb and a pupil's copy, British Museum 104096.

nippur-scribal-school-1740bce.dating_note: Textual dates for Mesopotamian kings depend on a chosen chronology; middle chronology figures are given here, short chronology runs about 64 years later. House F tablets dated by Samsu-iluna year names, c. 1740 BCE (middle).

erlitou-bronze-casting-1700bce.summary: At Erlitou in Henan's Luo valley, a palace-centred settlement of about 300 hectares includes a walled bronze foundry where, from around 1700 BCE, craftsmen cast thin-walled wine vessels (jue, jia) and bells in multi-part ceramic moulds, together with turquoise-inlaid plaques and a 70 cm turquoise dragon mosaic. Bayesian radiocarbon modelling dates Erlitou's four phases to about 1750-1520 BCE. Li Liu and Xingcan Chen treat Erlitou as China's earliest state-level society and as origin of a piece-mould casting tradition that Shang foundries developed into large ritual bronzes.

sources.title: Zhang, X. et al., 'Radiocarbon dating of Erlitou: new perspectives', Radiocarbon 63.6 (2021)
sources.author: Zhang, Xuelian et al.
sources.confirms: Bayesian model of radiocarbon dates places Erlitou phases I-IV c. 1750-1520 BCE.

sources.title: Liu, L. and Chen, X., The Archaeology of China: From the Late Paleolithic to the Early Bronze Age (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2012)
sources.author: Liu, Li; Chen, Xingcan
sources.confirms: Describes Erlitou's palaces, foundry and bronze vessels as the first Chinese state.

sources.title: Thorp, R. L., China in the Early Bronze Age: Shang Civilization (Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 2006)
sources.author: Thorp, Robert L.
sources.confirms: Discusses Erlitou bronze technology and the Xia question.

erlitou-bronze-casting-1700bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Zhang 2021 and Liu 2012.
erlitou-bronze-casting-1700bce.detail: No writing has been found at Erlitou, so its identification with Xia, a dynasty named in later texts, cannot be settled. Its bronze alloy already includes tin and lead. Piece-mould casting, distinct from western Asian lost-wax methods, shaped Chinese bronze design for a millennium. Erlitou vessels are small and thin, cast in moulds of two to four sections, and their shapes derive from pottery prototypes used in feasting.

picture.alt: Bronze jue wine vessel from Erlitou, National Museum of China.

erlitou-bronze-casting-1700bce.dating_note: Bayesian model c. 1750-1520 BCE (Zhang et al. 2021); earlier estimates began c. 1900 BCE.

knossos-plumbing-drains-1700bce.summary: Minoan palaces of Protopalatial and Neopalatial periods (c. 1900-1450 BCE) at Knossos, Phaistos, Mallia and Zakros contain tapered terracotta pressure pipes fitted end to end, stone-lined drains under floors, light wells that doubled as rainwater collectors, settling basins and, in the Knossos residential quarter, a latrine with a seat over a drain flushed by poured water. Rainwater and spring water from Mount Juktas were conveyed by aqueduct and pipe over several kilometres. Drainage was separated from water supply, a principle later lost and relearned.

sources.title: Angelakis, A. N., Koutsoyiannis, D. and Tchobanoglous, G., 'Urban wastewater and stormwater technologies in ancient Greece', Water Research 39.1 (2005), 210-220
sources.author: Angelakis, Andreas N.; Koutsoyiannis, Demetris; Tchobanoglous, George
sources.confirms: Describes Minoan drainage, sewerage and latrines at Knossos and other palaces.

sources.title: Angelakis, A. N., De Feo, G., Laureano, P. and Zourou, A., 'Major urban water and wastewater systems in Minoan Crete, Greece', Water Supply 13.3 (2013), 564-573
sources.author: Angelakis, Andreas N.; De Feo, Giovanni; Laureano, Pietro; Zourou, Anastasia
sources.confirms: Surveys aqueducts, terracotta pipes, cisterns and drains across Minoan sites.

knossos-plumbing-drains-1700bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Angelakis 2005 and Angelakis 2013.
knossos-plumbing-drains-1700bce.detail: Pipe segments taper so that each fits into the next, with collars and cement; flow acceleration at joints may have discouraged sediment. Whether the latrine was flushed routinely is inferred from its drain geometry. Similar hydraulic care appears in Indus cities centuries earlier, apparently without contact. Cisterns and stone-cut channels with parabolic curves at bends slowed water flow and reduced splashing, details that show empirical understanding of hydraulics.

picture.alt: Stone-lined drainage channel and gypsum blocks at the palace of Knossos, Crete.

knossos-plumbing-drains-1700bce.dating_note: Palace phases dated by Minoan pottery sequence; pipes and drains belong mainly to Middle Minoan II-III, c. 1800-1600 BCE.

poverty-point-earthworks-1700bce.summary: In north-east Louisiana, between about 1700 and 1100 BCE, people who fished, hunted and gathered without agriculture construct six concentric C-shaped earthen ridges 1.2 km across and several mounds, including Mound A, 22 metres high and about 240,000 cubic metres. Its stratigraphy shows it was built in a few months without pauses for erosion. Exchange brought copper from the Great Lakes, galena, soapstone and stone from across the mid-continent. Fired clay 'Poverty Point objects', shaped balls heated in earth ovens for cooking, were made by the thousands and were dated by thermoluminescence in 1972.

sources.title: Ortmann, A. L. and Kidder, T. R., 'Building Mound A at Poverty Point, Louisiana: Monumental Public Architecture, Ritual Practice, and Implications for Hunter-Gatherer Complexity', Geoarchaeology 28.1 (2013), 66-86
sources.author: Ortmann, Anthony L.; Kidder, Tristram R.
sources.confirms: Shows Mound A (c. 3261 cal BP) was built in a short period by a large labour force.

sources.title: Huxtable, J., Aitken, M. J. and Weber, J. C., 'Thermoluminescent dating of baked clay balls of the Poverty Point culture', Archaeometry 14.2 (1972), 269-275
sources.author: Huxtable, Joan; Aitken, Martin J.; Weber, J. C.
sources.confirms: TL dates on cooking balls give c. 1000 BCE with wide error, confirming Late Archaic age.

sources.title: Kidder, T. R., 'Poverty Point', in T. R. Pauketat (ed.), The Oxford Handbook of North American Archaeology (New York: Oxford University Press, 2012), 464-475
sources.author: Kidder, Tristram R.
sources.confirms: Overview of chronology, earthworks and exchange.

poverty-point-earthworks-1700bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Ortmann 2013 and Huxtable 1972.
poverty-point-earthworks-1700bce.detail: Monumental construction by foragers challenges assumptions tying monuments to agriculture and hierarchy. Poverty Point was inscribed by UNESCO in 2014. Radiocarbon on Mound A gives about 1260 BCE; ridges date earlier. Few burials or houses have been found, so population estimates vary widely. Clay cooking balls in standardised shapes allowed controlled heating in earth ovens where stone was absent, an adaptation to alluvial lowlands.

picture.alt: Mound A at Poverty Point World Heritage Site, Louisiana.
picture.credit: Jennifer R. Trotter, via Wikimedia Commons

poverty-point-earthworks-1700bce.dating_note: Radiocarbon places ridges c. 1700-1100 BCE and Mound A c. 1260 BCE; TL on clay objects c. 1000 ± 200 BCE.

chicken-domestication-ban-non-wat-1650bc.summary: Our earliest secure evidence for domestic chickens comes from Ban Non Wat in north-east Thailand, where red junglefowl bones occur in human burials and settlement deposits dated about 1650-1250 BCE; dry rice and millet cultivation drew junglefowl into villages. A 2022 reassessment of chicken bones from 600 sites rejected earlier claims for chickens in northern China around 6000 BCE and in Indus cities after re-identification of pheasant bones and redating. Chickens reached Mesopotamia and Egypt after 1500 BCE and Europe after 1000 BCE.

sources.title: Peters, J. et al., 'The biocultural origins and dispersal of domestic chickens', PNAS 119.24 (2022), e2121978119
sources.author: Peters, Joris; Lebrasseur, Ophélie; Irving-Pease, Evan K. et al.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Identifies Ban Non Wat c. 1650-1250 BCE as earliest secure domestic chicken evidence, linked to rice farming.

sources.title: Best, J. et al., 'Redefining the timing and circumstances of the chicken's introduction to Europe and north-west Africa', Antiquity 96.388 (2022), 868-882
sources.author: Best, Julia et al.
sources.confirms: Direct dating shows chickens reach Europe only in the first millennium BCE.

chicken-domestication-ban-non-wat-1650bc.verification_note: Date and core claims match Peters 2022 and Best 2022.
chicken-domestication-ban-non-wat-1650bc.detail: Direct dating of supposed early chicken bones from Europe found most intrusive or misidentified. Chickens spread first as exotic or ritual birds; eating them became common only centuries later. Lapita voyagers carried chickens into the Pacific after 1300 BCE. Chickens in Ban Non Wat graves accompany adults and children as offerings, which indicates symbolic value alongside any economic use at this early stage.

picture.alt: Red junglefowl (Gallus gallus) in Thailand, wild ancestor of the domestic chicken; modern photograph.

chicken-domestication-ban-non-wat-1650bc.dating_note: Ban Non Wat deposits c. 1650-1250 BCE; region assigned east-asia for mainland Southeast Asia (Thailand).

venus-tablet-ammisaduqa-1650bce.summary: Tablet 63 of omen series Enuma Anu Enlil preserves observations of first and last visibilities of Venus over Ammisaduqa's 21-year reign as king of Babylon, c. 1646-1626 BCE on middle chronology, each paired with an omen. Surviving copies are Neo-Assyrian, from Nineveh, about a thousand years after those observations were made. Because Venus phenomena repeat in an eight-year cycle, astronomers have long used this tablet to test Babylonian chronologies: Huber's analysis favours the middle or long chronology, while Gurzadyan and others argue its data are too corrupt to decide. It is our earliest sustained planetary record.

sources.title: Huber, P. J., 'Dating of Akkad, Ur III, and Babylon I', in G. Wilhelm (ed.), Organization, Representation, and Symbols of Power in the Ancient Near East (Winona Lake: Eisenbrauns, 2012), 715-733
sources.author: Huber, Peter J.
sources.confirms: Uses Venus tablet and month-length data to argue for a longer Old Babylonian chronology.

sources.title: Hunger, H., 'Uses of Enuma Anu Enlil for Chronology', Akkadica 119-120 (2000) 155-158
sources.author: Hunger, Hermann
sources.confirms: Reviews how the Venus tablet and eclipse omens have been used for absolute chronology and their limits.

sources.title: Gurzadyan, V. G., 'On the Astronomical Records and Babylonian Chronology', Akkadica 119-120 (2000) 177-186
sources.author: Gurzadyan, Vahe G.
sources.confirms: Argues the Venus data cannot fix chronology and favours a lower date.
sources.qualifies: Supports a short or ultra-short chronology against Huber.

venus-tablet-ammisaduqa-1650bce.verification_note: Observations are agreed to be from Ammisaduqa's reign; their use to fix absolute dates is contested.
venus-tablet-ammisaduqa-1650bce.detail: These observations show systematic watching of a planet's heliacal phenomena for divination, a practice that by 700 BCE had produced mathematical astronomy. Copyist errors and schematic insertions complicate use, and a 2010 study corrected earlier astronomical computations. Combined with Ur III lunar eclipse omens, this tablet remains central to middle versus short chronology debates. Omens pair each visibility event with predictions for kings, harvests and rain, so observation served statecraft; later Babylonian diaries from 650 BCE onward continued this habit with daily entries.

picture.alt: Neo-Assyrian copy of the Venus Tablet of Ammisaduqa (Enuma Anu Enlil tablet 63), British Museum.

venus-tablet-ammisaduqa-1650bce.dating_note: Ammisaduqa's reign 1646-1626 BCE (middle), 1582-1562 BCE (short); this tablet is the disputed evidence.

egyptian-medical-papyri-1600bce.summary: Egyptian medical papyri preserve systematic clinical writing. Kahun papyrus (c. 1825 BCE) treats gynaecological complaints and contraception. Edwin Smith papyrus, a Hyksos-period copy (c. 1600 BCE) of an older text, sets out 48 trauma cases from head to thorax, each with examination, diagnosis, verdict ('an ailment I will treat' or 'not to be treated') and treatment, including suturing, splints and observation of brain tissue. Ebers papyrus (c. 1550 BCE) collects about 870 remedies and incantations. Sanchez and Meltzer's 2012 edition and Nunn's survey treat Smith as our oldest surviving rational surgical text, though magic and medicine coexist across all three.

sources.title: Sanchez, G. M. and Meltzer, E. S., The Edwin Smith Papyrus: Updated Translation of the Trauma Treatise and Modern Medical Commentaries (Atlanta: Lockwood Press, 2012)
sources.author: Sanchez, Gonzalo M.; Meltzer, Edmund S.
sources.confirms: Translates the 48 cases with medical commentary and discusses date and composition.

sources.title: Breasted, J. H., The Edwin Smith Surgical Papyrus, Volume 1: Hieroglyphic Transliteration, Translation, and Commentary, Oriental Institute Publications 3 (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1930)
sources.author: Breasted, James Henry
sources.venue: University of Chicago Press, Oriental Institute
sources.confirms: First full edition with translation and commentary.

sources.title: Nunn, J. F., Ancient Egyptian Medicine (London: British Museum Press; Norman: University of Oklahoma Press, 1996)
sources.author: Nunn, John F.
sources.confirms: Surveys medical papyri, their dates and contents, including Kahun and Ebers.

sources.title: Collier, M. and Quirke, S., The UCL Lahun Papyri: Religious, Literary, Legal, Mathematical and Medical, BAR International Series 1209 (Oxford: Archaeopress, 2004)
sources.author: Collier, Mark; Quirke, Stephen
sources.confirms: Edits the Kahun medical papyrus.

egyptian-medical-papyri-1600bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Sanchez 2012 and Breasted 1930.
egyptian-medical-papyri-1600bce.detail: Breasted's 1930 edition first published Smith in full. Cases proceed in anatomical order and use consistent technical terms for wounds, fractures and dislocations. Dating is palaeographic: Smith's hand is Second Intermediate Period, while grammar suggests Old Kingdom composition. Ebers remedies draw on about 700 plant, animal and mineral substances, with dosages by measure, and a section on heart and vessels describes pulse as speaking from every limb.

picture.alt: Plates of the Edwin Smith surgical papyrus in hieratic script.

egyptian-medical-papyri-1600bce.dating_note: Kahun c. 1825 BCE (dated by year of Amenemhat III on verso), Smith copy c. 1600 BCE, Ebers c. 1550 BCE (calendar note naming Amenhotep I); all palaeographic within Egyptian chronology.

el-manati-rubber-balls-1600bce.summary: At El Manatí, a waterlogged spring site in Veracruz, offerings dated about 1600 BCE include solid rubber balls up to 30 cm across along with wooden busts and jade axes. Hosler, Burkett and Tarkanian's 1999 Science study showed that Mesoamerican peoples mixed latex from Castilla elastica with juice of the morning-glory vine Ipomoea alba, whose sulfur compounds cross-link polymer chains and transform sticky latex into elastic rubber, about 3,500 years before Goodyear's vulcanisation. Tarkanian and Hosler's 2011 experiments found that different latex-to-juice ratios produced properties suited to balls, sandal soles and bindings.

sources.title: Hosler, D., Burkett, S. L. and Tarkanian, M. J., 'Prehistoric Polymers: Rubber Processing in Ancient Mesoamerica', Science 284.5422 (1999), 1988-1991
sources.author: Hosler, Dorothy; Burkett, Sandra L.; Tarkanian, Michael J.
sources.confirms: Chemical and mechanical analysis shows Ipomoea alba juice converts Castilla latex into elastic rubber; El Manatí balls c. 1600 BCE.

sources.title: Tarkanian, M. J. and Hosler, D., 'America's First Polymer Scientists: Rubber Processing, Use and Transport in Mesoamerica', Latin American Antiquity 22.4 (2011), 469-486
sources.author: Tarkanian, Michael J.; Hosler, Dorothy
sources.confirms: Experiments show recipes tuned for balls, sandals and bindings.

sources.title: Ortiz, P. and Rodríguez, M. del C., 'The Sacred Hill of El Manatí: A Preliminary Discussion of the Site's Ritual Paradigms', in D. C. Grove and R. A. Joyce (eds), Social Patterns in Pre-Classic Mesoamerica (Washington: Dumbarton Oaks, 1999), 225-254
sources.author: Ortiz Ceballos, Ponciano; Rodríguez, María del Carmen
sources.confirms: Excavators' account of the offerings including rubber balls and their radiocarbon dates.

el-manati-rubber-balls-1600bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Hosler 1999 and Tarkanian 2011.
el-manati-rubber-balls-1600bce.detail: Rubber balls served the ballgame played across Mesoamerica for three millennia; 'Olmec' derives from a Nahuatl word for rubber people. Balls at El Manatí are the oldest known rubber artefacts. Rubber also waterproofed textiles and glued tool hafts. Waterlogged peat preserved wood and rubber that normally decay, so El Manatí offers a rare view of organic ritual goods, including wooden busts and infant remains.

picture.alt: Maya ceramic ballplayer figure, Cleveland Museum of Art 1990.180; later illustration of the Mesoamerican ballgame.

el-manati-rubber-balls-1600bce.dating_note: Earliest offering phase radiocarbon-dated c. 1600 BCE.

great-orme-copper-mine-1600bce.summary: Beneath a limestone headland at Llandudno, Wales, miners dig more than 8 km of passages, some too narrow for adults and worked by children, to extract malachite and other copper ores with hammerstones, bone and antler picks and fire-setting. Williams and Le Carlier de Veslud's 2019 study matched trace-element and lead-isotope signatures of Great Orme copper to bronze objects from Brittany to Sweden and dated a production boom to about 1600-1400 BCE, implying a full-time mining community rather than seasonal work. It is the largest known Bronze Age mine in Europe.

sources.title: Williams, R. A. and Le Carlier de Veslud, C., 'Boom and bust in Bronze Age Britain: major copper production from the Great Orme mine and European trade, c. 1600-1400 BC', Antiquity 93.371 (2019), 1178-1196
sources.author: Williams, R. Alan; Le Carlier de Veslud, Cécile
sources.confirms: Provenances bronze across north-west Europe to Great Orme and dates peak production 1600-1400 BCE.

sources.title: Timberlake, S., 'Mining and prospection for metals in Early Bronze Age Britain: making claims within the archaeological landscape', in J. Brück (ed.), Bronze Age Landscapes: Tradition and Transformation (Oxford: Oxbow, 2001), 179-192
sources.author: Timberlake, Simon
sources.confirms: Surveys British Bronze Age copper mines including Great Orme.

great-orme-copper-mine-1600bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Williams 2019 and Timberlake 2001.
great-orme-copper-mine-1600bce.detail: Earlier interpretations assumed small-scale working over a millennium. Great Orme copper, alloyed with tin from Cornwall and Devon, supplied the British and north European bronze industry; spearheads, palstaves and rapiers carry its signature. Workings were rediscovered in 1987 during landscaping. Over 2,400 hammerstones and some 30,000 bone tools have been recovered, and passages descend 70 metres below surface, with fire-setting used in harder rock.

picture.alt: Excavations at the Great Orme Bronze Age copper mine, Llandudno, Wales.

great-orme-copper-mine-1600bce.dating_note: Radiocarbon on charcoal and bone tools spans c. 1800-900 BCE; peak output modelled c. 1600-1400 BCE.

nebra-sky-disc-1600bce.summary: A 32 cm bronze disc with gold inlays of a full moon or sun, a crescent, a cluster of seven dots read as Pleiades, about 30 stars, two horizon arcs and a boat-like arc was looted from a hilltop near Nebra, Germany, in 1999 and recovered in 2002 with swords and axes. Its hoard dates to about 1600 BCE by typology of accompanying bronzes and radiocarbon from birch bark on a sword hilt, with copper from Austria's Mitterberg mines and gold from Cornwall. Interpretations treat it as a depiction of night sky and possibly a rule for intercalating lunar and solar calendars.

sources.title: Pernicka, E. et al., 'Why the Nebra Sky Disc Dates to the Early Bronze Age. An Overview of the Interdisciplinary Results', Archaeologia Austriaca 104 (2020), 89-122
sources.author: Pernicka, Ernst; Adam, Jörg; Borg, Gregor et al.
sources.confirms: Summarises typological, radiocarbon, soil and metal evidence for a date c. 1600 BCE.

sources.title: Gebhard, R. and Krause, R., 'Kritische Anmerkungen zum Fundkomplex der sog. Himmelsscheibe von Nebra', Archäologische Informationen 43 (2020), 325-346
sources.author: Gebhard, Rupert; Krause, Rüdiger
sources.confirms: Argues the disc is Iron Age and separate from the hoard.
sources.qualifies: Proposes a first millennium BCE date, rejected by the excavating team.

nebra-sky-disc-1600bce.verification_note: Date defended by Pernicka et al. but publicly challenged; astronomical reading is interpretive.
nebra-sky-disc-1600bce.detail: Rupert Gebhard and Rüdiger Krause argued in 2020 that this disc is an Iron Age object unconnected with its hoard; Ernst Pernicka replied that find circumstances, corrosion and metal composition tie disc and bronzes together.
