UNESCO listed it as Memory of the World in 2013. Its astronomical reading is inference, since no text accompanies it. Later additions, including horizon arcs and a boat, show reuse over generations before burial, with earlier star patterns partly covered by new gold.

picture.alt: Nebra sky disc, bronze with gold inlays of sun, moon and stars, State Museum of Prehistory, Halle.

nebra-sky-disc-1600bce.dating_note: Hoard typology and radiocarbon c. 1600 BCE; Iron Age redating proposed by Gebhard and Krause (2020) and contested.

thera-eruption-akrotiri-1600bce.summary: A volcanic eruption on Thera (Santorini) blankets Akrotiri town in pumice and ash, preserving multi-storey houses, frescoes of ships, monkeys and saffron gatherers, and drainage systems, with no bodies found, which suggests residents fled after precursor earthquakes. Tsunami deposits reached Crete. Its date has split archaeologists and scientists for forty years: Egyptian synchronisms favour about 1530-1500 BCE, while radiocarbon on an olive branch buried by ash gave about 1620 BCE. Annual tree-ring calibration in 2018 moved radiocarbon ranges into 1600-1500 BCE, and a 2023 olive shrub date supports about 1550 BCE, narrowing this gap.

sources.title: Manning, S. W. et al., 'Chronology for the Aegean Late Bronze Age 1700-1400 B.C.', Science 312.5773 (2006), 565-569
sources.author: Manning, Sturt W. et al.
sources.confirms: Radiocarbon places the eruption in the late seventeenth century BCE.

sources.title: Pearson, C. L. et al., 'Annual radiocarbon record indicates 16th century BCE date for the Thera eruption', Science Advances 4.8 (2018)
sources.author: Pearson, Charlotte L. et al.
sources.confirms: Tree-ring calibration shifts the eruption range toward the sixteenth century BCE.
sources.qualifies: Revises earlier seventeenth-century radiocarbon dates downward.

sources.title: Ehrlich, Y. et al., 'Olive shrub buried on Therasia supports a mid-16th century BCE date for the Thera eruption', Scientific Reports 13 (2023)
sources.author: Ehrlich, Yael et al.
sources.confirms: New olive shrub radiocarbon supports mid sixteenth century BCE.

sources.title: Bietak, M., 'Radiocarbon and the date of the Thera eruption', Antiquity 88.339 (2014), 277-282
sources.author: Bietak, Manfred
sources.confirms: Defends archaeological synchronisms placing the eruption c. 1530-1500 BCE.
sources.qualifies: Argues for a date a century later than early radiocarbon results.

thera-eruption-akrotiri-1600bce.verification_note: Event is certain; date is contested within about a century.
thera-eruption-akrotiri-1600bce.detail: Akrotiri's frescoes are among Europe's richest Bronze Age paintings outside Egypt. Eruption did not end Minoan Crete directly; palace destructions on Crete follow about a century later. Dating disputes here drove refinements in radiocarbon calibration that affect chronologies worldwide. Pumice from Thera has been found in Egyptian contexts at Tell el-Dab'a, and its stratigraphic position underlies archaeological arguments for a lower date.

picture.alt: Finds from the excavation at Akrotiri on Thera, National Archaeological Museum, Athens.
picture.credit: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China, via Wikimedia Commons

thera-eruption-akrotiri-1600bce.dating_note: Radiocarbon c. 1620-1540 BCE (narrowing toward 1560-1540); archaeological synchronisms c. 1530-1500 BCE.

dover-bronze-age-boat-1550bce.summary: A 9.5 metre surviving section of a sewn-plank boat, found in 1992 beneath a Dover street, was built around 1550 BCE from oak planks shaped with bronze tools, joined by yew withies through cleats and rails, with moss caulking held by oak laths. Clark's edited monograph publishes the hull and estimates an original length near 12-15 metres and a crew of up to 18 paddlers, capable of Channel crossings with cargo. It is the oldest known seagoing boat in Europe. Van de Noort's study of sewn-plank boats from the Humber and Severn estuaries places Dover in a British tradition from about 2000 BCE.

sources.title: Clark, P. (ed.), The Dover Bronze Age Boat (Swindon: English Heritage, 2004)
sources.author: Clark, Peter (ed.)
sources.confirms: Full publication of the hull, construction, dating and context.

sources.title: Van de Noort, R., 'An ancient seascape: the social context of seafaring in the early Bronze Age', World Archaeology 35.3 (2003), 404-415
sources.author: Van de Noort, Robert
sources.confirms: Sets Dover within British sewn-plank boat tradition and cross-Channel exchange.

dover-bronze-age-boat-1550bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Clark 2004 and Van de Noort 2003.
dover-bronze-age-boat-1550bce.detail: No sail or mast step was found; propulsion was by paddle. Cross-Channel movement of bronze, tin, gold and people is confirmed by Continental metalwork in Britain and by wrecks such as Salcombe and Langdon Bay. Radiocarbon on the timbers gives the date; dendrochronology failed because of short ring sequences. Timber conversion shows large oaks split and dressed with bronze axes and adzes, and tool marks record blade widths that match contemporary metalwork finds.

picture.alt: Sewn-plank Dover Bronze Age boat on display in Dover Museum.
picture.credit: Jim Linwood from London, via Wikimedia Commons

chinese-steamer-cooking-yan-1500bce.summary: Pottery steamers (zeng) set over tripod boilers (li) appear in Neolithic Yangshao and Longshan contexts, and by the Shang period combined bronze yan with a perforated grid between boiler and steaming bowl are cast as ritual vessels. Chang's edited history of Chinese food treats steaming of millet and rice as a defining technique of Chinese cuisine from this time, distinct from western Asian bread baking. Fuller and Rowlands contrast an East Asian tradition of boiling and steaming whole grains in pots with a West Asian tradition of grinding grain and baking, with consequences for pottery, ovens and taste.

sources.title: Chang, K. C. (ed.), Food in Chinese Culture: Anthropological and Historical Perspectives (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1977)
sources.author: Chang, Kwang-chih (ed.)
sources.confirms: Describes Shang cooking vessels including yan steamers and the role of steaming.

sources.title: Fuller, D. Q. and Rowlands, M., 'Ingestion and Food Technologies: Maintaining differences over the long-term in West, South and East Asia', in T. C. Wilkinson, S. Sherratt and J. Bennet (eds), Interweaving Worlds (Oxford: Oxbow, 2011), 37-60
sources.author: Fuller, Dorian Q.; Rowlands, Michael
sources.confirms: Contrasts East Asian boiling and steaming with West Asian grinding and baking traditions.

chinese-steamer-cooking-yan-1500bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Chang 1977 and Fuller 2011.
chinese-steamer-cooking-yan-1500bce.detail: Steaming required fuel-efficient control of water and heat and favoured sticky grain varieties. Tripod vessels with hollow legs (li) maximised heated surface. The distinction in cooking traditions Fuller and Rowlands describe is a hypothesis about long-term culinary culture rather than a dated event. Steamed grain eaten with separately cooked vegetables and meat established a fan-cai structure of meals that Chang identifies as persistent in Chinese food culture.

picture.alt: Shang bronze yan steamer from Anyang, Henan Provincial Museum, Zhengzhou.

chinese-steamer-cooking-yan-1500bce.dating_note: Pottery steamers from Neolithic c. 3000 BCE; bronze yan in Shang contexts c. 1500-1050 BCE.

egyptian-glass-faience-1500bce.summary: Egyptian faience, a glazed quartz-frit material, had been made since the fourth millennium, but glass made deliberately in quantity appears around 1500 BCE in Mesopotamia and Egypt. Core-formed vessels in cobalt blue, turquoise and yellow spread in Egypt from the reign of Thutmose III. Rehren and Pusch's 2005 excavation evidence from Qantir-Piramesses shows a two-stage process: raw materials fused in crucibles at 900-950 degrees to a semi-finished frit, then coloured and cast into ingots at 1000-1100 degrees. Smirniou and Rehren's Amarna study confirmed primary glassmaking there. Ingots then travelled, as on the Uluburun ship, to workshops that formed objects.

sources.title: Rehren, T. and Pusch, E. B., 'Late Bronze Age Glass Production at Qantir-Piramesses, Egypt', Science 308.5729 (2005), 1756-1758
sources.author: Rehren, Thilo; Pusch, Edgar B.
sources.confirms: Demonstrates primary glass production from raw materials in two temperature stages.

sources.title: Smirniou, M. and Rehren, T., 'Direct evidence of primary glass production in Late Bronze Age Amarna, Egypt', Archaeometry 53.1 (2011), 58-80
sources.author: Smirniou, Melina; Rehren, Thilo
sources.confirms: Identifies semi-finished glass and crucibles at Amarna.

sources.title: Nicholson, P. T. and Henderson, J., 'Glass', in P. T. Nicholson and I. Shaw (eds), Ancient Egyptian Materials and Technology (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2000), 195-224
sources.author: Nicholson, Paul T.; Henderson, Julian
sources.confirms: Surveys emergence of glass c. 1500 BCE and faience before it.

egyptian-glass-faience-1500bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Rehren 2005 and Smirniou 2011.
egyptian-glass-faience-1500bce.detail: Whether glass began in Mesopotamia or Egypt remains open; Mitanni and Nuzi texts describe glass recipes in the same period. Cobalt came from Egyptian Western Desert alum deposits. Glass was a luxury comparable to semi-precious stone, not a utilitarian material, until Roman blowing. Workshops at Amarna and Qantir were attached to royal residences, which indicates palace control of a prestige technology and its raw materials, including imported cobalt-free natron and local quartz pebbles.

picture.alt: Egyptian faience vessel from Malqata, Walters Art Museum 48.1732 (stands in for both glass and faience).

egyptian-glass-faience-1500bce.dating_note: Earliest dated Egyptian glass vessels bear names of Thutmose III (c. 1479-1425 BCE); Mesopotamian glass may be slightly earlier.

nok-culture-settlement-1500bce.summary: Frankfurt University's Nok research project, begun in 2005, has dated earliest Nok settlement sites in central Nigeria to about 1500 BCE, with pearl millet cultivation, pottery and pits, several centuries before terracotta figurines (from c. 900 BCE) and iron smelting (from c. 800 BCE) for which Nok is known. Pangwari is a site of 2,600 square metres with pits, pots and plant remains spanning Early to Late Nok. Nok forms one of West Africa's earliest known farming societies south of Sahel grasslands.

sources.title: Rupp, N., Ameje, J. and Breunig, P., 'New Studies on the Nok Culture of Central Nigeria', Journal of African Archaeology 3.2 (2005), 283-290
sources.author: Rupp, Nicole; Ameje, James; Breunig, Peter
sources.confirms: Launches settlement-focused Nok research and reports early results.

sources.title: Franke, G. et al., 'Pits, pots and plants at Pangwari: Deciphering the nature of a Nok Culture site', Azania 55.2 (2020), 129-188
sources.author: Franke, Gabriele; Höhn, Alexa; Schmidt, Annika et al.
sources.confirms: Large excavation with radiocarbon chronology from Early Nok (mid second millennium BCE) onward.

nok-culture-settlement-1500bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Rupp 2005 and Franke 2020.
nok-culture-settlement-1500bce.detail: Earlier chronologies, built on a few dates from tin-mining finds, placed Nok between 500 BCE and 200 CE. New radiocarbon series extend it back to about 1500 BCE. Iron and terracotta, Nok's famous traits, belong to later centuries and are not claimed here. Pearl millet and cowpea remains, plus oil palm and wild fruits, show a mixed economy, with few animal bones surviving in acidic soils.

picture.alt: Nok terracotta head, 5th century BCE to 4th century CE, Honolulu Museum of Art; later than the earliest Nok settlements.

nok-culture-settlement-1500bce.dating_note: Early Nok c. 1500-900 BCE by radiocarbon; figurines and iron are later.

rig-veda-oral-composition-1500bce.summary: Between about 1500 and 1200 BCE, priest-poets speaking Vedic Sanskrit in Punjab compose 1,028 hymns in fixed metres addressed to Indra, Agni, Soma and other gods, collected as Rig Veda. Witzel's analysis of its geography and language dates its core to this window and places it after Indus deurbanisation. Preservation relied on memorisation with word-by-word and permutation recitations (pada, krama and later jata, ghana) that reproduce accent and phonetics so precisely that modern printed editions vary hardly at all from recited versions; writing was not used for it until medieval times. Jamison and Brereton's 2014 translation is now standard in English.

sources.title: Jamison, S. W. and Brereton, J. P. (trans.), The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India, 3 vols (New York: Oxford University Press, 2014)
sources.author: Jamison, Stephanie W.; Brereton, Joel P.
sources.confirms: Complete translation with introduction on date, composition and oral transmission.

sources.title: Witzel, M., 'Early Indian history: linguistic and textual parametres', in G. Erdosy (ed.), The Indo-Aryans of Ancient South Asia: Language, Material Culture and Ethnicity (Berlin: de Gruyter, 1995), 85-125
sources.author: Witzel, Michael
sources.confirms: Dates Rig Vedic composition c. 1500-1200 BCE from geography, language and internal references.

sources.title: Jamison, S. W. and Brereton, J. P., The Rigveda: A Guide (New York: Oxford University Press, 2020)
sources.author: Jamison, Stephanie W.; Brereton, Joel P.
sources.confirms: Explains metre, recitation techniques and transmission.

rig-veda-oral-composition-1500bce.verification_note: Composition date is inferred from language and content; range of scholarly estimates is wide.
rig-veda-oral-composition-1500bce.detail: Dating is linguistic and internal: hymns mention horses, chariots, bronze (ayas) and no iron or cities, and share features with Mitanni Indo-Aryan names of c. 1400 BCE. Proposed dates range from 1900 to 1000 BCE. Recitation techniques constitute a mnemonic technology for exact copying without script. Recitation schools preserved accent marks (udatta, anudatta, svarita) that vanished from spoken Sanskrit, making this oral text a fossil of earlier pronunciation.

picture.alt: Rigveda manuscript page in Devanagari script; a modern copy, as the text was transmitted orally for most of its history.
picture.credit: Ms Sarah Welch, via Wikimedia Commons

rig-veda-oral-composition-1500bce.dating_note: Linguistic dating c. 1500-1200 BCE; no manuscripts before the medieval period; proposals range 1900-1000 BCE.

shaduf-nile-irrigation-1500bce.summary: Tomb paintings of New Kingdom Thebes, such as that of Ipuy at Deir el-Medina (c. 1250 BCE), show a pole pivoted on a post with a bucket at one end and a clay counterweight opposite, used to lift water from canal to garden plot. Butzer's hydraulic history of Egypt treats shadufs as introduced by about 1500 BCE and as Egypt's only mechanical water lift before Ptolemaic times, while Eyre's study of orchard water regimes shows it suited small vegetable and tree plots rather than basin field agriculture, which relied on annual floods. A person could raise a few cubic metres an hour, adequate for gardens.

sources.title: Butzer, K. W., Early Hydraulic Civilization in Egypt: A Study in Cultural Ecology (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1976)
sources.author: Butzer, Karl W.
sources.confirms: Dates shaduf introduction to the New Kingdom c. 1500 BCE and describes basin irrigation.

sources.title: Eyre, C. J., 'The Water Regime for Orchards and Plantations in Pharaonic Egypt', Journal of Egyptian Archaeology 80 (1994), 57-80
sources.author: Eyre, Christopher J.
sources.confirms: Analyses shaduf use for gardens and orchards from texts and tomb scenes.

shaduf-nile-irrigation-1500bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Butzer 1976 and Eyre 1994.
shaduf-nile-irrigation-1500bce.detail: A similar device appears on an Akkadian cylinder seal of about 2200 BCE, so Mesopotamian priority is possible. Shadufs remained in use along Egypt's river into the twentieth century. Larger lifts, saqiya wheels and Archimedean screws, arrive only after 300 BCE. Each lift depended on human effort rather than animal power, and gardens of New Kingdom estates employed teams of water carriers alongside shadufs according to tomb scenes.

picture.alt: Painting copy of a gardener raising water with a shaduf, tomb of Ipuy at Deir el-Medina (TT 217).
picture.credit: Norman de Garis Davies, via Wikimedia Commons

shaduf-nile-irrigation-1500bce.dating_note: Earliest Egyptian depictions are New Kingdom (c. 1500-1250 BCE); an Akkadian seal c. 2200 BCE may show an earlier Mesopotamian form.

zhengzhou-rammed-earth-walls-1500bce.summary: At Zhengzhou, Henan, an Erligang-period Shang city of about 1500 BCE is enclosed by a rammed-earth (hangtu) wall nearly 7 km long, up to 20 metres thick at its base and originally perhaps 10 metres high, built by compacting thin layers of earth between timber shuttering. Palace foundations inside and bronze foundries, bone workshops and pottery kilns outside show a planned capital. Reports in Chinese Archaeology describe its palace-area wall, and Campbell's study of Erligang expansion treats Zhengzhou as centre of a state whose bronze culture spread across the Yellow River basin. Labour estimates run to ten thousand workers over several years.

sources.title: Henan Provincial Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology, 'The Rammed-earth Wall in the Palace Area of Shang City at Zhengzhou in 1998', Chinese Archaeology 1.1 (2001), 117-121
sources.author: Henan Provincial Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology
sources.confirms: Reports excavation of the palace-area rammed-earth wall and its construction.

sources.title: Campbell, R. B., 'The Erligang Period', in Archaeology of the Chinese Bronze Age: From Erlitou to Anyang (Los Angeles: Cotsen Institute of Archaeology Press, 2014), 69-104
sources.author: Campbell, Roderick
sources.confirms: Analyses Zhengzhou's walls, workshops and the Erligang expansion.

sources.title: Liu, L. and Chen, X., The Archaeology of China (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2012)
sources.author: Liu, Li; Chen, Xingcan
sources.confirms: Summarises Zhengzhou wall dimensions and dating.

zhengzhou-rammed-earth-walls-1500bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Henan Provincial Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology 2001 and Campbell 2014.
zhengzhou-rammed-earth-walls-1500bce.detail: Rammed earth was used for walls and platforms from Longshan times and remained standard for Chinese monumental building, including later sections of China's Great Wall. Zhengzhou is usually identified with Shang capitals Bo or Ao of later texts, an identification not confirmed by inscriptions. Hoards outside Zhengzhou's wall held large bronze ding and fangding up to a metre tall, which shows casting at scale already in Erligang times.

picture.alt: Surviving section of the Shang rammed-earth city wall at Zhengzhou, Henan.

zhengzhou-rammed-earth-walls-1500bce.dating_note: Erligang period c. 1600-1400 BCE by radiocarbon; wall construction c. 1500 BCE.

rekhmire-bellows-metalworking-1450bce.summary: Paintings in the Theban tomb of Rekhmire, vizier under Thutmose III and Amenhotep II (c. 1450 BCE), show metalworkers standing on pairs of leather bag bellows, pumping with their feet and pulling cords to reinflate them, while others pour molten bronze through rows of funnels into a mould for temple doors. Davies' publication of the tomb recorded the scenes in detail, and Ogden's survey of Egyptian metallurgy treats them as the first clear evidence for bellows replacing blowpipes, allowing larger melts and hotter furnaces. Scenes also show weighing of metal under scribal supervision.

sources.title: Davies, N. de G., The Tomb of Rekh-mi-Rē at Thebes, 2 vols (New York: Metropolitan Museum of Art, 1943)
sources.author: Davies, Norman de Garis
sources.confirms: Publishes the tomb paintings including bellows and bronze-casting scenes.

sources.title: Ogden, J., 'Metals', in P. T. Nicholson and I. Shaw (eds), Ancient Egyptian Materials and Technology (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2000), 148-176
sources.author: Ogden, Jack
sources.confirms: Discusses bellows, furnaces and casting evidence from Rekhmire and other tombs.

rekhmire-bellows-metalworking-1450bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Davies 1943 and Ogden 2000.
rekhmire-bellows-metalworking-1450bce.detail: Blowpipe furnaces appear in Old Kingdom tombs; dish bellows mark a step in controlled air supply that later iron smelting required. Rekhmire's walls also depict glassmaking or faience work, brickmaking and carpentry, a rare visual inventory of state workshops. Bellows of this type remained standard in Egypt and western Asia for two millennia and appear in later Greek vase painting attached to iron forges.

picture.alt: Facsimile of metalworkers using foot bellows, tomb of Rekhmire (TT 100), Metropolitan Museum of Art.
picture.credit: Nina M. Davies, via Wikimedia Commons

rekhmire-bellows-metalworking-1450bce.dating_note: Rekhmire served Thutmose III and Amenhotep II; tomb decoration c. 1450-1420 BCE by Egyptian chronology.

hattusa-tablet-collections-1400bce.summary: At Hattusa (Boğazköy, Turkey), Hittite kings maintain tablet collections numbering tens of thousands of clay documents in Hittite, Akkadian, Hurrian, Luwian and other languages, stored in temple and palace buildings between about 1400 and 1180 BCE. Shelf lists catalogue holdings by title and note missing tablets, which Dardano reads as evidence for organised collection management. Among the texts are Mursili II's plague prayers (c. 1320 BCE), which treat an epidemic lasting twenty years as divine punishment and seek its cause through oracles; they are among the earliest attempts to reason about an epidemic in writing.

sources.title: Dardano, P., 'The Tablet Collections of the Hittite State, c.1650-1080 BCE', in K. Ryholt and G. Barjamovic (eds), Libraries before Alexandria: Ancient Near Eastern Traditions (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2019), 168-191
sources.author: Dardano, Paola
sources.confirms: Describes storage, shelf lists and cataloguing practices of Hittite tablet collections.

sources.title: Singer, I., Hittite Prayers, Writings from the Ancient World 11 (Atlanta: Society of Biblical Literature, 2002)
sources.author: Singer, Itamar
sources.confirms: Translates Mursili II's plague prayers with commentary on their date and reasoning about the epidemic's cause.

sources.title: Bryce, T., The Kingdom of the Hittites, new edn (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2005)
sources.author: Bryce, Trevor
sources.confirms: Narrative history including Mursili II's reign, the plague and the fall of Hattusa c. 1180 BCE.

hattusa-tablet-collections-1400bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Dardano 2019 and Singer 2002.
hattusa-tablet-collections-1400bce.detail: Hattusa was abandoned around 1180 BCE in the Late Bronze Age collapse, which sealed the archives. Tablets include treaties, laws, rituals, horse-training manuals (Kikkuli) and annals. Singer's translation of the plague prayers shows Mursili tracing the outbreak to Egyptian prisoners brought back by his father, a rare early epidemiological inference. Hittite scribes also kept a word-for-word Hittite version of Akkadian lexical lists and copied Mesopotamian omen series, which shows Hattusa participating in a wider cuneiform scholarly network.

picture.alt: Clay tablet on horse training (Kikkuli text), second half of the 14th century BCE, from Bogazkoy (Hattusa), Istanbul Archaeology Museums.

hattusa-tablet-collections-1400bce.dating_note: Hittite regnal dates are anchored to Egyptian and Assyrian synchronisms; Mursili II's plague prayers c. 1320 BCE, archive abandonment c. 1180 BCE.

hurrian-hymn-ugarit-notation-1400bce.summary: Clay tablets from Ugarit (Ras Shamra, Syria), written about 1400-1200 BCE, preserve hymns in Hurrian with instructions below each text naming intervals of a nine-string lyre and numbers, a notation whose vocabulary matches Babylonian music-theory texts from Nippur and Ur. Hymn h.6 to moon goddess Nikkal is nearly complete and has been realised in several competing modern performances. West's 1994 study sets out how Babylonian string-pair names (e.g. išartum, embūbum) define a heptatonic tuning cycle, and Crocker and Kilmer's Nippur fragment connects theory texts to Ugarit practice. No older musical notation is known.

sources.title: West, M. L., 'The Babylonian Musical Notation and the Hurrian Melodic Texts', Music & Letters 75.2 (1994), 161-179
sources.author: West, Martin L.
sources.confirms: Explains Babylonian tuning theory and offers a reading of the Hurrian hymn notation.

sources.title: Crocker, R. L. and Kilmer, A. D., 'The Fragmentary Music Text from Nippur', Iraq 46.2 (1984), 81-85
sources.author: Crocker, Richard L.; Kilmer, Anne Draffkorn
sources.confirms: Publishes a Nippur theory fragment linking string-pair terminology to the Ugarit texts.

sources.title: Koitabashi, M., 'A Hurrian Song with Musical Notation from Ugarit', Bulletin of the Society for Near Eastern Studies in Japan 32.1 (1989), 93-107
sources.author: Koitabashi, Matahisa
sources.venue: Bulletin of the Society for Near Eastern Studies in Japan
sources.confirms: Reviews interpretations of h.6.

hurrian-hymn-ugarit-notation-1400bce.verification_note: Existence and age of notation are secure; how to read it is unsettled.
hurrian-hymn-ugarit-notation-1400bce.detail: Interpretation is contested: whether numbers mark repetitions, two-note dyads or melody and accompaniment remains open, so transcriptions differ. Lyres with eleven strings are known from Ur's Royal Cemetery (c. 2500 BCE), and Shang China cast tuned bells in these same centuries, showing independent musical systems. Lyres with seven to nine strings appear on Ugaritic and Mesopotamian seals, matching string counts named in theory tablets, so instrument and notation agree.

picture.alt: Cuneiform tablet from Ugarit with the Hurrian hymn and its musical notation, National Museum of Damascus.

hurrian-hymn-ugarit-notation-1400bce.dating_note: Tablets from Ugarit's final centuries, c. 1400-1200 BCE, by archive context; destruction c. 1185 BCE gives a terminus.

linear-b-mycenaean-1400bce.summary: At Knossos from about 1400 BCE and at Pylos, Mycenae, Thebes and Tiryns until about 1200 BCE, palace scribes write Greek in Linear B, a syllabary of about 87 signs with logograms for commodities, on unbaked clay tablets preserved only because palace fires baked them. Tablets list rations, livestock, textiles, bronze allotments to smiths, chariot wheels and offerings to gods including Zeus, Hera and Dionysus. Ventris, an architect, deciphered the script in 1952 by assuming Greek, and his 1953 paper with Chadwick established the reading. Linear B vanished with the palaces; Greece was then without writing until the alphabet arrived around 800 BCE.

sources.title: Ventris, M. and Chadwick, J., 'Evidence for Greek Dialect in the Mycenaean Archives', Journal of Hellenic Studies 73 (1953), 84-103
sources.author: Ventris, Michael; Chadwick, John
sources.confirms: Announces decipherment of Linear B as Greek with sign values and sample texts.

sources.title: Chadwick, J., The Decipherment of Linear B, 2nd edn (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1967; reissue 2014)
sources.author: Chadwick, John
sources.confirms: Narrates the decipherment and summarises tablet contents and dates.

sources.title: Salgarella, E., Aegean Linear Script(s) (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2020)
sources.author: Salgarella, Ester
sources.confirms: Discusses derivation of Linear B from Linear A and chronology of the Knossos tablets.

linear-b-mycenaean-1400bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Ventris 1953 and Chadwick 1967.
linear-b-mycenaean-1400bce.detail: Knossos tablet dating is contested between c. 1400 and c. 1200 BCE because of Evans' excavation records. Tablets are annual accounts, not literature, and show no narrative texts. Chadwick's account of the decipherment remains standard. Pylos tablets from its final year record coastal watchers, bronze collected from sanctuaries and rowers assigned to ships, an administrative snapshot of a palace under pressure.

picture.alt: Linear B tablet Tn 316 from Pylos listing offerings to gods, National Archaeological Museum, Athens.

linear-b-mycenaean-1400bce.dating_note: Knossos tablets c. 1400 BCE (or c. 1200 BCE in alternative view); mainland tablets c. 1250-1200 BCE by destruction horizons.

san-lorenzo-olmec-1400bce.summary: On an artificially levelled plateau above the Coatzacoalcos river in Veracruz, San Lorenzo grows between about 1400 and 1000 BCE into Mesoamerica's first large centre, covering some 500 hectares with earthen platforms, a palace-like 'Red Palace' with basalt columns, aqueducts of carved basalt troughs and ten colossal heads up to 2.8 metres high carved from basalt quarried in the Tuxtla mountains 60 km away and moved without wheels or draught animals. Pool's synthesis and Cyphers' excavations describe a ranked society supported by levee agriculture and exchange in obsidian and greenstone. Olmec style, with its downturned mouths and were-jaguar motifs, spreads across Mesoamerica in this period.

sources.title: Pool, C. A., Olmec Archaeology and Early Mesoamerica (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2007)
sources.author: Pool, Christopher A.
sources.confirms: Synthesises San Lorenzo's chronology, architecture, sculpture and society.

sources.title: Hirth, K. G. and Cyphers, A., Olmec Lithic Economy at San Lorenzo (Boulder: University Press of Colorado, 2020)
sources.author: Hirth, Kenneth G.; Cyphers, Ann
sources.confirms: Analyses obsidian procurement and craft economy at San Lorenzo.

sources.title: Cyphers, A., Las bellas teorías y los terribles hechos: controversias sobre los olmecas del Preclásico inferior (Mexico City: UNAM, Instituto de Investigaciones Antropológicas, 2012)
sources.author: Cyphers, Ann
sources.confirms: Excavator's account of San Lorenzo's plateau, Red Palace and monuments.

san-lorenzo-olmec-1400bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Pool 2007 and Hirth 2020.
san-lorenzo-olmec-1400bce.detail: Hirth and Cyphers' 2020 study of obsidian shows San Lorenzo drawing on sources across highland Mexico and Guatemala. Colossal heads are thought to portray rulers. The centre declined around 1000 BCE and La Venta succeeded it. Radiocarbon dating of the San Lorenzo phase has shifted earlier over decades of research. Drainage lines of U-shaped basalt troughs with capstones carried water across the plateau, an engineered system of some 170 metres excavated so far.

picture.alt: Olmec colossal head from San Lorenzo, Veracruz, National Museum of Anthropology, Mexico City.

san-lorenzo-olmec-1400bce.dating_note: San Lorenzo phase c. 1400-1000 BCE by radiocarbon (calibrated).

egyptian-water-clock-karnak-1380bce.summary: A broken alabaster vessel from Karnak, inscribed for Amenhotep III (c. 1390-1352 BCE), is our oldest surviving water clock: a conical bowl with a small outlet near the base and twelve interior scales of hour marks, one per month, to allow for seasonal change in night length. Cotterell, Dickson and Kamminga's 1986 reappraisal tested how conical shape and scale spacing controlled outflow and found the marks approximate but workable. An inscription of an official named Amenemhat under Amenhotep I, two centuries earlier, claims he invented such a device, so such instruments may date to about 1500 BCE.

sources.title: Cotterell, B., Dickson, F. P. and Kamminga, J., 'Ancient Egyptian water-clocks: a reappraisal', Journal of Archaeological Science 13.1 (1986), 31-50
sources.author: Cotterell, Brian; Dickson, F. P.; Kamminga, Johan
sources.confirms: Analyses the Karnak clock's geometry and scale accuracy.

sources.title: Clagett, M., Ancient Egyptian Science, vol. 2: Calendars, Clocks, and Astronomy (Philadelphia: American Philosophical Society, 1995)
sources.author: Clagett, Marshall
sources.confirms: Describes the Karnak clock, the Amenemhat inscription and later water clocks.

egyptian-water-clock-karnak-1380bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Cotterell 1986 and Clagett 1995.
egyptian-water-clock-karnak-1380bce.detail: Water clocks let priests time night rituals when stars were hidden. Clagett's survey collects later Egyptian examples and Greek clepsydra traditions descended from them. Its scales reflect an accepted division of night into twelve hours, inherited from decan star clocks. Later inflow clocks, where a float rises in a filling vessel, appear in Ptolemaic temples; Greek engineers at Alexandria added gearing and alarms to this inherited principle.

picture.alt: Granite fragment of an Egyptian water clock with the god Min and a pharaoh, Museo Egizio, Turin.

egyptian-water-clock-karnak-1380bce.dating_note: Surviving clock inscribed for Amenhotep III c. 1380 BCE; a text claims invention under Amenhotep I c. 1500 BCE.

egtved-girl-burial-1370bce.summary: In 1370 BCE, dated by dendrochronology of her oak-trunk coffin, a woman aged 16-18 is buried under a mound at Egtved, Denmark, wearing a short corded skirt and woollen blouse, with a bronze belt plate, bronze bracelets, a birch-bark bucket that held a honey-sweetened beer, a comb and the cremated bones of a child. Waterlogged conditions preserved textiles, hair and nails. Karin Frei reads strontium isotopes in her hair, teeth and clothing as showing she grew up outside Denmark, possibly in southern Germany, and travelled in her last two years. Her clothing is a rare complete Bronze Age wardrobe.

sources.title: Frei, K. M. et al., 'Tracing the dynamic life story of a Bronze Age Female', Scientific Reports 5 (2015), 10431
sources.author: Frei, Karin Margarita et al.
sources.confirms: Strontium isotopes in hair, teeth and textiles indicate non-local origin and mobility; coffin dendro-dated to 1370 BCE.

sources.title: Thomsen, E. and Andreasen, R., 'Agricultural lime disturbs natural strontium isotope variations: Implications for provenance and migration studies', Science Advances 5.3 (2019)
sources.author: Thomsen, Erik; Andreasen, Rasmus
sources.confirms: Challenges the non-local interpretation on baseline grounds.
sources.qualifies: Argues the Egtved girl could be local.

sources.title: National Museum of Denmark, 'The Egtved Girl'
sources.author: National Museum of Denmark
sources.confirms: Museum account of the find, coffin, clothing and grave goods.

egtved-girl-burial-1370bce.verification_note: Date secure; her non-local origin is disputed.
egtved-girl-burial-1370bce.detail: Erik Thomsen and Rasmus Andreasen argue agricultural lime can shift local baseline values, so she could have been local. Oak-coffin burials from Jutland give precise tree-ring dates in a period otherwise reliant on radiocarbon, anchoring Nordic Bronze Age chronology. Wool textiles show spinning and weaving techniques of the period. Her corded skirt, 38 cm long, and short blouse show a summer costume; wool fibres came from sheep raised in regions matching her strontium signature.

picture.alt: Egtved Girl's woollen corded skirt and blouse in the oak coffin, National Museum of Denmark.
picture.credit: Roberto Fortuna & Kira Ursem, Nationalmuseet, Danmark, via Wikimedia Commons

egtved-girl-burial-1370bce.dating_note: Coffin oak felled 1370 BCE; one of few absolutely dated Bronze Age burials.

lapita-pottery-bismarcks-1350bce.summary: In the Bismarck Archipelago of Papua New Guinea around 1350 BCE, communities make pottery decorated with intricate dentate-stamped designs, including human faces, build stilt houses over lagoons, carry pigs, dogs and chickens, and exchange obsidian from Talasea and Lou over hundreds of kilometres. Bayesian analysis dates Lapita's emergence on Mussau to about 3,470 to 3,250 years ago and its dispersal to Vanuatu by 3,250 to 3,100 and Fiji by 3,130 to 3,010 years ago. Peter Sheppard reads the leap from Near to Remote Oceania as a rapid long-distance movement rather than a wave of advance. Lapita is ancestral to Polynesian and many Melanesian societies.

sources.title: Denham, T., Ramsey, C. B. and Specht, J., 'Dating the appearance of Lapita pottery in the Bismarck Archipelago and its dispersal to Remote Oceania', Archaeology in Oceania 47.1 (2012), 39-46
sources.author: Denham, Tim; Ramsey, Christopher Bronk; Specht, Jim
sources.confirms: Bayesian chronology: Lapita emerges on Mussau 3470-3250 cal BP, reaches Vanuatu 3250-3100 and Fiji 3130-3010 cal BP.

sources.title: Sheppard, P. J., 'Lapita Colonization across the Near/Remote Oceania Boundary', Current Anthropology 52.6 (2011), 799-840
sources.author: Sheppard, Peter J.
sources.confirms: Argues for rapid leapfrog colonisation across the Near/Remote Oceania boundary.

sources.title: Kirch, P. V., On the Road of the Winds: An Archaeological History of the Pacific Islands before European Contact, revised edn (Berkeley: University of California Press, 2017)
sources.author: Kirch, Patrick Vinton
sources.confirms: Synthesises Lapita origins, dispersal and material culture.

lapita-pottery-bismarcks-1350bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Denham 2012 and Sheppard 2011.
lapita-pottery-bismarcks-1350bce.detail: Lapita voyagers crossed open ocean gaps of over 800 km to reach Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa within about 300 years, using outrigger or double-hulled sailing canoes known only from later ethnography. Pottery decoration declined after settlement. Lapita's origins combine Austronesian arrivals from Island Southeast Asia with local Bismarck populations. Obsidian from Talasea has been found 3,000 km away in Fiji, which traces voyaging reach in a single durable material.

picture.alt: Dentate-stamped Lapita pot rim with lime infill from Bourewa, Fiji.

lapita-pottery-bismarcks-1350bce.dating_note: Bayesian model 3470-3250 cal BP for emergence (c. 1500-1300 BCE).

hittite-and-meteoritic-iron-1330bce.summary: Before smelted iron became common after 1200 BCE, iron appears as a prestige material. Tutankhamun's tomb (c. 1330 BCE) held an iron-bladed dagger with gold hilt; X-ray fluorescence in 2016 found about 11 percent nickel and 0.6 percent cobalt, matching iron meteorites, and mapping in 2022 found a Widmanstätten pattern confirming meteoritic origin and low-temperature forging. Hittite texts from that period list iron among valuable gifts. Small smelted iron objects come from Alaca Höyük and Kaman-Kalehöyük in the second millennium, with no evidence for Hittite monopoly on iron technology.

sources.title: Comelli, D. et al., 'The meteoritic origin of Tutankhamun's iron dagger blade', Meteoritics & Planetary Science 51.7 (2016), 1301-1309
sources.author: Comelli, Daniela et al.
sources.confirms: XRF analysis finds Ni 10.8 percent and Co 0.58 percent, consistent with meteoritic iron.

sources.title: Matsui, T. et al., 'The manufacture and origin of the Tutankhamen meteoritic iron dagger', Meteoritics & Planetary Science 57.4 (2022), 747-758
sources.author: Matsui, Takafumi et al.
sources.confirms: Detects Widmanstätten pattern and infers low-temperature forging; suggests the dagger may have come from Mitanni as a gift.

sources.title: Muhly, J. D. et al., 'Iron in Anatolia and the Nature of the Hittite Iron Industry', Anatolian Studies 35 (1985), 67-84
sources.author: Muhly, James D.; Maddin, Robert; Stech, Tamara; Özgen, Ergun
sources.confirms: Reviews Anatolian iron finds and rejects a Hittite iron monopoly.

hittite-and-meteoritic-iron-1330bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Comelli 2016 and Matsui 2022.
hittite-and-meteoritic-iron-1330bce.detail: Textual references to 'iron from heaven' in Egyptian match the meteoritic finds. Older claims that Hittites guarded a secret of iron smelting, built on a single letter of Hattusili III mentioning iron not yet ready, are no longer accepted. Carburised steel and widespread iron tools belong to the following period, after bronze supply networks broke down. Iron's high melting point meant early smiths worked it as a bloom hammered hot rather than cast, and without carburisation and quenching it stayed softer than good bronze.

picture.alt: Iron dagger with gold hilt from Tutankhamun's tomb, made from meteoritic iron, Egyptian Museum, Cairo.

hittite-and-meteoritic-iron-1330bce.dating_note: Tutankhamun's reign c. 1332-1323 BCE by Egyptian chronology; Anatolian iron finds dated by context across the second millennium.

uluburun-shipwreck-tin-copper-1320bce.summary: A merchant ship sinks off Uluburun near Kaş, Turkey, around 1320 BCE with about ten tonnes of Cypriot copper in oxhide ingots, roughly one tonne of tin ingots, glass ingots, ebony, ivory, resin, Canaanite jars, Mycenaean pottery and a gold scarab of Nefertiti. Cemal Pulak's 1984 to 1994 excavations revealed our richest Late Bronze Age cargo, with goods from at least seven cultures. Wayne Powell's isotope study traces about one third of its tin to Central Asia (Mushiston, Tajikistan) and two thirds to Anatolia's Taurus mountains, showing tin travelling thousands of kilometres overland before shipment. Copper to tin ratio, near ten to one, matches bronze recipes.

sources.title: Pulak, C., 'The Uluburun shipwreck: an overview', International Journal of Nautical Archaeology 27.3 (1998), 188-224
sources.author: Pulak, Cemal
sources.confirms: Excavator's overview of cargo, hull, date c. 1320 BCE and interpretation.

sources.title: Powell, W. et al., 'Tin from Uluburun shipwreck shows small-scale commodity exchange fueled continental tin supply across Late Bronze Age Eurasia', Science Advances 8.48 (2022)
sources.author: Powell, Wayne; Frachetti, Michael; Pulak, Cemal et al.
sources.confirms: Isotope and trace element data attribute about one third of the tin to Central Asia and two thirds to the Taurus.

sources.title: Berger, D. et al., 'Why Central Asia's Mushiston is not a source for the Late Bronze Age tin ingots from the Uluburun shipwreck', Frontiers in Earth Science 11 (2023)
sources.author: Berger, Daniel et al.
sources.confirms: Challenges the Mushiston attribution.
sources.qualifies: Argues isotope data do not support a Mushiston origin for the tin.

uluburun-shipwreck-tin-copper-1320bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Pulak 1998 and Powell 2022.
uluburun-shipwreck-tin-copper-1320bce.detail: Dendrochronology on firewood and a Mycenaean pottery sequence anchor a date near 1320 BCE. Daniel Berger argues that isotope data do not support a Mushiston origin for this tin. This cargo documents an interlocking Mediterranean exchange system whose breakdown a century later is part of the Bronze Age collapse. Hull remains show pegged mortise-and-tenon planking, an early Mediterranean example of a joinery method later standard in Phoenician and Greek ships, with a keel-plank and stone ballast.

picture.alt: Copper and tin ingot fragments recovered from the Uluburun shipwreck, Bodrum Museum of Underwater Archaeology.

uluburun-shipwreck-tin-copper-1320bce.dating_note: Dendro date on firewood c. 1305 BCE plus pottery; conventionally c. 1320 BCE.

cornish-tin-mediterranean-1300bce.summary: Trace-element, lead-isotope and tin-isotope analysis traces tin ingots from a shipwreck off Salcombe, Devon (c. 1300-1200 BCE) and from wrecks off Israel (Hishuley Carmel, Kfar Samir) and southern France to cassiterite ores of Cornwall and Devon. Israeli ingots were first matched to Cornish ores in 2019, and a 2025 analysis argues these accessible alluvial deposits supplied bronze production across Europe and the Mediterranean in the second millennium BCE. Archaeologists had doubted that British tin travelled so far before Phoenician trade in the first millennium.

sources.title: Williams, A. et al., 'From Land's End to the Levant: did Britain's tin sources transform the Bronze Age in Europe and the Mediterranean?', Antiquity 99 (2025)
sources.author: Williams, Alan; Montesanto, Mariacarmela et al.
sources.confirms: Provenances tin ingots from Israeli and French wrecks to south-west British ores using three independent methods.

sources.title: Berger, D. et al., 'Isotope systematics and chemical composition of tin ingots from Mochlos (Crete) and other Late Bronze Age sites in the eastern Mediterranean Sea', PLoS ONE 14.6 (2019), e0218326
sources.author: Berger, Daniel et al.
sources.confirms: Finds Israeli ingots consistent with Cornish ores while noting limits of tin isotope provenance.
sources.qualifies: Stresses that isotopic overlap between ore fields leaves some attributions uncertain.

cornish-tin-mediterranean-1300bce.verification_note: British origin for some Mediterranean tin is now well supported but isotopic provenance remains debated.
cornish-tin-mediterranean-1300bce.detail: Tin sources were scarce: Erzgebirge, Iberia, Brittany, Cornwall, Anatolia and Central Asia. Tin isotopes fractionate during smelting and ores overlap in signature, so attribution relies on combining several methods. Cornwall's streams also yielded gold, and Bronze Age Britain exported both. Tin ore in Cornwall occurs as cassiterite pebbles in stream gravels, workable by panning without mining, which explains early exploitation by small communities.

picture.alt: Late Bronze Age copper alloy and tin ingot fragments from a British hoard, Portable Antiquities Scheme record 2015 T64.
picture.credit: The Portable Antiquities Scheme, Frank Basford, 2015-02-01 15:48:52, via Wikimedia Commons
picture.changes: re-encoded as JPEG at source size 958x1080; source smaller than 1200px

cornish-tin-mediterranean-1300bce.dating_note: Salcombe wreck c. 1300-1200 BCE by associated bronzes; Israeli wrecks c. 1300-1200 BCE; provenance published 2019-2025.

shang-oracle-bones-1250bce.summary: At Yinxu near Anyang, from Wu Ding's reign (c. 1250-1192 BCE), royal diviners heat prepared cattle shoulder blades and turtle shells, read cracks, then carve each charge, sometimes a prognostication and outcome, into bone. About 150,000 inscribed fragments record questions on harvests, rain, war, illness, childbirth, sacrifices and dreams in a script ancestral to modern Chinese characters, with some 4,500 distinct graphs. Keightley's Sources of Shang History set out their palaeography and dating by diviner groups, and his later work used them to reconstruct Shang religion and politics. They confirm Shang king lists transmitted by Sima Qian.

sources.title: Keightley, D. N., Sources of Shang History: The Oracle-Bone Inscriptions of Bronze Age China (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1978)
sources.author: Keightley, David N.
sources.confirms: Comprehensive account of oracle bone production, script, periodisation and dating.

sources.title: Keightley, D. N., The Ancestral Landscape: Time, Space, and Community in Late Shang China, ca. 1200-1045 B.C. (Berkeley: Institute of East Asian Studies, 2000)
sources.author: Keightley, David N.
sources.venue: Institute of East Asian Studies, University of California
sources.confirms: Uses the inscriptions to reconstruct Shang calendar, religion and politics.

sources.title: Bagley, R., 'Shang Archaeology', in M. Loewe and E. L. Shaughnessy (eds), The Cambridge History of Ancient China (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1999), 124-231
sources.author: Bagley, Robert
sources.confirms: Places Anyang and the inscriptions in archaeological context.

shang-oracle-bones-1250bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Keightley 1978 and Keightley 2000.
shang-oracle-bones-1250bce.detail: Oracle bone script already shows mature principles of pictographs, phonetic loans and semantic-phonetic compounds, implying earlier writing on perishable materials now lost. Bones were recognised as inscribed only in 1899 when sold as 'dragon bones' for medicine. Dates rest on later textual king lists and on astronomical records among them. Inscriptions record about 30 kings in a lineage, royal consorts, named diviners and sacrifices on fixed days, with royal ancestors receiving offerings in a ten-day ritual cycle.

picture.alt: Inscribed Shang oracle bone from Xiaotun, Anyang, Henan.

shang-oracle-bones-1250bce.dating_note: Wu Ding's reign c. 1250-1192 BCE per the Xia-Shang-Zhou Chronology Project; traditional dates differ by decades; anchored partly by eclipse records.

shang-silk-sericulture-1250bce.summary: Bronzes from Anyang tombs, including Fu Hao's, carry corroded imprints of silk wrappings in plain tabby and in patterned weaves with lozenge designs, showing that Shang workshops reeled filament from domesticated Bombyx mori cocoons and wove it on looms with pattern devices. Oracle bone graphs for silk, mulberry and silkworm occur, and sacrifices to a silkworm spirit are recorded. Silk goes back to Neolithic finds such as a cut cocoon at Xiyincun and silk fragments at Qianshanyang (c. 2700 BCE).

sources.title: Kuhn, D., Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 5 part 9: Textile Technology: Spinning and Reeling (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1988)
sources.author: Kuhn, Dieter
sources.confirms: Analyses Neolithic and Shang silk evidence, reeling technology and oracle bone graphs.

sources.title: Good, I. L., Kenoyer, J. M. and Meadow, R. H., 'New Evidence for Early Silk in the Indus Civilization', Archaeometry 51.3 (2009), 457-466
sources.author: Good, Irene L.; Kenoyer, Jonathan Mark; Meadow, Richard H.
sources.confirms: Notes Shang silk weaving evidence while reporting Harappan wild silk.

sources.title: Bagley, R., 'Shang Archaeology', in The Cambridge History of Ancient China (1999)
sources.author: Bagley, Robert
sources.confirms: Mentions silk pseudomorphs on Anyang bronzes.

shang-silk-sericulture-1250bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Kuhn 1988 and Good 2009.
shang-silk-sericulture-1250bce.detail: Wild silk fibres on Harappan ornaments show silk use outside China by 2450 BCE, from different moth species and without reeling. Shang silk stayed within elite circles; export westward is documented only in the first millennium. Preservation as pseudomorphs means weave structure is known but colour and scale are not. Silk production required mulberry orchards, controlled rearing of larvae and reeling of unbroken filament from softened cocoons, a sequence that ties textile craft to agriculture.

picture.alt: Bombyx mori silk moth on its cocoon; modern photograph for illustration.

shang-silk-sericulture-1250bce.dating_note: Anyang tomb contexts c. 1250-1050 BCE; Neolithic silk finds earlier but less secure.

tiryns-flood-dam-1250bce.summary: East of Tiryns in Greece's Argolid, a dam about 10 metres high and 100 metres long of earth faced with cyclopean masonry blocks a stream bed and diverts its flow through a 1.5 km artificial channel to another valley. Zangger's 1994 geoarchaeological study showed a flash flood had buried part of Tiryns' lower town in mud around 1200 BCE, and that dam and channel were built in response, late in Mycenaean palatial times. Balcer's 1974 study first described this structure. It is among Europe's earliest flood-control works, built in masonry matching its citadel walls.

sources.title: Zangger, E., 'Landscape Changes around Tiryns during the Bronze Age', American Journal of Archaeology 98.2 (1994), 189-212
sources.author: Zangger, Eberhard
sources.confirms: Documents the flood that buried the lower town and dates the dam and diversion to LH IIIB.

sources.title: Balcer, J. M., 'The Mycenaean Dam at Tiryns', American Journal of Archaeology 78.2 (1974), 141-149
sources.author: Balcer, Jack Martin
sources.confirms: Describes the dam and canal and argues for Mycenaean date.

tiryns-flood-dam-1250bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Zangger 1994 and Balcer 1974.
tiryns-flood-dam-1250bce.detail: Mycenaean hydraulic engineering also drained Lake Kopais in Boeotia through dykes and canals. These works show palace states organising labour for landscape management shortly before their collapse. Dating depends on pottery in flood deposits and on LH IIIB2 pottery. Dam masonry uses blocks of similar size to citadel walls, pointing to a shared workforce and to palace direction of both defensive and hydraulic construction.

picture.alt: Mycenaean dam at Tiryns, near Agios Adrianos, Greece.

tiryns-flood-dam-1250bce.dating_note: Flood deposit and dam dated by LH IIIB2 pottery to c. 1250-1200 BCE.

anyang-piece-mould-houmuwu-1200bce.summary: Shang foundries at Yinxu cast ritual vessels by building a clay model, pressing sectional outer moulds against it, carving decoration into mould faces, shaving that model to form a core, and pouring bronze into an assembled mould. Their largest product, Houmuwu ding (formerly read Simuwu), a rectangular four-legged cauldron 133 cm high weighing about 833 kg, was cast around 1200 BCE for a royal consort and required coordinated pouring from many crucibles. Bagley's catalogue and Cambridge History chapter explain this technique and its design consequences: symmetrical taotie masks and flanges follow mould divisions. Foundry debris at Anyang covers hectares.

sources.title: Bagley, R. W., Shang Ritual Bronzes in the Arthur M. Sackler Collections (Washington, DC: Arthur M. Sackler Foundation; Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1987)
sources.author: Bagley, Robert W.
sources.confirms: Detailed account of piece-mould casting technology and Shang bronze design.

sources.title: Bagley, R., 'Shang Archaeology', in The Cambridge History of Ancient China (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1999), 124-231
sources.author: Bagley, Robert
sources.confirms: Describes Anyang foundries and the Houmuwu ding.

sources.title: National Museum of China, 'Houmuwu square cauldron (ding)' collection record
sources.author: National Museum of China
sources.confirms: Gives height 133 cm, mouth 112 by 79.2 cm, weight 832.84 kg, the inscription Hou Mu Wu as the temple title of a Shang king's mother, and casting of body and feet as one pour with composite moulds.

anyang-piece-mould-houmuwu-1200bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Bagley 1987 and Bagley 1999.
anyang-piece-mould-houmuwu-1200bce.detail: Piece-mould casting allowed precise repeated decoration without lost-wax. Lead additions improved fluidity for large castings. Workshops specialised by product and were state-controlled. Weight figures for Houmuwu differ (875 kg earlier, 832.84 kg after 1994 reweighing). Mould sections were fired before assembly, and joint lines on finished bronzes were concealed by flanges, so mould technology shaped Shang ornament as much as taste did.

picture.alt: Houmuwu ding, the heaviest surviving Shang bronze, National Museum of China.

anyang-piece-mould-houmuwu-1200bce.dating_note: Houmuwu ding dated by inscription and tomb context to late Shang, c. 1200 BCE.

bronze-age-collapse-1200bce.summary: Between about 1200 and 1150 BCE, Hattusa is abandoned, Ugarit burns, Mycenaean palaces at Pylos and Mycenae fall, Cypriot and Levantine cities are destroyed and Egypt fights 'Sea Peoples' on land and sea under Ramesses III (year 8, c. 1177 BCE). Linear B and Hittite cuneiform cease; Greece loses writing for four centuries. Pollen data from Cyprus and Syria show a three-century drought beginning around 1200 BCE. Causes varied by region among drought, earthquakes, migration, systems collapse and warfare, and interdependence in tin, copper and grain trade spread failure. Iron working expands in the aftermath.

sources.title: Knapp, A. B. and Manning, S. W., 'Crisis in Context: The End of the Late Bronze Age in the Eastern Mediterranean', American Journal of Archaeology 120.1 (2016), 99-149
sources.author: Knapp, A. Bernard; Manning, Sturt W.
sources.confirms: Reviews evidence and causes region by region, dating the crisis c. 1200-1150 BCE.

sources.title: Kaniewski, D. et al., 'Environmental Roots of the Late Bronze Age Crisis', PLoS ONE 8.8 (2013), e71004
sources.author: Kaniewski, David et al.
sources.confirms: Pollen records from Cyprus indicate drought beginning c. 1200 BCE and lasting about 300 years.

sources.title: Cline, E. H., 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2014)
sources.author: Cline, Eric H.
sources.confirms: Synthesises textual and archaeological evidence for multi-causal collapse.

bronze-age-collapse-1200bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Knapp 2016 and Kaniewski 2013.
bronze-age-collapse-1200bce.detail: Eric Cline frames events as a 'perfect storm'. Ugarit's final letters mention famine and enemy ships. Not every polity fell: Assyria, Egypt and Phoenician cities survived in reduced form, and Cyprus adapted. Chronology rests on Egyptian regnal dates and Aegean pottery phases; radiocarbon from destruction layers broadly agrees. Recovery took centuries; when writing returned to Greece it was an alphabet from Phoenicia, and new states in Israel, Phrygia and Assyria rose on a landscape of fallen palaces.

picture.alt: Relief at Medinet Habu, first court of the temple of Ramesses III, with hieroglyphs naming the Sea Peoples.

bronze-age-collapse-1200bce.dating_note: Egyptian regnal dates (Ramesses III year 8 c. 1177 BCE) and Aegean pottery phases; radiocarbon broadly concordant.

chariot-reaches-china-1200bce.summary: Chariot pits at Yinxu, from about 1200 BCE, hold two-horse vehicles with wheels of 18 to 26 spokes, a single draught pole and yoke, often with driver and horses buried in place. No earlier wheeled vehicles are known in China. Shaughnessy's 1988 study argued the chariot arrived fully formed from the steppe through contacts documented by northern-style bronzes, and Wu's 2013 monograph compares Chinese chariots with Caucasian and steppe finds. Oracle bones record chariots in hunting and warfare and a graph for chariot shows wheels and pole. Horse domestication in China also begins with this horizon.

sources.title: Shaughnessy, E. L., 'Historical Perspectives on the Introduction of the Chariot into China', Harvard Journal of Asiatic Studies 48.1 (1988), 189-237
sources.author: Shaughnessy, Edward L.
sources.confirms: Argues for steppe origin of the Chinese chariot and dates its appearance to c. 1200 BCE.

sources.title: Wu, H.-Y., Chariots in Early China: Origins, Cultural Interaction, and Identity, BAR International Series 2457 (Oxford: Archaeopress, 2013)
sources.author: Wu, Hsiao-yun
sources.confirms: Compares Anyang chariots with steppe and Caucasian finds.

chariot-reaches-china-1200bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Shaughnessy 1988 and Wu 2013.
chariot-reaches-china-1200bce.detail: Chinese chariots had larger wheels and more spokes than Near Eastern examples, pointing to steppe rather than Mesopotamian intermediaries. Transmission across 3,000 km of steppe from Sintashta took about eight centuries. Later Zhou texts treat chariots as the measure of a state's power. Inscriptions describe chariot accidents during royal hunts, and chariot pits accompany royal and elite tombs, so vehicles marked status as much as military power.

picture.alt: Shang chariot burial with horses at the Yin Ruins, Anyang, Henan.

chariot-reaches-china-1200bce.dating_note: Anyang chariot pits belong to Yinxu periods II-IV, c. 1200-1050 BCE.

fu-hao-tomb-1200bce.summary: Tomb 5 at Yinxu, excavated intact in 1976, belongs to Fu Hao, a consort of Wu Ding named in about 200 oracle bone inscriptions as leading armies of up to 13,000, conducting rituals and owning estates. Her grave held 468 bronze objects including ritual vessels, weapons, mirrors and bells, 755 jades, 6,900 cowrie shells, ivory cups inlaid with turquoise and 16 human sacrifices. Chang's Shang Civilization and Thorp's synthesis present it as the only unlooted Shang royal tomb and a key for dating bronze styles. Vessels bear her name and her posthumous temple name.

sources.title: Chang, K. C., Shang Civilization (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1980)
sources.author: Chang, Kwang-chih
sources.confirms: Describes Tomb 5 and Fu Hao's place in oracle bone records.

sources.title: Thorp, R. L., China in the Early Bronze Age: Shang Civilization (Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 2006)
sources.author: Thorp, Robert L.
sources.confirms: Inventories the tomb and discusses its dating significance.

sources.title: Keightley, D. N., Sources of Shang History (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1978)
sources.author: Keightley, David N.
sources.confirms: Oracle bone references to Fu Hao's military and ritual activity.

fu-hao-tomb-1200bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Chang 1980 and Thorp 2006.
fu-hao-tomb-1200bce.detail: The inscriptions make her one of few individuals from the second millennium BCE known from both texts and an excavated burial. Bronze weapons in her tomb include northern-style knives, pointing to contacts with steppe cultures. Jades include Neolithic heirlooms a thousand years old. Oracle bones record divinations about her pregnancies and illnesses, with Wu Ding asking whether childbirth would be fortunate, which gives rare personal detail for a Bronze Age woman.

picture.alt: Reconstructed display of Fu Hao's tomb at Yinxu, Anyang; originals held in Beijing and Zhengzhou.

fu-hao-tomb-1200bce.dating_note: Wu Ding's reign c. 1250-1192 BCE; tomb assigned to Yinxu period II.

sanxingdui-bronze-masks-1200bce.summary: At Sanxingdui near Guanghan, Sichuan, two pits found in 1986 and six more excavated from 2019 contained burned and broken bronze heads with gold foil masks, a standing figure 2.62 metres tall on a pedestal, masks with protruding eyes over a metre wide, bronze trees up to four metres high, elephant tusks, jade blades and cowrie shells. Li, Qiu and Guo's 2022 Antiquity report summarises these new pits, whose radiocarbon dates cluster around 1200-1000 BCE. Bagley's publications first presented Sanxingdui to Western scholarship. Sanxingdui shares piece-mould casting with Shang foundries but its imagery and absence of writing or ritual vessels of Shang type mark an independent culture.

sources.title: Li, X., Qiu, T. and Guo, J., 'New discoveries at the Sanxingdui Bronze Age site in south-west China', Antiquity 97.391 (2023)
sources.author: Li, Xin; Qiu, Tianran; Guo, Jianbo
sources.confirms: Reports six new pits with radiocarbon dates c. 1200-1000 BCE and inventories of bronzes, gold and ivory.

sources.title: Ge, Y. and Linduff, K. M., 'Sanxingdui: a new Bronze Age site in southwest China', Antiquity 64.244 (1990), 505-513
sources.author: Ge, Yan; Linduff, Katheryn M.
sources.confirms: First English report on pits 1 and 2 and their contents.

sources.title: Bagley, R., 'Sacrificial pits of the Shang period at Sanxingdui in Guanghan county, Sichuan Province', Arts asiatiques 43 (1988), 78-86
sources.author: Bagley, Robert
sources.confirms: Analyses casting and iconography of the pit 1 and 2 bronzes.

sanxingdui-bronze-masks-1200bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Li 2023 and Ge 1990.
sanxingdui-bronze-masks-1200bce.detail: Interpretation of these pits as sacrifice, destruction after regime change or ritual burial is unresolved. Ge and Linduff's 1990 Antiquity article introduced Sanxingdui to Antiquity's readers. Sanxingdui's walled city dates from about 1700 BCE and pit deposits mark its end; Jinsha near Chengdu continued this tradition. Metal analysis shows lead-rich alloys with isotopic signatures shared with Anyang bronzes, which points to common ore sources or exchange despite different imagery.

picture.alt: Bronze animal mask from Sanxingdui, Sanxingdui Museum, Sichuan.

sanxingdui-bronze-masks-1200bce.dating_note: New pits radiocarbon-dated c. 1200-1000 BCE; pits 1 and 2 placed c. 1250-1100 BCE by typology.

shang-bronze-bells-nao-1200bce.summary: Late Shang tombs at Anyang contain sets of three to five nao, clapperless bronze bells mounted mouth upward on a hollow shank and struck with a mallet, cast in graded sizes so that each set spans several pitches. Fu Hao's tomb held a set of five. Larger single nao from the Yangzi region weigh over 200 kg. Falkenhausen's Suspended Music traces how these developed into the Zhou chime-bell sets whose almond-shaped cross section produces two distinct tones per bell. Bells, drums with crocodile-skin heads, chime stones and ocarinas appear together in elite burials, and oracle bone graphs record music in ritual.

sources.title: Falkenhausen, L. von, Suspended Music: Chime-Bells in the Culture of Bronze Age China (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1993)
sources.author: Falkenhausen, Lothar von
sources.confirms: Traces Shang nao and their development into Zhou chime bells with acoustic analysis.

sources.title: Bagley, R., 'Shang Archaeology', in The Cambridge History of Ancient China (1999)
sources.author: Bagley, Robert
sources.confirms: Describes nao sets in Anyang tombs including Fu Hao's.

shang-bronze-bells-nao-1200bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Falkenhausen 1993 and Bagley 1999.
shang-bronze-bells-nao-1200bce.detail: Acoustic analysis of Shang bells shows irregular tuning compared with Zhou sets, suggesting pitch standards were emerging rather than fixed. Casting bells demanded control of wall thickness that piece-mould technique supplied. Mesopotamian notation of the same centuries records a different, string-based theory. Nao sets from Fu Hao's tomb span roughly a fifth in pitch, and tuning marks inside later bells show post-casting adjustment by grinding.

picture.alt: Late Shang bronze nao bell, National Palace Museum, Taipei.

shang-eclipse-records-ganzhi-1200bce.summary: Oracle bone inscriptions date each divination by a day name formed from ten 'heavenly stems' and twelve 'earthly branches', a sixty-day cycle that has run without interruption into the modern Chinese calendar. Some inscriptions record that 'the moon was eclipsed', and five such lunar eclipses from the reign of Wu Ding and his successors have been matched to computed eclipses between about 1200 and 1180 BCE, providing anchors for Shang chronology. Pankenier's study analyses these records and the Shang luni-solar calendar with intercalary thirteenth months, while Keightley describes how diviners tracked time by ten-day weeks.

sources.title: Pankenier, D. W., Astrology and Cosmology in Early China: Conforming Earth to Heaven (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2013)
sources.author: Pankenier, David W.
sources.confirms: Analyses Shang eclipse records, the ganzhi cycle and their use for chronology.

sources.title: Keightley, D. N., The Ancestral Landscape (Berkeley: Institute of East Asian Studies, 2000)
sources.author: Keightley, David N.
sources.confirms: Describes Shang timekeeping by ten-day weeks, lunar months and intercalation.

shang-eclipse-records-ganzhi-1200bce.verification_note: Cycle and eclipse records are secure; specific eclipse dates are debated.
shang-eclipse-records-ganzhi-1200bce.detail: Eclipse identifications depend on reading damaged graphs and on assumptions about observation at Anyang, so proposed absolute dates vary by decades among scholars. The ganzhi cycle later extended to years. Shang astronomers also recorded a 'new great star' near Antares, interpreted by some as a nova. Diviners also recorded solar eclipses and a star near Antares in inscriptions whose astronomical reading remains debated among specialists.

picture.alt: Ox scapula Heji 37986 inscribed with a complete ganzhi sexagenary table, Shang period.
picture.credit: rotated and cropped by Kanguole, via Wikimedia Commons

shang-eclipse-records-ganzhi-1200bce.dating_note: Eclipse records matched to computed lunar eclipses c. 1200-1180 BCE; identifications vary among scholars.

deir-el-medina-strike-1157bce.summary: In year 29 of Ramesses III, about 1157 BCE, craftsmen cutting royal tombs in Thebes' Valley of the Kings walk out of their village at Deir el-Medina after monthly grain rations fall weeks overdue. Turin Strike Papyrus records them crossing enclosure walls, sitting at mortuary temples of Thutmose III and Ramesses II and declaring 'we are hungry', then negotiating with scribes and the vizier until rations arrive. Edgerton's 1951 translation made this our earliest documented labour stoppage. Lesko's edited volume sets it in a decade of grain shortages and administrative strain late in Dynasty 20.

sources.title: Edgerton, W. F., 'The Strikes in Ramses III's Twenty-Ninth Year', Journal of Near Eastern Studies 10.3 (1951), 137-145
sources.author: Edgerton, William F.
sources.confirms: Translates and analyses the Turin Strike Papyrus.

sources.title: Lesko, L. H. (ed.), Pharaoh's Workers: The Villagers of Deir el Medina (Ithaca: Cornell University Press, 1994)
sources.author: Lesko, Leonard H. (ed.)
sources.confirms: Essays on the village economy, rations and the strikes of Ramesses III's reign.

sources.title: Museo Egizio, Turin, 'Turin Strike Papyrus' (Papyrus Turin Cat. 1880)
sources.author: Museo Egizio
sources.confirms: Digitised papyrus with description and dating to year 29 of Ramesses III.

deir-el-medina-strike-1157bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Edgerton 1951 and Lesko 1994.
deir-el-medina-strike-1157bce.detail: Deir el-Medina's thousands of ostraca and papyri preserve attendance registers, absence excuses, laundry lists and lawsuits, giving an unusually full picture of a skilled workforce paid in kind. Repeated stoppages over following years point to failing state logistics as wider Late Bronze Age collapse unfolded. Workers framed grievances in moral terms, invoking Pharaoh's duty to feed them, and officials responded by borrowing grain from temple stores rather than by punishment.

picture.alt: Turin Strike Papyrus written by the scribe Amennakht reporting the Deir el-Medina work stoppage, Museo Egizio, Turin.

deir-el-medina-strike-1157bce.dating_note: Year 29 of Ramesses III, c. 1157 BCE by Egyptian chronology (range 1159-1155 BCE in different schemes).

indian-iron-working-ganga-1000bce.summary: Excavations at Malhar, Raja Nala ka Tila and Dadupur in Uttar Pradesh produced iron artefacts, slag, tuyeres and furnace remains in layers radiocarbon dated between about 1800 and 1000 BCE. Those dates push iron working in north India several centuries earlier than older schemes that tied it to Painted Grey Ware around 1000 BCE. Dilip Chakrabarti argued in 1976 that Indian iron arose locally rather than arriving from Iran. These finds make Ganga plain and eastern Vindhyas one of several places where bloomery smelting began in the second millennium BCE.

sources.title: Tewari, Rakesh, 'The origins of iron working in India: new evidence from the Central Ganga Plain and the Eastern Vindhyas', Antiquity 77 (2003)
sources.author: Tewari, Rakesh
sources.confirms: Iron artefacts, slag and furnaces at Malhar and other sites dated c. 1800 to 1000 BCE

sources.title: Chakrabarti, Dilip K., 'The beginning of iron in India', Antiquity 50 (1976)
sources.author: Chakrabarti, Dilip K.
sources.confirms: Argues for indigenous origin of Indian iron

indian-iron-working-ganga-1000bce.detail: Malhar has furnace bases, slag heaps and iron tools, linked to local ores in the Vindhya range. Rakesh Tewari dates them from 1800 to 1000 BCE; critics question whether charcoal behind early dates is securely associated with iron. Many archaeologists accept iron in common use across the Ganga basin by about 1000 BCE; that year is approximate. Later Indian crucible steel built on this bloomery base.

picture.alt: Painted Grey Ware sherds from Sonkh, about 1000 to 600 BCE, Government Museum Mathura

indian-iron-working-ganga-1000bce.dating_note: Tewari's dates run 1800 to 1000 BCE; older schemes placed Ganga iron c. 1000 BCE, used here as a conservative anchor.

iron-age-eurasia-africa-era-1000bce.summary: Between about 1200 and 500 BCE, iron smelting passed from a rare Anatolian craft into everyday use for blades, axes and ploughshares across Anatolia, Canaan, Greece, Iran, India and Europe, with independent or parallel traditions in West Africa and Sudan. Archaeometric work shows carburized iron (steel) appearing in Canaan by about 1000 BCE, and bloomery furnaces spreading as bronze supply networks broke down after 1200 BCE. Iron ore was common where tin was scarce, so smiths who mastered high-temperature smelting and quenching gained a cheap, hard metal. This era record frames regional entries on Hallstatt, Ganga plain, Chinese cast iron, Meroe, Nok and Urewe iron.

sources.title: Erb-Satullo, Nathaniel L., 'The Innovation and Adoption of Iron in the Ancient Near East', Journal of Archaeological Research 27 (2019)
sources.author: Erb-Satullo, Nathaniel L.
sources.confirms: Anatolian origin for extractive iron; spread explained through craft and exchange networks

sources.title: Yahalom-Mack, Naama; Eliyahu-Behar, Adi, 'The Transition from Bronze to Iron in Canaan: Chronology, Technology, and Context', Radiocarbon 57 (2015)
sources.author: Yahalom-Mack, Naama; Eliyahu-Behar, Adi
sources.confirms: Transition from bronze to iron in Canaan dated to Iron I to IIA, about 1150 to 900 BCE

sources.title: Killick, David; Fenn, Thomas, 'Archaeometallurgy: The Study of Preindustrial Mining and Metallurgy', Annual Review of Anthropology 41 (2012)
sources.author: Killick, David; Fenn, Thomas
sources.confirms: Bloomery smelting as a worldwide preindustrial technology

iron-age-eurasia-africa-era-1000bce.detail: Erb-Satullo's 2019 review supports an Anatolian origin for extractive iron and ties its spread to craft networks rather than any single collapse. Yahalom-Mack and Eliyahu-Behar date Canaan's transition to Iron I and IIA, roughly 1150 to 900 BCE, with smelting evidence at Tell Hammeh. Killick and Fenn frame bloomery smelting as a worldwide preindustrial technology whose spread varied by region. Sub-Saharan Africa appears to have developed iron without a copper or bronze stage, which is why African entries sit alongside Eurasian ones here.

picture.alt: Late Bronze Age to earliest Iron Age metal hoard recorded by the Portable Antiquities Scheme, England
picture.credit: Salisbury and South Wiltshire Museum, Katie Hinds, 2012-07-12 10:39:12

iron-age-eurasia-africa-era-1000bce.dating_note: Start dates for iron use differ by region, from about 1200 BCE in Anatolia to after 500 BCE in parts of Africa and East Asia.

las-capas-irrigation-tucson-1000bce.summary: At Las Capas on the Santa Cruz River, farmers of San Pedro phase, about 1200 to 800 BCE, built canals, laterals and bordered fields covering some 15 hectares of irrigable land, which Archaeology Southwest describes as 'the best example of Early Agricultural period farming technology known to date'. Huckleberry, Rittenour and Vint combined radiocarbon and single-grain optically stimulated luminescence to date these preceramic canals in Journal of Archaeological Science in 2014. Maize had reached this region from Mexico by about 2000 BCE, and Las Capas shows irrigation managed by village communities centuries before Hohokam canals.

sources.title: Huckleberry, Gary; Rittenour, Tammy; Vint, James, 'Combining radiocarbon and single-grain optically stimulated luminescence methods to accurately date pre-ceramic irrigation canals, Tucson, Arizona', Journal of Archaeological Science 41 (2014)
sources.author: Huckleberry, Gary; Rittenour, Tammy; Vint, James
sources.confirms: Radiocarbon and OSL dating of preceramic canals at Las Capas

sources.title: Gann, Kate Sarther, 'The Archaeology of Southern Arizona's Early Farmers', Archaeology Southwest (2015)
sources.author: Gann, Kate Sarther
sources.confirms: San Pedro phase c. 1200 to 800 BCE; canals and fields; 15 hectares irrigable

las-capas-irrigation-tucson-1000bce.detail: Excavations ahead of a wastewater plant in 2008 and 2009 exposed stacked layers of fields and canals preserved by flood silts, with footprints of farmers and children. Fields were small plots fed by gated laterals. Dating combines charcoal, maize fragments and luminescence on canal sediments. Canals were abandoned and rebuilt as river channels shifted, and successive generations added new field grids above old ones.

phoenician-alphabet-byblos-1000bce.summary: Scribes in Phoenician cities reduced earlier West Semitic letter forms to a fixed set of 22 consonant signs written right to left, an alphabet seen in tenth-century BCE royal inscriptions from Byblos such as Ahiram's sarcophagus. Richey's chapter in the Oxford Handbook of the Phoenician and Punic Mediterranean argues that standardization was complete at Tyre by about 850 BCE and that Byblos inscriptions were not 'the fount' of standard Phoenician. Finkelstein and Sass reassess dates of West Semitic inscriptions from Late Bronze and Iron ages. This script became parent to Greek, Aramaic and, through them, most alphabets.

sources.title: Richey, Madadh, 'The Alphabet and its Legacy', in The Oxford Handbook of the Phoenician and Punic Mediterranean (Oxford University Press, 2019)
sources.author: Richey, Madadh
sources.confirms: Phoenician script standardized at Tyre by c. 850 BCE with 22 graphemes; Byblos 10th-century inscriptions noted

sources.title: McCarter, P. Kyle, The Antiquity of the Greek Alphabet and the Early Phoenician Scripts (Brill, 1975)
sources.author: McCarter, P. Kyle
sources.confirms: Monograph on antiquity of Greek alphabet and early Phoenician scripts

sources.title: Finkelstein, Israel; Sass, Benjamin, 'The West Semitic Alphabetic Inscriptions, Late Bronze II to Iron IIA: Archeological Context, Distribution and Chronology', Hebrew Bible and Ancient Israel 2 (2013)
sources.author: Finkelstein, Israel; Sass, Benjamin
sources.confirms: Archaeological reassessment of West Semitic alphabetic inscription dates

phoenician-alphabet-byblos-1000bce.verification_note: Richey confirms Tyre about 850 BCE and tenth-century Byblos inscriptions; McCarter and Finkelstein and Sass (2013) are cited as supporting literature.
phoenician-alphabet-byblos-1000bce.detail: McCarter's 1975 study and later work compare letter shapes to date early inscriptions on arrowheads and stone. Finkelstein and Sass, writing in Hebrew Bible and Ancient Israel in 2013, lower some conventional dates by arguing from archaeological context rather than palaeography. Scholars disagree whether to anchor the alphabet at tenth-century Byblos or ninth-century Tyre, so 1000 BCE is an approximate year.

picture.alt: Phoenician inscription on the sarcophagus of Ahiram, National Museum of Beirut

phoenician-alphabet-byblos-1000bce.dating_note: Richey places standardization at Tyre c. 850 BCE while tenth-century Byblos inscriptions are often taken as the earliest Phoenician; Finkelstein and Sass argue for lower dates.

teouma-lapita-cemetery-vanuatu-950bce.summary: At Teouma on Efate in Vanuatu, Lapita settlers created a cemetery within a generation or two of arrival, placing bodies in dentate-stamped pots and later removing skulls. Radiocarbon dates its regular use to about 990 to 930 BCE, with last burials about 820 to 760 BCE. Teouma is among Vanuatu's earliest known sites and is Remote Oceania's largest Lapita cemetery. Those same decades saw voyagers continue east: uranium-thorium coral dates put first settlement of Tonga about 890 BCE. Vanuatu's early dates and Tonga's lie within a century of each other, a pace of expansion with few parallels.

sources.title: Burley, David; Edinborough, Kevan; Weisler, Marshall; Zhao, Jian-xin, 'Bayesian Modeling and Chronological Precision for Polynesian Settlement of Tonga', PLOS ONE 10 (2015)
sources.author: Burley, David; Edinborough, Kevan; Weisler, Marshall; Zhao, Jian-xin
