sources.confirms: Earliest U/Th date 2838 plus or minus 8 cal BP beneath Nukuleka; overlap model 2863 to 2835 cal BP for Tongatapu

sources.title: Petchey, Fiona; Spriggs, Matthew; Bedford, Stuart; Valentin, Frédérique; Buckley, Hallie, 'Radiocarbon dating of burials from the Teouma Lapita cemetery, Efate, Vanuatu', Journal of Archaeological Science 50 (2014)
sources.author: Petchey, Fiona; Spriggs, Matthew; Bedford, Stuart; Valentin, Frédérique; Buckley, Hallie
sources.confirms: Teouma cemetery regular use c. 2940 to 2880 BP; last burials 2770 to 2710 cal BP

sources.title: Kirch, Patrick Vinton, On the Road of the Winds: An Archaeological History of the Pacific Islands before European Contact, rev. ed. (University of California Press, 2017)
sources.author: Kirch, Patrick Vinton
sources.confirms: Synthesis of Pacific island archaeology

teouma-lapita-cemetery-vanuatu-950bce.detail: Teouma was found in 2003 during quarrying for a prawn farm. Excavations recovered over 60 burials with associated decorated pots, including a vessel bearing modelled birds. Skull removal and rearrangement of bones indicate mortuary rites performed over time. Pottery decoration with toothed stamps shows shared identity across 4,000 kilometres of ocean. Teouma anchors chronology for Vanuatu settlement: radiocarbon gives 2,940 to 2,880 years before 1950 for regular use, about 990 to 930 BCE, and 2,770 to 2,710 for last burials, about 820 to 760 BCE. Uranium-thorium dates on coral put Tonga's Nukuleka landfall at 2,838 years before 1950, about 890 BCE.

picture.alt: Dentate-stamped Lapita potsherd from the Bourewa site, Fiji

teouma-lapita-cemetery-vanuatu-950bce.dating_note: Teouma's regular use is dated c. 2940 to 2880 BP; Tonga's first settlement is modelled at c. 2838 BP, so Vanuatu and Tonga dates overlap within a century.

chavin-de-huantar-metallurgy-900bce.summary: Andean smiths of the early first millennium BCE produced gold and gold-silver alloy objects by hammering sheets, soldering and joining; Heather Lechtman links these techniques to Andean values favouring surface transformation over casting. Copper and gold artefacts from Mina Perdida in Lurin valley, dated about 1410 to 1090 BCE, show hammered and annealed foil before Chavin. Chavin de Huantar, a pilgrimage centre with carved stone and galleries, flourished about 900 to 200 BCE. Gold crowns and ornaments from Chavin-related sites such as Kuntur Wasi show mastery of sheet metal.

sources.title: Lechtman, Heather, 'Andean Value Systems and the Development of Prehistoric Metallurgy', Technology and Culture 25 (1984)
sources.author: Lechtman, Heather
sources.confirms: Andean value systems and development of prehistoric metallurgy

sources.title: Burger, Richard L.; Gordon, Robert B., 'Early Central Andean Metalworking from Mina Perdida, Peru', Science 282 (1998)
sources.author: Burger, Richard L.; Gordon, Robert B.
sources.confirms: Copper and gold artefacts at Mina Perdida dated c. 1410 to 1090 BCE; hammered foil

sources.title: Rick, John W., 'The Evolution of Authority and Power at Chavín de Huántar, Peru', Archeological Papers of the American Anthropological Association 14 (2005)
sources.author: Rick, John W.
sources.venue: Archeological Papers of the American Anthropological Association
sources.confirms: Evolution of authority and power at Chavin de Huantar

chavin-de-huantar-metallurgy-900bce.detail: Andean metallurgy began with native gold and copper worked cold, then annealed. Lechtman argued that depletion gilding and surface colour expressed ideas about essence. Chavin's temple used drainage canals and acoustic galleries, and its art spread an iconography of fanged deities. Chavin spans an era from about 900 to 200 BCE, and gold work there set patterns for Moche smiths.

picture.alt: Chavín-style gold crown with deity figures, Dallas Museum of Art

nok-terracottas-900bce.summary: In central Nigeria, Nok communities produced terracotta figures with elongated heads, pierced eyes and detailed hairstyles, from small pieces to nearly life-size, which Franke's 2024 Oxford Research Encyclopedia article dates from early first millennium BCE with standardized forms from about 900 BCE. Fagg and Fleming applied thermoluminescence dating to a Nok terracotta in Archaeometry in 1970. Rupp, Ameje and Breunig's 2005 article reports new studies by a Frankfurt team. Figures were apparently broken and deposited deliberately, perhaps in rituals. Franke notes no proven link between figurines and iron working, which began at least a century later.

sources.title: Franke, Gabriele, 'The Archaeology of Nok Culture in Nigeria (2nd/1st Millennium BCE)', Oxford Research Encyclopedia of African History (2024)
sources.author: Franke, Gabriele
sources.venue: Oxford Research Encyclopedia of African History
sources.confirms: Figurines early 1st millennium BCE, standardized from 900 BCE; iron at least 100 years later; no link proven

sources.title: Rupp, Nicole; Ameje, James; Breunig, Peter, 'New Studies on the Nok Culture of Central Nigeria', Journal of African Archaeology 3 (2005)
sources.author: Rupp, Nicole; Ameje, James; Breunig, Peter
sources.confirms: New Frankfurt studies on Nok culture

sources.title: Fagg, Bernard; Fleming, S. J., 'Thermoluminescent Dating of a Terracotta of the Nok Culture, Nigeria', Archaeometry 12 (1970)
sources.author: Fagg, Bernard; Fleming, S. J.
sources.confirms: Thermoluminescence dating of a Nok terracotta

nok-terracottas-900bce.verification_note: Franke's encyclopedia article is this entry's principal source; Fagg and Fleming and Rupp, Ameje and Breunig are cited as supporting literature.
nok-terracottas-900bce.detail: Nok terracottas were first found in tin mines near Jos in 1928 and named for Nok village. Frankfurt excavations since 2005 at sites such as Pangwari, Ungwar Kura and Ifana found figurines in pits with pottery and stone axes. Nok culture ends around 100 BCE; this culture record runs 900 to 100 BCE. Looting for art markets has stripped many sites of context, making excavated examples all the more valuable.

picture.alt: Terracotta head of the Nok culture, Nigeria, Honolulu Museum of Art

nok-terracottas-900bce.dating_note: Figurines are dated by radiocarbon from pit contexts and by thermoluminescence; standardized style from c. 900 BCE.

olmec-la-venta-900bce.summary: On a low salt dome near Tabasco's Gulf Coast, Olmec people built La Venta, a planned ceremonial centre with a clay pyramid over 30 metres high, basalt colossal heads, buried mosaic pavements and massive offerings of serpentine blocks. Settlement along levees of the Rio Bari began about 1750 to 1400 BCE, with the centre flourishing roughly 900 to 400 BCE. Susan Gillespie and Michael Volk read so-called royal tombs in Mound A-2 as a single construction episode.

sources.title: Rust, William F.; Sharer, Robert J., 'Olmec Settlement Data from La Venta, Tabasco, Mexico', Science 242 (1988)
sources.author: Rust, William F.; Sharer, Robert J.
sources.confirms: Initial occupation c. 1750 to 1400 BCE along Rio Bari levees; La Venta as major Olmec centre

sources.title: Pool, Christopher A., Olmec Archaeology and Early Mesoamerica (Cambridge University Press, 2007)
sources.author: Pool, Christopher A.
sources.confirms: Synthesis of Olmec archaeology

sources.title: Gillespie, Susan D.; Volk, Michael, 'An archaeological evaluation of the Olmec "royal tombs" at La Venta, Mexico', Ancient Mesoamerica 34 (2023)
sources.author: Gillespie, Susan D.; Volk, Michael
sources.confirms: Mound A-2 tombs and caches as single construction episode

olmec-la-venta-900bce.detail: Basalt for heads and altars came from Tuxtla mountains over 80 kilometres away, moved without draft animals. La Venta's layout along a north-south axis prefigures later Mesoamerican site planning. Drains of U-shaped basalt troughs show water management. Olmec iconography and possibly early glyphs influenced Maya and Zapotec neighbours. La Venta's main phase ran from about 900 to 400 BCE, when it was abandoned and monuments defaced.

picture.alt: Olmec colossal head from La Venta, Parque-Museo La Venta, Villahermosa

yayoi-rice-farming-japan-900bce.summary: Wet-rice agriculture with paddy fields, together with bronze and iron tools and new pottery, spread into northern Kyushu from the Korean peninsula and then across Honshu, marking Japan's Yayoi period. AMS dates on carbonized residues pushed Yayoi's start from about 500 BCE back to around 900 or 1000 BCE, a shift some specialists accept and others reject. Minoru Sakamoto used tree-ring radiocarbon in 2023 to date Yayoi's beginning and end. Yayoi farming villages led toward state formation. Yayoi runs roughly 900 BCE to 250 CE.

sources.title: Shoda, Shinya, 'Radiocarbon and Archaeology in Japan and Korea: What has Changed Because of the Yayoi Dating Controversy?', Radiocarbon 52 (2010)
sources.author: Shoda, Shinya
sources.confirms: Radiocarbon and the Yayoi dating controversy

sources.title: Sakamoto, Minoru; et al., 'Radiocarbon dating of tree rings from the beginning and end of the Yayoi period, Japan', Radiocarbon 65 (2023)
sources.author: Sakamoto, Minoru; et al.
sources.confirms: Tree-ring radiocarbon dating of Yayoi's beginning and end

sources.title: Mizoguchi, Koji, The Archaeology of Japan: From the Earliest Rice Farming Villages to the Rise of the State (Cambridge University Press, 2013), ch. 'Beginnings'
sources.author: Mizoguchi, Koji
sources.confirms: Chapter on earliest rice farming villages

yayoi-rice-farming-japan-900bce.verification_note: Shoda's title confirms an early-start controversy over Yayoi dating; Sakamoto and Mizoguchi are cited as supporting literature.
yayoi-rice-farming-japan-900bce.detail: Early paddies at Itazuke and Nabatake show ditches, bunds and wooden tools. Objections to early dates rest on marine reservoir effects in cooking residues and calibration curve plateaus between 800 and 400 BCE. Wiggle-matched tree-ring dates span start and end phases. Migration from Korea and local adoption by Jomon descendants both played roles in Yayoi origins, as skeletal and genetic studies show.

picture.alt: Yayoi period earthenware jar from Takakura-cho, Aichi, Tokyo National Museum

yayoi-rice-farming-japan-900bce.dating_note: Yayoi's start was placed c. 500 BCE; AMS dating since 2003 suggests c. 900 to 1000 BCE, still debated.

lapita-reaches-tonga-890bce.summary: Lapita canoes reach Nukuleka on Tongatapu's lagoon, Tonga, and establish a founding settlement of what becomes Polynesia. Uranium-thorium dating of coral abraders from Nukuleka fixes first occupation at about 890 BCE, to within 8 years, with occupation developing over the next 250 years. Excavations by David Burley showed western Lapita pottery styles distinct from Fiji's. Within a few generations settlers spread north through Vava'u to Samoa, where a pause of more than a thousand years followed before voyagers moved on to East Polynesia.

sources.title: Burley, D., Weisler, M. I. and Zhao, J.-x., 'High Precision U/Th Dating of First Polynesian Settlement', PLoS ONE 7.11 (2012), e48769
sources.author: Burley, David; Weisler, Marshall I.; Zhao, Jian-xin
sources.confirms: U/Th dates on coral abraders fix founding of Nukuleka at 2838 ± 8 BP.

sources.title: Burley, D. V., Barton, A., Dickinson, W. R., Connaughton, S. P. and Taché, K., 'Nukuleka as a Founder Colony for West Polynesian Settlement: New Insights from Recent Excavations', Journal of Pacific Archaeology 1.2 (2010), 128-144
sources.author: Burley, David V.; Barton, Andrew; Dickinson, William R.; Connaughton, Sean P.; Taché, Karine
sources.confirms: Excavations support Nukuleka as first landfall c. 2850-2900 cal BP.

sources.title: Burley, D. V. and Connaughton, S. P., 'First Lapita Settlement and its Chronology in Vava'u, Kingdom of Tonga', Radiocarbon 49.1 (2007), 131-137
sources.author: Burley, David V.; Connaughton, Sean P.
sources.confirms: Dates rapid northward spread within Tonga.

lapita-reaches-tonga-890bce.verification_note: Date is precise; included at the period boundary because it completes the Lapita record begun c. 1350 BCE.
lapita-reaches-tonga-890bce.detail: Nukuleka's date is one of the most precise for any prehistoric colonisation event because coral tools can be dated by U/Th independent of radiocarbon reservoir problems. Decorated Lapita ceramics disappeared rapidly after settlement in Tonga, giving way to plain ware and eventually to no pottery at all in Polynesia. Settlers brought pigs, chickens, dogs and root crops, and cleared forest for gardens, with bird extinctions following within centuries.

picture.alt: Eastern arm of Fanga'uta Lagoon on Tongatapu, Tonga, where the earliest Lapita sites lie.

lapita-reaches-tonga-890bce.dating_note: U/Th date 2838 ± 8 BP (c. 888 BCE) on coral tools; radiocarbon concordant. Falls just after 1000 BCE but is included as the end point of Lapita dispersal in this period.

greek-alphabet-vowels-800bce.summary: Greeks borrowed Phoenician consonant letters and repurposed several for vowels, producing a script in which every sound of speech had a sign. Janko's study of inscriptions from Gabii, Gordion, Eretria and Methone finds that some of our earliest alphabetic Greek texts come from Latium and Phrygia, which he reads as evidence for an eighth-century spread along trade routes. Powell argued in 1991 that one adapter devised the alphabet to record Homeric verse. Waal's 2018 article makes a case for transmission by the eleventh century BCE at latest, against the prevailing eighth-century date, so dating remains debated.

sources.title: Janko, Richard, 'From Gabii and Gordion to Eretria and Methone: the rise of the Greek alphabet', Bulletin of the Institute of Classical Studies 58 (2015)
sources.author: Janko, Richard
sources.venue: Bulletin of the Institute of Classical Studies
sources.confirms: Earliest alphabetic inscriptions seem to come from Gabii and Gordion; Methone inscriptions in Eretrian script; three phases of adaptation

sources.title: Powell, Barry B., Homer and the Origin of the Greek Alphabet (Cambridge University Press, 1991)
sources.author: Powell, Barry B.
sources.confirms: Thesis that alphabet was adapted to record Homeric poetry

sources.title: Waal, Willemijn, 'On the "Phoenician Letters": The Case for an Early Transmission of the Greek Alphabet from an Archaeological, Epigraphic, and Linguistic Perspective', Aegean Studies 1 (2018)
sources.author: Waal, Willemijn
sources.confirms: Argues for transmission by the 11th century BCE at latest against the 8th-century consensus

greek-alphabet-vowels-800bce.detail: Earliest Greek inscriptions, such as the Dipylon jug and Nestor's cup, date to about 740 to 720 BCE on pottery typology. Waal argues that perishable writing surfaces could hide centuries of earlier use. Janko sees three phases of adaptation and treats Methone finds in Eretrian script as evidence of Euboean traders. Vowel letters alpha, epsilon, iota, omicron and upsilon came from Phoenician consonants with no Greek equivalent.

picture.alt: The Dipylon inscription scratched on an eighth-century BCE oinochoe, National Archaeological Museum Athens

greek-alphabet-vowels-800bce.dating_note: Most scholars date adoption to the eighth century BCE; Waal 2018 argues for the eleventh century or earlier.

hallstatt-iron-working-800bce.summary: From about 800 BCE, communities of west-central Europe grouped by archaeologists under Hallstatt C began forging long iron swords, iron horse bits and wagon fittings, with salt mining at Hallstatt in Austria funding a rich grave culture. A dendrochronological date of 778 plus or minus 5 BCE for a wagon grave at Wehringen in Bavaria anchors this phase and agrees with radiocarbon results. Iron came into general use across the Alps and Danube basin during Hallstatt C and D, between about 800 and 450 BCE, before La Tene styles took over. Britannica dates Hallstatt's later phase to about 800/700 to 450 BCE.

sources.title: Friedrich, Michael; Hennig, Hermann, 'A dendrodate for the Wehringen Iron Age wagon grave (778 ± 5 BC) in relation to other recently obtained absolute dates for the Hallstatt period in southern Germany', Journal of European Archaeology 4 (1996)
sources.author: Friedrich, Michael; Hennig, Hermann
sources.confirms: Dendrodate 778 plus or minus 5 BCE for Wehringen wagon grave anchors Hallstatt C

sources.title: Arnold, Bettina, 'West-Central European Early Iron Age', in Encyclopedia of Prehistory vol. 4 (Springer, 2001)
sources.author: Arnold, Bettina
sources.confirms: Iron Age west-central Europe: hillforts, wagon burials, trade with Mediterranean

sources.title: 'Hallstatt', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Britannica editors
sources.confirms: Hallstatt culture later phase c. 800/700 to 450 BCE; iron in general use; long iron swords; over 2,000 graves

hallstatt-iron-working-800bce.detail: More than 2,000 graves at Hallstatt yielded bronze vessels, amber, glass and iron weapons, while the salt mine preserved wooden tools and textiles. Arnold's encyclopedia entry describes hillforts, wagon burials and long-distance exchange with Mediterranean cities as features of this Early Iron Age. Friedrich and Hennig's tree-ring date from Wehringen settled a long debate about when Hallstatt C began in southern Germany, pushing it a generation earlier than many older typological schemes.

picture.alt: Iron dagger in its scabbard displayed at the Hallstatt Museum, Austria

hallstatt-iron-working-800bce.dating_note: Hallstatt C start was placed c. 750 BCE on typology; the Wehringen tree-ring date of 778 plus or minus 5 BCE moved it earlier.

qanat-iran-700bce.summary: Across the Iranian plateau, diggers sank lines of vertical shafts and linked them with a tunnel sloping gently from an aquifer at a hill's foot to fields many kilometres away, delivering water by gravity with little evaporation. Lightfoot's 2000 article in Geographical Journal concludes that qanats originated in Persia and spread into Arabia first by Persians during Achaemenid rule. Laessoe's 1951 study of Sargon II's 714 BCE campaign account describes an irrigation system at Ulhu in Urartu that some read as an early qanat. Magee's work on Iron Age Iran provides chronological background. Qanats later spread from Morocco to Xinjiang.

sources.title: Magee, Peter, 'The Chronology and Environmental Background of Iron Age Settlement in Southeastern Iran and the Question of the Origin of the Qanat Irrigation System', Iranica Antiqua 40 (2005)
sources.author: Magee, Peter
sources.confirms: Iron Age Iran chronology and environment

sources.title: Lightfoot, Dale R., 'The Origin and Diffusion of Qanats in Arabia: New Evidence from the Northern and Southern Peninsula', Geographical Journal 166 (2000)
sources.author: Lightfoot, Dale R.
sources.confirms: Qanats originated in Persia and spread to Arabia first by Persians

sources.title: Laessøe, Jørgen, 'The Irrigation System at Ulhu, 8th Century B.C.', Journal of Cuneiform Studies 5 (1951)
sources.author: Laessøe, Jørgen
sources.confirms: Irrigation system at Ulhu in Sargon's 714 BCE account

qanat-iran-700bce.verification_note: Lightfoot and Magee support these claims; Laessoe (1951) is cited as supporting literature.
qanat-iran-700bce.detail: A qanat begins with a mother well sunk to test water depth, followed by shafts every 20 to 50 metres for spoil removal and ventilation. Gradient must stay below about 1 in 500 to avoid erosion. Lightfoot's survey of Arabian qanats found Persian and later Islamic introductions. Whether Ulhu's channels were true qanats is debated, so 700 BCE is approximate, and the Persian-origin thesis is one of several.

picture.alt: Line of vertical access shafts of a qanat crossing the Iranian desert

qanat-iran-700bce.dating_note: Lightfoot argues a Persian origin; Laessoe reads Sargon's 714 BCE Ulhu account as an early qanat; Urartian or Arabian origins are also proposed.

siloam-tunnel-jerusalem-700bce.summary: Workers dug a winding tunnel 533 metres long through bedrock beneath Jerusalem's City of David, carrying water from Gihon spring to a pool inside fortifications, with two teams meeting mid-rock as a Hebrew inscription found in 1880 records. Radiocarbon and uranium-thorium dates on plaster and stalactites give an Iron Age II date consistent with Hezekiah around 700 BCE. Ronny Reich and Eli Shukron argue that archaeological context shows 'the tunnel predates Hezekiah's reign', while Amihai Sneh, Ram Weinberger and Eyal Shalev propose Manasseh in early seventh century, estimating at least four years of cutting.

sources.confirms: Radiocarbon and U-Th dating give Iron Age II date for Siloam Tunnel

sources.title: Reich, Ronny; Shukron, Eli, 'The Date of the Siloam Tunnel Reconsidered', Tel Aviv 38 (2011)
sources.author: Reich, Ronny; Shukron, Eli
sources.confirms: Tunnel predates Hezekiah's reign; completion at least early 8th century BCE

sources.title: Sneh, Amihai; Weinberger, Ram; Shalev, Eyal, 'The Why, How, and When of the Siloam Tunnel Reevaluated', Bulletin of the American Schools of Oriental Research 359 (2010)
sources.author: Sneh, Amihai; Weinberger, Ram; Shalev, Eyal
sources.venue: Bulletin of the American Schools of Oriental Research
sources.confirms: At least four years to cut; not a siege response; Manasseh early 7th century BCE

sources.title: Shimron, Aryeh E.; Frumkin, Amos, 'The Why, How, and When of the Siloam Tunnel Reevaluated: A Reply to Sneh, Weinberger, and Shalev', BASOR 364 (2011)
sources.author: Shimron, Aryeh E.; Frumkin, Amos
sources.venue: Bulletin of the American Schools of Oriental Research
sources.confirms: Reply rejecting karstic-route model

siloam-tunnel-jerusalem-700bce.detail: Biblical texts credit Hezekiah with bringing water into Jerusalem before Sennacherib's 701 BCE siege. Sneh, Weinberger and Shalev argue that a karst conduit guided diggers and that four years' work rules out a siege response; Shimron and Frumkin reply that no groundwater route existed. Reich and Shukron place completion by early eighth century BCE on pottery from a related pool. Dating thus spans about 800 to 680 BCE.

picture.alt: Inside the Siloam tunnel beneath the City of David, Jerusalem

siloam-tunnel-jerusalem-700bce.dating_note: Frumkin 2003 supports c. 700 BCE; Reich and Shukron 2011 date it before Hezekiah (early 8th century); Sneh et al. 2010 propose Manasseh, early 7th century.

chinese-spade-knife-money-600bce.summary: During the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, states of the Zhou world cast bronze tokens shaped like farming spades and knives, often inscribed with place names or weights, that circulated as money. Von Glahn's monetary history traces this bronze coinage alongside uncoined metal and cowries, while Scheidel's comparison of Han and Roman systems notes that Chinese bronze coinages were supplemented by uncoined bullion before Qin unification standardized currency in the third century BCE. Spade money from Jin and Zhou and knife money from Qi and Yan were replaced by round coins with square holes.

sources.title: von Glahn, Richard, Fountain of Fortune: Money and Monetary Policy in China, 1000-1700 (University of California Press, 1996), ch. 1
sources.author: von Glahn, Richard
sources.confirms: Monetary history of China including early bronze coinage

sources.title: Scheidel, Walter, 'The Monetary Systems of the Han and Roman Empires', in Rome and China (Oxford University Press, 2009)
sources.author: Scheidel, Walter
sources.confirms: China: bronze coinages supplemented by uncoined bullion; unification from 3rd century BCE standardizes currency

chinese-spade-knife-money-600bce.verification_note: Scheidel confirms bronze coinages alongside bullion before third-century BCE unification; von Glahn is cited as supporting literature, and a sixth-century BCE date for spade and knife money rests on general scholarship.
chinese-spade-knife-money-600bce.detail: Hoards and tomb finds date spade coins to the sixth century BCE or earlier, though scholars dispute whether early hollow-handled spades were tools, ritual objects or money. Inscriptions name cities such as Anyi and Jinyang. Von Glahn's Fountain of Fortune, available on Internet Archive, treats early coinage as background to later Chinese monetary policy. Qin's round banliang coin set a pattern for two millennia.

picture.alt: Eastern Zhou bronze spade coins, China

chinese-spade-knife-money-600bce.dating_note: Sixth-century BCE start rests on hoard typology; whether early hollow-handled spades were money is debated.

lydian-electrum-coinage-600bce.summary: In western Anatolia, Lydian kings or their mints began striking lumps of electrum, a natural gold and silver alloy washed from Pactolus river sands, into stamped pieces of standard weight. Konuk's survey in the Oxford Handbook of Greek and Roman Coinage places earliest coins probably at Sardis in mid seventh century BCE, with Ionian Greek cities adopting them soon after. A foundation deposit at Ephesus's Artemision containing 93 coins, including a hoard of 19 electrum pieces in a jug, shows coins in use by about 630 to 620 BCE. Kroll traces Lydia's weighed bullion economy before coinage.

sources.title: Kroll, John H., 'The Monetary Background of Early Coinage', in The Oxford Handbook of Greek and Roman Coinage (Oxford University Press, 2012)
sources.author: Kroll, John H.
sources.confirms: Electrum native to Lydia, extracted from the Pactolus by the 7th century BCE; weighed bullion preceded coinage

sources.title: Konuk, Koray, 'Asia Minor to the Ionian Revolt', in The Oxford Handbook of Greek and Roman Coinage (Oxford University Press, 2012)
sources.author: Konuk, Koray
sources.confirms: Earliest coins probably minted at Sardis c. mid-7th century BCE; Artemision deposit of 93 coins, 19 electrum in an olpe, in use c. 630/620 BCE

lydian-electrum-coinage-600bce.detail: Electrum coins carried a lion's head or other badges punched in relief on one face and incuse marks on another. Croesus, king from about 560 BCE, is credited with separate gold and silver issues. Kroll argues that weighed silver had circulated as money in Mesopotamia and the Levant for centuries, so coinage added state guarantee rather than inventing money. Dating depends on Artemision stratigraphy and comparison with Greek pottery.

picture.alt: Lydian electrum trite with lion head and incuse punch, about 600 to 530 BCE, British Museum

lydian-electrum-coinage-600bce.dating_note: Earliest coinage placed c. 650 to 620 BCE on Artemision deposit evidence; older schemes said c. 600 BCE.

zapotec-script-san-jose-mogote-600bce.summary: A carved stone slab at San Jose Mogote in Oaxaca shows a slain captive with a glyph between his feet read as a calendrical name, 1 Earthquake. Flannery and Marcus argued in PNAS in 2003 that charcoal from a layer sealing Monument 3 dates to 2580 and 2510 radiocarbon years BP, giving a terminus ante quem around 600 BCE and making it a candidate for Mesoamerica's earliest writing. Cahn and Winter had argued in 1993 that the monument belongs to Monte Alban II, several centuries later. Justeson surveys early Mesoamerican writing systems in the Oxford Handbook of Mesoamerican Archaeology.

sources.title: Flannery, Kent V.; Marcus, Joyce, 'The origin of war: New 14C dates from ancient Mexico', PNAS 100 (2003)
sources.author: Flannery, Kent V.; Marcus, Joyce
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Charcoal above Monument 3 dated 2580 plus or minus 40 and 2510 plus or minus 40 BP as terminus ante quem

sources.title: Justeson, John, 'Early Mesoamerican Writing Systems', in The Oxford Handbook of Mesoamerican Archaeology (Oxford University Press, 2012)
sources.author: Justeson, John
sources.confirms: Survey of early Mesoamerican writing systems

sources.title: Cahn, Robert; Winter, Marcus, 'The San José Mogote Danzante', Indiana 13 (1993)
sources.author: Cahn, Robert; Winter, Marcus
sources.confirms: Argues Monument 3 dates to Monte Alban II

zapotec-script-san-jose-mogote-600bce.detail: Monument 3 was set as a threshold stone in a corridor between two public buildings, so visitors stepped on its carved captive. Flannery and Marcus counter Cahn and Winter by citing stratigraphy they say rules out a later date. Zapotec script went on to appear on hundreds of Danzante slabs at Monte Alban after 500 BCE. A 600 BCE date is approximate and disputed.

picture.alt: Monument 3 at San José Mogote, Oaxaca, carved stone with an early Zapotec glyph

zapotec-script-san-jose-mogote-600bce.dating_note: Flannery and Marcus date Monument 3 before c. 600 BCE by charcoal above it; Cahn and Winter assign it to Monte Alban II, after c. 100 BCE.

thales-miletus-585bce.summary: Herodotus reports that Thales of Miletus foretold to Ionians a loss of daylight that fell during a battle between Lydians and Medes, fixing it within a year; modern astronomers identify this eclipse with 28 May 585 BCE. Kahn's Oxford Classical Dictionary entry notes that Aristotle treated Thales as first of those who sought a material principle, naming water as origin of all. Stephenson and Fatoohi examined in 1997 whether any Babylonian method available to Thales could have produced such a prediction. Whatever his method, later Greeks counted him among seven sages and credited him with geometry learned in Egypt.

sources.title: Stephenson, F. Richard; Fatoohi, Louay J., 'Thales's Prediction of a Solar Eclipse', Journal for the History of Astronomy 28 (1997)
sources.author: Stephenson, F. Richard; Fatoohi, Louay J.
sources.venue: Journal for the History of Astronomy
sources.confirms: Study of Thales's eclipse prediction in Journal for the History of Astronomy 1997
sources.qualifies: Metadata only; argument known from abstract tradition

sources.title: Kahn, Charles H., 'Thales of Miletus', Oxford Classical Dictionary (2016)
sources.author: Kahn, Charles H.
sources.confirms: Eclipse attributed to Thales dated by moderns to 585 BCE; water as first principle; Aristotle's first natural philosopher

sources.title: Herodotus, Histories 1.74 (Godley translation), Perseus Digital Library
sources.author: Herodotus
sources.confirms: Thales foretold loss of daylight to Ionians within the year

thales-miletus-585bce.detail: No writings by Thales survive, so claims rest on Herodotus, Aristotle and later doxographers. Stephenson and Fatoohi doubt that saros-type cycles known in his day could predict visibility at a given place. Kahn summarizes traditions crediting Thales with measuring pyramids by shadow and with explaining earthquakes by a floating earth. This person record marks Ionian inquiry into nature as a distinct practice.

picture.alt: Roman marble head identified as Thales of Miletus, second century CE

thales-miletus-585bce.dating_note: Identification of Herodotus' eclipse with 585 BCE is conventional; Stephenson and Fatoohi question whether Thales could have predicted it.

eupalinos-tunnel-samos-540bce.summary: Herodotus lists among Samian wonders a tunnel through a mountain 150 fathoms high, seven furlongs long, with a channel carrying water to the city, designed by Eupalinos of Megara. Rediscovered in 1882 and cleared in the twentieth century, it runs about 1,036 metres and was dug from both ends, meeting with a small offset. Olson's 2012 article in Anatolia Antiqua offers an empirical account of how Eupalinos navigated with surveying around a hill, using a deliberate zigzag near the meeting point to guarantee intersection. Built under tyrant Polycrates around 550 to 530 BCE, it carried water for over a thousand years.

sources.title: Herodotus, Histories 3.60 (Macaulay translation), ToposText
sources.author: Herodotus
sources.confirms: Tunnel through mountain, seven furlongs, water channel, Eupalinos of Megara

sources.title: Olson, Åke, 'How Eupalinos navigated his way through the mountain: An empirical approach to the geometry of Eupalinos', Anatolia Antiqua 20 (2012)
sources.author: Olson, Åke
sources.confirms: Empirical reconstruction of Eupalinos's surveying geometry

eupalinos-tunnel-samos-540bce.detail: Surveyors probably set out a line over the mountain and transferred it to both portals, then kept direction with sightings on lamps. Where diggers met, a dogleg shows how they corrected. A separate water channel beneath the walking tunnel's floor carried terracotta pipes. Hero of Alexandria later described such a surveying method. Date is approximate within Polycrates's reign, and some scholars place construction a decade or two before he seized power.

picture.alt: Interior of the Tunnel of Eupalinos on Samos

eupalinos-tunnel-samos-540bce.dating_note: Construction is placed in Polycrates's reign, c. 550 to 522 BCE; some scholars date it earlier.

pythagoras-croton-530bce.summary: Around 530 BCE Pythagoras of Samos settled at Croton in southern Italy and gathered followers who treated number as a key to music, cosmos and conduct. Huffman's Stanford Encyclopedia entry sifts early testimony from Porphyry, Dicaearchus and Aristotle, concluding that Pythagoras was known in his lifetime for teaching about the soul's fate and a way of life rather than for proofs. Zhmud's 2012 monograph and Burkert's 1972 study disagree over how much mathematics early Pythagoreans did. Later tradition credited this group with discovering that musical intervals correspond to simple ratios of string lengths.

sources.title: Zhmud, Leonid, Pythagoras and the Early Pythagoreans (Oxford University Press, 2012)
sources.author: Zhmud, Leonid
sources.confirms: Monograph on Pythagoras and early Pythagoreans defending early mathematics

sources.title: Huffman, Carl, 'Pythagoras', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.author: Huffman, Carl
sources.confirms: Early testimony on Pythagoras; Porphyry cites Dicaearchus and Nicomachus; teaching on soul and way of life

sources.title: Burkert, Walter, Lore and Science in Ancient Pythagoreanism (Harvard University Press, 1972)
sources.author: Burkert, Walter
sources.confirms: Argues Pythagoras was a religious figure whose mathematical fame grew later

pythagoras-croton-530bce.verification_note: Huffman's full entry confirms chronology and sources; Zhmud was seen only as DOI metadata; Burkert's book was seen as an Internet Archive item page.
pythagoras-croton-530bce.detail: Burkert argued that Pythagoras was a religious leader whose mathematical reputation grew in Plato's Academy. Zhmud defends an early scientific Pythagoreanism including number theory and harmonics. Huffman notes that Porphyry quotes reliable sources, including Dicaearchus, for Pythagoras's arrival at Croton. Whatever his own contributions, this community made ratio and proportion central to Greek mathematics, shaped Plato's cosmology in Timaeus and gave Euclid's number theory much of its material.

picture.alt: Roman bust identified as Pythagoras, Capitoline Museums, Rome

pythagoras-croton-530bce.dating_note: Pythagoras's arrival at Croton is placed c. 530 BCE from later chronographers; scholars dispute how much mathematics he practised.

adena-earthworks-500bce.summary: From about 500 BCE, people of the Ohio, Kentucky and West Virginia river valleys built conical burial mounds, some over 20 metres high such as Grave Creek Mound, and circular ditched enclosures used for gatherings. Dragoo's 1963 Mounds for the Dead analysed Adena culture from excavations at Cresap Mound. Clay's 1998 article in Southeastern Archaeology identifies ritual features shared across Adena sites, including paired post circles and log tombs, and argues mounds served dispersed communities as meeting points. Grave goods include copper bracelets, mica, tubular pipes and engraved tablets. This culture record spans roughly 500 BCE to 100 CE.

sources.title: Clay, R. Berle, 'The Essential Features of Adena Ritual and Their Implications', Southeastern Archaeology 17 (1998)
sources.author: Clay, R. Berle
sources.confirms: Essential features of Adena ritual

sources.title: Dragoo, Don W., 'Mounds for the Dead: An Analysis of the Adena Culture', Annals of the Carnegie Museum 37 (1963)
sources.author: Dragoo, Don W.
sources.confirms: Analysis of Adena culture from mound excavations

adena-earthworks-500bce.verification_note: Clay's article and Dragoo's monograph are cited as supporting literature; dating rests on general scholarship.
adena-earthworks-500bce.detail: Adena people were hunter-gatherers who also grew squash, sunflower and goosefoot. Mounds accumulated through repeated burials and cappings over generations. Copper came from Lake Superior and marine shell from the Gulf, evidence of long exchange. Dating rests on radiocarbon from mound layers. Hopewell traditions grew from Adena bases after about 100 BCE, adding geometric enclosures and wider exchange. Adena's name comes from an estate near Chillicothe where a mound was excavated in 1901.

picture.alt: Grave Creek Mound, an Adena burial mound at Moundsville, West Virginia

aramaic-alphabet-achaemenid-500bce.summary: Persian kings ruling from Egypt to the Indus used Aramaic, written in a 22-letter alphabet derived from Phoenician, as a shared language of administration. Folmer's chapter in The Semitic Languages treats Imperial Aramaic as Achaemenid administration's language, with letters, legal deeds and accounts surviving on papyrus and leather from Elephantine in Egypt to Bactria. Gzella's cultural history traces Aramaic from its beginnings to Islam. Its script later gave rise to Hebrew square script, Nabataean, Syriac and, in India, Kharosthi.

sources.title: Folmer, Margaretha, 'Imperial Aramaic as an Administrative Language of the Achaemenid Period', in The Semitic Languages: An International Handbook (De Gruyter, 2011)
sources.author: Folmer, Margaretha
sources.confirms: Imperial Aramaic as administrative language of the Achaemenid period

sources.title: Gzella, Holger, A Cultural History of Aramaic: From the Beginnings to the Advent of Islam (Brill, 2015)
sources.author: Gzella, Holger
sources.confirms: Cultural history of Aramaic from beginnings to Islam

aramaic-alphabet-achaemenid-500bce.verification_note: Folmer's chapter confirms Aramaic's chancery role; Gzella is cited as supporting literature, and neither work fixes a specific date.
aramaic-alphabet-achaemenid-500bce.detail: Aramaic had spread under the Assyrian and Babylonian empires before Cyrus and Darius made it a chancery standard around 500 BCE. Scribes used reed pens and ink on papyrus or leather, and a cursive hand developed. Standardized spelling across far-flung provinces let officials in Persepolis read letters from Egypt. Date here is approximate, marking Achaemenid consolidation rather than a single decree.

picture.alt: Fifth-century BCE Aramaic papyrus from Elephantine narrating the story of Ahiqar, Neues Museum Berlin

banana-cameroon-500bce.summary: Mbida, Van Neer, Doutrelepont and Vrydaghs reported in Journal of Archaeological Science in 2000 banana phytoliths and animal bones from pits at Nkang in southern Cameroon dated to the first millennium BCE, evidence that a crop domesticated in New Guinea had crossed the Indian Ocean and reached central Africa's forest early. Vansina replied in Azania in 2003 under the title 'Bananas in Cameroun c. 500 BCE? Not proven', questioning phytolith identification and context. Neumann and Hildebrand's 2009 review of early bananas in Africa weighs this and other claims. Bananas later became a staple across Africa's forest and Great Lakes.

sources.title: Mbida, Christophe M.; Van Neer, Wim; Doutrelepont, Hugues; Vrydaghs, Luc, 'Evidence for Banana Cultivation and Animal Husbandry During the First Millennium BC in the Forest of Southern Cameroon', Journal of Archaeological Science 27 (2000)
sources.author: Mbida, Christophe M.; Van Neer, Wim; Doutrelepont, Hugues; Vrydaghs, Luc
sources.confirms: Evidence for banana cultivation in first millennium BCE southern Cameroon

sources.title: Vansina, Jan, 'Bananas in Cameroun c. 500 BCE? Not proven', Azania 38 (2003)
sources.author: Vansina, Jan
sources.confirms: Bananas in Cameroun c. 500 BCE? Not proven

sources.title: Neumann, Katharina; Hildebrand, Elisabeth, 'Early Bananas in Africa: The state of the art', Ethnobotany Research and Applications 7 (2009) 353-362
sources.author: Neumann, Katharina; Hildebrand, Elisabeth
sources.confirms: Review of early bananas in Africa

banana-cameroon-500bce.verification_note: Mbida's article title states its claim and Vansina's reply title states his objection; Neumann and Hildebrand review both.
banana-cameroon-500bce.detail: Phytoliths are silica bodies that survive in soil after plants decay; Musa phytoliths can be confused with those of wild Ensete, which is Vansina's main objection. If accepted, Nkang implies maritime contact between Southeast Asia and Africa a millennium before Austronesian settlement of Madagascar. Most researchers now treat Nkang as possible but unconfirmed.
banana-cameroon-500bce.dating_note: Mbida et al. 2000 claim first-millennium BCE bananas; Vansina 2003 calls this not proven; Neumann and Hildebrand 2009 treat it as unconfirmed.

chinese-cast-iron-blast-furnace-500bce.summary: By the fifth century BCE, foundries in Zhou states were running furnaces hot enough to tap liquid iron and pour it into moulds for hoes, ploughshares and axes, a practice Craddock's 2015 review in Antiquity and Wagner's 1993 Brill monograph trace through excavated artefacts. Cast iron is brittle, so Chinese smiths also annealed castings into malleable iron and later decarburized them toward steel. Wagner describes a two-tier industry attested in third-century BCE sources, with large state-run furnaces producing tools at scale. Europe did not cast iron routinely until the late medieval period, over 1,500 years later.

sources.title: Wagner, Donald B., Iron and Steel in Ancient China (Brill, 1993), ch. 'The Earliest Evidence of the Use of Iron in China'
sources.author: Wagner, Donald B.
sources.confirms: Monograph on iron and steel in ancient China with metallographic examinations

sources.title: Craddock, Paul, 'Iron and steel in ancient China: origins and technical change', Antiquity 68 (1994)
sources.author: Craddock, Paul
sources.confirms: Review of origins and technical change in Chinese iron and steel
sources.qualifies: Fetched page shows references, no abstract

sources.title: Wagner, Donald B., 'Brass tacks on iron: Ferrous metallurgy in Science and Civilisation in China', Cultures of Science 3 (2020)
sources.author: Wagner, Donald B.
sources.confirms: Han cast-iron ploughshare; two-tier iron industry in 3rd-century BCE sources; blast furnace scale economies

chinese-cast-iron-blast-furnace-500bce.verification_note: Wagner's work discusses third-century BCE and Han evidence; a fifth-century BCE date rests on Craddock's review.
chinese-cast-iron-blast-furnace-500bce.detail: Craddock reviews metallographic evidence for white cast iron, malleable cast iron and fined steel in Warring States and Han contexts. Wagner's memoir on Science and Civilisation in China volume 5 part 11 notes a Han cast-iron ploughshare and blast furnace economies of scale, though his fetched text gives no fifth-century date. Early castings come from tombs and sites in Jiangsu and Hunan dated by typology and inscriptions. Bellows driven by people, later by water wheels, supplied the air blast.

picture.alt: Cast iron ploughshare of the Warring States period, China

chinese-cast-iron-blast-furnace-500bce.dating_note: Earliest cast iron is dated by tomb context and typology to the sixth to fifth century BCE; exact start is approximate.

dong-son-bronze-drums-500bce.summary: In the Red River valley of northern Vietnam, Dong Son communities cast bronze drums up to a metre across by lost-wax and piece-mould methods, decorating tympana with sunbursts, birds, boats and feathered dancers. From about 500 BCE such drums were carried or copied across mainland and island Southeast Asia. Oliveira, O'Connor and Bellwood reported drums from Timor-Leste in Antiquity in 2019, extending their known range. Calo's 2009 study maps drum distribution as evidence for exchange routes. Higham's Bronze Age of Southeast Asia sets Dong Son within regional metallurgy.

sources.author: Oliveira, Nuno Vasco; O'Connor, Sue; Bellwood, Peter
sources.confirms: Dong Son drums found in Timor-Leste

sources.title: Calò, Ambra, The Distribution of Bronze Drums in Early Southeast Asia: Trade Routes and Cultural Spheres (BAR International Series 1913, 2009)
sources.author: Calò, Ambra
sources.confirms: Distribution of bronze drums and trade routes

sources.title: Higham, Charles, The Bronze Age of Southeast Asia (Cambridge University Press, 1996)
sources.author: Higham, Charles
sources.confirms: Regional Bronze Age survey

dong-son-bronze-drums-500bce.verification_note: Oliveira, Calo and Higham are cited as supporting literature; none states a start date, which rests on general scholarship.
dong-son-bronze-drums-500bce.detail: Drums served as ritual instruments, prestige goods and perhaps rain-calling devices. Heger's typology of 1902 still organizes them. Dating depends on tomb associations at Dong Son and Co Loa and on Chinese records after Han conquest in 111 BCE. Some drums travelled over 2,000 kilometres to eastern Indonesia and New Guinea, showing seaborne exchange networks long before Indian and Chinese traders arrived.

picture.alt: The Ngoc Lu bronze drum of the Dong Son culture, Vietnam National Museum of History

dong-son-bronze-drums-500bce.dating_note: Dong Son drum production is dated c. 600 to 100 BCE by tomb typology; 500 BCE is approximate.

dorset-soapstone-lamps-500bce.summary: Palaeo-Inuit people of Dorset tradition, emerging in eastern Canadian Arctic around 500 BCE, carved shallow rectangular and oval lamps from soapstone, burning seal and whale oil with moss wicks to heat snow houses and cook. Savelle and Dyke's 2009 study of Foxe Basin in American Antiquity traces Dorset origins in a core area of Pre-Dorset occupation. Maxwell's Prehistory of the Eastern Arctic describes Dorset tool kits. Erwin's 2016 systematic study in Arctic examined over 3,600 Palaeo-Inuit soapstone vessel fragments, inferring function from morphology and carbonized residues.

sources.author: Savelle, James M.; Dyke, Arthur S.
sources.confirms: Palaeoeskimo occupation of Foxe Basin and Dorset origins

sources.title: Maxwell, Moreau S., Prehistory of the Eastern Arctic (Academic Press, 1985)
sources.author: Maxwell, Moreau S.
sources.confirms: Survey of eastern Arctic prehistory

sources.title: Erwin, John C., 'A Large-Scale Systematic Study of Palaeoeskimo Soapstone Vessel Fragments from Newfoundland and Labrador', Arctic 69 (2016)
sources.author: Erwin, John C.
sources.confirms: 3,600 soapstone vessel fragments analysed for function

dorset-soapstone-lamps-500bce.verification_note: Savelle and Dyke's page shows title and authors; Maxwell's book is an archive item; Erwin's abstract confirms the vessel study. Dorset date comes from these works as known rather than quoted.
dorset-soapstone-lamps-500bce.detail: Dorset people lacked bows and dogsleds known to earlier and later groups but developed snow knives for building snow houses, where lamps were essential. Soapstone was quarried at known outcrops and traded. Vessel soot and residues record oil burning. This home record marks lamp technology that made winter life on sea ice possible, later refined by Thule Inuit who added larger lamps and pots.

picture.alt: Carved soapstone lamp of a type used by Arctic peoples, shown in a museum in Osaka in 2014; this example is later Inuit work.
picture.credit: Yanajin33, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

dorset-soapstone-lamps-500bce.dating_note: Dorset emergence is dated c. 800 to 500 BCE depending on region.

indian-punch-marked-coins-500bce.summary: Silver pieces struck with several small punches, each bearing symbols such as sun, wheel or animals, appear in northern India around the sixth to fifth century BCE and became standard coinage of Magadha and later of Mauryan rulers. Cribb's 2003 article in South Asian Studies examines where this tradition came from and whether contact with Achaemenid Persia played a role. Kosambi applied statistical weight analysis to hoards in 1940, inferring circulation time from wear. Punch-marked coins weighed around 3.4 grams, following a local karshapana standard rather than Greek or Persian weights.

sources.title: Cribb, Joe, 'The Origins of the Indian Coinage Tradition', South Asian Studies 19 (2003)
sources.author: Cribb, Joe
sources.confirms: Origins of the Indian coinage tradition

sources.title: Kosambi, D. D., 'A Statistical Study of the Weights of Old Indian Punch-Marked Coins', reprinted in D.D. Kosambi: Selected Works in Mathematics and Statistics (Springer, 2016)
sources.author: Kosambi, D. D.
sources.confirms: Statistical study of weights of old Indian punch-marked coins

indian-punch-marked-coins-500bce.verification_note: Cribb's article and Kosambi's 1940 paper are cited as supporting literature; a fifth-century BCE date rests on general scholarship.
indian-punch-marked-coins-500bce.detail: Coins were cut from sheets of silver, adjusted to weight, then stamped with up to five punches whose combinations may identify issuing authorities. Hoards from Taxila and the Ganga valley give relative chronologies, with absolute dates resting on stratigraphy at Northern Black Polished Ware sites. Cribb's study questions early dates and argues for a later start, so a fifth-century date is approximate.

picture.alt: Silver punch-marked karshapana of the Magadha kingdom, about 430 to 320 BCE

indian-punch-marked-coins-500bce.dating_note: Start dates range from the sixth to the fourth century BCE; Cribb argues for a later origin than traditional Indian scholarship.

meroe-iron-smelting-500bce.summary: At Meroe on the Nile in Sudan, Kushite workers smelted iron in bloomery furnaces over roughly a thousand years, leaving slag mounds now dated with 97 radiocarbon determinations. These place production from potentially the seventh century BCE through the sixth century CE, with peaks under Meroitic kings. Furnace bases, tuyeres and charcoal pits show organized production for tools and weapons supplied to a royal capital. Meroe is often described as a major African iron centre, though its slag heaps are smaller than early popular estimates suggested.

sources.title: Humphris, Jane; Scheibner, Thomas, 'A New Radiocarbon Chronology for Ancient Iron Production in the Meroe Region of Sudan', African Archaeological Review 34 (2017)
sources.author: Humphris, Jane; Scheibner, Thomas
sources.confirms: 97 radiocarbon dates give new chronology for iron production at Meroe

sources.title: Humphris, Jane; Bussert, Robert; Alshishani, Fareed; Scheibner, Thomas, 'The ancient iron mines of Meroe', Azania 53 (2018)
sources.author: Humphris, Jane; Bussert, Robert; Alshishani, Fareed; Scheibner, Thomas
sources.confirms: Kushite iron production potentially 7th century BCE to 6th century CE; slag mounds; AMS date AD 419 to 539

meroe-iron-smelting-500bce.detail: Jane Humphris and Thomas Scheibner's dating program sampled slag mounds and furnace deposits across Meroe's Royal City and eastern mounds. One AMS date from slag falls at 419 to 539 CE, and production spans Napatan to post-Meroitic times. Egypt, Assyria and Kush are each proposed as source of Meroe's iron technology. A 500 BCE anchor is approximate within a range beginning possibly in the seventh century BCE.

picture.alt: Pyramids of the royal cemetery at Meroë, Sudan, the Kushite capital known for its iron slag heaps

meroe-iron-smelting-500bce.dating_note: Production start placed potentially in the seventh century BCE; 500 BCE used as approximate anchor.

nok-taruga-iron-smelting-500bce.summary: Nok communities of central Nigeria smelted iron in shaft and bowl furnaces during the first millennium BCE, with Taruga yielding furnaces and slag that Bernard Fagg excavated in the 1960s. A reassessment of those dates places Nok iron within a West African sequence where smelting appears without a preceding bronze stage. Pangwari dates Nok occupation to about 1500 to 500 BCE, with iron arriving at least a century after terracotta figurines began. Nok iron is among Africa's earliest securely dated metallurgy.

sources.title: Fagg Rackham, Angela; Junius, Hannah; et al., 'Early West African Iron Smelting: The Legacy of Taruga in Light of Recent Nok Research', African Archaeological Review 34 (2017)
sources.author: Fagg Rackham, Angela; Junius, Hannah; Breunig, Peter
sources.confirms: Reassessment of early West African iron and Nok dates

sources.author: Franke, Gabriele; Höhn, Alexa; Schmidt, Annika; Ozainne, Sylvain; Breunig, Peter; Neumann, Katharina

nok-taruga-iron-smelting-500bce.detail: Taruga's furnaces produced charcoal dated by Fagg to the mid first millennium BCE. Later radiocarbon programs from Frankfurt place Nok iron smelting between about 800 and 400 BCE, though old-wood effects and plateau problems in the calibration curve make precision hard. Angela Fagg Rackham argues for careful handling of legacy dates. Pangwari's ritual deposits around 800 BCE connect iron with terracotta production.

nok-taruga-iron-smelting-500bce.dating_note: Nok iron dates cluster c. 800 to 400 BCE but calibration plateaus make exact start uncertain.

royal-road-postal-relay-500bce.summary: Herodotus describes a road from Sardis to Susa with 111 stations and inns over about 2,700 kilometres, a journey of ninety days on foot, and a courier relay in which riders handed messages to fresh horses and men at each stage so that nothing stopped them, 'neither snow nor rain nor heat nor darkness'. Henry Colburn argues this road network and courier system kept the Achaemenid empire well connected despite its size. GIS modelling of court logistics between Susa and Persepolis followed in 2025.

sources.title: Herodotus, Histories 8.98 and 5.52-54 (Macaulay translation), ToposText
sources.author: Herodotus
sources.confirms: Royal Road stages and courier relay

sources.title: Colburn, Henry P., 'Connectivity and Communication in the Achaemenid Empire', Journal of the Economic and Social History of the Orient 56 (2013)
sources.author: Colburn, Henry P.
sources.venue: Journal of the Economic and Social History of the Orient
sources.confirms: Road network and communication made Achaemenid empire connected

sources.title: Salaris, Davide; et al., '"Royal" road, "royal" needs: a GIS-based approach to Achaemenid court logistics', Antiquity 99 (2025)
sources.author: Salaris, Davide; et al.
sources.confirms: GIS model of court logistics between Susa and Persepolis

royal-road-postal-relay-500bce.detail: Persepolis Fortification tablets record rations issued to travellers carrying sealed authorizations, confirming a state-run system of way stations around 500 BCE. Roads reused Assyrian routes and extended toward Egypt and Bactria. Relay posts influenced later Roman, Mongol and Mamluk systems. Herodotus's phrase about couriers became a motto inscribed on New York's main post office in 1914, long after Persian relays had vanished.

picture.alt: Map of the Achaemenid Empire with the Royal Road from Sardis to Susa (modern map)

urewe-bantu-iron-great-lakes-500bce.summary: Around Lake Victoria, in what is now Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, Kenya and Tanzania, an Early Iron Age tradition marked by Urewe pottery and shaft furnaces appears abruptly in archaeological records. Dates for its onset range from 2,500 years ago or earlier to about 1,500 years ago. Many archaeologists link Urewe to Bantu-speaking farmers whose expansion from Cameroon reached eastern and southern Africa during the last millennium BCE. Koen Bostoen connects that movement to climate shifts that opened forest corridors.

sources.title: Bostoen, Koen; et al., 'Middle to Late Holocene Paleoclimatic Change and the Early Bantu Expansion in the Rain Forests of Western Central Africa', Current Anthropology 56 (2015)
sources.author: Bostoen, Koen; Clist, Bernard; Doumenge, Charles; Grollemund, Rebecca; Hombert, Jean-Marie; Muluwa, Joseph Koni; Maley, Jean
sources.confirms: Bantu expansion and mid to late Holocene climate change

sources.title: de Maret, Pierre, 'Archaeologies of the Bantu Expansion', in The Oxford Handbook of African Archaeology (Oxford University Press, 2013)
sources.author: de Maret, Pierre
sources.confirms: Great Lakes Early Iron Age begins abruptly with shaft furnaces and Urewe ceramics; dating controversial from 2500 BP or earlier to c. 1500 BP

urewe-bantu-iron-great-lakes-500bce.verification_note: De Maret's chapter confirms Urewe's Early Iron Age and its disputed dating; Bostoen 2015 supplies the climate-expansion link.
urewe-bantu-iron-great-lakes-500bce.detail: Urewe furnaces were slag-pit shafts producing bloomery iron for hoes and axes that aided forest clearance. Early radiocarbon dates from Rwanda and Buhaya in Tanzania, some before 500 BCE, have been questioned for old-wood effects and poor context. Bostoen ties Bantu dispersal through the rainforest to a drier phase around 2,500 years ago.

picture.alt: Map of the Urewe culture area around Lake Victoria in East Africa (modern map)

urewe-bantu-iron-great-lakes-500bce.dating_note: De Maret calls Urewe dating controversial, from 2500 BP or earlier to c. 1500 BP; early dates may suffer old-wood effects.

vedanga-jyotisha-calendar-500bce.summary: Vedanga Jyotisha, a short Sanskrit text attributed to Lagadha, lays out a five-year cycle (yuga) of 1,830 days with 62 synodic months and 67 sidereal lunar months, with rules to compute positions of Sun and Moon among 27 nakshatras for scheduling sacrifices. Pingree argued in 1973 that its arithmetic period relations derive from Mesopotamian astronomy of the Achaemenid period, which would place it after about 500 BCE. Plofker's Mathematics in India discusses Vedic-period calendrical computation. Its solstice reference, with winter solstice at a Dhanishtha star, has been used to argue for dates from 1400 to 400 BCE.

sources.title: Pingree, David, 'The Mesopotamian Origin of Early Indian Mathematical Astronomy', Journal for the History of Astronomy 4 (1973)
sources.author: Pingree, David
sources.venue: Journal for the History of Astronomy
sources.confirms: Mesopotamian origin of early Indian mathematical astronomy

sources.title: Plofker, Kim, Mathematics in India (Princeton University Press, 2009), ch. 2
sources.author: Plofker, Kim
sources.confirms: Mathematical thought in Vedic India

vedanga-jyotisha-calendar-500bce.verification_note: Pingree's article and Plofker's chapter on Vedic mathematics are cited as supporting literature; dates rest on those works as generally known.
vedanga-jyotisha-calendar-500bce.detail: Two recensions survive, one attached to Rigveda and one to Yajurveda, totalling under fifty verses. Rules use ratios and a water clock for time units. Dating from precession of its solstice position suggests 1400 to 1200 BCE, but Pingree and others treat that as inherited data and date composition to the mid first millennium BCE. A date of 500 BCE is approximate, within a range scholars still debate.
vedanga-jyotisha-calendar-500bce.dating_note: Internal solstice data suggest c. 1400 to 1200 BCE; Pingree dates composition to c. 500 to 400 BCE from Mesopotamian borrowings.

trireme-salamis-480bce.summary: Herodotus reports that Themistocles persuaded Athenians to spend silver from Laurion mines on 200 ships rather than distribute it, and that this fleet of triremes, warships with three banks of oars and bronze rams, fought Xerxes's navy in the straits of Salamis in 480 BCE. Morrison, Coates and Rankov's Athenian Trireme, reviewed by Simonsen in 2001, reconstructs these ships and documents the full-scale replica Olympias. Eliav's 2022 study in International Journal of Nautical Archaeology analyses their lightweight construction. A trireme carried about 170 rowers and could reach speeds near nine knots in sprints.

sources.title: Simonsen, Kirsten, review of Morrison, Coates and Rankov, The Athenian Trireme: The History and Reconstruction of an Ancient Greek Warship (2nd ed., Cambridge University Press, 2000), Phoenix 55 (2001)
sources.author: Simonsen, Kirsten
sources.confirms: Review of standard reconstruction study

sources.title: Eliav, Joseph, 'Lightweight Construction of an Athenian Trireme', International Journal of Nautical Archaeology 51 (2022)
sources.author: Eliav, Joseph
sources.confirms: Lightweight construction analysis of an Athenian trireme

sources.title: Herodotus, Histories 7.144 and 8.84-96 (Macaulay translation), ToposText
sources.author: Herodotus
sources.confirms: Themistocles persuades Athenians to build ships from Laurion silver; battle of Salamis
sources.qualifies: Primary source, Macaulay translation 7.144 and 8.84 to 96

trireme-salamis-480bce.detail: Triremes were about 37 metres long, built shell-first with mortise-and-tenon planking and tensioned by a hypozoma cable. They were drawn up on beaches at night and depended on manpower from citizen rowers, which linked naval power with democracy. Olympias trials in 1987 to 1994 tested rowing arrangements. Carthaginian and Roman navies later moved to larger quinqueremes with more rowers per oar, as Marsala's wreck shows.

picture.alt: The reconstructed Athenian trireme Olympias at Palaio Faliro (modern reconstruction)

zeng-hou-yi-bells-433bce.summary: A tomb at Leigudun in Hubei, closed about 433 BCE, held a set of 65 bronze bells hung on a lacquered frame, each cast so that striking its centre and its side produced two notes about a third apart, with inscriptions naming pitches across regional scales. Shen Sinyan's 1987 Scientific American article explains how their almond-shaped cross section produces two distinct fundamentals. Von Falkenhausen's Suspended Music treats Zhou chime-bells as the only Bronze Age instruments still playable and studies Zeng inscriptions. Cook's 2020 article in T'oung Pao reexamines musical theory in this inscriptional corpus.

sources.title: von Falkenhausen, Lothar, Suspended Music: Chime-Bells in the Culture of Bronze Age China (University of California Press, 1993)
sources.author: von Falkenhausen, Lothar
sources.confirms: Zhou chime-bells as only Bronze Age instruments still playable; Zeng inscriptions

sources.title: Shen, Sinyan, 'Acoustics of Ancient Chinese Bells', Scientific American 256 (April 1987)
sources.author: Shen, Sinyan
sources.confirms: Bell chime's acoustical design; two-tone bells

sources.title: Cook, Scott, 'Technology in a New Key: Toward a Reexamination of Musical Theory and Practice in the Zeng Hou Yi Bell Inscriptions', T'oung Pao 106 (2020)
sources.author: Cook, Scott
sources.confirms: Reexamination of musical theory in bell inscriptions

zeng-hou-yi-bells-433bce.detail: Bells weigh from a few kilograms to over 200, spanning five octaves. Inscriptions in gold inlay give over 2,800 characters of pitch names, revealing a twelve-tone system with tonal correspondences between states. Casting such precise two-tone bells required control of alloy, wall thickness and shape. Date rests on an inscription recording a gift from King Hui of Chu in his 56th year.

picture.alt: The bronze chime bells from the tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng, Hubei Provincial Museum

athens-kleroterion-400bce.summary: Aristotle's Constitution of the Athenians, chapters 63 to 66, describes how prospective jurors inserted bronze tickets into columns of slots on allotment machines, after which an official released black and white bronze balls down a tube; each white ball selected a whole row of tickets. Fragments of such kleroteria, stone slabs with rows of slots, were identified by Sterling Dow in 1939 and discussed by Bishop in 1970. They randomized jury selection to resist bribery and were also used for magistrates. Fourth-century BCE evidence is firm; earlier allotment used simpler methods.

sources.title: Dow, Sterling, 'Aristotle, the Kleroteria, and the Courts', Harvard Studies in Classical Philology 50 (1939)
sources.author: Dow, Sterling
sources.confirms: Identification of kleroteria and their relation to Aristotle's account

sources.title: Bishop, J. D., 'The Cleroterium', Journal of Hellenic Studies 90 (1970)
sources.author: Bishop, J. D.
sources.confirms: The Cleroterium

sources.title: Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 63-66 (Kenyon translation), Internet Classics Archive, MIT
sources.author: Aristotle (attributed)
sources.confirms: Jurors' tickets, allotment machines, balls and staves

athens-kleroterion-400bce.detail: Jurors carried tickets bearing name, father's name and deme, with a letter assigning them to a section. Machines stood at court entrances, one per tribe pair. Coloured staves and acorns then routed jurors to courtrooms. Dow identified surviving fragments in the Athenian Agora as kleroteria matching Aristotle's description. This computing record marks a mechanical randomizing device in civic service, centuries before dice-based lotteries were formalized elsewhere.

picture.alt: Marble kleroterion allotment machine fragment, Museum of the Ancient Agora, Athens

athens-kleroterion-400bce.dating_note: Aristotle describes machines in use by the 320s BCE; 400 BCE is an approximate anchor for fourth-century allotment practice.

babylonian-zodiac-mathematical-astronomy.summary: In fifth-century BCE Babylon, scribes divided the ecliptic into twelve equal signs of 30 degrees, creating a coordinate zodiac that Britton's 2010 study in Archive for History of Exact Sciences dates to about 400 BCE as part of developing lunar theories known as Systems A and B. Those systems predicted new moons, eclipses and planetary phenomena with step and zigzag functions on cuneiform tablets, without geometric models. Ossendrijver showed in Science in 2016 that some tablets computed Jupiter's position from an area under a velocity-time graph. Rochberg's Heavenly Writing traces how omen divination gave rise to horoscopes and mathematical astronomy.

sources.title: Britton, John P., 'Studies in Babylonian lunar theory: part III. The introduction of the uniform zodiac', Archive for History of Exact Sciences 64 (2010)
sources.author: Britton, John P.
sources.venue: Archive for History of Exact Sciences
sources.confirms: Third part of study on Babylonian lunar theory; introduction of uniform zodiac

sources.title: Ossendrijver, Mathieu, 'Ancient Babylonian astronomers calculated Jupiter's position from the area under a time-velocity graph', Science 351 (2016)
sources.author: Ossendrijver, Mathieu
sources.confirms: Babylonian astronomers computed Jupiter's position from area under a graph; 360-degree division

sources.title: Rochberg, Francesca, The Heavenly Writing: Divination, Horoscopy, and Astronomy in Mesopotamian Culture (Cambridge University Press, 2004)
sources.author: Rochberg, Francesca
sources.confirms: Divination, horoscopy and astronomy in Mesopotamian culture

babylonian-zodiac-mathematical-astronomy.detail: Astronomical diaries recorded observations from the eighth century BCE onward, supplying data for period relations. Zodiacal signs enabled horoscopes, earliest dated 410 BCE. Greek astronomers, including Hipparchus, adopted Babylonian parameters and sexagesimal degrees. Britton's three-part study reconstructs how empirical elements were separated to isolate lunar and solar anomaly. Its zodiac and arithmetic methods remain in use in astronomy and astrology today.

picture.alt: Babylonian astronomical diary tablet for 331 to 330 BCE recording the Battle of Gaugamela, British Museum BM 36761

babylonian-zodiac-mathematical-astronomy.dating_note: Zodiac introduction is dated c. 450 to 400 BCE from dated tablets; Britton places it with early lunar theory development.

chinese-crossbow-trigger-400bce.summary: Warring States armies adopted crossbows whose bronze trigger assemblies, cast in several interlocking parts within a housing, released a heavy draw with a light pull and could be mass-produced to fit standard stocks. Triggers from Qin's Terracotta Army show tight dimensional consistency that points to organized workshop production. Texts supply further evidence for these mechanisms. Crossbows gave infantry a weapon against cavalry centuries before Europe adopted them widely.

sources.title: Li, Xiuzhen; Bevan, Andrew; Martinón-Torres, Marcos; et al., 'Crossbows and imperial craft organisation: the bronze triggers of China's Terracotta Army', Antiquity 88 (2014)

sources.confirms: Bronze triggers of Terracotta Army and imperial craft organisation

chinese-crossbow-trigger-400bce.detail: Triggers from the Terracotta Army, buried around 210 BCE, show casting flashes and tool marks indicating batch production with final fitting. Earlier triggers come from fourth-century BCE tombs in Chu and other states. Chinese writers credited Chu inventors; mechanisms featured a nut, a sear and a lever pinned in a bronze box. Europe's medieval crossbows used simpler rotating nuts without such multi-part housings.

picture.alt: Bronze crossbow trigger mechanism of the Warring States period, China

chinese-crossbow-trigger-400bce.dating_note: Earliest bronze triggers come from fourth-century BCE tombs; a fifth-century origin is possible.

counting-rods-china-400bce.summary: Chinese calculators laid small bamboo or bone rods on a board in columns to represent digits, alternating vertical and horizontal orientations for successive places, with an empty column for zero. Lam and Ang's Fleeting Footsteps argues that this rod numeral system was a full decimal place-value notation and that arithmetic procedures later found in Hindu-Arabic numerals resemble rod methods. Needham and Wang Ling's volume 3 of Science and Civilisation in China surveys rod arithmetic, including multiplication, division, root extraction and negative numbers shown by red and black rods. Rods were in use by Warring States times, attested by texts and later by finds.

sources.title: Lam Lay Yong; Ang Tian Se, Fleeting Footsteps: Tracing the Conception of Arithmetic and Algebra in Ancient China (World Scientific, rev. ed. 2004)
sources.author: Lam Lay Yong; Ang Tian Se
sources.confirms: Rod numerals as decimal place-value system and ancestor of Hindu-Arabic arithmetic

sources.title: Needham, Joseph; Wang Ling, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 3: Mathematics and the Sciences of the Heavens and the Earth (Cambridge University Press, 1959)
sources.author: Needham, Joseph; Wang Ling
sources.confirms: Survey of Chinese mathematics including rod arithmetic

counting-rods-china-400bce.detail: Rods appear in texts such as Laozi's remark that a good reckoner needs no tallies, and excavated bundles date to Han tombs. Rod layouts underlie algorithms in the Nine Chapters and later polynomial methods. Abacus beads replaced rods in late medieval China. Dating of first use is approximate; 400 BCE marks textual attestation rather than invention, and some historians push rod use back to Spring and Autumn times.

picture.alt: Lead counting rods of the Western Han period, China

counting-rods-china-400bce.dating_note: Rods are attested in Warring States texts; earliest excavated rods are Han.

hippocratic-corpus-400bce.summary: Around sixty medical texts attributed to Hippocrates of Cos were composed mostly in the fifth and fourth centuries BCE, forming a corpus in which, as Totelin writes, diseases are considered to have natural causes. Attribution to Hippocrates himself was debated already in antiquity. Treatises such as Airs, Waters and Places, which MIT's Internet Classics Archive dates to about 400 BCE, link health to climate and location, while Epidemics records case histories and On the Sacred Disease denies divine origin for epilepsy. Craik's 2014 survey treats each work's content and context.

sources.title: Craik, Elizabeth M., The 'Hippocratic' Corpus: Content and Context (Routledge, 2014)
sources.author: Craik, Elizabeth M.
sources.confirms: Survey of content and context of each Hippocratic treatise

sources.title: Totelin, Laurence, 'Hippocratic Corpus', Oxford Classical Dictionary (2021)
sources.author: Totelin, Laurence
sources.confirms: Around sixty texts, mostly fifth to fourth century BCE; natural causes of disease; attribution debated since antiquity

sources.title: Hippocrates, On Airs, Waters, and Places (Adams translation), Internet Classics Archive, MIT
sources.author: Hippocratic authors
sources.confirms: Airs, Waters and Places dated c. 400 BCE

hippocratic-corpus-400bce.detail: Authors wrote in Ionic Greek across several generations, so this corpus reflects a tradition rather than one author. Theories of four humours, prognosis and regimen shaped Galen and medieval medicine for two millennia. Craik examines the dating of each treatise and argues some are later than usually thought. Hippocratic oath, though later and varied in form, still names this tradition.

picture.alt: Bust of Hippocrates, Pushkin Museum cast

hippocratic-corpus-400bce.dating_note: Individual treatises span the fifth to the fourth century BCE and some later; 400 BCE is an approximate midpoint.

mohist-canon-optics-logic-400bce.summary: Followers of Mozi compiled terse canons and explanations, probably in the fourth and third centuries BCE, covering definitions, logic, geometry, mechanics and optics. Optical propositions describe shadow formation, an inverted image through a small aperture, reflection in plane and curved mirrors and how image size changes with distance. Fraser's Stanford Encyclopedia entry presents their theory of names, inference and disputation. Schemmel's 2022 study treats theoretical knowledge in these canons as practitioners' knowledge formalized. Zhou's 2021 article reads Mohist use of gnomon shadows as a model for valid reasoning.

sources.title: Schemmel, Matthias, Theoretical Knowledge in the Mohist Canon (Springer, 2022)
sources.author: Schemmel, Matthias
sources.confirms: Theoretical knowledge in Mohist Canon

sources.title: Fraser, Chris, 'Mohist Canons', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.author: Fraser, Chris
sources.confirms: Mohist Canons: logic, names, disputation

sources.author: Zhou, Yunzhi
sources.confirms: Gnomon shadows as metaphor for valid argument in Mohist thought

mohist-canon-optics-logic-400bce.detail: Canons also define point, line and circle, discuss levers and balances, and distinguish kinds of knowledge. Text transmission is corrupt, so readings are debated. Mohism faded after Qin, and these canons were little read until Qing scholars such as Sun Yirang revived them. Under this project's domain rules, a formal treatment of inference and classification counts as an ai precursor, alongside Aristotle's logic.
mohist-canon-optics-logic-400bce.dating_note: Canons are dated to the 4th to 3rd century BCE on linguistic grounds; 400 BCE is approximate.

panini-ashtadhyayi-400bce.summary: Panini, a grammarian from Gandhara whom Britannica places in the sixth to fifth century BCE, composed eight chapters of about 4,000 terse sutras that derive Sanskrit words and sentences from roots and affixes by ordered rules. Cardona's Britannica entry calls his grammar 'generative as well as descriptive'. Kadvany's 2007 article in Journal of Indian Philosophy links Panini's use of markers and recursion to positional notation and formal language theory. Kiparsky's encyclopedia survey explains metarules, rule ordering and a compressed metalanguage. Twentieth-century linguists compared Panini's system to formal grammars used in computer science.

sources.author: Kadvany, John
sources.confirms: Panini's grammar linked to positional notation and recursion

sources.confirms: Survey of Paninian linguistics

panini-ashtadhyayi-400bce.detail: Rules use abbreviations (pratyaharas) formed from fourteen Shiva sutras listing sounds, and apply in a fixed order with later rules overriding earlier ones. Panini's date is inferred from his language and from references in later authors such as Katyayana and Patanjali; estimates range from sixth to fourth century BCE. Panini's grammar is an early formal rule system, and Backus acknowledged him when describing notation for programming languages.

picture.alt: Palm-leaf manuscript of Panini's Ashtadhyayi written in Grantha script, a later copy photographed in 2018.

panini-ashtadhyayi-400bce.dating_note: Panini's date is debated between the sixth and the fourth century BCE; 400 BCE is a conventional approximation.

paracas-textiles-400bce.summary: On Peru's Paracas peninsula, communities wrapped their dead in bundles of up to dozens of textiles, including large mantles embroidered in camelid wool with hundreds of figures of flying shamans, felines and birds in dozens of colours. Unkel, Kromer, Reindel, Wacker and Wagner's 2007 Radiocarbon article presents over a hundred AMS dates placing Paracas and Nasca cultures between about 800 BCE and 650 CE, and Unkel's 2012 Journal of Archaeological Science paper gives a comprehensive numerical chronology. Paul's Paracas Ritual Attire analyses garments as symbols of authority. Necropolis of Wari Kayan, excavated by Tello in 1927, yielded 429 bundles.
