paracas-textiles-400bce.detail: Textiles combined plain weave cotton grounds with stem-stitch embroidery; some mantles exceed 2.5 metres. Dyes came from plants and cochineal. Dry desert conditions preserved them. Dating of Paracas phases places Necropolis bundles around 400 BCE to 200 CE, so 400 BCE is approximate. Textile skill passed to Nasca weavers, who added weft-faced weaving and featherwork, and Paracas mantles remain among the most complex embroideries known from any ancient culture.

picture.alt: Paracas ceremonial mantle with embroidered figures

paracas-textiles-400bce.dating_note: Paracas Necropolis textiles are dated c. 400 BCE to 200 CE within Unkel's 800 BCE to 650 CE Paracas-Nasca chronology.

plato-phaedrus-writing-370bce.summary: In Plato's dialogue Phaedrus, Socrates tells how Egyptian god Theuth offered letters to King Thamus as a remedy for memory, and Thamus replied that writing would produce forgetfulness in learners, who would trust external marks rather than recollect, gaining 'the appearance of wisdom, not true wisdom'. Written words, Socrates adds, cannot answer questions and fall into any hands. Werner's chapter reads this myth as a critique of writing within a written work. Yunis's Cambridge edition dates the dialogue to about 370 BCE. This is often cited as the earliest recorded fear of a communication technology.

sources.title: Plato, Phaedrus 274c-275b (Fowler translation, Loeb), Perseus Digital Library
sources.author: Plato
sources.confirms: Theuth and Thamus; writing produces forgetfulness and appearance of wisdom

sources.title: Werner, Daniel S., 'Theuth, Thamus, and the Critique of Writing', in Myth and Philosophy in Plato's Phaedrus (Cambridge University Press, 2012)
sources.author: Werner, Daniel S.
sources.confirms: Analysis of critique of writing in Phaedrus

sources.title: Yunis, Harvey (ed.), Plato: Phaedrus (Cambridge University Press, 2011)
sources.author: Yunis, Harvey
sources.confirms: Edition of Phaedrus with dating discussion

plato-phaedrus-writing-370bce.detail: Phaedrus 274c to 275b sets this myth near the dialogue's end, after discussion of rhetoric and love. Plato wrote dialogues, so scholars debate whether he condemned writing or only its misuse. Later worries about printing, novels, television and search engines have echoed Thamus's complaint. Under this project's rules this is a fear record attached to communications, and it opens a long series of such anxieties.

picture.alt: Papyrus fragment of Plato's Phaedrus

plato-phaedrus-writing-370bce.dating_note: Composition of Phaedrus is placed c. 370 BCE on stylistic grounds; proposals range from 380 to 360 BCE.

aristotle-lyceum-biology-335bce.summary: Returning to Athens in 335 BCE, Aristotle taught at a gymnasium called the Lyceum, where he and his students collected observations on more than 500 animal kinds. His History of Animals, translated by D'Arcy Thompson in 1910, describes anatomy, reproduction and behaviour of fish, birds, insects and mammals, including dissections of cuttlefish and a day-by-day account of chick embryo development. Lennox's Stanford Encyclopedia entry explains how this work sought causes and classified by shared features. Lynch's 1972 study examines how this Peripatetic school functioned as an educational institution.

sources.title: Lynch, John Patrick, Aristotle's School: A Study of a Greek Educational Institution (University of California Press, 1972), ch. 3
sources.author: Lynch, John Patrick
sources.confirms: Study of Aristotle's school as an educational institution, including its founding

aristotle-lyceum-biology-335bce.detail: Aristotle's biology includes Parts of Animals and Generation of Animals as well as History of Animals. He grouped blooded and bloodless animals, noted that dolphins breathe air and bear live young, and described a shark's placenta-like structure confirmed only in the nineteenth century. Theophrastus continued plant studies after him. Aristotle's framework dominated natural history until early modern naturalists revised it.

picture.alt: Roman marble bust of Aristotle after a Greek bronze by Lysippos, Palazzo Altemps, Rome

aqua-appia-312bce.summary: Frontinus, water commissioner in 97 CE, records that Rome drew on Tiber, wells and springs for 441 years until Appius Claudius Crassus, censor in 312 BCE, brought water into the city by a channel named Aqua Appia, running about 16 kilometres almost wholly underground from springs east of Rome to a distribution point near the Forum Boarium. Evans's Water Distribution in Ancient Rome analyses Frontinus's evidence for how aqueducts were planned and distributed. Hodge's Roman Aqueducts and Water Supply explains gradients, settling tanks and lead pipes. Ten more aqueducts followed over five centuries.

sources.confirms: Aqua Appia built by Appius Claudius, censor 312 BCE, after 441 years of wells and springs

aqua-appia-312bce.detail: Aqua Appia was cut as a covered channel to protect water and to hide it from enemies. Later lines such as Anio Vetus (272 BCE) and Aqua Marcia (144 BCE) ran on arches where valleys required. Frontinus gives discharge figures in quinariae for each line. Roman water engineering relied on gravity flow with gradients of a few metres per kilometre, surveyed with chorobates and groma.

picture.alt: Plan of the Aqua Appia's course into Rome (modern plan)

via-appia-312bce.summary: As censor in 312 BCE, Appius Claudius Caecus had a road built from Rome south across the Pontine marshes to Capua, about 200 kilometres, later paved with fitted basalt blocks and extended to Brundisium. Livy records that in his censorship 'the road and the aqueduct which bear his name' were built. Humm's 1996 article in Melanges de l'Ecole francaise de Rome notes that ancient tradition unanimously credits Appius with this road. Laurence's Roads of Roman Italy examines how roads changed mobility and culture. Roman roads with layered foundations, drainage and milestones became a template for state infrastructure.

via-appia-312bce.verification_note: Humm's article and Livy's text support this entry; Laurence's book is cited as supporting literature.
via-appia-312bce.detail: Early Roman roads were gravelled; paving with polygonal basalt came later in sections. Via Appia served military movement during Samnite wars and later carried trade and officials. Milestones, way stations and bridges followed. Roman engineers built over 80,000 kilometres of paved roads by late antiquity. Appius also built Rome's first aqueduct in that same censorship, recorded here as a separate entry on water supply.

picture.alt: Basalt paving of the Via Appia Antica near Rome

arthashastra-kautilya-300bce.summary: Arthashastra, attributed to Kautilya, minister to Chandragupta Maurya around 300 BCE, treats administration, revenue, law, espionage, war and management of mines, forests and irrigation in fifteen books. Olivelle's 2013 translation argues for a layered composition between the first century BCE and third century CE, while McClish's 2019 history holds that an originally pragmatic text had dharma material added when 'redacted in the late classical period'. Trautmann's 1971 statistical study found several authors. Britannica judges it unlikely that all of this text goes back to Maurya times, though parts may. It documents salaries, weights and a superintendent of mines.

sources.author: Olivelle, Patrick
sources.confirms: Translation with introduction arguing layered composition

arthashastra-kautilya-300bce.verification_note: McClish and Britannica support these readings; Olivelle's introduction is cited for layered composition and Trautmann's study for multiple authorship.
arthashastra-kautilya-300bce.detail: Rediscovered in 1905 by R. Shamasastry from a manuscript in Mysore, Arthashastra has been read as evidence for Mauryan government, though philologists now see it as compiled later from older material. Its chapters on metals describe assaying and coinage. Dating is contested, so 300 BCE is traditional and approximate. Its detailed treatment of a mines superintendent and of assaying makes it a source for ancient metallurgy whatever its date.

arthashastra-kautilya-300bce.dating_note: Tradition dates the text c. 300 BCE; Olivelle, McClish and Trautmann argue for composition and redaction between c. 100 BCE and 300 CE.

brahmi-kharosthi-scripts-300bce.summary: Two scripts recorded Indian languages by the third century BCE: Brahmi, written left to right and later parent of most South and Southeast Asian scripts, and Kharosthi, a right-to-left script derived from Aramaic used in Gandhara. Ashoka's edicts around 250 BCE are their best-dated early monuments. Potsherds from Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka carry Brahmi letters in layers radiocarbon dated to the fourth or even fifth century BCE, pushing Brahmi earlier. Theories of Brahmi's origin run from Semitic borrowing to indigenous invention.

brahmi-kharosthi-scripts-300bce.detail: Kharosthi's descent from Aramaic under Achaemenid rule in Gandhara is widely accepted by epigraphists. On Brahmi they divide: some see adaptation from Aramaic or South Semitic scripts, others an invention under Mauryan state patronage. Coningham's Anuradhapura dates would place Brahmi before the Mauryas; critics question the sherds' contexts. Brahmi letters record vowels with marks attached to consonants, an abugida design copied across Asia from Tibet to Java.

brahmi-kharosthi-scripts-300bce.dating_note: Anuradhapura sherds suggest Brahmi by the fourth century BCE; many epigraphists date secure Brahmi to Ashoka c. 250 BCE.

euclid-elements-300bce.summary: Working in Alexandria around 300 BCE, Euclid compiled thirteen books that derive geometry and number theory from definitions, postulates and common notions. MacTutor's biography notes that this treatise influenced Western mathematics for more than 2,000 years. Book VII Proposition 2 gives a procedure for finding a greatest common measure of two numbers by repeated subtraction, now called Euclid's algorithm and still used in computing. Netz's study of Greek deduction analyses how lettered diagrams and formulaic language made such proofs possible. Elements remained a school text into the twentieth century.

sources.confirms: Study of how Greek mathematical deduction was shaped by diagrams and formulaic language

euclid-elements-300bce.detail: Little is known of Euclid's life; Proclus places him under Ptolemy I. Books I to VI treat plane geometry, VII to IX number theory, X incommensurables, XI to XIII solids. Heath's translation with commentary, hosted by Joyce at Clark University, presents each proposition with diagrams. Netz argues that cognitive practices of diagram and formula, rather than any single genius, shaped Greek mathematical rigor.

picture.alt: Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 29, a fragment of Euclid's Elements Book II, about 100 CE

euclid-elements-300bce.dating_note: Euclid's floruit c. 300 BCE rests on Proclus and his relation to Ptolemy I; no contemporary record exists.

maya-writing-san-bartolo-300bce.summary: Painted glyphs on a plastered block buried inside Las Pinturas pyramid at San Bartolo, Guatemala, are among the earliest Maya writing known. Carbonized wood associated with this text dates to 300 to 200 BCE calibrated, centuries before Classic-period inscriptions. A fragment published in 2022 bears a '7 Deer' day sign dated by radiocarbon to 300 to 200 BCE, earliest datable evidence of a 260-day calendar. Both finds show a mature script in a Preclassic ritual building.

sources.title: Saturno, William A.; Stuart, David; Beltrán, Boris, 'Early Maya Writing at San Bartolo, Guatemala', Science 311 (2006)
sources.author: Saturno, William A.; Stuart, David; Beltrán, Boris
sources.confirms: San Bartolo glyphs; associated carbonized wood dated 200 to 300 BCE calibrated

sources.author: Stuart, David; Hurst, Heather; Beltrán, Boris; Saturno, William
sources.confirms: Fragment 4778 with '7 Deer' day sign radiocarbon dated 300 to 200 BCE; earliest datable 260-day calendar evidence

maya-writing-san-bartolo-300bce.detail: Glyphs were painted in black line on white plaster by skilled hands, then buried under later construction phases, which preserved them and allowed stratigraphic dating. Some signs resemble later Maya logographs, though most cannot yet be read. The 2022 fragment, numbered 4778, carries no Long Count date. San Bartolo murals also depict maize god mythology, suggesting writing served ritual as well as record keeping.

picture.alt: Central section of the west wall mural at San Bartolo, Guatemala (Pinturas Sub-1)

meroitic-script-300bce.summary: In Kush, scribes created a script of 23 signs to write their own language, in two forms: hieroglyphs for monuments and a cursive derived from Egyptian demotic for everyday texts. Rilly and de Voogt's 2012 Cambridge monograph presents its decipherment history and shows it was alphasyllabic, with an inherent vowel and separate vowel signs. Earliest dated inscriptions belong to the second century BCE, with origins placed in the third century. Rilly's encyclopedia entry classifies Meroitic within Northern East Sudanic. Texts can be read aloud but only partly understood.

sources.author: Rilly, Claude; de Voogt, Alex
sources.confirms: Monograph on Meroitic language and writing system

meroitic-script-300bce.detail: Meroitic abandoned Egyptian's hundreds of signs for a compact alphabet with word dividers, unusual for ancient scripts. Francis Llewellyn Griffith worked out sign values in 1909 using Egyptian and Meroitic bilingual royal names on funerary texts. Rilly's comparative work with Nubian and other Sudanic languages has recovered some vocabulary. Earliest texts come from Meroe and from Queen Shanakdakhete's reign, including temple inscriptions at Naqa.

picture.alt: The Hamadab stela with Meroitic cursive inscription, British Museum

meroitic-script-300bce.dating_note: Earliest dated Meroitic texts are second century BCE; origin in the third century is inferred.

sushruta-samhita-surgery-300bce.summary: Sushruta Samhita, a Sanskrit medical compendium whose core Jan Meulenbeld dates to the last centuries BCE with later revision, describes over a hundred surgical instruments, techniques for suturing, removing bladder stones and couching cataracts, and reconstruction of a nose with a cheek or forehead flap. Its instruments include tubular endoscopes, and plastic surgeons count Sushruta as a founder of their field. Students practised incisions on gourds and watermelons. Dating of its layers ranges from 600 BCE to several centuries CE.

sushruta-samhita-surgery-300bce.detail: Meulenbeld argues from manuscript evidence for a core text revised by Nagarjuna in perhaps the third or fourth century CE. Popular claims placing Sushruta at 600 BCE lack firm support. Its nose reconstruction method was reported from India in a 1794 London magazine letter and influenced European plastic surgery through Carpue's operations in 1814.

wootz-crucible-steel-kodumanal-300bce.summary: Smiths in southern India sealed bloomery iron with carbon-rich plant matter inside clay crucibles and fired them until a hypereutectoid steel ingot formed, a process Srinivasan documented at Mel-siruvalur and compared with megalithic and early historic finds from Tamil Nadu such as Kodumanal. Her 1994 and 2007 studies describe ultrahigh-carbon steel made by crucible carburization. Europeans later called this metal wootz, a term Dube traces to a 1794 letter by Helenus Scott and shows to be a mistransliteration of a Sanskrit or Kannada word. Crucible steel became famous as the raw material for watered-pattern blades.

wootz-crucible-steel-kodumanal-300bce.detail: Srinivasan's field survey found crucible fragments with adhering steel at Mel-siruvalur in South Arcot district, and metallographic analysis showed carbon above 1 percent. Dating of the earliest Tamil crucible steel rests on associations with megalithic burials and early historic sites around 300 BCE, so 300 BCE is approximate. Dube's 2014 paper in JOM reconstructs how Scott's spelling 'wootz' entered scientific English through the Royal Society.

wootz-crucible-steel-kodumanal-300bce.dating_note: Kodumanal crucible steel is dated by association with megalithic and early historic layers; absolute dates for the earliest wootz remain approximate.

library-of-alexandria-295bce.summary: Ptolemy I Soter, advised by Demetrius of Phalerum, established at Alexandria a Museum, a shrine to the Muses housing salaried scholars, and a library intended to gather Greek literature and foreign texts in translation. Erskine's 1995 article in Greece and Rome reads these institutions as instruments of Ptolemaic power and Greek cultural identity in Egypt. Fraser's Ptolemaic Alexandria remains the standard account. Bagnall's 2002 essay warns that ancient figures of 400,000 or 700,000 scrolls are implausible and that much of the library's fame is later legend. Scholars there edited Homer, compiled grammar and advanced mathematics and astronomy.

library-of-alexandria-295bce.detail: Foundation is usually placed between 300 and 283 BCE, with growth under Ptolemy II. Librarians included Zenodotus, Apollonius of Rhodes, Eratosthenes and Aristarchus of Samothrace. Decline came with a fire during Caesar's war in 48 BCE and later disturbances; no single destruction is documented. This Museum model of state-funded research later influenced Pergamon, Baghdad's House of Wisdom and modern academies. Bagnall's scepticism concerns scale rather than existence.

library-of-alexandria-295bce.dating_note: Foundation date is not recorded; c. 295 BCE falls within the range 300 to 283 BCE given by most historians.

herophilus-dissection-alexandria-280bce.summary: In Alexandria during the first half of the third century BCE, Herophilus of Chalcedon and his younger contemporary Erasistratus performed systematic dissections of human cadavers, an activity von Staden calls unique in ancient science. Von Staden's Yale Journal of Biology and Medicine article also reports that in all probability they conducted vivisections of condemned criminals supplied by Ptolemaic kings. Herophilus distinguished sensory from motor nerves, described brain ventricles and named the duodenum. Wills's 1999 Lancet article treats this pair as founders of neuroscience. His Oxford Classical Dictionary dates are about 330 to 260 BCE.

herophilus-dissection-alexandria-280bce.detail: Greek religious attitudes toward corpses had prevented human dissection before and after this window; Ptolemaic royal patronage in a new city made it possible. Herophilus also measured pulse with a water clock and wrote on midwifery. His writings are lost and known through Galen and others. Von Staden's 1989 edition collects his fragments. Erasistratus went further in physiology, tracing heart valves and arguing that arteries carried pneuma.

picture.alt: Detail of an early modern woodcut depicting Herophilus and Erasistratus, Wellcome Collection

aristarchus-heliocentric-270bce.summary: Aristarchus, active around 280 to 260 BCE, wrote a surviving treatise On the Sizes and Distances of the Sun and Moon that used eclipse geometry and a half-moon angle to estimate that our Sun lies about 18 to 20 times farther away than our Moon. Archimedes reports in his Sand Reckoner that Aristarchus also hypothesized that fixed stars and Sun remain unmoved while Earth revolves around that Sun in a circle. Heath's 1913 study called him 'the ancient Copernicus'. Berggren and Sidoli edited Greek and Arabic versions of his surviving work in 2007.

aristarchus-heliocentric-270bce.detail: His heliocentric hypothesis survives only in Archimedes' report and a note in Plutarch, and few ancient astronomers adopted it. His measured angle of 87 degrees for the half-moon was far from 89.85, so his distances were too small, but his geometric method was sound. Copernicus knew of Aristarchus through Renaissance scholarship. Dates are approximate and derive from a solstice observation attributed to him.

picture.alt: Page from a tenth-century Greek manuscript of Aristarchus on the sizes and distances of the Sun and Moon

ctesibius-pneumatics-270bce.summary: Ctesibius, a third-century BCE innovator in Alexandria, applied air and water pressure to machines. Vitruvius describes his force pump with bronze cylinders, pistons and valves for raising water, used for fire fighting, and credits him with a water organ and improved water clocks that drove figures and sounded alarms. Irby's encyclopedia entry summarizes him as employing pneumatics and hydraulics to invent and improve devices. Landels's Engineering in the Ancient World reconstructs his mechanisms. His writings are lost, surviving only through Vitruvius, Philo and Hero of Alexandria.

sources.title: Vitruvius, De Architectura 9.8 and 10.7 (Gwilt translation), LacusCurtius
sources.author: Vitruvius
sources.confirms: Machine of Ctesibius raising water by pistons; screws and presses

sources.title: Irby, Georgia L., 'Ktesibios (Ctesibius) of Alexandria', in The Encyclopedia of Ancient History (Wiley, 2023)
sources.author: Irby, Georgia L.
sources.confirms: Third-century BCE innovator using pneumatics and hydraulics; water pumps for fires

sources.title: Landels, J. G., Engineering in the Ancient World (University of California Press, 1978), ch. 3
sources.author: Landels, J. G.
sources.confirms: Survey of ancient engineering including Ctesibius

ctesibius-pneumatics-270bce.detail: Tradition says Ctesibius began as a barber's son who devised a counterweighted mirror and heard air whistle from its tube. His hydraulis used water pressure to steady air supply to organ pipes. His clepsydra with a float and rack drove pointers and automata. Under this project's rules, such programmable water clocks and automata count as early precursors in the ai domain.

picture.alt: Modern reconstruction of the force pump of Ctesibius and Hero, Kotsanas Museum of Ancient Greek Technology (reconstruction)

dujiangyan-irrigation-256bce.summary: Around 256 BCE Li Bing, Qin governor of Shu, directed construction of a levee splitting Min River into inner and outer channels, a spillway to flush sediment and a cut through Mount Yulei, the Baopingkou, that fed irrigation canals across the Chengdu plain. Li and Xu's 2006 paper in Irrigation and Drainage describes its initiation under Li Bing in 256 BCE and analyses its hydraulics with current theory. UNESCO's listing dates it to about 256 BCE. Sima Qian recorded Li Bing's works in a treatise on rivers. It still irrigates over 600,000 hectares.

sources.title: Li, Kerong; Xu, Zhifang, 'Overview of Dujiangyan Irrigation Scheme of ancient China with current theory', Irrigation and Drainage 55 (2006)
sources.author: Li, Kerong; Xu, Zhifang
sources.confirms: Initiated by Li Bing, governor of Shu, in Qin dynasty in 256 BCE

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Mount Qingcheng and the Dujiangyan Irrigation System'
sources.author: UNESCO
sources.confirms: Constructed around 256 BCE under Li Bing

dujiangyan-irrigation-256bce.detail: Workers heated rock with fire and quenched it to crack a channel through Yulei hill. Bamboo cages filled with stones formed weirs that could be rebuilt yearly. The Fish Mouth levee directs about 60 percent of flow to inner channels in dry season and reverses in flood. Dating comes from Shiji and Han sources. Dujiangyan is often cited as an example of engineering with sediment rather than against it.

picture.alt: The Fish Mouth levee dividing the Min River at Dujiangyan, Sichuan

archimedes-screw-syracuse-250bce.summary: Archimedes, working in Syracuse in the mid third century BCE, is credited with a helical pump that lifts water when rotated inside a cylinder, and with war engines used against Rome in 213 to 212 BCE. Polybius describes beams swung over city walls dropping stones and an 'iron hand attached to a chain' that gripped Roman ships by their prows and lifted them. Rorres analysed optimal design of such screws in 2000. Dalley and Oleson argue that a water screw may already have irrigated Sennacherib's gardens at Nineveh in the seventh century BCE, so priority is disputed.

sources.title: Dalley, Stephanie; Oleson, John Peter, 'Sennacherib, Archimedes, and the Water Screw: The Context of Invention in the Ancient World', Technology and Culture 44 (2003)
sources.author: Dalley, Stephanie; Oleson, John Peter
sources.confirms: Argues water screw may have been used at Sennacherib's Nineveh centuries before Archimedes
sources.qualifies: Abstract via Crossref; journal page blocked

sources.title: Rorres, Chris, 'The Turn of the Screw: Optimal Design of an Archimedes Screw', Journal of Hydraulic Engineering 126 (2000)
sources.author: Rorres, Chris
sources.confirms: Engineering analysis of Archimedes screw design

sources.title: Polybius, Histories 8.3-7 (Paton translation, Loeb), LacusCurtius
sources.author: Polybius
sources.confirms: Beams swung over walls and an iron hand on a chain lifting Roman ships at Syracuse

archimedes-screw-syracuse-250bce.detail: Ancient sources credit Archimedes with inventing his screw in Egypt, though Dalley and Oleson read an Assyrian cuneiform text as describing a bronze screw. His mathematical works on spheres, spirals and floating bodies survive; his engines are known only through historians. Polybius, writing within a century, is our best witness to Syracuse's defence. Screws of this type remain in use for irrigation and sewage lifting.

picture.alt: Engraving of an Archimedean screw for raising water, Chambers's Encyclopaedia 1908

archimedes-screw-syracuse-250bce.dating_note: Dalley and Oleson 2003 argue a water screw existed at Nineveh c. 700 BCE; most historians still credit Archimedes.

ashoka-edicts-250bce.summary: Mauryan emperor Ashoka, ruling about 268 to 232 BCE, ordered proclamations inscribed on rock faces and polished sandstone pillars from Afghanistan to Karnataka, in Prakrit written in Brahmi and Kharosthi and, in the northwest, in Greek and Aramaic. They announce his remorse after conquering Kalinga, promote dharma, tolerance between sects, medical care for people and animals, planting of trees and wells along roads, and officers to oversee morals. Hultzsch's 1925 corpus remains the standard edition. Thapar's and Olivelle's studies read them as a ruler's public philosophy and as administrative policy.

sources.title: Hultzsch, E., Inscriptions of Asoka, Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum vol. I (Oxford, 1925), Internet Archive
sources.author: Hultzsch, Eugen
sources.confirms: Standard edition of Ashoka's inscriptions

sources.title: Thapar, Romila, Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (Oxford University Press, 1961; rev. 1997)
sources.author: Thapar, Romila
sources.confirms: Study of Ashoka and Mauryan decline

sources.title: Olivelle, Patrick, Ashoka: Portrait of a Philosopher King (Yale University Press, 2023)
sources.author: Olivelle, Patrick
sources.confirms: Biography of Ashoka as philosopher king

ashoka-edicts-250bce.verification_note: Hultzsch's edition and Thapar's book are cited as supporting literature, and Olivelle's Yale biography is confirmed; content of these edicts is known from those editions.
ashoka-edicts-250bce.detail: Major rock edicts number fourteen, with separate Kalinga edicts and minor rock and pillar edicts. James Prinsep's decipherment of them in 1837 made Brahmi readable. Pillars, some over 12 metres tall with animal capitals, were quarried at Chunar and transported hundreds of kilometres. Edicts mention Hellenistic kings Antiochus, Ptolemy, Antigonus, Magas and Alexander, which anchors their chronology. Edicts served as state communication of policy.

picture.alt: Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts carved on the Girnar rock, Gujarat

djenne-djenno-founded-250bce.summary: On a floodplain of the Middle Niger in Mali, people settled Jenne-jeno around 250 BCE, farming African rice, fishing and working iron, and by the first centuries CE their settlement grew into a dense cluster of mounds covering tens of hectares. Susan and Roderick McIntosh's excavations, reported in Journal of African History in 1981, showed urban growth without evidence of a centralized state or North African stimulus. UNESCO's listing says Djenne has been inhabited since 250 BCE and notes Djenne-Djeno's metal artefacts and slag. Roderick McIntosh's chapter on different cities presents Jenne-jeno as a clustered city with little hierarchy.

sources.title: McIntosh, Susan Keech; McIntosh, Roderick J., 'The Inland Niger Delta before the Empire of Mali: Evidence from Jenne-Jeno', Journal of African History 22 (1981)
sources.author: McIntosh, Susan Keech; McIntosh, Roderick J.
sources.confirms: Inland Niger Delta before Mali empire; evidence from Jenne-jeno

sources.title: McIntosh, Roderick J., 'Different cities: Jenne-jeno and African urbanism', in The Cambridge World History, vol. 3 (Cambridge University Press, 2015)
sources.author: McIntosh, Roderick J.
sources.confirms: African urbanism; clustered cities with little hierarchy

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Old Towns of Djenné'
sources.author: UNESCO
sources.confirms: Djenne inhabited since 250 BCE; Djenne-Djeno metal artefacts and slag

djenne-djenno-founded-250bce.detail: Jenne-jeno's earliest phase shows iron tools, pottery and domesticated rice, with trade in stone and copper arriving from afar. Clustered satellite mounds housed specialists such as smiths and potters. Jenne-jeno declined around 1400 CE as nearby Djenne rose with its famous Great Mosque of mud brick. McIntosh's model of heterarchical urbanism challenged assumptions that African cities began with Islamic trade across Sahara.

picture.alt: Terracotta figure from Jenne-jeno, Mali, 900 to 1400 CE, National Museum of Natural History (later than the founding)

marsala-punic-ship-241bce.summary: A ship found in 1971 off western Sicily near Marsala and excavated under Honor Frost preserved a stern section with shipwrights' letters painted on planks before assembly, mortise-and-tenon joints, lead sheathing below waterline and iron nails fixing frames. Frost proposed it sank after a battle of 10 March 241 BCE that ended the First Punic War. Epigraphy and radiocarbon place it in mid third century BCE. Painted letters show standardized assembly of hulls from prefabricated parts.

sources.title: Armetta, Francesco; Ponterio, Rosina Celeste; Pibiri, Ivana; Saladino, Maria Luisa, 'New Insight on Archaeological Metal Finds, Nails and Lead Sheathings of the Punic Ship from Battle of the Egadi Islands', Molecules 28 (2023)
sources.author: Armetta, Francesco; et al.
sources.confirms: Found 1971 off western Sicily; Honor Frost; hypothesis of loss after 10 March 241 BCE; lead sheathing; iron nails

sources.title: Frost, Honor, 'The Punic Ship Museum, Marsala: Its Presentation and Some Structural Observations', The Mariner's Mirror 67 (1981)
sources.author: Frost, Honor
sources.confirms: Punic Ship Museum presentation and structural observations

sources.title: Honor Frost Foundation, 'The Punic Ship of Marsala'
sources.confirms: Discovered 1971; shipwrights' marks; epigraphy and C-14 mid 3rd century BCE

marsala-punic-ship-241bce.detail: Ram-bow warships of this kind were long and narrow, rowed by dozens of oarsmen. Marked planks suggest shipyards building hulls to pattern rather than shaping each piece in place, which would explain how Carthage and Rome launched fleets quickly. Cannabis stems were found aboard. Frost's battle attribution is a hypothesis; dating by letters and carbon fits about 250 to 230 BCE.

picture.alt: Prow timbers of the Punic ship from Marsala, Museo Archeologico Baglio Anselmi

marsala-punic-ship-241bce.dating_note: Frost linked the wreck to the Battle of the Aegates in 241 BCE; this remains a hypothesis supported by mid-3rd-century epigraphy and radiocarbon.

eratosthenes-earth-circumference-240bce.summary: Eratosthenes of Cyrene, head of Alexandria's library from about 245 BCE, compared a noon shadow at Alexandria with a shadowless well at Syene on midsummer day and, taking their distance as 5,000 stades, computed Earth's circumference at 250,000 stades, later rounded to 252,000. Roller's 2010 edition collects his geographical fragments. How accurate this was depends on his stade's length: Engels argued in 1985 for a stade of about 185 metres, and Shcheglov in 2018 rejected a short 'itinerary stade', finding the common 185-metre stade attested by most sources, which gives about 46,000 kilometres.

sources.title: Shcheglov, Dmitry A., 'The so-called "Itinerary Stade" and the Accuracy of Eratosthenes' Measurement of the Earth', Klio 100 (2018)
sources.author: Shcheglov, Dmitry A.
sources.confirms: Rejects a short itinerary stade; common stade of 185 m attested by most sources

sources.title: Roller, Duane W., Eratosthenes' Geography: Fragments Collected and Translated (Princeton University Press, 2010)
sources.author: Roller, Duane W.
sources.confirms: Edition of Eratosthenes' geographical fragments

sources.title: Engels, Donald, 'The Length of Eratosthenes' Stade', American Journal of Philology 106 (1985)
sources.author: Engels, Donald
sources.confirms: Argues Eratosthenes' stade was c. 185 m

eratosthenes-earth-circumference-240bce.verification_note: Shcheglov's abstract was read; Roller and Engels were confirmed only through DOI metadata. The measurement account comes from Cleomedes as summarized in these works.
eratosthenes-earth-circumference-240bce.detail: Cleomedes preserves the method. Alexandria and Syene are not on one meridian and the distance was an estimate, so modern praise for near-exact accuracy rests partly on a convenient stade. Shcheglov argues that Eratosthenes' figure overshot by about 15 percent, still a remarkable result from geometry and a gnomon. Eratosthenes also devised a sieve for primes and a calendar with leap days.

picture.alt: Diagram of Eratosthenes' method for measuring Earth's circumference using shadows at Syene and Alexandria (modern diagram)

eratosthenes-earth-circumference-240bce.dating_note: Length of Eratosthenes' stade is disputed; Shcheglov 2018 argues for 185 m against a short stade that would make his result near exact.

south-pointing-spoon-dispute-240bce.summary: A passage in Wang Chong's Lunheng (first century CE) says that when a south-pointing ladle is thrown on the ground it comes to rest pointing south, and Han Feizi (third century BCE) mentions a 'south-pointer' used to fix bearings. Needham's Science and Civilisation in China volume 4 part 1 took these as evidence for a lodestone spoon on a bronze diviner's board, reconstructed by Wang Zhenduo. Li Shu-hua argued in Isis in 1954 that textual evidence for a magnetic instrument before the Song dynasty is weak. Huang Xingzong's 2019 experiments tested whether carved lodestone spoons point south.

sources.title: Li Shu-hua, 'Origine de la Boussole II. Aimant et Boussole', Isis 45 (1954)
sources.author: Li Shu-hua
sources.confirms: Questions evidence for a pre-Song magnetic instrument

sources.title: Needham, Joseph, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 4 part 1: Physics (Cambridge University Press, 1962), section on magnetism
sources.author: Needham, Joseph
sources.confirms: Lodestone spoon on diviner's board as early compass

sources.title: Huang Xingzong, 'Experimental Research on the South-Pointing Loadstone Spoon (sinan)', Chinese Annals of History of Science and Technology 3 (2019)
sources.author: Huang Xingzong
sources.venue: Chinese Annals of History of Science and Technology
sources.confirms: Experimental reconstruction of south-pointing spoon

south-pointing-spoon-dispute-240bce.verification_note: Needham's volume was accessed as an archive full text; Li Shu-hua's and Huang's articles were confirmed only through journal and DOI metadata.
south-pointing-spoon-dispute-240bce.detail: No ancient lodestone spoon has been excavated; Wang Zhenduo's 1940s reconstruction is a model, often shown in museums as if an artefact. Li Shu-hua read 'sinan' as possibly a non-magnetic device. Secure evidence for magnetic compasses comes with Shen Kuo in 1088 and Zhu Yu in 1119. This concept record marks a disputed origin rather than a confirmed invention, and it stays in communications as a navigation aid.
south-pointing-spoon-dispute-240bce.dating_note: Needham accepts a Han lodestone spoon; Li Shu-hua 1954 finds pre-Song evidence weak; no physical spoon survives.

philo-byzantium-mechanics-230bce.summary: Philo of Byzantium, active about 200 BCE according to Toomer's Oxford Classical Dictionary entry, composed a multi-book Mechanike Syntaxis of which parts survive on artillery (Belopoeica), siegecraft and pneumatics. His Belopoeica reports that Alexandrian engineers improved torsion catapults by testing many models and found that all dimensions should scale from a spring-hole diameter set by a cube-root formula; Schiefsky analyses this as a method of technical knowledge. His Pneumatica, known in Arabic and Latin versions reviewed by Drachmann, describes siphons, automatic wine dispensers and an eight-sided inkwell that stays upright.

sources.title: Schiefsky, Mark, 'Technē and Method in Ancient Artillery Construction: The Belopoeica of Philo of Byzantium', in The Frontiers of Ancient Science (De Gruyter, 2015)
sources.author: Schiefsky, Mark
sources.confirms: Analysis of method in Philo's Belopoeica

sources.title: Toomer, G. J., 'Philon (2), of Byzantium, mechanician', Oxford Classical Dictionary (2016)
sources.author: Toomer, G. J.
sources.confirms: Philon of Byzantium, mechanician, fl. c. 200 BCE

sources.title: Drachmann, A. G., review of 'Philo of Byzantium: Pneumatica', Technology and Culture 17 (1976)
sources.author: Drachmann, A. G.
sources.confirms: Review of Prager's edition of Philo's Pneumatica

philo-byzantium-mechanics-230bce.verification_note: Toomer's dictionary entry title confirms floruit c. 200 BCE; Schiefsky's chapter and Drachmann's review were confirmed only through DOI metadata.
philo-byzantium-mechanics-230bce.detail: Philo visited Alexandria and Rhodes and reports engineers' experiments, which makes his work evidence for state-funded research under the Ptolemies. His pneumatic devices use air pressure, floats and valves developed by Ctesibius. Prager's 1974 edition of the Pneumatica was reviewed by Drachmann in Technology and Culture. Dates for his life range from about 280 to 200 BCE, so 230 BCE is an approximate midpoint. Later Arabic engineers drew heavily on his pneumatic designs.

picture.alt: Modern reconstruction of the automatic servant described by Philo of Byzantium, Kotsanas Museum (reconstruction)

philo-byzantium-mechanics-230bce.dating_note: Philo's dates are uncertain between c. 280 and 200 BCE.

qin-standardization-221bce.summary: After conquering rival states in 221 BCE, Qin's First Emperor and his chancellor Li Si imposed uniform weights and measures, a single coinage, standard axle gauges for carts and a simplified small seal script for official writing, replacing regional variants. Bodde's chapter in the Cambridge History of China recounts these measures alongside road building and legal codes. Sanft's 2014 study argues that Qin publicized standards through inscribed weights, measures and stone inscriptions as mass communication to win cooperation. Bronze and pottery weights bearing an imperial edict of 221 BCE survive in many collections.

sources.title: Bodde, Derk, 'The State and Empire of Ch'in', in The Cambridge History of China, vol. 1 (Cambridge University Press, 1986)
sources.author: Bodde, Derk
sources.confirms: Qin's rise and imperial measures

sources.title: Sanft, Charles, Communication and Cooperation in Early Imperial China: Publicizing the Qin Dynasty (SUNY Press, 2014), ch. 'Mass Communication and Standardization'
sources.author: Sanft, Charles
sources.confirms: Qin publicized standards as mass communication

qin-standardization-221bce.detail: Standard axle width let carts follow ruts across an empire of dirt roads. Small seal script, attributed to Li Si, became ancestor of clerical and regular scripts. Qin also unified currency on round banliang coins. Bodde notes Qin's half-millennium as a small state before its conquests. Standardization served control and taxation, and later dynasties kept it as a mark of legitimate rule.

picture.alt: Rubbing of the Qin imperial edict on a bronze plate attached to an iron standard weight

qin-great-wall-214bce.summary: Around 215 to 214 BCE, general Meng Tian led hundreds of thousands of soldiers and convicts to join and extend rammed-earth walls built earlier by Qin, Zhao and Yan into a continuous frontier against Xiongnu horsemen. UNESCO's listing says that around 220 BCE under Qin Shi Huang 'sections of earlier fortifications were joined together to form a united defence system', with building continuing to the seventeenth century. Waldron's 1983 article and his later book argue that a single 'Great Wall' is a myth assembled from many walls of different eras, as Perdue's review discusses. Most surviving brick and stone walls are Ming.

sources.title: Waldron, Arthur N., 'The Problem of The Great Wall of China', Harvard Journal of Asiatic Studies 43 (1983)
sources.author: Waldron, Arthur N.
sources.confirms: Problem of the Great Wall as a unified concept

sources.title: Perdue, Peter C., 'The Great Wall of China: From History to Myth' (review), Journal of Interdisciplinary History 23 (1992)
sources.author: Perdue, Peter C.
sources.confirms: Review of Waldron's From History to Myth

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'The Great Wall'
sources.author: UNESCO World Heritage Centre
sources.confirms: c. 220 BCE earlier fortifications joined into a united defence system; over 20,000 km in total

qin-great-wall-214bce.detail: Qin walls were built of tamped earth between wooden frames, often following ridges north of the Ordos. Sima Qian's biography of Meng Tian describes a line over 10,000 li. Waldron showed that later writers merged separate projects into one monument. UNESCO measures all walls at over 20,000 kilometres. Qin's forced labour on walls and roads fed resentment that toppled the dynasty in 206 BCE.

picture.alt: The Great Wall of China photographed by Herbert Ponting in 1907 (Ming-era masonry section, not Qin rammed earth)

qin-great-wall-214bce.dating_note: Waldron argues the Great Wall as a single structure is a later construct; Qin wall building c. 215 to 214 BCE rests on Sima Qian.

huangdi-neijing-200bce.summary: Huangdi Neijing, cast as dialogues between Yellow Emperor and his ministers, sets out a medicine of correspondence between body and cosmos: qi circulating through channels, balance of yin and yang, five agents, pulse diagnosis, acupuncture and moxibustion, with emphasis on prevention. Unschuld's 2003 study of its Su wen half holds that short medical essays composed in final centuries BCE were assembled into a text whose present form dates to eleventh century CE. Britannica dates it to about third century BCE. Sivin's bibliographical essay in Early Chinese Texts reviews its history. It remains a foundational text of Chinese medicine.

sources.title: Unschuld, Paul U., Huang Di Nei Jing Su Wen: Nature, Knowledge, Imagery in an Ancient Chinese Medical Text (University of California Press, 2003)
sources.author: Unschuld, Paul U.
sources.confirms: Text originated in final centuries BCE from short essays; present form 11th century; yin-yang, five agents, qi, acupuncture

sources.title: Sivin, Nathan, 'Huang ti nei ching', in Loewe (ed.), Early Chinese Texts: A Bibliographical Guide (Society for the Study of Early China, 1993)
sources.author: Sivin, Nathan
sources.venue: Society for the Study of Early China
sources.confirms: Bibliographical review of Huang ti nei ching

sources.title: 'Huangdi neijing', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Britannica editors
sources.confirms: Dated c. 3rd century BCE; teachings addressed to Yellow Emperor; prevention

huangdi-neijing-200bce.detail: Two parts survive, Su wen (Basic Questions) and Ling shu (Spiritual Pivot), each in 81 chapters. Wang Bing's 762 CE edition and Song editors reshaped them. Mawangdui manuscripts of 168 BCE show earlier channel theories without acupuncture needles, which supports a Han date for mature doctrine. A 200 BCE date is approximate for its earliest layers. Unschuld's translation project, completed in 2011, made Su wen fully available in English.

picture.alt: Chinese woodcut portrait of Qibo, the physician who answers the Yellow Emperor in the Huangdi Neijing, Wellcome Collection

huangdi-neijing-200bce.dating_note: Earliest layers date to the final centuries BCE; present form is 11th century CE per Unschuld; Britannica says c. 3rd century BCE.

pingala-chandahsastra-binary-200bce.summary: Pingala's treatise on Sanskrit prosody classifies metres by sequences of light and heavy syllables and gives rules to list every pattern of a given length, to find a pattern's position in that list and to recover a pattern from its position. Van Nooten showed in 1993 that these procedures amount to binary numbers and binary-to-decimal conversion. Pingala also describes meru prastara, an arrangement of counts equal to binomial coefficients later known as Pascal's triangle, and his commentators derive a sequence now called Fibonacci numbers, as Singh documented in 1985. Varshney connects this work to constrained codes.

sources.title: Van Nooten, B., 'Binary numbers in Indian antiquity', Journal of Indian Philosophy 21 (1993)
sources.author: Van Nooten, B.
sources.confirms: Binary numbers in Indian antiquity from Pingala's prosody

sources.title: Singh, Parmanand, 'The so-called Fibonacci numbers in ancient and medieval India', Historia Mathematica 12 (1985)
sources.author: Singh, Parmanand
sources.confirms: So-called Fibonacci numbers in ancient and medieval India

sources.title: Varshney, Lav R., 'Local fidelity, constrained codes, and the Meru Prastara', IEEE Potentials 27 (2008)
sources.author: Varshney, Lav R.
sources.confirms: Meru prastara and constrained codes

pingala-chandahsastra-binary-200bce.verification_note: Van Nooten's article and Singh and Varshney are cited as supporting literature; none fixes Pingala's date.
pingala-chandahsastra-binary-200bce.detail: Pingala's date is uncertain, with estimates from fourth to second century BCE; 200 BCE is a conventional approximation. His sutras are terse and were expanded by Halayudha in tenth century CE, who gave a fuller meru prastara. Counting metres of n syllables yields 2 to power n, and rules for doubling and halving resemble later algorithms, an early combinatorial method.

picture.alt: Opening leaves of a Sanskrit Chandas manuscript on metrics, copied in 1569 and held in Paris.
picture.credit: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

pingala-chandahsastra-binary-200bce.dating_note: Pingala is dated between the fourth and the second century BCE; attribution of binary interpretation partly rests on later commentators.

pergamon-parchment-190bce.summary: Pliny the Elder, citing Varro, reports that parchment was invented at Pergamum when Ptolemaic kings, jealous of Eumenes II's library, cut off papyrus exports. Scraped and stretched animal skins had long been written on, but Pergamene workshops produced a thinner, smoother sheet that took ink on both sides, and Latin 'pergamena' preserves this origin. Johnson's 1970 article examines ancient and medieval accounts of this 'invention' and finds the story simplified. Reed's Ancient Skins, Parchments and Leathers describes liming and stretching processes. Parchment later displaced papyrus for codices across Europe.

sources.title: Johnson, Richard R., 'Ancient and Medieval Accounts of the "Invention" of Parchment', California Studies in Classical Antiquity 3 (1970)
sources.author: Johnson, Richard R.
sources.confirms: Examines ancient and medieval accounts of parchment's invention

sources.title: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 13.21 (13.70 Rackham numbering), ToposText
sources.author: Pliny the Elder
sources.confirms: Parchment invented at Pergamum amid library rivalry, citing Varro

sources.title: Reed, Ronald, Ancient Skins, Parchments and Leathers (Seminar Press, 1972)
sources.author: Reed, Ronald
sources.confirms: Technical history of skins and parchment

pergamon-parchment-190bce.verification_note: Pliny's text was read; Johnson's article was confirmed through DOI metadata; Reed's book was seen as an archive item page.
pergamon-parchment-190bce.detail: Eumenes II ruled 197 to 159 BCE, so Pliny's story fits around 190 BCE. Skins were soaked in lime, dehaired, stretched on frames and scraped with a lunar knife, then whitened with chalk. Unlike leather, parchment was not tanned, so it stayed pale and could be erased and reused as palimpsest. Durability made it medieval Europe's main manuscript medium until paper mills spread from the twelfth century.

picture.alt: Room behind the north stoa in the Sanctuary of Athena at Pergamon, identified as part of the library

pergamon-parchment-190bce.dating_note: Pliny's account is anecdotal; Johnson 1970 shows parchment predates Pergamon and the story records refinement and naming.

fangmatan-paper-map-170bce.summary: Excavations at Fangmatan near Tianshui, Gansu, in 1986 recovered from tomb 5 a fragment of hemp paper about 5.6 centimetres wide bearing a brush-and-ink drawing of rivers and roads, dated to early Western Han, around the second century BCE. Tomb 1 nearby held seven maps drawn on four wooden boards, dated by scholars anywhere from 317 BCE to early Western Han, as Wang's 2023 chapter notes. Britannica describes this fragment as the oldest surviving paper map and as pushing paper back about 300 years before Cai Lun's 105 CE report. Tsien's volume on paper and printing sets it within early paper finds.

sources.title: Wang, Michelle H., 'Fangmatan and the Bureaucratization of Space', in The Art of Terrestrial Diagrams in Early China (University of Chicago Press, 2023), ch. 2
sources.author: Wang, Michelle H.
sources.confirms: Tomb 1 seven diagrams on four boards, dating proposals 317 BCE to early Western Han; tomb 5 paper drawing 5.6 cm wide dated Western Han

sources.title: Tsien Tsuen-Hsuin, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 5 part 1: Paper and Printing (Cambridge University Press, 1985)
sources.author: Tsien Tsuen-Hsuin
sources.confirms: Early paper finds in China

fangmatan-paper-map-170bce.detail: Paper fragments from Han sites such as Baqiao and Xuanquan show that felted plant-fibre sheets existed before Cai Lun improved them. Hsu's 1993 article in Imago Mundi analyses Qin map conventions on the wooden boards. Wang reads Fangmatan maps as part of bureaucratic ordering of space. Dating of this paper rests on tomb typology and associated objects. Whether such early sheets were used for writing or wrapping remains debated.

picture.alt: Fragment of the Fangmatan paper map from a Western Han tomb, Gansu

fangmatan-paper-map-170bce.dating_note: Tomb 5 paper is dated to early Western Han by typology; tomb 1 boards are variously dated 317 BCE to early Western Han.

mawangdui-medical-silk-texts-168bce.summary: Tomb 3 at Mawangdui near Changsha, closed in 168 BCE, held a lacquer box of silk and bamboo texts including, as Harper reported in 1982, two scrolls containing six medical treatises and a set of illustrations of therapeutic calisthenics. Harper's 1998 translation presents these as our earliest Chinese medical manuscripts: recipes for 52 ailments, texts on cauterization channels without acupuncture, breath cultivation, sexual hygiene and a chart of exercise postures. Hinrichs reviewed his edition in 2001. Because they are dated by burial, they give a fixed point before Huangdi Neijing's compilation.

sources.title: Harper, Donald, 'Mawangdui Tomb Three: Documents. I - The Medical Documents', Early China 2 (1976)
sources.author: Harper, Donald
sources.confirms: Two scrolls contained six medical treatises and illustrations of therapeutic calisthenics; scrolls fused in lacquer box

sources.title: Hinrichs, TJ, review of Harper, 'Early Chinese Medical Literature: The Mawangdui Medical Manuscripts', Bulletin of the History of Medicine 75 (2001)
sources.author: Hinrichs, TJ
sources.venue: Bulletin of the History of Medicine
sources.confirms: Review of Harper's translation

sources.title: Harper, Donald, Early Chinese Medical Literature: The Mawangdui Medical Manuscripts (Routledge, 2013 reprint of 1998)
sources.author: Harper, Donald
sources.confirms: Translation and study of Mawangdui medical manuscripts

mawangdui-medical-silk-texts-168bce.detail: Recipes combine drugs, incantations and surgical measures such as treating hemorrhoids. Channel texts name eleven vessels for moxibustion, one fewer than later theory. The Daoyin chart shows 44 figures exercising. Harper's Early China article describes how fused scrolls were separated after excavation in 1973. These manuscripts show medicine before Han standardization, mixing magic and physiology, and were found with maps, divination texts and a copy of Laozi.

picture.alt: The Daoyin tu exercise chart on silk from Mawangdui tomb 3, Wellcome Collection reproduction

cato-greek-doctors-160bce.summary: Marcus Porcius Cato, Roman censor and author of De Agri Cultura, told his son Marcus in a letter preserved by Pliny that Greeks had 'conspired together to murder all foreigners with their physic' and that he forbade him to have dealings with doctors. Plutarch's Life of Cato reports his suspicion of Greeks practising medicine at Rome, his retelling of a story about Hippocrates refusing to treat Persians, and his own notebook of remedies with which he treated his household. Nutton's Ancient Medicine discusses this episode in his chapter on medicine's transplantation to Rome.

sources.title: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 29.7 (29.14 Rackham numbering), ToposText
sources.author: Pliny the Elder
sources.confirms: Cato's letter: Greeks conspired to murder foreigners with their medicine

sources.title: Nutton, Vivian, Ancient Medicine (Routledge, 2004), ch. 11 'Rome and the transplantation of Greek medicine'
sources.author: Nutton, Vivian
sources.confirms: Chapter on Rome and transplantation of Greek medicine

sources.title: Plutarch, Life of Cato the Elder 23 (Perrin translation, Loeb), LacusCurtius
sources.author: Plutarch
sources.confirms: Cato suspicious of Greek doctors at Rome; Hippocrates story; own book of recipes

cato-greek-doctors-160bce.detail: Cato's hostility combined moral conservatism, dislike of fees and fear of Greek cultural influence after Rome's eastern conquests. His remedies relied on cabbage, wine and incantations. Greek doctors nonetheless flourished at Rome; Asclepiades of Bithynia arrived a generation later. Pliny himself echoed Cato's complaint two centuries on. This project treats it as a fear record about an imported medical technology.

picture.alt: The so-called Patrizio Torlonia, a Roman republican portrait bust once identified as Cato the Elder

cato-greek-doctors-160bce.dating_note: Date of Cato's letter is unknown; c. 160 BCE falls within his later life (he died 149 BCE).

roman-concrete-opus-caementicium-150bce.summary: By the second century BCE, builders in Rome and Latium were mixing lime with volcanic ash (pozzolana) and rubble into a mortar that set hard, even under water, enabling vaulted substructures, harbours and later domes. Marcello Mogetta places concrete's origins in Rome and its hinterland in the second century BCE; traditional accounts placed them earlier, in Campania. Vitruvius writes that sand found near Baiae and Vesuvius mixed with lime and rubble hardens under water. Seawater reacting with ash grew interlocking minerals that strengthened marine concrete over centuries. Pont du Gard, often shown as an example, dates to the mid first century CE.

sources.title: Mogetta, Marcello, The Origins of Concrete Construction in Roman Architecture: Technology and Society in Republican Italy (Cambridge University Press, 2021)
sources.author: Mogetta, Marcello
sources.confirms: Origins of concrete construction in Roman architecture

sources.author: Jackson, Marie D.; Mulcahy, Sean R.; Chen, Heng; et al.
sources.confirms: Phillipsite and tobermorite cements grow in Roman marine concrete

sources.author: Vitruvius
sources.confirms: Sand near Baiae and Vesuvius mixed with lime and rubble hardens under water

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Pont du Gard (Roman Aqueduct)'
sources.author: UNESCO
sources.confirms: Pont du Gard built in mid 1st century CE

roman-concrete-opus-caementicium-150bce.detail: Opus caementicium was faced with stone or brick patterns such as opus incertum and reticulatum. Arches and barrel vaults in concrete allowed Pantheon's 43-metre dome in the second century CE. Harbour concrete at Portus Cosanus and elsewhere holds phillipsite and aluminous tobermorite crystals. Dating of first use is approximate; Mogetta argues for a later and more gradual adoption than traditional accounts.

picture.alt: Exposed Roman concrete, opus caementicium, in a tomb core on the Via Appia Antica
picture.credit: No machine-readable author provided. MM assumed (based on copyright claims).

roman-concrete-opus-caementicium-150bce.dating_note: Mogetta dates concrete's origin to 2nd century BCE Rome; older accounts placed it in 3rd-century Campania.

hipparchus-precession-star-catalogue-130.summary: Hipparchus of Nicaea, observing from Rhodes around 150 to 125 BCE, compiled positions of hundreds of stars and, comparing them with earlier Alexandrian records, found that equinox points drift slowly westward along the ecliptic. Ptolemy's Almagest preserves his results and credits him with discovering precession. In 2022 multispectral imaging of the Codex Climaci Rescriptus recovered fragments of his catalogue, giving coordinates for about 129 BCE accurate to within one degree. He also developed trigonometry and a lunar theory.

sources.title: Gysembergh, Victor; Williams, Peter J.; Zingg, Emanuel, 'New evidence for Hipparchus' Star Catalogue revealed by multispectral imaging', Journal for the History of Astronomy 53 (2022)
sources.author: Gysembergh, Victor; Williams, Peter J.; Zingg, Emanuel
sources.venue: Journal for the History of Astronomy
sources.confirms: Codex Climaci Rescriptus fragments of Hipparchus's catalogue; coordinates c. 129 BCE accurate within one degree

sources.title: Kwan, Alan, 'Hipparchus of Nicaea', in Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers (Springer, 2014)
sources.author: Kwan, Alan
sources.confirms: Biographical entry on Hipparchus

sources.title: Toomer, G. J. (trans.), Ptolemy's Almagest (Princeton University Press, 1998), VII.2 on Hipparchus and precession
sources.author: Toomer, G. J.
sources.confirms: Ptolemy's Almagest preserving Hipparchus's observations and precession

hipparchus-precession-star-catalogue-130.detail: Hipparchus combined Babylonian eclipse records with Greek geometry, built a chord table that is an ancestor of trigonometry, and estimated lunar distance. His catalogue was long thought lost except through Ptolemy and the Farnese Atlas. Recovered fragments show he used equatorial coordinates. Applying precession rates to recovered coordinates dates his observations to around 129 BCE, a method independent of ancient testimony. This find also confirms that Ptolemy did not simply copy his predecessor.

picture.alt: The Farnese Atlas, a Roman marble statue bearing a celestial globe, Naples National Archaeological Museum

antikythera-mechanism-100bce.summary: A bronze device recovered in 1901 from a shipwreck off Antikythera carried over 30 interlocking gears that modelled motions of Sun, Moon and probably planets, displayed calendars and predicted eclipses. X-ray tomography in 2006 decoded its inscriptions and gearing, identified a pin-and-slot device for lunar anomaly and placed manufacture toward the end of the second century BCE. A model of its front cosmos display followed in 2021. Its Saros dial starts from an epoch in 205 BCE, pointing to an earlier design. It stands as a precursor to computing machines.

sources.title: Freeth, Tony; et al., 'Decoding the ancient Greek astronomical calculator known as the Antikythera Mechanism', Nature 444 (2006)
sources.author: Freeth, Tony; Bitsakis, Yanis; Moussas, Xenophon; et al.
sources.confirms: Made toward the end of the second century BCE; 30 gears; eclipse prediction

sources.title: Carman, Christián C.; Evans, James, 'On the epoch of the Antikythera mechanism and its eclipse predictor', Archive for History of Exact Sciences 68 (2014)
sources.author: Carman, Christián C.; Evans, James
sources.venue: Archive for History of Exact Sciences
sources.confirms: Saros dial epoch dated to 205 BCE

sources.title: Freeth, Tony; et al., 'A Model of the Cosmos in the ancient Greek Antikythera Mechanism', Scientific Reports 11 (2021)
sources.author: Freeth, Tony; Higgon, David; Dacanalis, Aris; et al.
sources.confirms: 82 fragments; a third survives; model of front cosmos display

antikythera-mechanism-100bce.detail: Only about a third survives in 82 fragments. Gears encode a 19-year Metonic cycle, a 76-year Callippic cycle and a 223-month Saros eclipse cycle. Inscriptions in Koine Greek act as a user manual. Letter forms put its making at about 150 to 100 BCE; astronomical epoch analysis points to 205 BCE. No comparable device is known for over a thousand years, until Islamic geared astrolabes and Su Song's clock.

picture.alt: Fragments of the Antikythera mechanism displayed at the National Archaeological Museum, Athens

antikythera-mechanism-100bce.dating_note: Freeth 2006 places manufacture late second century BCE on letter forms; Carman and Evans 2014 put the Saros dial epoch at 205 BCE.

charaka-samhita-100bce.summary: Charaka Samhita, built on an older text of Agnivesha and revised by Charaka, then completed by Dridhabala, is the chief treatise of Ayurvedic internal medicine, covering diagnosis, causes of disease in three doshas, hundreds of plant and mineral drugs, diet and a code for physicians. Britannica places its present form around the first century CE, while Meulenbeld's survey reviews proposals from the second century BCE onward. Maas's 2010 article traces what became of Charaka's text after Dridhabala's revision. It frames medicine as a rational inquiry into causes and remedies, with debate protocols for physicians.

sources.title: Maas, Philipp A., 'On What Became of the Carakasaṃhitā after Dṛḍhabala's Revision', eJournal of Indian Medicine 3 (2010)
sources.author: Maas, Philipp A.
sources.confirms: Fate of Charaka's text after Dridhabala's revision

sources.title: Meulenbeld, G. Jan, A History of Indian Medical Literature, vol. IA (Egbert Forsten, 1999), ch. on the Carakasamhita
sources.author: Meulenbeld, G. Jan
sources.confirms: Philological history of Charaka Samhita and its dating proposals

sources.title: 'Charaka-samhita', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Britannica editors
sources.confirms: Present text c. 1st century CE; Agnivesha original, Charaka revision; diagnosis and drugs

charaka-samhita-100bce.verification_note: Britannica confirms a first-century CE present text; Maas and Meulenbeld are cited as supporting literature. The 100 BCE anchor marks an early textual stage, not a documented date.
charaka-samhita-100bce.detail: Charaka's text has eight sections and about 120 chapters, with a long pharmacology. Dridhabala, perhaps in fourth or fifth century CE, supplied missing chapters. A 100 BCE date marks an Agnivesha-Charaka stage rather than final redaction and is approximate. Along with Sushruta's compendium it formed a basis for later Ayurveda and for Arabic translations made in Abbasid Baghdad.

picture.alt: Manuscript page from the Sutrasthana of the Charaka Samhita, Wellcome Collection

charaka-samhita-100bce.dating_note: Britannica dates the present text to c. 1st century CE; proposals for Charaka's revision range from 2nd century BCE to 2nd century CE.

hippalus-monsoon-sailing-100bce.summary: Pliny the Elder records that a pilot named Hippalus discovered that a steady southwest wind could carry ships from Arabia's coast straight across open sea to India, and that merchants named this wind after him; with it a voyage from Ocelis took about forty days. Strabo reports that under Aelius Gallus about 120 ships sailed each year from Myos Hormos to India, where under Ptolemies scarcely any had dared. Casson's edition of the Periplus Maris Erythraei, a first-century CE merchant's guide, discusses this route. Open-sea monsoon sailing, probably learned from Arab and Indian seafarers, linked Roman Egypt with Indian ports.

sources.title: Casson, Lionel, The Periplus Maris Erythraei: Text with Introduction, Translation, and Commentary (Princeton University Press, 1989), Internet Archive
sources.author: Casson, Lionel
sources.confirms: Edition and commentary on the Periplus Maris Erythraei

sources.title: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 6.26 (6.100-106 Rackham numbering), ToposText
sources.author: Pliny the Elder
sources.confirms: Hippalus wind; forty-day voyage from Ocelis to India

sources.title: Strabo, Geography 2.5.12 (Hamilton and Falconer translation), ToposText
sources.author: Strabo
sources.confirms: About 120 ships a year from Myos Hormos to India under Gallus; scarcely any under Ptolemies

hippalus-monsoon-sailing-100bce.verification_note: Pliny and Strabo were read in full; Casson's edition is an access-restricted archive item seen at catalogue level. No source fixes Hippalus's date.
hippalus-monsoon-sailing-100bce.detail: Hippalus's date is unknown; proposals run from the second century BCE to the early first century CE, so 100 BCE is approximate. Indian and Arab sailors had used monsoon winds earlier, and Greek sources record what Greeks learned. Return voyages used northeast winds in winter. Trade carried pepper, gems and cotton west and wine, glass and coin east, as Roman coin hoards in south India show.

picture.alt: Modern map of names, routes and locations in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea

hippalus-monsoon-sailing-100bce.dating_note: Hippalus's date is debated between the 2nd century BCE and 1st century CE; Pliny and Strabo give no year.

hopewell-newark-earthworks-100bce.summary: In central Ohio, Hopewell communities built Newark Earthworks, a complex of a circle 320 metres across, an octagon enclosing 20 hectares and connecting walls, within a tradition UNESCO dates to 1 to 400 CE. Octagon and circle walls align with moonrise and moonset extremes over an 18.6-year cycle, a pattern tested statistically. New radiocarbon dates have refined Ohio Hopewell chronology. Hopewell people obtained obsidian from Yellowstone, copper from Lake Superior and shells from the Gulf.

sources.title: Hively, Ray; Horn, Robert, 'A Statistical Study of Lunar Alignments at the Newark Earthworks', Midcontinental Journal of Archaeology 31 (2006)
sources.author: Hively, Ray; Horn, Robert
sources.confirms: Statistical study of lunar alignments at Newark

sources.title: Seeman, Mark F.; et al., 'Building the Ohio Hopewell Chronology: An Incremental Approach to Historical Reckoning', American Antiquity 88 (2023)
sources.author: Seeman, Mark F.; Nolan, Kevin C.; Hill, Mark A.
sources.confirms: Ohio Hopewell chronology refined

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks'
sources.author: UNESCO
sources.confirms: Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks built 1 to 400 CE; Newark; solar and lunar alignments

hopewell-newark-earthworks-100bce.detail: Earthworks were built of basket-loaded soil to precise geometry; squares and circles at different sites share a unit of measure. Hopewell groups lived in dispersed hamlets and gathered at these centres. Early Hopewell in Illinois and Ohio begins about 100 BCE, and the tradition runs to 400 CE. Newark's octagon now lies partly within a golf course, a preservation dispute resolved in 2024.

picture.alt: Central mound within the Great Circle of the Newark Earthworks, Ohio

hopewell-newark-earthworks-100bce.dating_note: UNESCO dates Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks to 1 to 400 CE; Hopewell origins c. 100 BCE are included here as era start.

nabataean-petra-water-100bce.summary: Nabataean engineers at Petra in southern Jordan collected flash floods and spring water through dams, rock-cut channels, ceramic pipelines, settling tanks and hundreds of cisterns, supporting a caravan city of tens of thousands in a desert. Ortloff's 2005 article in Cambridge Archaeological Journal analyses this system between 300 BCE and 300 CE, and his 2020 study in Water applies hydraulic engineering analysis to pipelines dating 100 BCE to 300 CE, finding designs that matched flow rates to pipe capacity. UNESCO's listing describes Petra as a Nabataean caravan city from the fourth century BCE to the first century CE with dams, channels and cisterns.

sources.title: Ortloff, Charles R., 'The Water Supply and Distribution System of the Nabataean City of Petra (Jordan), 300 BC-AD 300', Cambridge Archaeological Journal 15 (2005)
sources.author: Ortloff, Charles R.
sources.confirms: Water supply and distribution at Petra, 300 BCE to 300 CE

sources.title: Ortloff, Charles R., 'Hydraulic Engineering at 100 BC-AD 300 Nabataean Petra (Jordan)', Water 12 (2020)
sources.author: Ortloff, Charles R.
sources.confirms: Hydraulic engineering at Petra 100 BCE to 300 CE; pipeline analysis

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Petra'
sources.author: UNESCO
sources.confirms: Caravan city 4th century BCE to 1st century CE; dams, channels, cisterns

nabataean-petra-water-100bce.detail: A tunnel diverted Wadi Musa floods away from the Siq, whose walls carry channels on both sides. Pipes of interlocking ceramic segments ran at gradients that kept flow partial to avoid pressure surges. Ortloff estimates that aggregate storage let Petra survive drought years. Date here is approximate; most surviving works belong to first centuries BCE and CE, when caravan wealth from incense peaked.

picture.alt: Rock-cut water channel along the Siq at Petra, Jordan

nazca-lines-100bce.summary: Between about 500 BCE and 500 CE, people of Peru's south coast cleared dark stones from pale desert ground to form straight lines kilometres long, trapezoids and figures of a hummingbird, monkey, spider and others, visible whole only from hills or the air. UNESCO's listing covers about 450 square kilometres of Nasca and Palpa geoglyphs. Many lines link to ray centres and water. In 2024 an AI-assisted survey nearly doubled known figurative geoglyphs to over 700. Figures were laid out with stakes and cords.

sources.title: Sakai, Masato; et al., 'AI-accelerated Nazca survey nearly doubles the number of known figurative geoglyphs and sheds light on their purpose', PNAS 121 (2024)
sources.author: Sakai, Masato; Sakurai, Akihisa; Lu, Siyuan; et al.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: AI-accelerated survey nearly doubles known figurative geoglyphs

sources.title: Aveni, Anthony F. (ed.), The Lines of Nazca (American Philosophical Society, 1990), ch. 2 'Order in the Nazca Lines'
sources.author: Aveni, Anthony F.
sources.confirms: Order in the Nazca lines; ray centres

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Lines and Geoglyphs of Nasca and Palpa'
sources.author: UNESCO
sources.confirms: Nasca and Palpa lines 500 BCE to 500 CE; about 450 square kilometres

nazca-lines-100bce.detail: Lines were made by removing oxidized surface stones to expose lighter soil; arid climate preserved them. Interpretations range from ritual pathways and water cults to astronomical sightlines, which Anthony Aveni tested statistically. Smaller relief-type figures, often near paths, appear earlier than large line-type figures. A date of 100 BCE is an approximate midpoint of Paracas-to-Nasca geoglyph making, which runs to 500 CE.

picture.alt: The hummingbird geoglyph of the Nazca lines seen from the air

nazca-lines-100bce.dating_note: UNESCO gives 500 BCE to 500 CE; individual figures are dated by associated pottery and surface weathering.

nine-chapters-mathematical-art-100bce.summary: Jiuzhang Suanshu, compiled during the Han dynasty with roots in Qin and earlier texts, presents 246 problems on field measurement, grain exchange, proportional distribution, extraction of square and cube roots, volumes, taxation, excess and deficit, systems of linear equations solved by array elimination, and right triangles. Shen, Crossley and Lun's 1999 translation calls it the most important mathematical source in China for 2,000 years, comparable to Euclid's Elements. Chemla's encyclopedia entry explains its algorithmic form. Dauben's translation of the Suan shu shu, a bamboo text buried about 186 BCE, shows an earlier stage of this tradition.

sources.author: Shen Kangshen; Crossley, John N.; Lun, Anthony W.-C.
sources.confirms: Most important mathematical source in China for 2,000 years, comparable to Euclid

sources.title: Chemla, Karine, 'Jiuzhang Suanshu', in Encyclopaedia of the History of Science, Technology, and Medicine in Non-Western Cultures (Springer, 2016)
sources.author: Chemla, Karine
sources.confirms: Entry on Jiuzhang Suanshu

sources.author: Dauben, Joseph W.
sources.venue: Archive for History of Exact Sciences
sources.confirms: Suan shu shu translation, pp. 91 to 178

nine-chapters-mathematical-art-100bce.detail: Problems give a rule (shu) as a procedure executed with counting rods, including negative numbers and Gaussian-style elimination for simultaneous equations. Liu Hui's commentary of 263 CE added proofs and a pi estimate. Dating of compilation ranges from second century BCE to first century CE; 100 BCE is approximate. Its influence spread to Korea and Japan as a state examination textbook.

picture.alt: Page from a printed edition of the Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art with commentary

nine-chapters-mathematical-art-100bce.dating_note: Compilation is dated between the 2nd century BCE and 1st century CE; Suan shu shu (before 186 BCE) shows earlier material.

screw-press-olive-oil-100bce.summary: Pliny writes that within the past hundred years a press using a wooden screw on a vertical post was introduced, replacing or supplementing long lever-and-windlass presses, and that a later design used a short screw with a box. Cato's De Agri Cultura, written around 160 BCE, gives detailed instructions for building lever presses for olives in a pressing room with crushing mill (trapetum) and vats. Curtis's Ancient Food Technology surveys oil and wine processing. Screw presses, drawing on Hellenistic mechanics, let smaller workshops press oil and wine, and oil became a traded commodity shipped in amphorae across the Roman world.

sources.title: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 18.74 (18.317 Rackham numbering), ToposText
sources.author: Pliny the Elder
sources.confirms: Screw press introduced within the last hundred years; later short screw with box

sources.title: Cato, De Agri Cultura 18-19 (Hooper and Ash translation, Loeb), LacusCurtius
sources.author: Cato the Elder
sources.confirms: Instructions for building an olive pressing room and lever press
sources.qualifies: Primary source, Hooper and Ash translation

sources.title: Curtis, Robert I., Ancient Food Technology (Brill, 2001), ch. on olive oil and wine presses
sources.author: Curtis, Robert I.
sources.confirms: Survey of ancient food technology including oil and wine

screw-press-olive-oil-100bce.verification_note: Pliny's and Cato's texts were read; Curtis's Brill book was confirmed through DOI metadata only.
screw-press-olive-oil-100bce.detail: Olive oil served as food, lamp fuel, soap and medicine, so pressing technology affected daily life. Cato's lever press used a 25-foot beam, windlass and stone weights. Pliny's note dates screw presses to about 100 BCE or after. Archaeological press beds and weights survive across North Africa, Spain and Syria. Roman screw-making, cut by hand in wood, also underlies later printing and coining presses.

picture.alt: Roman-period olive press at Capernaum, Israel

screw-press-olive-oil-100bce.dating_note: Pliny (c. 77 CE) says screw presses appeared within the last hundred years; the 100 BCE anchor is approximate.

shiji-sima-qian-91bce.summary: Sima Qian, Grand Scribe at Emperor Wu's court, finished around 91 BCE a history in 130 chapters that Britannica dates to about 85 BCE and describes as eighteen years' work. He arranged annals of rulers, chronological tables, treatises on rites, music, calendar, astronomy, rivers and economy, hereditary houses and biographies of individuals from generals to merchants and assassins. Durrant's Cloudy Mirror calls it China's first comprehensive history and shows its tensions between duty and self-expression, since Sima Qian wrote on after castration for defending a disgraced general. Its five-part structure became a template for later dynastic histories.

sources.title: Durrant, Stephen W., The Cloudy Mirror: Tension and Conflict in the Writings of Sima Qian (SUNY Press, 1995)
sources.author: Durrant, Stephen W.
sources.confirms: Shiji as China's first comprehensive history; tension between history and self-expression

sources.title: 'Shiji', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Written c. 85 BCE over 18 years; 130 chapters; five-part structure as pattern for later histories

shiji-sima-qian-91bce.detail: Sima Qian inherited his father Sima Tan's project and access to imperial archives. His treatise on calendar and his account of Li Bing's waterworks and Qin's wall are key sources for technology in this period. Durrant describes Shiji as 'as much his story as it is history'. Completion is dated between 91 and 86 BCE from his letter to Ren An, which also explains his motives.

picture.alt: Portrait of Sima Qian from a Ming-dynasty album of sages and worthies (later portrait)
picture.credit: 歷代聖賢半身像　冊　司馬遷. 故宮典藏資料檢索. National Palace Museum.

shiji-sima-qian-91bce.dating_note: Completion is placed c. 91 BCE from Sima Qian's letter to Ren An; Britannica gives c. 85 BCE.

roman-hypocaust-80bce.summary: Roman bath buildings of the early first century BCE raised floors on pillars of brick so that hot gases from a furnace could circulate beneath and rise through hollow wall tiles, heating rooms evenly without smoke inside. Pliny credits Sergius Orata, a wealthy entrepreneur around 90 BCE, with inventing 'shower-baths' or hanging baths (balneae pensiles), and later writers made him inventor of hypocausts. Fagan's 1996 article in Phoenix doubts this attribution, arguing Orata installed heated fish tanks or baths for profit. Yegul's Baths and Bathing in Classical Antiquity sets hypocausts within bath architecture. Heated floors spread with baths across the empire.

sources.title: Fagan, Garrett G., 'Sergius Orata: Inventor of the Hypocaust?', Phoenix 50 (1996)
sources.author: Fagan, Garrett G.
sources.confirms: Doubts that Orata invented hypocaust

sources.title: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 9.79 (9.168 Rackham numbering), ToposText
sources.author: Pliny the Elder
sources.confirms: Orata invented shower-baths or hanging baths

sources.title: Yegül, Fikret, Baths and Bathing in Classical Antiquity (MIT Press, 1992)
sources.author: Yegül, Fikret
sources.confirms: Baths and bathing architecture

roman-hypocaust-80bce.verification_note: Pliny's text was read; Fagan's article was confirmed through DOI metadata; Yegul's publisher page gives no details.
roman-hypocaust-80bce.detail: Excavated hypocausts at Pompeii's Stabian Baths and in Greek baths at Olympia show gradual development from channel heating in the third and second centuries BCE.
