Fuel was wood or charcoal burned in a praefurnium. Hypocausts heated caldaria to over 40 degrees. Date here is approximate; Orata's floruit is around 90 BCE, and pillared hypocausts appear in early first century BCE baths in Campania and Latium.

picture.alt: Pilae stacks supporting the floor of a Roman hypocaust, Thermenmuseum Heerlen

roman-hypocaust-80bce.dating_note: Pliny credits Orata c. 90 BCE with hanging baths; Fagan 1996 argues hypocaust attribution is a later inference.

lucretius-progress-55bce.summary: In Book 5 of De Rerum Natura, Lucretius narrates how people learned to use fire, then discovered copper, gold, iron, silver and lead when forest fires melted ore from rocks, and how weaving, farming, music and writing followed one improvement at a time, driven by need and by reason. He wrote that practice and experience of eager minds taught each art gradually. Sedley's Stanford Encyclopedia entry places this Epicurean poem around 55 BCE, and Campbell's commentary treats its account of creation and development. Unlike myths of a golden age, Lucretius saw culture as cumulative human invention.

sources.title: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura Book 5 (W. E. Leonard translation), Project Gutenberg
sources.author: Lucretius
sources.confirms: Book 5: discovery of metals through forest fires; stepwise progress of arts

sources.title: Campbell, Gordon, Lucretius on Creation and Evolution: A Commentary on De Rerum Natura Book Five, Lines 772-1104 (Oxford University Press, 2003)
sources.author: Campbell, Gordon
sources.confirms: Commentary on Lucretius' account of creation and development

sources.title: Sedley, David, 'Lucretius', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.author: Sedley, David
sources.confirms: Lucretius' life, date and Epicurean physics

lucretius-progress-55bce.verification_note: Leonard's translation and Sedley's entry support this entry; Campbell's commentary is cited as supporting literature.
lucretius-progress-55bce.detail: Leonard's translation on Project Gutenberg renders Lucretius' account of early metallurgy and the passage from bronze to iron arms. Lucretius tempered optimism with warnings that wealth and war grew with technique. His poem was lost for centuries and recovered in 1417, influencing Renaissance and Enlightenment ideas of progress. Under this project's rules this is a hope record about cumulative technical change.

picture.alt: First page of Lucretius, De rerum natura, in a ninth-century manuscript, Leiden VLF 30

lucretius-progress-55bce.dating_note: Lucretius died c. 55 BCE according to Jerome; the poem's date is inferred from Cicero's 54 BCE letter mentioning it.

sheep-southern-africa-50bce.summary: Fragmentary bones from South African sites dated to about 2000 years ago are domestic sheep, an identification made by palaeoproteomics in 2021 that settled doubts about distinguishing early livestock from similar-sized wild antelope. Karim Sadr argues that livestock reached southern Africa in two separate events. One view holds that Khoe-speaking migrants from East Africa brought them; another that local hunter-gatherers acquired them through exchange. Sheep allowed pastoral life in Cape grasslands with no earlier farming. Pottery appears at about the same time.

sources.title: Coutu, Ashley N.; et al., 'Palaeoproteomics confirm earliest domesticated sheep in southern Africa ca. 2000 BP', Scientific Reports 11 (2021)
sources.author: Coutu, Ashley N.; Taurozzi, Alberto J.; Mackie, Meaghan; Jensen, Theis Zetner Trolle; Collins, Matthew J.; Sealy, Judith
sources.confirms: Palaeoproteomics confirms earliest domesticated sheep in South Africa c. 2000 BP

sources.title: Sadr, Karim, 'Livestock First Reached Southern Africa in Two Separate Events', PLOS ONE 10 (2015)
sources.author: Sadr, Karim
sources.confirms: Livestock reached southern Africa in two events; migration versus diffusion debate

sheep-southern-africa-50bce.detail: Sites such as Spoegrivier, Blombos and Die Kelders yielded early sheep remains. Sheep descended from Southwest Asian stock and came via East Africa, moving south through Zambia and Botswana or along the Atlantic coast. Cattle arrived later, perhaps centuries afterward. Genetic studies of Khoe-San populations show East African admixture consistent with pastoralist migration. Earliest sheep dates fall around 50 BCE.
sheep-southern-africa-50bce.dating_note: Earliest sheep dates cluster around 2000 BP; whether they arrived by migration or diffusion is debated.

julian-calendar-45bce.summary: Suetonius reports that Caesar, as dictator and pontifex maximus, adjusted a calendar so disordered by neglected intercalations that harvest festivals fell in winter, fixing a year of 365 days, abolishing an intercalary month and adding one day every fourth year, after inserting two extra months between November and December in 46 BCE to realign seasons. Feeney's Caesar's Calendar studies how this reform reshaped Roman conceptions of time. Stern's Calendars in Antiquity compares it with other ancient systems. The Julian year ran about eleven minutes long, a drift corrected by Gregory XIII in 1582.

sources.title: Feeney, Denis, Caesar's Calendar: Ancient Time and the Beginnings of History (University of California Press, 2007)
sources.author: Feeney, Denis
sources.confirms: Reformed calendar and Roman conception of time

sources.title: Stern, Sacha, Calendars in Antiquity: Empires, States, and Societies (Oxford University Press, 2012), ch. 4
sources.author: Stern, Sacha
sources.confirms: Comparative study of ancient calendars

sources.title: Suetonius, Life of Julius Caesar 40 (Rolfe translation, Loeb), LacusCurtius
sources.author: Suetonius
sources.confirms: 365 days; intercalary month abolished; one day every fourth year; two months inserted

julian-calendar-45bce.detail: Caesar drew on Alexandrian astronomy, with Sosigenes named by Pliny as adviser. Pontiffs at first intercalated every third year by mistake, which Augustus corrected. Months were renamed Julius and later Augustus. Julian reckoning became standard across Europe and remains in use for liturgy in Orthodox churches. It was both a computational rule for time and a policy imposed by a state.

picture.alt: The Fasti Antiates Maiores, a painted pre-Julian Roman calendar from Antium, Palazzo Massimo Rome

long-count-chiapa-de-corzo-36bce.summary: Stela 2 at Chiapa de Corzo in Chiapas carries a fragmentary Long Count date read as 7.16.3.2.13, corresponding to 36 BCE in the usual correlation, earliest such date yet found; Tres Zapotes Stela C follows at 32 BCE. Long Count notation records days elapsed from a base date in 3114 BCE using positional place values of 20 and 18, requiring a placeholder concept for empty positions. These Cycle 7 monuments come from epi-Olmec contexts. A find at San Bartolo shows 260-day calendar use centuries earlier.

sources.title: Coe, Michael D., 'Cycle 7 Monuments in Middle America: A Reconsideration', American Anthropologist 59 (1957)
sources.author: Coe, Michael D.
sources.confirms: Reconsideration of Cycle 7 monuments

sources.title: Pool, Christopher A., Olmec Archaeology and Early Mesoamerica (Cambridge University Press, 2007), ch. 7 on Tres Zapotes Stela C
sources.author: Pool, Christopher A.
sources.confirms: Epi-Olmec context of early Long Count monuments

sources.title: Stuart, David; et al., 'An early Maya calendar record from San Bartolo, Guatemala', Science Advances 8 (2022)
sources.author: Stuart, David; Hurst, Heather; Beltrán, Boris; Saturno, William
sources.confirms: San Bartolo 7 Deer day sign c. 300 to 200 BCE; no Long Count

long-count-chiapa-de-corzo-36bce.verification_note: Coe's article was seen as journal metadata; Pool's book as a publisher page; Stuart 2022 was read in full but concerns San Bartolo, not Chiapa de Corzo. The 36 BCE reading comes from general scholarship.
long-count-chiapa-de-corzo-36bce.detail: Dates were carved as bar-and-dot numerals in a vertical column. A shell-like zero glyph appears explicitly on later monuments, though positional logic was already needed at Chiapa de Corzo. Correlation of Maya dates with our calendar follows the GMT constant, debated within a few days. Stela 2 marks positional notation with placeholder in the Americas, independent of Old World systems.

picture.alt: Mound at the archaeological zone of Chiapa de Corzo, Chiapas

long-count-chiapa-de-corzo-36bce.dating_note: Reading of Stela 2 as 36 BCE depends on reconstructing a damaged baktun coefficient and on the GMT correlation.

vitruvius-water-wheel-25bce.summary: In Book 10 of De Architectura, written about 25 BCE, Vitruvius describes undershot water wheels that lift water in buckets and then a mill in which a wheel in a stream turns an axle with a toothed drum engaging a horizontal toothed wheel on a vertical shaft that spins a millstone, with a hopper feeding grain. This is the earliest clear description of geared water power for grinding. Wilson's 2002 article in Journal of Roman Studies argues that water mills spread more widely in Roman times than once thought. Wikander's handbook chapter surveys evidence for mills from Hellenistic to late antique times.

sources.title: Vitruvius, De Architectura 10.5 (Gwilt translation), LacusCurtius
sources.author: Vitruvius
sources.confirms: Water mills with toothed drum-wheel driving millstone

sources.title: Wilson, Andrew, 'Machines, Power and the Ancient Economy', Journal of Roman Studies 92 (2002)
sources.author: Wilson, Andrew
sources.confirms: Machines and power in the ancient economy; wider use of water mills

sources.title: Wikander, Örjan, 'The Water-Mill', in Handbook of Ancient Water Technology (Brill, 2000)
sources.author: Wikander, Örjan
sources.confirms: Survey of the ancient water mill

vitruvius-water-wheel-25bce.detail: Earlier references include a Greek epigram by Antipater praising water-driven mills and a mention at Mithridates' palace at Cabira around 65 BCE. Vitruvius's design transmitted vertical wheel motion through right-angle gearing, allowing speed change. Roman mills at Barbegal in Gaul later ran sixteen wheels. Water power for grinding grain freed human and animal labour and became medieval Europe's main energy source.

picture.alt: Remains of the Barbegal aqueduct and watermill complex near Arles, France (second century CE)

vitruvius-water-wheel-25bce.dating_note: De Architectura is dated c. 30 to 20 BCE from its dedication to Augustus.

bantu-iron-spread-1.summary: Between about 200 BCE and 400 CE, farming communities speaking Bantu languages move from East Africa's Great Lakes region down both sides of Lake Malawi into Zimbabwe, Mozambique and South Africa, bringing bloomery iron smelting, pearl millet and sorghum, cattle and distinctive pottery styles (Urewe, Kwale, Gokomere, Ziwa, Mzonjani). David Killick's review assesses radiocarbon dates for sub-Saharan iron and finds secure evidence for smelting in East and southern Africa from about 500 BCE onward, while older claims for independent invention before 1000 BCE in West and Central Africa remain contested. Gokomere and Ziwa village sites on Zimbabwe's plateau, with iron tools, slag and cattle bone, form an agricultural foundation on which Mapungubwe and Great Zimbabwe later build.

sources.title: Killick, David, 'Cairo to Cape: The Spread of Metallurgy through Eastern and Southern Africa', Journal of World Prehistory 22 (2009)
sources.author: Killick, David
sources.confirms: Reviews radiocarbon evidence for iron smelting in eastern and southern Africa and its association with Bantu-speaking farming communities from about 500 BCE to 500 CE.

sources.title: Mitchell, Peter, 'Southern African Iron Age', in Mitchell and Lane (eds), 'The Oxford Handbook of African Archaeology', Oxford University Press (2013)
sources.author: Mitchell, Peter
sources.confirms: Surveys Early Iron Age settlement in southern Africa, including Gokomere, Ziwa and coastal Mzonjani sites, dated from the second to fifth centuries CE.

sources.title: Huffman, Thomas N., 'Handbook to the Iron Age: The Archaeology of Pre-Colonial Farming Societies in Southern Africa', University of KwaZulu-Natal Press (2007); reviewed in Choice 46 (2008)
sources.author: Huffman, Thomas N.
sources.confirms: Catalogues ceramic facies and radiocarbon dates for Early Iron Age farming settlement in Zimbabwe and South Africa.

bantu-iron-spread-1.verification_note: Range c. 200 BCE to 400 CE from radiocarbon on Early Iron Age villages; claims for earlier independent African iron remain disputed.
bantu-iron-spread-1.detail: Year 1 is a placeholder within a range of c. 200 BCE to 400 CE. Linguistic reconstruction and ceramics agree on eastward and southward streams; dating is radiocarbon on charcoal from settlement layers. Debate continues over whether iron arrived with migrating farmers or was adopted by existing populations, and over disputed early dates from Nigeria and Gabon. Lydenburg heads (c. 500 CE), seven fired-clay heads from Mpumalanga, show ceramic art of these communities. Furnaces were low shaft or bowl types with bellows and clay tuyeres, producing bloom that smiths forged into hoes, axes, arrowheads and bangles.

picture.alt: Lydenburg head, fired clay, c. 500 CE, Iziko Museums
picture.credit: Nkansahrexford, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

bantu-iron-spread-1.dating_note: Range c. 200 BCE to 400 CE from radiocarbon on Early Iron Age villages; claims for earlier independent African iron remain disputed.

polynesia-long-pause-1.summary: Lapita settlers reach Fiji, Tonga and Samoa by about 900 BCE and then stop; for some 1,500 to 2,000 years no islands east of Samoa are settled. In this interval, West Polynesian communities develop Polynesian language, double-hulled sailing canoes and navigation by stars, swells and birds. Over 1,400 radiocarbon dates on short-lived materials place initial colonisation of Society Islands around 1025 to 1120 CE and of remote archipelagos (Hawaii, Marquesas, Rapa Nui, New Zealand) in 1190 to 1290, overturning earlier claims of settlement in 300 to 600 CE based on older dates. Lake sediment from Atiu shows people in southern Cooks by about 900. Micronesian settlement of Pohnpei and Kosrae occurs within this period, around 1 to 500 CE.

sources.title: Wilmshurst, Janet M.; Hunt, Terry L.; Lipo, Carl P.; Anderson, Atholl J., 'High-precision radiocarbon dating shows recent and rapid initial human colonization of East Polynesia', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 108 (2011)
sources.author: Wilmshurst, Janet M.; Hunt, Terry L.; Lipo, Carl P.; Anderson, Atholl J.
sources.confirms: Analyses 1,434 radiocarbon dates and concludes East Polynesia was colonised in two pulses, c. 1025 to 1120 CE (Societies) and c. 1190 to 1290 CE (remote islands), rejecting earlier first-millennium dates.

sources.title: Sear, David A. et al., 'Human settlement of East Polynesia earlier, incremental, and coincident with prolonged South Pacific drought', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 117 (2020)
sources.author: Sear, David A.
sources.confirms: Lake sediment evidence from Atiu indicates human presence in the southern Cook Islands by c. 900 CE.
sources.qualifies: Proposes an earlier and more incremental settlement than Wilmshurst's model; both agree against 300 to 600 CE dates.

sources.title: Rainbird, Paul, 'The Archaeology of Micronesia', Cambridge University Press (2004)
sources.author: Rainbird, Paul
sources.confirms: Dates settlement of Pohnpei and Kosrae in eastern Micronesia to the first centuries CE.

polynesia-long-pause-1.verification_note: East Polynesian settlement is now dated c. 900 to 1290 CE (Sear 2020 earlier, Wilmshurst 2011 later); older claims of 300 to 600 CE are superseded.
polynesia-long-pause-1.detail: Years 1 to 500 fall inside a pause running from c. 900 BCE to 1200 CE, with voyaging technology developing but no dated eastern settlement. Earlier chronologies (Marquesas c. 300 CE, Hawaii c. 400 to 600) relied on radiocarbon on unidentified wood with inbuilt age and are no longer accepted. Sweet potato transfer from South America is dated to about 1000 to 1200. Explanations for a pause include wind patterns, since prevailing easterlies oppose eastward sailing until El Nino reversals, and development of shunting outrigger rigs. Pohnpei and Kosrae ceramics and radiocarbon place Micronesian high-island settlement at about 1 to 500 CE.

picture.alt: Polynesian double-hulled and outrigger canoes
picture.credit: Nurg, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

polynesia-long-pause-1.dating_note: East Polynesian settlement is now dated c. 900 to 1290 CE (Sear 2020 earlier, Wilmshurst 2011 later); older claims of 300 to 600 CE are superseded.

terra-preta-1.summary: Along bluffs of Amazon tributaries, settlements accumulate dark earths up to two metres deep, formed from charcoal, pottery, bone, fish waste and excrement over centuries of occupation. Glaser and Birk's 2012 review shows these soils hold three times as much organic carbon and far more phosphorus and calcium than surrounding oxisols, with charcoal (biochar) stabilising nutrients. Radiocarbon dates place most formation between about 500 BCE and 1500 CE, with many sites starting in early centuries CE. Terra preta allowed sedentary farming and populations later reported by Orellana's 1542 expedition, and inspired modern biochar research. Whether formation was deliberate soil management or a byproduct of refuse is debated; both views agree on human origin.

sources.title: Glaser, Bruno and Birk, Jago Jonathan, 'State of the scientific knowledge on properties and genesis of Anthropogenic Dark Earths in Central Amazonia (terra preta de Indio)', Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta 82 (2012)
sources.author: Glaser, Bruno; Birk, Jago Jonathan
sources.confirms: Reviews composition, charcoal content, nutrient retention and radiocarbon chronology of Amazonian dark earths from c. 500 BCE onward.

sources.title: Neves, Eduardo G. et al., 'Historical and Socio-cultural Origins of Amazonian Dark Earths', in Lehmann et al. (eds), 'Amazonian Dark Earths: Origin, Properties, Management', Kluwer (2003)
sources.author: Neves, Eduardo G.; Petersen, James B.; Bartone, Robert N.; da Silva, Carlos Augusto
sources.confirms: Presents radiocarbon dates from Central Amazon sites showing dark earth formation beginning in the first centuries CE.

terra-preta-1.verification_note: Formation spans c. 500 BCE to 1500 CE; intensity and intent are debated.
terra-preta-1.detail: Year 1 is a placeholder within a long range; this is an era-like process. Dates come from charcoal in soil profiles and from pottery phases such as Manacapuru and Paredao in central Amazonia. Arroyo-Kalin and others argue for intentional management through burning and mulching; Glaser's review leaves intent open. Estimated extent ranges from 0.1 to 3 percent of Amazonia, with sites averaging 20 hectares and some over 200. A 2021 study of Marajo and Xingu sites found pre-Columbian populations increased soil fertility in a few decades, and farmers today seek out terra preta plots for papaya and maize.

picture.alt: Profile of terra preta dark earth beside pale Amazonian oxisol
picture.credit: Bruno Glaser, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

terra-preta-1.dating_note: Formation spans c. 500 BCE to 1500 CE; intensity and intent are debated.

wang-mang-currency-9.summary: Wang Mang takes Han's throne in 9 CE and over six years issues four coinage reforms, reviving knife and spade money alongside round cash in 28 denominations, while nationalising land, banning slave sales, and setting up wujun liuguan, Five Equalisations and Six Controls: market offices in major cities to buy surplus goods, sell at posted prices, lend to farmers, and run salt, iron, liquor and coinage monopolies. Dubs's 1939 analysis of Hanshu's account shows these reforms produced counterfeiting, confiscation and collapse of trust; most were repealed by 14 CE and his regime fell in 23. His episode becomes a reference point for later Chinese debates on state price management and currency, including Tang and Song paper money.

sources.title: Dubs, Homer H., 'Wang Mang and His Economic Reforms', T'oung Pao 35 (1939)
sources.author: Dubs, Homer H.
sources.confirms: Describes the currency reforms of 7 to 14 CE, the wujun liuguan market and credit offices, monopolies, and their failure as recorded in the Hanshu.

sources.title: Ban Gu, 'Hanshu 99, Wang Mang zhuan' (c. 100 CE), digitized at Chinese Text Project
sources.author: Ban Gu
sources.confirms: Primary account of Wang Mang's accession in 9 CE, coinage changes and market regulation decrees.

sources.title: Thierry, Francois, 'Monnaies chinoises I: L'antiquite preimperiale', Bibliotheque nationale de France (1997); knife coins of Wang Mang in BnF and British Museum collections
sources.confirms: Museum documentation of Xin dynasty knife and spade coinage types.

wang-mang-currency-9.detail: Han equal-transport (junshu) and price-stabilisation (pingzhun) offices founded by Sang Hongyang in 110 BCE are precedents; Wang Mang's version added credit and wider monopolies. Scholars disagree whether his reforms were Confucian idealism or fiscal desperation; Dubs reads them as both. Han coin moulds and knife coins survive in quantity, including gold-inlaid 'one knife worth five thousand' pieces of 7 CE. Hanshu 99 reports that each currency change left people 'weeping in markets and roads' and that counterfeiters were enslaved by hundreds of thousands. Land nationalisation (wangtian) was withdrawn after three years. Later historians, from Ban Gu onward, wrote him as a usurper.

picture.alt: Knife coin issued under Wang Mang
picture.credit: Gary Lee Todd, Ph.D., CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

ennion-glass-25.summary: Glassblowing begins on Syro-Palestinian coasts in the mid first century BCE; within decades workshops combine blowing with multi-part moulds. Vessels signed 'Ennion made it' in Greek, found from Jerusalem to Italy and Spain, carry fine relief ornament and a maker's name, among the first branded products in glass. Christopher Lightfoot's 2014 Metropolitan Museum study dates Ennion's activity to the first half of the first century CE and locates his workshop at or near Sidon. Mould blowing allows series production of identical shapes. Pliny names Sidon as home of glass craft, and blown glass soon fills Roman tables, windows and burials, base for Roman window glass and later Islamic and Venetian traditions.

sources.title: Lightfoot, Christopher S., 'Ennion: Master of Roman Glass', Metropolitan Museum of Art (2014); reviewed in Journal of Glass Studies / American Journal of Archaeology
sources.author: Lightfoot, Christopher S.
sources.confirms: Catalogues signed Ennion vessels, dates them to the first half of the first century CE and discusses mould-blowing technique and the Sidonian workshop.

sources.title: Stern, E. Marianne, 'Roman Glassblowing in a Cultural Context', American Journal of Archaeology 103 (1999)
sources.author: Stern, E. Marianne
sources.confirms: Discusses the origins of glassblowing on the Levantine coast and the spread of mould-blown wares.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, 'Glass jug signed by Ennion', accession 17.194.226
sources.confirms: Museum record of a signed Ennion mould-blown vessel dated first half of the first century CE.

ennion-glass-25.verification_note: Year is approximate within the span given in the summary.
ennion-glass-25.detail: Year 25 is approximate within Ennion's floruit of about 1 to 50 CE. Over 50 signed pieces are known, in one- and two-handled cups, jugs and bowls, with inscriptions set in tabulae ansatae. Debate continues over whether Ennion worked in Sidon or in Italy, since many finds come from Italian sites; Lightfoot favours a Levantine origin with wide export. Other named glassmakers of this generation include Aristeas, Meges and Jason. Mould seams visible on surviving vessels show two- and three-part moulds of clay or stone, and matching cups from distant findspots prove single moulds served many castings.

picture.alt: Mould-blown glass jug signed by Ennion, Metropolitan Museum of Art
picture.credit: Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

du-shi-water-bellows-31.summary: Hou Hanshu records that in 31 CE Du Shi, as governor of Nanyang, 'made water-powered bellows (shuipai) for casting agricultural implements, using little labour and achieving much, so the people found it convenient'. Nanyang was a centre of Han iron smelting with state foundries, and blast furnaces there reached temperatures for liquid cast iron. Donald Wagner's study of Chinese iron treats this as antiquity's earliest dated use of water power for metallurgical blowing, several centuries before European water-driven bellows. Han furnace sites and pottery models of blower installations survive. Evidence is textual: a single sentence in an official biography, with no surviving mechanism, so reconstruction of its drive (a horizontal wheel with crank or a vertical wheel) is inferred from later illustrations.

sources.title: Fan Ye, 'Hou Hanshu 31, Biography of Du Shi' (5th c.), digitized at Wikisource
sources.author: Fan Ye
sources.confirms: Text: 造作水排，鑄為農器，用力少，見功多，百姓便之, in the seventh year of Jianwu (31 CE) after Du Shi's transfer to Nanyang.

sources.title: Wagner, Donald B., 'Iron and Steel in Ancient China', Brill (1993)
sources.author: Wagner, Donald B.
sources.confirms: Discusses Han blast-furnace iron production, Nanyang state ironworks and Du Shi's water-powered bellows of 31 CE as the earliest dated metallurgical use of water power.

sources.title: Wagner, Donald B., 'Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 5 part 11: Ferrous Metallurgy', Cambridge University Press (2008)
sources.author: Wagner, Donald B.
sources.confirms: Full treatment of Han ironworks, cast-iron technology and the shuipai evidence.

du-shi-water-bellows-31.detail: Dating rests on Hou Hanshu's entry year; later texts (Sanguozhi on Han Ji, c. 238) say water bellows gave three times output of horse-powered ones. Needham reconstructed its drive as a horizontal water wheel with crank and connecting rod on a model of Wang Zhen's 1313 Nong shu illustration, which scholars treat as plausible but unproven. Han bellows were probably leather or wooden box types worked by pistons or by a pushing bar, as shown on a Shandong tomb relief. Nanyang's Wafangzhuang foundry site yielded furnace bases, moulds and slag over 120,000 square metres. Du Shi's biography also praises him for cutting ponds and expanding farmland.

picture.alt: Eastern Han pottery model of a blast furnace blower installation
picture.credit: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

arikamedu-50.summary: Excavated by Wheeler in 1945 and re-examined by Vimala Begley from 1989, Arikamedu on India's Coromandel coast yields Arretine sigillata stamped by Italian potters, Mediterranean amphorae, Roman glass, a brick warehouse and dyeing tanks. Begley's reassessment pushes occupation back to the second century BCE and shows a local bead industry in glass and semiprecious stone exporting across the Indian Ocean and to Southeast Asia. Roman gold and silver coin hoards across Tamil Nadu and Periplus references to Poduke confirm this trade. Arikamedu shows how monsoon routes connected Mediterranean consumers, south Indian producers and Southeast Asian markets in the first century CE.

sources.title: Begley, Vimala, 'Arikamedu Reconsidered', American Journal of Archaeology 87 (1983)
sources.author: Begley, Vimala
sources.confirms: Re-dates Arikamedu's occupation from the second century BCE, documents Arretine ware, amphorae and the bead industry.

sources.title: Tomber, Roberta, 'Indo-Roman Trade: From Pots to Pepper', Duckworth (2008); reviewed by Whitehouse, Journal of Roman Archaeology 23 (2010)
sources.author: Tomber, Roberta
sources.confirms: Synthesises ceramic evidence for Indo-Roman trade including Arikamedu and the Red Sea ports.

sources.title: 'Periplus of the Erythraean Sea' (1st c. CE), trans. Schoff, Fordham Internet History Sourcebooks
sources.confirms: Section 60 names Poduke among the market towns of the east coast.

arikamedu-50.verification_note: Year is approximate within the span given in the summary.
arikamedu-50.detail: Arretine ware dates Roman-contact layers to c. 10 BCE to 50 CE, so year 50 is approximate for peak trade. Wheeler's 'Roman trading station' model has given way to a picture of an Indian port receiving Mediterranean imports and run by local merchants. Identification with Poduke is accepted but unproven. Begley's project found no break in occupation, and bead workshops continued after Roman imports stopped. Finds include Tamil-Brahmi graffiti on sherds, Rouletted Ware distributed from Sri Lanka to Vietnam, and a sherd inscribed in Greek, now housed at Pondicherry Museum.

picture.alt: Brick remains at Arikamedu, Early Historic site near Pondicherry
picture.credit: Jayaseerlourdhuraj, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

gandhara-scrolls-50.summary: In 1994 the British Library acquired 29 birch-bark scroll fragments stored in clay pots, written in Kharosthi script and Gandhari language and dated by palaeography and radiocarbon to around 50 CE. Richard Salomon's 1999 study identifies them as Dharmaguptaka school texts, including verses, avadanas and commentaries, probably interred at a monastery near Hadda in Afghanistan. Further collections (Senior, Schoyen, Bajaur) followed, some radiocarbon-dated to the first century BCE. These scrolls show Buddhist texts in written form centuries before any surviving Pali manuscript and document scroll format, pot burial and scribal practice in a region through which Buddhism passed to Central Asia and China.

sources.title: Salomon, Richard, 'Ancient Buddhist Scrolls from Gandhara: The British Library Kharosthi Fragments', University of Washington Press (1999); reviewed by Oskar von Hinuber in Journal of the American Oriental Society 120 (2000)
sources.author: Salomon, Richard
sources.confirms: Describes the 29 British Library scrolls, their Kharosthi script and Gandhari language, first-century dating and Dharmaguptaka affiliation.

sources.title: Allon, Mark et al., 'Radiocarbon Dating of Kharosthi Fragments from the Schoyen and Senior Manuscript Collections', in Braarvig (ed.), 'Buddhist Manuscripts in the Schoyen Collection III', Hermes (2006)
sources.author: Allon, Mark; Salomon, Richard; Jacobsen, Geraldine; Zoppi, Ugo
sources.confirms: Reports radiocarbon dates for Gandharan scrolls ranging from the first century BCE to the second century CE.

sources.title: British Library Archives and Manuscripts, 'Or 14915: Fragments of birch bark manuscript in Kharosthi'
sources.confirms: Institutional description of the birch-bark Kharosthi scrolls as the oldest surviving Buddhist manuscripts.

gandhara-scrolls-50.verification_note: Palaeography places the British Library scrolls in the first century CE; radiocarbon on related collections spans c. 100 BCE to 200 CE.
gandhara-scrolls-50.detail: Dating is palaeographic for the British Library group, with radiocarbon support from related collections; 50 CE is approximate within a span from 100 BCE to 200 CE. Provenance is unexcavated, so findspot is inferred from dealer reports and pot inscriptions. Scrolls were already damaged when buried, suggesting ritual interment of worn texts once recopied. Salomon's team in Seattle continues editing them in a Gandharan Buddhist Texts series, and Harry Falk's Bajaur collection adds Mahayana material of similar date.

picture.alt: Fragment of a Gandharan birch-bark Kharosthi scroll, British Library Or. 14915
picture.credit: British Library, Or. 14915, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

gandhara-scrolls-50.dating_note: Palaeography places the British Library scrolls in the first century CE; radiocarbon on related collections spans c. 100 BCE to 200 CE.

indian-crucible-steel-50.summary: Iron and carbon sealed in clay crucibles and heated for hours yield a high-carbon ingot that forges into blades with a watered pattern. Sharada Srinivasan's survey of Tamil Nadu sites such as Mel-siruvalur, and Gill Juleff's excavations of wind-powered furnaces at Samanalawewa in Sri Lanka, show crucible steel production in southern India and Sri Lanka by early centuries CE, with Kodumanal crucible fragments dated to late centuries BCE. Pliny praises iron 'sent to us by the Seres' and the Periplus lists Indian iron and steel among exports carried to Red Sea ports. Traded west as ferrum indicum, this metal becomes raw material for later Damascus blades and a benchmark European metallurgists tried to reproduce into the nineteenth century.

sources.title: Srinivasan, Sharada, 'Wootz Crucible Steel: A Newly Discovered Production Site in South India', Papers from the Institute of Archaeology 5 (1994)
sources.author: Srinivasan, Sharada
sources.venue: Papers from the Institute of Archaeology
sources.confirms: Reports the Mel-siruvalur crucible steel site and argues wootz production was widespread in south India.

sources.title: Juleff, Gill, 'An ancient wind-powered iron smelting technology in Sri Lanka', Nature 379 (1996)
sources.author: Juleff, Gill
sources.confirms: Excavated and experimentally tested monsoon-wind-driven furnaces at Samanalawewa dated to the first millennium CE producing high-carbon steel.

sources.title: 'Periplus of the Erythraean Sea' (1st c. CE), trans. W. H. Schoff (1912), Fordham Internet History Sourcebooks
sources.confirms: Section 6 lists Indian iron and steel among goods carried to the East African ports.

indian-crucible-steel-50.verification_note: Production dates rely on radiocarbon from Kodumanal and Sri Lankan sites plus first-century Roman texts; exact start uncertain.
indian-crucible-steel-50.detail: Year 50 is approximate; crucible technique is older in Tamil country (Kodumanal, c. 300 BCE) and Roman references cluster in the first century CE. Whether Pliny's 'Seric iron' means Indian or Chinese metal is debated; most metallurgists read it as south Indian steel shipped through Chera ports. Juleff's Samanalawewa furnaces, set on hill crests to catch monsoon wind, run from the seventh to eleventh centuries, with earlier smelting nearby. Metallographic study of Mel-siruvalur crucibles shows slag and glassy lids matching later Deccan wootz practice described by Buchanan in 1807.

picture.alt: South Indian wootz steel sword, seventeenth to eighteenth century (later object)
picture.credit: Mr McIntyre, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

indian-crucible-steel-50.dating_note: Production dates rely on radiocarbon from Kodumanal and Sri Lankan sites plus first-century Roman texts; exact start uncertain.

la-graufesenque-50.summary: At La Graufesenque near Millau in southern Gaul, workshops produce terra sigillata, glossy red tableware, on an industrial scale from about 20 CE to the early second century. Kiln records scratched on plates list firings of 25,000 to 30,000 vessels shared among named potters, each of whom stamps his products. Pieces travel to Britain, the Rhine frontier, Italy and North Africa; a crate found unopened at Pompeii in 79 CE still held Graufesenque cups. Standard shapes, makers' marks and shared kilns make this one of the best-documented cases of coordinated mass production before modern factories, and the stamps let archaeologists date sites across the Roman west to within decades.

sources.title: Fulle, Gunnar, 'The Internal Organization of the Arretine Terra Sigillata Industry: Problems of Evidence and Interpretation', Journal of Roman Studies 87 (1997)
sources.author: Fulle, Gunnar
sources.confirms: Analyses sigillata workshop organisation, potters' stamps and kiln records including the Graufesenque firing lists, and debates factory versus dispersed-workshop models.

sources.title: Marichal, Robert, 'Les graffites de La Graufesenque', Gallia Supplement 47, CNRS (1988); reviewed by Bird, Britannia 22 (1991)
sources.author: Marichal, Robert
sources.confirms: Edits the kiln-load graffiti recording tens of thousands of vessels per firing.
sources.qualifies: Fulle cautions that the term 'factory' overstates centralisation; production was shared among independent potters using common kilns.

la-graufesenque-50.verification_note: Workshop activity runs c. 20 to 120 CE; stamps and Pompeii finds anchor the mid first century peak.
la-graufesenque-50.detail: Firing lists (bordereaux d'enfournement) written in Gaulish and Latin on plates record vessel counts by potter and form; Marichal's 1988 edition publishes over 200 such graffiti. Peak output falls between 40 and 80 CE; year 50 is a midpoint and approximate. Fulle's 1997 article argues against reading these works as factories with wage labour, preferring a model of many small workshops sharing kilns and distribution. Kilns at La Graufesenque fired in a reducing-then-oxidising cycle with vessels stacked in saggars; largest known kiln held about 30,000 pieces. Clay came from local Jurassic marls, and slip was refined by levigation to give a glossy red surface.

picture.alt: Kiln firing list scratched on a sigillata plate from La Graufesenque, Musee Fenaille, Rodez
picture.credit: Pierre Tribhou, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

la-graufesenque-50.dating_note: Workshop activity runs c. 20 to 120 CE; stamps and Pompeii finds anchor the mid first century peak.

las-medulas-50.summary: From Augustus's conquest of Asturia onward, Roman state mining in northwest Spain uses water on a scale without earlier parallel. At Las Medulas in Leon, canals totalling over 100 km bring water to tanks above auriferous conglomerate; miners tunnel galleries, then release water so hillsides collapse and wash through sluices. Pliny, who served in Spain, describes gold mines where 'the earth sinks in, and the workmen are crushed beneath', rivers brought 'a distance in many instances of one hundred miles', and a yield of twenty thousand pounds of gold a year from Asturia, Gallaecia and Lusitania. Modern survey and OSL dating confirm first-century operation and show the red badlands visible today are mining waste.

sources.title: Pliny the Elder, 'Natural History 33.21' (77 CE), trans. Bostock and Riley, Perseus Digital Library
sources.author: Pliny the Elder
sources.confirms: Describes arrugiae mines, mountain collapse, rivers brought one hundred miles for washing, and a yearly yield of twenty thousand pounds of gold from Asturia, Gallaecia and Lusitania.

sources.title: Curras, Brais X. et al., 'Landscape archaeology of Roman gold mining in Lusitania: the Aurifer Tagus project', Antiquity 95 (2021)
sources.author: Curras, Brais X.; Lopez-Sanchez, Jesus; Romero, Damian; Sanchez-Palencia, F. Javier
sources.confirms: Documents Roman hydraulic gold-mining landscapes in Iberia using survey and LiDAR, confirming first to second century state-run operation and water-supply networks.

sources.title: Mattingly, David J., 'Imperialism, Power, and Identity: Experiencing the Roman Empire', Princeton University Press (2011), ch. 7
sources.author: Mattingly, David J.
sources.confirms: Treats metal mining in northwest Spain as a state-directed extractive industry of the early empire.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Las Medulas'
sources.confirms: Describes the first-century Roman hydraulic mining landscape and its canal network.

las-medulas-50.verification_note: Operation spans roughly 25 BCE to the early third century; Pliny's text and OSL dates place peak activity in the first century.
las-medulas-50.detail: Year 50 is a midpoint for an industry running from about 25 BCE to early third century; it is marked approximate. Sanchez-Palencia's teams mapped 600 million cubic metres of displaced material and water channels cut into hillsides over 100 km. Debate continues over whether gold yields justified cost, since Pliny's figure of twenty thousand pounds a year cannot be checked against mint output. Pliny describes a sequence: galleries propped on timber, miners working by lamplight for months, then water released from tanks 200 feet across so hillsides fall with a roar; gorse mats catch gold in sluices. UNESCO inscribed Las Medulas in 1997.

picture.alt: Red eroded hillsides of Las Medulas, Leon, remains of Roman hydraulic gold mining
picture.credit: Frayle from Salamanca, España, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

las-medulas-50.dating_note: Operation spans roughly 25 BCE to the early third century; Pliny's text and OSL dates place peak activity in the first century.

periplus-monsoon-50.summary: An anonymous Egyptian Greek trader, writing around 40 to 70 CE, lists ports, anchorages, goods and rulers from Red Sea harbours down East Africa to Rhapta and across to Barbarikon, Barygaza, Muziris and Poduke in India, with notes on China ('Thina') as a source of silk. He credits a pilot Hippalus with charting open-sea routes using monsoon winds, and in section 57 says sailors 'take their departure with the Indian wind' at a set season. Casson's edition analyses dating and geography. Roman coin hoards in Tamil Nadu, Indian pepper at Berenike and Muziris papyrus loan contract confirm a seasonal trade in which ships of 500 tonnes carried wine, glass and coin out and pepper, gems and textiles back.

sources.title: Casson, Lionel, 'The Periplus Maris Erythraei: Text with Introduction, Translation, and Commentary', Princeton University Press (1989)
sources.author: Casson, Lionel
sources.confirms: Critical edition dating the text to c. 40 to 70 CE and analysing monsoon navigation and Indian Ocean ports.

sources.title: 'Periplus of the Erythraean Sea', trans. W. H. Schoff (1912), Fordham Internet History Sourcebooks
sources.confirms: Section 57 on Hippalus and monsoon departure; section 64 on Thina and silk.

sources.title: Sidebotham, Steven E., 'Berenike and the Ancient Maritime Spice Route', University of California Press (2011)
sources.author: Sidebotham, Steven E.
sources.confirms: Archaeological evidence from Berenike for Indian Ocean trade including pepper, teak and Tamil-Brahmi graffiti.

periplus-monsoon-50.verification_note: Year is approximate within the span given in the summary.
periplus-monsoon-50.detail: Casson's date of c. 40 to 70 rests on named rulers (Malichus II of Nabataea, Manbanos/Nahapana) and is approximate. Whether Hippalus was a person or a wind name is debated; Pliny also names him. Region is global because this text spans Africa, Arabia, India and references to China. A single tenth-century manuscript, Heidelberg Palatinus gr. 398, preserves it. Muziris papyrus (second century) records a loan on a cargo worth nearly seven million sesterces, including Gangetic nard, ivory and textiles, showing scale of single voyages. Berenike excavations found 7.5 kilograms of Indian black pepper in one jar.

picture.alt: Map of ports and routes named in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (modern map)
picture.credit: George Wynn Brereton Huntingford, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

hero-aeolipile-60.summary: In Pneumatica Hero describes a cauldron heated beneath a pivoted hollow sphere; steam passes through a tube into it and escapes from two bent nozzles, so reaction makes it spin. He presents this among devices using air, water and steam pressure to work temple doors, singing birds and fountains. Paul Keyser's 1992 analysis treats it as a demonstration of pneumatic principle, not a power source; no ancient author reports work done by it. Hero's date rests on his reference to a lunar eclipse of 13 March 62 CE in Dioptra, though Masia argues he may have taken it from tables rather than observing. This is antiquity's only described steam reaction turbine and recurs in every later history of steam.

sources.title: Keyser, Paul, 'A new look at Heron's Steam Engine', Archive for History of Exact Sciences 44 (1992)
sources.author: Keyser, Paul
sources.venue: Archive for History of Exact Sciences
sources.confirms: Analyses the aeolipile's description and performance, concluding it was a demonstration device of pneumatic principle.

sources.title: Masia, Ramon, 'On dating Hero of Alexandria', Archive for History of Exact Sciences 69 (2015)
sources.author: Masia, Ramon
sources.venue: Archive for History of Exact Sciences
sources.confirms: Reviews Neugebauer's identification of the eclipse of 62 CE in Dioptra 35.
sources.qualifies: Argues the eclipse may be an example taken from tables, so Hero's date is less certain than usually stated.

sources.title: Hero of Alexandria, 'Pneumatica' (1st c. CE), trans. Bennet Woodcroft (1851), section 50
sources.author: Hero of Alexandria
sources.confirms: Section 50 describes the steam-driven rotating sphere.

hero-aeolipile-60.verification_note: Floruit c. 62 CE rests on an eclipse reference whose evidential value Masia (2015) questions; proposed dates range over two centuries.
hero-aeolipile-60.detail: Year 60 is approximate; Hero's floruit is placed in the 60s CE on eclipse evidence, with alternatives from the first century BCE to the second century CE. Pneumatica survives in over 100 manuscripts; its earliest, Venice Marcianus gr. 516, is thirteenth century. Hero credits Ctesibius and Philo for earlier pneumatic work. Keyser estimates a reconstructed sphere spins at about 1,500 rpm with negligible torque, consistent with a toy. Vitruvius, two generations earlier, describes an aeolipile as a bronze vessel that blows steam to show wind's nature, so Hero's rotating version adds motion to an existing demonstration.

picture.alt: Modern reconstruction of Hero's aeolipile
picture.credit: Gts-tg, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

hero-aeolipile-60.dating_note: Floruit c. 62 CE rests on an eclipse reference whose evidential value Masia (2015) questions; proposed dates range over two centuries.

hero-automata-60.summary: Hero's Peri automatopoietikes describes a mobile theatre driven by a falling weight whose cord, wound round axles with pegs and reversals, makes a cart advance, stop, turn and return on a set programme, and a stationary theatre playing a five-act Nauplius drama with moving figures, sound and changing scenery. In Pneumatica he describes a vessel releasing a measured dose of water when a five-drachma coin drops onto a balance arm. Karin Tybjerg reads these works as displays of mechanical knowledge in which wonder is a product in its own right. Together they give antiquity's most detailed record of sequence control by a stored pattern of cords and pegs and its only coin-operated machine.

sources.title: Tybjerg, Karin, 'Wonder-making and philosophical wonder in Hero of Alexandria', Studies in History and Philosophy of Science 34 (2003)
sources.author: Tybjerg, Karin
sources.venue: Studies in History and Philosophy of Science Part A
sources.confirms: Analyses Hero's Automata and Pneumatica as demonstrations of mechanical wonder and knowledge, including the mobile and stationary theatres.

sources.title: Hero of Alexandria, 'Pneumatica' (1st c. CE), trans. Woodcroft (1851), section 21, 'Sacrificial vessel which flows only when money is introduced'
sources.author: Hero of Alexandria
sources.confirms: Section 21 describes a coin dropping onto a lever that opens a valve to dispense a measured quantity of water.

sources.title: Murphy, Susan, 'Heron of Alexandria's On Automaton-Making', History of Technology 17 (1995)
sources.author: Murphy, Susan
sources.confirms: English translation and commentary of the Automata treatise, describing weight drive, peg-and-cord programming of motion and the Nauplius theatre.

hero-automata-60.verification_note: Year is approximate within the span given in the summary.
hero-automata-60.detail: Dating follows Hero's eclipse reference and is approximate. Automata draws on Philo of Byzantium (third century BCE), whom Hero cites. Manuscript diagrams are medieval; reconstructions by Noel Sharkey in 2007 and in Giovanni Battista Aleotti's 1589 Italian edition demonstrate that described programming works. Cord wound in alternating directions around an axle encodes forward and backward motion, and slack loops encode pauses, so a single falling weight plays out a fixed sequence, an arrangement historians compare to later cam and punched-card control. Imagery here shows a 1589 printed diagram and a labelled modern model.

picture.alt: Diagram from the 1589 Italian edition of Hero's Automata (1589 printed edition)
picture.credit: Hero of Alexandria, 1589 Italian edition, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

seneca-epistle-90-64.summary: In Letter 90 to Lucilius, written around 64 CE, Seneca rejects Posidonius's claim that philosophers invented crafts. He lists recent novelties: glazed windows letting in light through transparent panes, baths heated through pipes set in walls, polished marble, and shorthand that keeps pace with speech. He writes that such inventions were 'devised by the lowest grade of slaves', coming from a mind 'nimble and keen, but not great or exalted' and serving luxury rather than virtue. Letter 90 is among antiquity's fullest surviving statements that technical novelty deserves suspicion, and it documents window glass and heated baths as recent arrivals in his lifetime.

sources.title: Seneca, 'Moral letters to Lucilius, Letter 90' (c. 64 CE), trans. R. M. Gummere (1920), digitized at Wikisource
sources.author: Seneca
sources.confirms: Quotes verbatim: windows admitting light through transparent tiles, vaulted baths with heating pipes, shorthand, all 'devised by the lowest grade of slaves', and inventors with minds 'nimble and keen, but not great or exalted'.

sources.title: Blankert, Albert, 'Seneca's Letters to Lucilius', The Classical Journal 60 (1965)
sources.author: Blankert, Albert
sources.confirms: Places the Letters in Seneca's retirement years of 62 to 65 CE and discusses their moral programme.

seneca-epistle-90-64.verification_note: Letters to Lucilius are dated to 62 to 65 CE from internal references; 64 is conventional.
seneca-epistle-90-64.detail: Letter 90 is a primary witness for dating two technologies: glazed windows and hypocaust piping in walls, both described as inventions 'within our own memory'. Historians of attitudes to technology read Seneca alongside Pliny's complaints about luxury and later Christian writers on curiosity as evidence that Roman elites separated moral worth from mechanical ingenuity. Seneca also credits a slave with inventing shorthand (notae) and describes a wise man of early times living in caves without such comforts. Letter 90 belongs to his final years under Nero, between retirement in 62 and forced suicide in 65; Richard Gummere's Loeb translation supplies quoted wording.

picture.alt: Engraving of a bust identified as Seneca, by Andries Vaillant, 1680 (1680 engraving)
picture.credit: Andries Vaillant (1655-1693), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

seneca-epistle-90-64.dating_note: Letters to Lucilius are dated to 62 to 65 CE from internal references; 64 is conventional.

dioscorides-70.summary: Pedanius Dioscorides of Anazarbus in Cilicia, who travelled with Roman forces, writes five books around 70 CE arranging remedies by plant, animal and mineral and by physiological effect, recording habitat, preparation, dosage and adulterations. John Riddle shows that arrangement by drug affinity was a working classification which later copyists destroyed by alphabetising. Vienna Dioscurides of about 512, made for princess Anicia Juliana with nearly 400 full-page plant paintings, is Europe's oldest surviving illustrated herbal. Translated into Arabic in Baghdad in the ninth century and printed in Greek in 1499, it remained pharmacy's reference text until the seventeenth century. Galen drew on it; Ge Hong's handbook belongs to a parallel empirical drug tradition in China.

sources.title: Riddle, John M., 'Dioscorides on Pharmacy and Medicine', University of Texas Press (1985)
sources.author: Riddle, John M.
sources.confirms: Analyses the structure and drug-affinity arrangement of De materia medica, dates it to c. 65 to 75 CE and assesses its pharmacological content.

sources.title: Nutton, Vivian, 'Ancient Medicine', 2nd ed., Routledge (2013)
sources.author: Nutton, Vivian
sources.confirms: Places Dioscorides in Neronian-Flavian Rome and describes his work's later authority.

sources.title: Osterreichische Nationalbibliothek, 'Vienna Dioscurides', Cod. med. gr. 1, UNESCO Memory of the World
sources.confirms: Describes the c. 512 CE illustrated manuscript of Dioscorides made for Anicia Juliana.

dioscorides-70.verification_note: Year is approximate within the span given in the summary.
dioscorides-70.detail: Composition in the 60s or 70s CE rests on a dedication to Areius of Tarsus and on use by Pliny and Galen; 70 is approximate. Whether Dioscorides served as an army physician is inferred from his preface about travel. Vienna manuscript plant paintings derive from an earlier illustrated tradition attributed to Krateuas, physician to Mithridates VI. Entries number about 600 plants, 35 animal products and 90 minerals, with over 1,000 preparations. Riddle finds modern pharmacology confirms many recorded actions, including willow bark for pain and autumn crocus (colchicine) for gout.

picture.alt: Peacock page from the Vienna Dioscurides manuscript, c. 512 (c. 512 manuscript)
picture.credit: Unknown author, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

last-cuneiform-75.summary: An astronomical almanac in the British Museum (W22340a), giving predicted planetary positions for Seleucid year 385, corresponding to 74 to 75 CE, is cuneiform's latest securely dated text. Hunger and de Jong's 2014 edition confirms date and content: positions of planets, lunar phenomena and eclipse possibilities computed by Babylonian arithmetical schemes. Temple astronomers at Babylon and Uruk had kept astronomical diaries since the eighth century BCE and developed predictive methods that Hipparchus and Ptolemy used; by 75 CE Esagil's temple community was cuneiform's last user. Greek and Aramaic had replaced it in all other functions. This tablet marks an end for a 3,000-year written tradition while its astronomical methods lived on in Greek.

sources.title: Hunger, Hermann and de Jong, Teije, 'Almanac W22340a from Uruk: The Latest Datable Cuneiform Tablet', Zeitschrift fur Assyriologie und Vorderasiatische Archaologie 104 (2014)
sources.author: Hunger, Hermann; de Jong, Teije
sources.confirms: Edits the almanac and dates it to 74/75 CE as the latest datable cuneiform text.

sources.title: Geller, M. J., 'The Last Wedge', Zeitschrift fur Assyriologie 87 (1997)
sources.author: Geller, M. J.
sources.confirms: Surveys the end of cuneiform writing in the first centuries CE and argues the script may have persisted in limited use into the second or third century.
sources.qualifies: Suggests cuneiform literacy may have outlived the last dated tablet.

last-cuneiform-75.detail: Its date is fixed by its own Seleucid year, so 75 CE is secure. Pliny notes in this decade that Bel's temple at Babylon still stood with astronomers active. Earlier claims for a tablet of 79/80 CE have been withdrawn. Geller's argument for later survival rests on Graeco-Babyloniaca, clay tablets with Babylonian text transliterated into Greek letters, perhaps as late as the second or third century CE. Predicted planetary positions in W22340a match modern computation within a few degrees, showing arithmetical schemes still in working order after Hellenistic astronomy had moved to geometric models.

picture.alt: Babylonian astronomical diary tablet of 141 BCE, same genre as the last dated almanac (earlier tablet of same genre)
picture.credit: Zunkir, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

pliny-natural-history-77.summary: Gaius Plinius Secundus dedicates his Natural History to Titus in 77 CE, two years before dying at Vesuvius. He claims to have gathered 'in thirty-six books 20,000 topics' from 'about 2000 volumes' by '100 select authors'. Books 33 to 37 cover metals, stone, pigments, glass and gems; book 18 agriculture; book 36 building and concrete. He records glass-making at Sidon, hydraulic gold mining in Spain, a Gallic reaping machine, and papyrus manufacture, usually naming sources. Copied continuously through late antiquity and medieval centuries, it becomes a model for encyclopedias from Isidore to Vincent of Beauvais. For technology history it is Rome's single richest inventory of materials and techniques, and also a record of anxiety about luxury and novelty.

sources.title: Pliny the Elder, 'Natural History, Preface' (77 CE), trans. Bostock and Riley, Perseus Digital Library
sources.author: Pliny the Elder
sources.confirms: Preface states the work contains in thirty-six books 20,000 topics from about 2000 volumes by 100 select authors.

sources.title: Pliny the Elder, 'Natural History 18.72' (77 CE), Perseus Digital Library
sources.author: Pliny the Elder
sources.confirms: Describes the Gallic reaping frame with teeth driven through standing corn by a yoked animal.

sources.title: Murphy, Trevor, 'Pliny the Elder's Natural History: The Empire in the Encyclopedia', Oxford University Press (2004)
sources.author: Murphy, Trevor
sources.confirms: Analyses the Natural History as an encyclopedic project tied to imperial knowledge and dates dedication to 77 CE.

pliny-natural-history-77.detail: Pliny's text is cited throughout this period's records because it documents techniques otherwise unrecorded: Sidonian glassblowing, Spanish arrugiae, Gaul's vallus reaper, and pozzolana concrete. His moralising about luxury (gold, pearls, marble) sits alongside admiration for ingenuity. Over 200 medieval manuscripts survive; a first printed edition appeared in Venice in 1469. His nephew's letter (Ep. 3.5) describes his working method: reading at meals, dictating to a secretary in his carriage, and leaving 160 notebooks written on both sides in tiny script. Trevor Murphy's 2004 study reads Natural History as an inventory of empire.

picture.alt: Opening page of a 1481 printed edition of Pliny's Naturalis Historia
picture.credit: Master of Pico, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

vallus-reaper-77.summary: Pliny writes in 77 CE that on Gaul's vast provincial estates 'a large hollow frame, armed with teeth and supported on two wheels, is driven through the standing corn, the beasts being yoked behind it', so that ears are torn off and fall within its frame. Palladius repeats this account in his fourth-century Opus agriculturae, and stone reliefs from Trier, Buzenol, Arlon, Reims and Koblenz show a mule or donkey pushing such a cart while a worker clears its comb. It is antiquity's only known mechanical harvester. Use seems confined to large estates on flat northern Gallic land, and knowledge of it disappears after 500 CE.

sources.title: Pliny the Elder, 'Natural History 18.72' (77 CE), trans. Bostock and Riley, Perseus Digital Library
sources.author: Pliny the Elder
sources.confirms: Verbatim description of the toothed reaping frame on two wheels pushed through standing corn by yoked beasts.

sources.title: White, K. D., 'The Gallo-Roman Harvesting Machine', Antiquity 41 (1967, Crossref lists 1966); see also White, 'Agricultural Implements of the Roman World', Cambridge University Press (1967)
sources.author: White, K. D.
sources.confirms: Collects Pliny, Palladius and the Belgic reliefs as evidence for the vallus and reconstructs its operation.

vallus-reaper-77.verification_note: Pliny's 77 CE text is the earliest witness; reliefs date between 100 and 300 CE.
vallus-reaper-77.detail: Reliefs were identified as reaper images only in 1958 at Buzenol, which resolved doubts about Pliny's text. Scholars disagree on why so efficient a device vanished: labour abundance, estate structure, and terrain are proposed. Year 77 is Pliny's publication date; his machine is older, so that date is approximate. Palladius (Opus agriculturae 7.2) adds detail: a driver adjusts frame height by raising or lowering its shafts, and heads collected in its box are threshed later, leaving straw standing. Experimental reconstructions by Belgian and French teams in 1958 and 2000 harvested about a hectare in a day with two workers.

picture.alt: Relief of a Gallo-Roman vallus reaping machine pushed by a mule, Rheinisches Landesmuseum Trier
picture.credit: Unknown author, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

vallus-reaper-77.dating_note: Pliny's 77 CE text is the earliest witness; reliefs date to the second and third centuries.

roman-window-glass-79.summary: Glassblowing, developed on Syro-Palestinian coasts in the first century BCE, spreads through Italy under Augustus and makes glass vessels cheap. Larson's 2019 study shows this shift took decades and depended on workshop organisation and markets rather than a single technique. Window glass follows: cast panes in wooden or bronze frames appear in baths and houses, and Vesuvius seals examples at Pompeii and Herculaneum in 79 CE, among them panes from Pompeii's Forum Baths and House of the Faun. Seneca, writing a decade earlier, counts glazed windows among inventions 'within our own memory'. Glazed openings let bath builders keep heat while admitting light, changing how Roman interiors were lit and warmed.

sources.title: Larson, Katherine A., 'Cheap, fast, good: the Roman glassblowing revolution reconsidered', Journal of Roman Archaeology 32 (2019)
sources.author: Larson, Katherine A.
sources.confirms: Documents widespread adoption of glass vessels in the first century BCE and first century CE alongside glassblowing, arguing for a gradual process driven by markets and workshop practice.

sources.title: Stern, E. Marianne, 'Roman Glassblowing in a Cultural Context', American Journal of Archaeology 103 (1999)
sources.author: Stern, E. Marianne
sources.confirms: Surveys evidence for glassblowing's origin and spread and for Roman glass workshops in Italy in the first century CE.

sources.title: Seneca, 'Moral letters to Lucilius, Letter 90' (c. 64 CE), Wikisource
sources.author: Seneca
sources.confirms: Names windows 'which admit the clear light through transparent tiles' as a device within living memory.

roman-window-glass-79.verification_note: 79 CE is the eruption date fixing a terminus ante quem; first use of window glass is earlier and undated.
roman-window-glass-79.detail: Vesuvius gives a terminus ante quem of 79 CE for cast window glass; manufacture began earlier, probably in early first century. Early panes are cast in trays and ground on one side, typically bluish-green; cylinder-blown sheet glass only becomes common from third century. Pane sizes at Herculaneum reach about 54 by 72 cm, held in bronze frames with pivots in Suburban Baths. Chemical analysis shows Roman glass was made from Egyptian natron and Levantine sand at a few primary furnaces, then shipped as chunks to secondary workshops across provinces. Window glass fragments appear at villas and forts in Britain from 60s CE.

picture.alt: Fragment of Roman cast window glass recorded by the Portable Antiquities Scheme
picture.credit: North Lincolnshire Museum, Martin Foreman, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

roman-window-glass-79.dating_note: 79 CE is the eruption date fixing a terminus ante quem; first use of window glass is earlier and undated.

lodestone-sinan-83.summary: In Lunheng, chapter Shiying, completed around 83 CE, Wang Chong writes: 司南之杓，投之於地，其柢指南, 'the south-pointing ladle: throw it on the ground and its handle points south'. Li Shu-hua's 1954 studies in Isis argue this is history's earliest clear record of magnetic directivity used in an instrument, though a ladle on a bronze board was a diviner's tool, not a navigational compass. No ancient sinan survives; its familiar spoon-on-plate model is Wang Zhenduo's 1940s reconstruction, which experiments show works poorly with natural lodestone. Needham accepted a lodestone reading; some sinologists read sinan here as a south-pointing chariot or a constellation. Magnetised needles and a floating compass appear only in Shen Kuo's Mengxi bitan of 1088.

sources.title: Wang Chong, 'Lunheng, chapter 52 Shiying' (c. 83 CE), digitized at Wikisource
sources.author: Wang Chong
sources.confirms: Verbatim text: 司南之杓，投之於地，其柢指南.

sources.title: Li Shu-hua, 'Origine de la Boussole I. Aimant et Boussole', Isis 45 (1954)
sources.author: Li Shu-hua
sources.confirms: Reviews Chinese texts on lodestone and the sinan, arguing for Han knowledge of magnetic polarity while placing the navigational compass much later.

sources.title: Li Shu-hua, 'Origine de la Boussole II. Aimant et Boussole', Isis 45 (1954)
sources.author: Li Shu-hua
sources.qualifies: Questions Needham's confidence that the sinan was a working lodestone instrument and notes the absence of surviving examples.

lodestone-sinan-83.verification_note: Textual witness is secure; interpretation as a magnetic device is debated.
lodestone-sinan-83.detail: Lunheng's date of c. 83 CE is secure from Wang Chong's biography. His sinan passage occurs in an argument against omens, comparing a plant said to point at flatterers with a ladle that points south by nature. Han bronze diviner's boards (shi) survive, but none with a lodestone. This is a concept record; a navigational compass belongs to eleventh century. Earlier Han texts (Hanfeizi, Guiguzi) mention sinan as a guide for jade collectors, and Lunheng's own 'Luan long' chapter notes lodestone attracting needles (頓牟掇芥，磁石引針), so Han writers knew magnetic attraction even if directional use remains uncertain.

picture.alt: Modern model of a Han sinan lodestone ladle on a bronze board (Wang Zhenduo reconstruction) (modern reconstruction)
picture.credit: Unknown author, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

lodestone-sinan-83.dating_note: Reading of sinan as a lodestone instrument is accepted by Needham and Li Shu-hua but contested by some philologists; no artefact survives.

frontinus-aqueducts-97.summary: Sextus Julius Frontinus becomes curator aquarum in 97 CE and writes a treatise for his own instruction and for successors. He lists nine aqueducts, their sources, lengths and intake dates from Aqua Appia (312 BCE) to Claudia and Anio Novus (52 CE), measures discharge in quinariae, and exposes fraud: illegal taps, oversize pipes, and water diverted by watermen for private sale. He compares his structures with 'the idle pyramids or the useless, though famous, works of the Greeks'. His text is the only surviving administrative manual of a Roman public utility, and it preserves the technical vocabulary of pipes, settling tanks and distribution castella used for urban water supply.

sources.title: Frontinus, 'De aquaeductu urbis Romae' (97 CE), trans. C. E. Bennett (1925), LacusCurtius
sources.author: Frontinus
sources.confirms: Text records Frontinus's appointment under Nerva, the list of nine aqueducts with dates, quinaria measurements and fraud by watermen.

sources.title: Rodgers, Robert H. (ed.), 'Frontinus: De Aquaeductu Urbis Romae', Cambridge Classical Texts and Commentaries 42, Cambridge University Press (2004); reviewed by Ehlers, Gnomon 78 (2006)
sources.author: Rodgers, Robert H.
sources.confirms: Critical edition and commentary dating composition to 97 to 98 CE under Nerva and analysing the quinaria system.

sources.title: Hodge, A. Trevor, 'Aqueducts and Water Supply', in Evans (ed.), 'A Companion to the Archaeology of the Roman Republic', Wiley-Blackwell (2013); see also Hodge, 'Roman Aqueducts and Water Supply', Duckworth (1992)
sources.author: Hodge, A. Trevor
sources.confirms: Standard engineering history of Roman water supply, drawing on Frontinus for Rome's system and discharge figures.

frontinus-aqueducts-97.detail: Frontinus's discharge figures do not add up, and modern hydraulic analysis (Hodge, Rodgers) shows quinaria measured pipe cross-section, not flow, so his totals cannot be converted to litres with confidence. Composition date rests on his statement that Nerva appointed him; Nerva ruled from September 96 to January 98. His tally lists 24,000 quinariae of supply, serving 247 castella and 591 public basins, and he reports recovering water stolen by puncturers of pipes (punctores). Frontinus also records legal rules: a senatorial decree of 11 BCE on access strips beside channels, and penalties of 100,000 sesterces for damaging aqueducts. Rodgers's 2004 Cambridge edition is standard.

picture.alt: Arches of Aqua Claudia in Rome, one of the aqueducts Frontinus audited

barbegal-mills-100.summary: An aqueduct branch feeds two parallel flights of eight overshot wheels down a slope at Barbegal near Arles, each driving millstones in a building beside it. Excavated by Benoit in 1937 and reinterpreted since, this complex ground flour for Arelate and perhaps for ships supplying grain. Carbonate deposits from wooden flumes, analysed in 2018, show construction in early second century, about a century of operation, and seasonal use that may have targeted shipping biscuit. Barbegal sits within wider Roman use of water power for grain, ore-crushing and sawing. With Vitruvius's gearing and Hierapolis's water-driven stone saw, it shows Roman engineers converting flowing water into mechanical work at scale.

sources.title: Surmelihindi, Gul et al., 'The second century CE Roman watermills of Barbegal: Unraveling the enigma of one of the oldest industrial complexes', Science Advances 4 (2018), eaar3620
sources.author: Surmelihindi, Gul; Leveau, Philippe; Spotl, Christoph; Bernard, Vincent; Passchier, Cees W.
sources.confirms: Carbonate deposits date construction to the early second century CE, show about a century of operation and seasonal running of the wheels.

sources.title: Wilson, Andrew, 'Machines, Power and the Ancient Economy', Journal of Roman Studies 92 (2002)
sources.author: Wilson, Andrew
sources.confirms: Surveys water-lifting, water-powered grain mills and water power in mining, arguing Roman use of mechanical power was wider than Finley's model allowed.

sources.title: Ritti, Tullia; Grewe, Klaus; Kessener, Paul, 'A relief of a water-powered stone saw mill on a sarcophagus at Hierapolis and its implications', Journal of Roman Archaeology 20 (2007)
sources.author: Ritti, Tullia; Grewe, Klaus; Kessener, Paul
sources.confirms: Publishes a third-century sarcophagus relief of a water wheel driving two stone saws through a crank and connecting rods.

barbegal-mills-100.verification_note: Benoit dated the complex to c. 300 CE; carbonate analysis (2018) places construction in the early second century with a century of use.
barbegal-mills-100.detail: Benoit dated Barbegal to about 300 CE; carbonate analysis in 2018 moved construction back to early second century, so year 100 is approximate. Carbonate layers record seasonal water chemistry, suggesting mills ran mainly in late summer and autumn and stood idle for months, which fits supply of ship's biscuit for Mediterranean sailing seasons rather than a city's daily bread. Each wheel measured about 2.1 metres across; estimated total output is 4.5 tonnes of flour a day. Hierapolis's sawmill relief (mid third century) and Gerasa and Ephesus sawmills (sixth century) extend Roman water power beyond grain; see hierapolis-sawmill-250.

picture.alt: Remains of the aqueduct and mill flights at Barbegal near Arles
picture.credit: Carole Raddato from FRANKFURT, Germany, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

barbegal-mills-100.dating_note: Benoit dated the complex to c. 300 CE; carbonate analysis (2018) places construction in the early second century with a century of use.

garamantes-foggara-100.summary: Survey by David Mattingly's Fazzan Project mapped over 600 foggaras, underground channels with access shafts tapping aquifers under escarpments, feeding fields around Garama (Germa) and other oasis settlements in Libya's Sahara. These towns, with mud-brick fortified centres, cemeteries of thousands of tombs and imports of Roman wine and glass, flourished from about 500 BCE to 500 CE, with foggara construction concentrated in early centuries CE. Mattingly and Sterry's 2013 paper argues these were urban communities sustained by intensive irrigated agriculture of wheat, barley, dates and grapes in hyper-arid terrain. Andrew Wilson's analysis shows labour investment comparable to Roman aqueducts, built without imperial engineering.

sources.title: Mattingly, David J. and Sterry, Martin, 'The first towns in the central Sahara', Antiquity 87 (2013)
sources.author: Mattingly, David J.; Sterry, Martin
sources.confirms: Presents survey evidence for Garamantian urban settlements of the late first millennium BCE and early first millennium CE supported by intensive irrigated agriculture.

sources.title: Wilson, Andrew, 'The Garamantes and the Origins of Saharan Foggara Irrigation', in Mattingly et al. (eds), 'The Archaeology of Fazzan', Society for Libyan Studies
sources.author: Wilson, Andrew
sources.confirms: Analyses foggara technology, distribution and dating in Fazzan and argues for Garamantian origin in the first millennium BCE to CE.

sources.title: Mattingly, David J. (ed.), 'The Archaeology of Fazzan, vol. 1: Synthesis', Society for Libyan Studies (2003), open access on JSTOR
sources.author: Mattingly, David J.
sources.confirms: Synthesis of the Fazzan Project's survey of Garamantian settlements, foggaras and chronology.

garamantes-foggara-100.verification_note: Foggara construction spans several centuries; OSL and settlement dating centre on the first to fourth centuries CE.
garamantes-foggara-100.detail: Foggara dating relies on OSL and radiocarbon from associated settlements and spans from mid first millennium BCE to fourth century CE, so 100 is approximate. Decline follows falling water tables as fossil aquifers were drawn down; no recharge reaches them today. Garama is Garamantian capital described by Pliny after Cornelius Balbus's expedition of 19 BCE, and Roman-Garamantian relations alternated between raids and trade in slaves, carnelian and natron. Shafts spaced about 10 metres apart allowed cleaning; channel lengths run to 4.5 kilometres. Total combined length is estimated at several hundred kilometres across Wadi al-Ajal.

picture.alt: Ruins of Garama (Germa), Garamantian capital in Fazzan, Libya
picture.credit: Franzfoto, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

garamantes-foggara-100.dating_note: Foggara construction spans several centuries; OSL and settlement dating centre on the first to fourth centuries CE.

han-iron-plough-100.summary: Excavations at Guxing near Zhengzhou and at Tieshenggou reveal Han state ironworks with blast furnaces and stacks of clay moulds for ploughshares, hoes and mouldboards, cast in large batches. Iron shares, often as caps over wooden bodies, and cast-iron mouldboards that turn sod appear from Western Han and become standard by first century CE; Hanshu credits Zhao Guo around 90 BCE with promoting ox-drawn ploughing and daitian ridge cultivation. Louche seed drills, a frame with one to three tubes feeding seed from a hopper into furrows, are described in Cui Shi's Simin yueling (c. 160 CE) and shown in Han tomb art. Francesca Bray's volume of Science and Civilisation in China documents these tools, which Europe acquires only in seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.

sources.title: Bray, Francesca, 'Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 6 part 2: Agriculture', Cambridge University Press (1984); reviewed by Elvin in Technology and Culture 26 (1985)
sources.author: Bray, Francesca
sources.confirms: Documents Han cast-iron ploughshares, mouldboards, the multi-tube seed drill and their textual and archaeological evidence.

sources.title: Wagner, Donald B., 'Iron and Steel in Ancient China', Brill (1993)
sources.author: Wagner, Donald B.
sources.confirms: Describes Han ironworks including Guxing and the mass casting of agricultural tools in clay moulds.

sources.title: Ban Gu, 'Hanshu 24A, Shihuo zhi' (c. 100 CE), Chinese Text Project
sources.author: Ban Gu
sources.confirms: Records Zhao Guo's daitian system and promotion of ox ploughing under Emperor Wu.

han-iron-plough-100.verification_note: Year is approximate within the span given in the summary.
han-iron-plough-100.detail: Year 100 is approximate for spread of these tools; iron shares appear from fourth century BCE and mouldboards from Western Han. Guxing's site includes a furnace estimated at 50 cubic metres and over 300 iron objects stamped with state foundry marks. Mouldboard dating and extent of ox ploughing among smallholders remain debated; Bray stresses regional variation. Han iron was cast then often annealed into malleable iron, a process (chaogang) Wagner documents at Tieshenggou. Mural art at Pinglu in Shanxi shows a two-ox plough and a three-tube drill. Comparable European mouldboards appear in late Roman contexts without wide adoption.

picture.alt: Han dynasty cast-iron ploughshare
picture.credit: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

hopewell-exchange-100.summary: Between about 100 BCE and 400 CE, communities in Ohio's Scioto and Miami valleys build geometric earthworks and burial mounds and deposit objects of materials from across North America: obsidian from Obsidian Cliff in Yellowstone, 2,400 kilometres away, mica from Appalachia, copper and silver from Lake Superior, marine shells and shark teeth from Gulf coasts, and grizzly bear canines from Rocky Mountains. Trace-element sourcing confirmed Yellowstone as origin of Hopewell obsidian, with a single Hopewell Mound deposit holding over 136 kilograms. Older accounts read this as long-distance trade networks; later ones read it as a few pilgrimage journeys. Hopewell peoples farmed squash, sunflower and goosefoot and lived in dispersed hamlets, so monuments were gathering places, not cities.

sources.title: Hatch, James W.; Michels, Joseph W.; Stevenson, Christopher M.; Scheetz, Barry E.; Geidel, Richard A., 'Hopewell Obsidian Studies: Behavioral Implications of Recent Sourcing and Dating Research', American Antiquity 55 (1990)
sources.author: Hatch, James W.
sources.confirms: Sources Ohio Hopewell obsidian to Obsidian Cliff, Yellowstone, and dates acquisition episodes within the Middle Woodland period.

sources.title: Carr, Christopher and Case, D. Troy (eds), 'Gathering Hopewell: Society, Ritual, and Ritual Interaction', Springer (2005)
sources.author: Carr, Christopher; Case, D. Troy
sources.confirms: Synthesises Ohio Hopewell social organisation, exotic materials and ceremonial earthworks.

sources.title: National Park Service, 'Hopewell Culture National Historical Park'
sources.confirms: Describes Hopewell earthworks and the range of exotic materials deposited c. 100 BCE to 400 CE.

hopewell-exchange-100.verification_note: Year is approximate within the span given in the summary.
hopewell-exchange-100.detail: Year 100 is approximate within a range of 100 BCE to 400 CE; dating is radiocarbon and obsidian hydration. Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks were inscribed by UNESCO in 2023. Interpretation shifted from Caldwell's 'interaction sphere' of trade, proposed in 1964, toward pilgrimage and gift models. Bow and arrow reach Ohio only after Hopewell decline, around 500 to 700 CE. Craft objects include copper breastplates and ear spools, cut mica hands and claws, platform pipes carved as animals, and obsidian bifaces too thin for use. Mound City near Chillicothe holds 23 mounds within a square enclosure; Hopewell Mound Group's enclosure covers 45 hectares.

picture.alt: Obsidian blade from Hopewell Mound Group, Hopewell Culture National Historical Park
picture.credit: NPS, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

roman-valetudinarium-100.summary: Fortresses at Vetera, Novaesium, Inchtuthil, Vindonissa and forts such as Housesteads contain large courtyard buildings with rows of small rooms, which excavators since 1890s have called valetudinaria, following Hyginus's camp manual and Vegetius.
