Finds of surgical instruments and medicinal plants at some sites support this identification; Vindolanda's strength report lists sick and wounded as separate categories. Patricia Baker warns that most identifications rest on plan alone and that no building is securely proven a hospital, while Galen and Celsus describe medicine as civilian, household practice. Whatever their exact function, these are Europe's earliest buildings plausibly designed for institutional care of sick people.

sources.title: Baker, Patricia A., 'Medical Care for the Roman Army on the Rhine, Danube and British Frontiers in the First, Second and Early Third Centuries AD', BAR International Series 1286, Archaeopress (2004)
sources.author: Baker, Patricia A.
sources.confirms: Reviews all claimed frontier valetudinaria and medical finds.
sources.qualifies: Argues that identification of courtyard buildings as hospitals is unproven in most cases and that medical care was less institutional than earlier scholarship assumed.

sources.title: Israelowich, Ido, 'Medical Care in the Roman Army during the High Empire', in Harris (ed.), 'Popular Medicine in Graeco-Roman Antiquity', Brill (2016)
sources.author: Israelowich, Ido
sources.confirms: Surveys textual and archaeological evidence for army physicians (medici) and infirmaries in the first and second centuries.

sources.title: Pormann, Peter E. and Savage-Smith, Emilie, 'Medieval Islamic Medicine', Edinburgh University Press (2007)
sources.author: Pormann, Peter E.; Savage-Smith, Emilie
sources.qualifies: Shows the claim that Gundeshapur in Sasanian Persia hosted a famous teaching hospital rests on late sources and is a modern construct.

roman-valetudinarium-100.verification_note: Function of the buildings is disputed; presence of army medici is documented.
roman-valetudinarium-100.detail: A Sasanian academy-hospital at Gundeshapur, often dated to Shapur I around 271, lacks contemporary evidence and rests on late sources; Christian xenodocheia from Basil's foundation at Caesarea (c. 370) are first institutions documented as caring for sick poor. Most identified fortress buildings were built around 100. Novaesium's building, excavated by Koenen in 1887 to 1900, had 60 rooms off a corridor around a courtyard, with an operating room identified from instruments. Hyginus (De munitionibus castrorum 4) places a valetudinarium away from workshops for quiet.

picture.alt: Foundations of a courtyard building identified as a valetudinarium at Housesteads Roman fort
picture.credit: Victuallers, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

roman-valetudinarium-100.dating_note: Identification of these buildings as hospitals is contested (Baker 2004); dates of construction run from the Flavian period to the early second century.

silk-road-sericulture-100.summary: Hou Hanshu records that in 97 CE Ban Chao sent Gan Ying toward Daqin (Rome), who reached Tiaozhi on a great sea and turned back when Parthian sailors warned of a voyage lasting years, and that in 166 envoys claiming to come from Daqin's king Andun (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus) arrived by sea at Rinan with ivory, rhinoceros horn and tortoiseshell. Woven and raw silk flows through Parthian and Kushan middlemen to Rome, where Pliny complains of gold drained east. China guards silkworm rearing; Procopius reports monks smuggling eggs to Justinian around 552. Along these routes move glass, horses, Buddhism and paper. Hill's annotated translation and Thorley's study of second-century silk trade document both ends of a commerce neither empire controlled.

sources.title: Thorley, John, 'The Silk Trade between China and the Roman Empire at Its Height, circa A.D. 90-130', Greece and Rome 18 (1971)
sources.author: Thorley, John
sources.confirms: Analyses Gan Ying's mission of 97 CE, Parthian intermediaries and silk trade volumes with Rome.

sources.title: Hill, John E., 'Through the Jade Gate to Rome: A Study of the Silk Routes during the Later Han Dynasty, 1st to 2nd Centuries CE', annotated translation of Hou Hanshu 88 (2009)
sources.author: Fan Ye; Hill, John E.
sources.venue: Silk Road Seattle, University of Washington
sources.confirms: Translation of Hou Hanshu chapter 88: Gan Ying's journey to Tiaozhi in 97 and the Daqin embassy of 166 under 'Andun'.

sources.title: Fan Ye, 'Hou Hanshu' juan 88, Xiyu zhuan (5th c.), Chinese text at Wikisource
sources.author: Fan Ye
sources.confirms: Original text: 和帝永元九年，都護班超遣甘英使大秦，抵條支 and 桓帝延熹九年，大秦王安敦遣使自日南徼外獻象牙、犀角、瑇瑁.

sources.title: Hansen, Valerie, 'The Silk Road: A New History', Oxford University Press (2012)
sources.author: Hansen, Valerie
sources.confirms: Reassesses scale of silk trade and argues much exchange was regional and state-driven rather than long-distance commerce.
sources.qualifies: Cautions against overstating direct Rome-China commerce.

silk-road-sericulture-100.verification_note: Year 100 is approximate within the span 97 to 166.
silk-road-sericulture-100.detail: Year 100 is approximate between two dated events (97 and 166). Whether that 166 'embassy' was official or merchants posing as envoys is debated; most historians favour merchants. Pliny's figure of 100 million sesterces a year lost to India, China and Arabia (NH 12.84) is rhetorical. This trade spanned Han China, Parthia, Kushan India and Rome. Palmyrene tomb textiles and Han silks at Loulan and Niya show weaving types that moved west, and Roman glass vessels appear in Chinese tombs from Guangzhou to Luoyang. Hou Hanshu's Daqin account describes Roman cities, postal relays and coinage, in part reworked from Parthian hearsay.

picture.alt: Western Han embroidered silk from Mawangdui, Changsha
picture.credit: Ismoon, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

vindolanda-tablets-100.summary: Excavations from 1973 at Vindolanda, a fort south of Hadrian's Wall, recover hundreds of postcard-thin wooden leaves written in ink between about 85 and 130 CE. They include strength reports, supply accounts, requests for leave, and a letter from Claudia Severa inviting Sulpicia Lepidina to her birthday on 11 September, dated by the British Museum to 97 to 103 CE and counted among the earliest surviving Latin written by a woman. The tablets show literate administration deep in a provincial garrison, a postal exchange between forts, and everyday use of a cheap writing medium alongside wax tablets and papyrus. Their survival in anaerobic soil makes them Britain's oldest handwritten documents.

sources.title: Bowman, Alan K. and Thomas, J. David, 'Vindolanda 1985: The New Writing-Tablets', Journal of Roman Studies 76 (1986)
sources.author: Bowman, Alan K.; Thomas, J. David
sources.confirms: Reports the ink leaf tablets, their dating by stratigraphy to c. 85 to 130 CE and their content as military and private correspondence.

sources.title: British Museum, 'Writing-tablet 1986,1001.64: letter from Claudia Severa to Lepidina'
sources.confirms: Gives production date 97 to 103 CE, findspot Vindolanda, and describes the birthday invitation as among the earliest Latin writing by a woman.

vindolanda-tablets-100.verification_note: Tablets span c. 85 to 130 CE by stratigraphy; the Severa letter is dated 97 to 103.
vindolanda-tablets-100.detail: Tablets were cut from alder and birch to about 2 mm, folded, and addressed on outer faces; most come from period 3 occupation (c. 97 to 103 CE). Year 100 is a midpoint. Tablet 154 records 31 sick, wounded and eye-sufferers out of 752 men, cited in debates about fort medical care. Ink was carbon black in gum; reading depends on infrared photography, since text fades on exposure. Over 1,700 tablets have been published online by Oxford's Centre for the Study of Ancient Documents. Content ranges from a request for more beer for soldiers to accounts of socks, sandals and underpants sent from home, and a draft petition complaining of a beating.

picture.alt: Vindolanda tablet 291, Claudia Severa's birthday invitation, British Museum
picture.credit: Fæ, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

vindolanda-tablets-100.dating_note: Tablets span c. 85 to 130 CE by stratigraphy; the Severa letter is dated 97 to 103.

cai-lun-paper-105.summary: Hou Hanshu says that before Cai Lun 'writing was mostly on bamboo slips' and silk was costly, so 'Lun conceived the idea of making paper from tree bark, hemp ends, old rags and fishing nets', presenting it in Yuanxing's first year (105 CE). Archaeology shows paper is older: hemp-fibre sheets from Baqiao near Xi'an, a paper map fragment from Fangmatan in Gansu (Western Han, second century BCE), and dated paper at Xuanquanzhi. Tsien Tsuen-hsuin's study of Chinese paper and printing treats Cai Lun as improver and standardiser of a craft rather than inventor. Paper spreads to Korea and Japan by seventh century and to Samarkand by 751, reaching Xativa and Europe through Islamic workshops.

sources.title: Fan Ye, 'Hou Hanshu 78, Biographies of Eunuchs: Cai Lun' (5th c.), Chinese Text Project
sources.author: Fan Ye
sources.confirms: Text: 自古書契多編以竹簡 ... 倫乃造意，用樹膚、麻頭及敝布、魚網以為紙, presented in 元興元年 (105 CE).

sources.title: Tsien, Tsuen-hsuin, 'Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 5 part 1: Paper and Printing', Cambridge University Press (1985)
sources.author: Tsien, Tsuen-hsuin
sources.confirms: Reviews pre-Cai Lun paper finds at Baqiao and elsewhere and treats Cai Lun as improver of an existing craft.

sources.title: Pan Jixing, 'Invention and Development of Papermaking Techniques', in 'History of Printing Techniques in China', Springer (2025)
sources.author: Pan Jixing
sources.confirms: Surveys Western Han paper finds (Baqiao, Fangmatan, Xuanquan) and Cai Lun's improvement of 105 CE.
sources.qualifies: Fangmatan paper map (excavated 1986) postdates this article; its Western Han date rests on tomb typology and is accepted by most but not all specialists.

cai-lun-paper-105.verification_note: Hou Hanshu fixes presentation in 105 CE; archaeological paper from Baqiao and Fangmatan predates it by two centuries, so Cai Lun is improver rather than inventor.
cai-lun-paper-105.detail: 105 is his presentation date in official history; priority is contested: Baqiao fragments (found 1957) and Fangmatan's map place paper-like hemp sheets in second century BCE, and some scholars doubt whether early Baqiao material was writing paper. Cai Lun's contribution is read as process improvement and official adoption. Xuanquanzhi near Dunhuang yielded paper with writing in strata dated by wooden slips to 8 BCE to 23 CE. Cai Lun was a eunuch official in charge of palace workshops (shangfang ling), which gave him authority over craft standards. Later Chinese papermakers honoured him as patron deity.

picture.alt: Fragment of Western Han hemp paper
picture.credit: Ytrottier, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

cai-lun-paper-105.dating_note: Hou Hanshu fixes presentation in 105 CE; archaeological paper from Baqiao and Fangmatan predates it by two centuries, so Cai Lun is improver rather than inventor.

alcantara-bridge-106.summary: An inscription over its central arch names Gaius Julius Lacer as builder and dates dedication to 104 to 106 CE under Trajan, funded by eleven Lusitanian municipalities. Six unmortared granite arches span 194 metres; two central arches open nearly 29 metres each and carry a roadway 48 metres above Tagus water. A triumphal arch stands mid-bridge and a small temple holds Lacer's epitaph claiming his bridge will last for ages. In Trajan's same reign Apollodorus of Damascus bridges Danube for his Dacian war with twenty masonry piers and timber arches over 1,100 metres. Alcantara remains in use and is, with Trajan's Danube bridge, clearest evidence of Roman long-span masonry engineering.

sources.title: O'Connor, Colin, 'Roman Bridges', Cambridge University Press (1993); reviewed in Journal of Roman Archaeology 8 (1995)
sources.author: O'Connor, Colin
sources.confirms: Catalogues Roman bridges including Alcantara (dedicated 104 to 106 CE, builder C. Julius Lacer, six arches, 48 m high) and Trajan's Danube bridge by Apollodorus.

sources.title: Taylor, Rabun, review of O'Connor, 'Roman Bridges', Journal of Roman Archaeology 8 (1995)
sources.author: Taylor, Rabun
sources.confirms: Review assessing O'Connor's catalogue and structural analysis of Roman bridges including Alcantara.

sources.title: Boletin Oficial del Estado, 'Puente de Alcantara, Arco Honorifico y Templo', heritage declaration BOE-A-2023-3100 (2023)
sources.confirms: Spanish heritage listing noting Monument status since 1924 and the honorific arch dedicated to Trajan in 103 to 104.

alcantara-bridge-106.detail: Dedication year is epigraphic and secure. Lacer's inscription reads 'Pontem perpetui mansurum in saecula mundi'. Trajan's Danube bridge at Drobeta (103 to 105 CE), known from Cassius Dio and Trajan's Column, was dismantled under Hadrian or Aurelian; its pier footings survive. Roman road engineering, with layered agger construction and milestones, underpins cursus publicus relays recorded on Peutinger's map. Alcantara's piers rise from bedrock on granite blocks joined by iron clamps set in lead, and voussoirs were raised by cranes with lewis holes still visible. Its second arch was blown up in 1809 during Peninsular War and rebuilt in 1860.

picture.alt: Roman bridge of Alcantara over the Tagus with its central triumphal arch
picture.credit: Alta Falisa, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

zhang-heng-armillary-125.summary: Appointed Grand Astrologer (taishi ling) under Emperor An, Zhang Heng 'made an armillary sphere (huntianyi) and wrote Ling Xian and Suanwang lun', according to Hou Hanshu. Later sources say his bronze sphere was turned by a water clock so its rotation followed sky motion, history's first known powered celestial model. Ling Xian describes a spherical heaven, explains lunar eclipses by Earth's shadow and moonlight as reflected sunlight, and counts 2,500 named stars. Christopher Cullen's Heavenly Numbers analyses Zhang Heng's cosmology within Han court astronomy, where calendar-making and omen reading were state functions. His instruments set a line of development running to Su Song's astronomical clock tower of 1092.

sources.title: Fan Ye, 'Hou Hanshu 59, Biography of Zhang Heng' (5th c.), digitized at Wikisource
sources.author: Fan Ye
sources.confirms: Text: 再遷為太史令。遂乃研核陰陽，妙盡琁機之正，作渾天儀，著靈憲、筭罔論.

sources.title: Cullen, Christopher, 'Heavenly Numbers: Astronomy and Authority in Early Imperial China', Oxford University Press (2017)
sources.author: Cullen, Christopher
sources.confirms: Analyses Zhang Heng's Ling Xian, his armillary instrument and Han astronomical office.

sources.title: Yan, Hong-Sen, 'Reconstruction Designs of Lost Ancient Chinese Machinery', Springer (2007), chapter on Zhang Heng's instruments
sources.author: Yan, Hong-Sen
sources.confirms: Reviews textual evidence for the water-driven armillary and proposes mechanical reconstructions.

zhang-heng-armillary-125.verification_note: Year is approximate within the span given in the summary.
zhang-heng-armillary-125.detail: Zhang Heng held his astrologer's post from about 115 to 120 and again from 126; sphere construction is placed in his first tenure, so 125 is approximate. Water drive is reported in Jin-era sources quoting his own Hun yi text, not in Hou Hanshu. Star counts and eclipse theory in Ling Xian are quoted in Kaiyuan zhanjing of eighth century. Hun yi describes graduated rings for equator, ecliptic and horizon with a sighting tube, and Jin shu's astronomical treatise reports his sphere kept pace with stars so that observers inside could call out risings matched by watchers outside. Beijing's Ancient Observatory holds a Ming replica.

picture.alt: Ming dynasty armillary sphere at Beijing Ancient Observatory, a later instrument in Zhang Heng's tradition (Ming replica)
picture.credit: Hans A. Rosbach, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

pantheon-dome-126.summary: Rome's Pantheon rotunda rises on brick-faced concrete walls six metres thick to a hemispherical dome 43.3 metres across, lit by a nine-metre oculus. Builders grade aggregate from travertine at its base to light volcanic scoria near its top, cut weight with coffers, and rely on pozzolanic mortar that cures by reaction with lime. Brick stamps cluster in 123 to 125 CE, so its dome is usually dated to Hadrian's reign and finished around 126 to 128. Lise Hetland argues from stamp statistics and construction logic that work began under Trajan about 114. Lynne Lancaster's study of vaulted construction shows Pantheon as peak of a century of experiments with lightweight aggregates and relieving arches. No larger unreinforced dome has been built.

sources.title: Hetland, Lise M., 'Dating the Pantheon', Journal of Roman Archaeology 20 (2007)
sources.author: Hetland, Lise M.
sources.confirms: Analyses brick stamps.
sources.qualifies: Argues construction began under Trajan c. 114 rather than Hadrian in 118, with completion under Hadrian.

sources.title: Hetland, Lise M., 'New Perspectives on the Dating of the Pantheon', in Marder and Wilson Jones (eds), 'The Pantheon from Antiquity to the Present', Cambridge University Press (2015)
sources.author: Hetland, Lise M.
sources.confirms: Restates the Trajanic-start hypothesis against the conventional Hadrianic dating of 118 to 128.

sources.title: Lancaster, Lynne C., 'Concrete Vaulted Construction in Imperial Rome: Innovations in Context', Cambridge University Press (2005)
sources.author: Lancaster, Lynne C.
sources.confirms: Documents graded lightweight aggregates, pumice and scoria, relieving arches and the structural logic of Roman concrete vaults culminating in the Pantheon.

pantheon-dome-126.verification_note: Brick stamps of 123 to 125 support Hadrianic completion c. 126 to 128; Hetland (2007) argues construction began under Trajan c. 114.
pantheon-dome-126.detail: Hadrian's reign (117 to 138) and stamp dates of 123 to 125 fix conventional dating; Hetland's Trajanic start is debated. Roman concrete (opus caementicium) uses lime and volcanic ash; materials studies by Admir Masic's group in 2023 find lime clasts that heal cracks when water enters, explaining durability. Porch inscription names Agrippa, builder of a first Pantheon of 27 BCE destroyed by fire in 80 CE. Dome thickness tapers from 6.4 metres at its base to 1.2 metres at its oculus, and step rings outside load its haunches. Interior floor drains carry rain entering through that open oculus.

picture.alt: Coffered concrete dome of the Pantheon in Rome seen from below with its oculus
picture.credit: Ank Kumar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

pantheon-dome-126.dating_note: Brick stamps of 123 to 125 support Hadrianic completion c. 126 to 128; Hetland (2007) argues construction began under Trajan c. 114.

zhang-heng-seismoscope-132.summary: In Yangjia's first year (132 CE) Zhang Heng 'made a seismoscope (houfeng didong yi) of fine bronze, eight chi in diameter, with a domed lid, shaped like a wine jar', Hou Hanshu says. Inside stood a central column with eight channels and trigger mechanisms; outside, eight dragons each held a bronze ball above a toad with open mouth. When ground moved, one dragon released its ball and its clang alerted observers to a quake's direction. Once a dragon triggered with no tremor felt in Luoyang, and scholars doubted it until a courier reported an earthquake in Longxi days later. Sleeswyk and Sivin's 1983 study reconstructs an inverted pendulum design. It is history's earliest recorded instrument for detecting distant earthquakes.

sources.title: Fan Ye, 'Hou Hanshu 59, Biography of Zhang Heng' (5th c.), digitized at Wikisource
sources.author: Fan Ye
sources.confirms: Verbatim: 陽嘉元年，復造候風地動儀。以精銅鑄成，員徑八尺 ... 外有八龍，首銜銅丸，下有蟾蜍，張口承之 ... 後數日驛至，果地震隴西.

sources.title: Sleeswyk, Andre Wegener and Sivin, Nathan, 'Dragons and Toads: The Chinese Seismoscope of A.D. 132', Chinese Science 6 (1983)
sources.author: Sleeswyk, Andre Wegener; Sivin, Nathan
sources.confirms: Analyses the Hou Hanshu text and proposes a mechanical reconstruction with an inverted pendulum and eight triggers; dates the instrument to 132 CE.

zhang-heng-seismoscope-132.detail: No part of this instrument survives, and all modern versions are reconstructions; common museum models follow Wang Zhenduo's 1951 design, whose internal mechanism is conjectural. Whether it could discriminate direction is debated; Sleeswyk and Sivin argue an inverted pendulum could register a distant quake's first motion, and Feng Rui's 2005 team built a working version on that principle. Eight chi is about 1.9 metres. Longxi lies roughly 600 kilometres west of Luoyang, and Hou Hanshu's annals record earthquakes in 133, 134 and 138, one of which may be that confirmed event. Imagery here shows a replica, labelled as such.

picture.alt: Modern replica of Zhang Heng's seismoscope, Museo Oriental, Valladolid

ptolemy-almagest-150.summary: Claudius Ptolemy's Mathematike Syntaxis, in thirteen books, builds on Hipparchus and Babylonian records to model each heavenly body with eccentric circles, epicycles and an equant, derives parameters from dated observations between 127 and 141 CE, tabulates chords (a trigonometric table), and catalogues 1,022 stars by longitude, latitude and magnitude. Gerald Toomer's translation and commentary remain standard in English. Its tables allow computation of positions and eclipses for any date, which is why Arabic astronomers named it al-Majisti, 'the greatest', and why it governed astronomy until Copernicus and Kepler. Aryabhata and later Indian astronomers knew related Greek material through Yavanajataka transmissions.

sources.title: Toomer, G. J. (trans.), 'Ptolemy's Almagest', Princeton University Press (1998; first published 1984)
sources.author: Toomer, G. J.
sources.confirms: Complete annotated translation; dates Ptolemy's observations to 127 to 141 CE and the work's completion to about 150.

sources.title: Jones, Alexander (ed.), 'Ptolemy in Perspective: Use and Criticism of his Work from Antiquity to the Nineteenth Century', Springer (2010)
sources.author: Jones, Alexander
sources.confirms: Studies the Almagest's methods, transmission and critiques including Newton's accusation of data fabrication.

sources.title: Ptolemy, 'Almagest', BnF Grec 2392, digitised manuscript
sources.author: Ptolemy
sources.confirms: Medieval Greek manuscript witness used for imagery.

ptolemy-almagest-150.verification_note: Year is approximate within the span given in the summary.
ptolemy-almagest-150.detail: Completion around 150 is inferred from his latest observation (141 CE) and dedication to Syrus; it is approximate. Robert Newton's 1977 charge that Ptolemy fabricated observations is largely rejected, though adjustment of data to theory is acknowledged. Dependence of his star catalogue on Hipparchus is debated; a 2022 multispectral reading of a palimpsest recovered part of Hipparchus's own catalogue for comparison. Books survive in Greek manuscripts from the ninth century and in Arabic translations from around 800, with Latin versions by Gerard of Cremona in 1175. BnF Grec 2392 supplies imagery.

picture.alt: Page of Ptolemy's Almagest in BnF manuscript Grec 2392 (medieval manuscript)
picture.credit: Bibliotheque nationale de France, Grec 2392, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

ptolemy-geography-150.summary: Ptolemy's Geographike Hyphegesis gives latitude and longitude for about 8,000 localities from Ireland to Southeast Asia, instructions for two conic-type projections and a third globe-like projection, and a critique of Marinus of Tyre's data on distances and itineraries. Berggren and Jones's annotated translation of its theoretical chapters shows how he converted travellers' reports and shadow measurements into coordinates and how his overestimate of Asia's length later encouraged Columbus. Whether his text included drawn maps is debated; surviving maps are Byzantine reconstructions. Translated into Arabic in the ninth century and Latin in 1406, it set a model of a map as a coordinate grid.

sources.title: Berggren, J. Lennart and Jones, Alexander, 'Ptolemy's Geography: An Annotated Translation of the Theoretical Chapters', Princeton University Press (2000)
sources.author: Berggren, J. Lennart; Jones, Alexander
sources.confirms: Translates and analyses Ptolemy's projections, coordinate method, use of Marinus, and the question of original maps.

sources.title: Talbert, Richard J. A., 'Rome's World: The Peutinger Map Reconsidered', Cambridge University Press (2010)
sources.author: Talbert, Richard J. A.
sources.confirms: Contrasts Ptolemy's coordinate cartography with the itinerary-based Peutinger map tradition.

sources.title: Ptolemy, 'Geography', Vatican Urb. gr. 82, 13th century, digitised
sources.author: Ptolemy
sources.confirms: Earliest surviving manuscript with world and regional maps, used for imagery.

ptolemy-geography-150.verification_note: Whether the original Geography contained maps is disputed; surviving maps are from thirteenth-century manuscripts.
ptolemy-geography-150.detail: Composition after Almagest, around 150 CE, is approximate. Longitude values stretch Mediterranean length by about a third because Ptolemy adopted a degree length too short, following Posidonius. Berggren and Jones argue his original probably lacked maps; Stuckelberger and Grasshoff take an opposite view in their 2006 edition. Vatican Urb. gr. 82 of about 1300 holds his earliest surviving maps. Coordinates for Chinese and Southeast Asian places (Sinae, Kattigara) came from merchants' reports via Marinus, and his enclosed Indian Ocean persisted on European maps until Portuguese voyages. Place lists give modern archaeologists a check on Roman-era toponymy.

picture.alt: World map from a manuscript of Ptolemy's Geography, British Library Add MS 19391 (later manuscript)
picture.credit: Anonymous Byzantine scribe, British Library Add MS 19391, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

ptolemy-geography-150.dating_note: Whether the original Geography contained maps is disputed; surviving maps are from thirteenth-century manuscripts.

teotihuacan-grid-150.summary: In Mexico's central highlands, Teotihuacan grows after about 100 CE into a city of perhaps 100,000 people, with a four-kilometre Street of the Dead, Pyramids of Sun and Moon, and more than 2,000 stone-walled apartment compounds, all set on one orientation of about 15.5 degrees east of north that even redirects San Juan river into a canal. George Cowgill's synthesis, drawing on Rene Millon's 1960s mapping project, dates grid and main pyramids to about 100 to 250 CE and reads apartment compounds as planned multi-family housing with drains and plastered floors. Obsidian workshops, Thin Orange ceramics and merchants' quarters show state-scale production and trade across Mesoamerica. No ruler's name survives; governance remains debated.

sources.title: Cowgill, George L., 'Ancient Teotihuacan: Early Urbanism in Central Mexico', Cambridge University Press (2015)
sources.author: Cowgill, George L.
sources.confirms: Synthesises chronology, grid orientation, apartment compounds, pyramids and economy of Teotihuacan with main construction c. 100 to 250 CE.

sources.title: Cowgill, George L., 'State and Society at Teotihuacan, Mexico', Annual Review of Anthropology 26 (1997)
sources.author: Cowgill, George L.
sources.confirms: Reviews urban planning, population estimates and political organisation.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Pre-Hispanic City of Teotihuacan'
sources.confirms: Describes the city's geometric layout and monuments built between the first and seventh centuries.

teotihuacan-grid-150.verification_note: Year is approximate within the span given in the summary.
teotihuacan-grid-150.detail: Year 150 is approximate for grid completion; chronology rests on ceramic phases (Tzacualli, Miccaotli) cross-checked by radiocarbon. Grid orientation is explained by astronomical alignments to sunset on 13 August and 29 April or to Pleiades setting; no consensus exists. Apartment compounds date mostly after 250. Collapse with burning of civic buildings is dated around 550 to 600. Pyramid of the Sun, 65 metres high over a tunnel and cave, was built in one campaign around 200 CE; Feathered Serpent Pyramid, dedicated around 200 to 250, held over 200 sacrificed soldiers. Pecked-cross markers in rock around the city record survey lines.

picture.alt: Avenue of the Dead and Pyramid of the Sun seen from the Pyramid of the Moon, Teotihuacan
picture.credit: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

la-mojarra-stela-156.summary: Pulled from Acula river in Veracruz in 1986, Stela 1 of La Mojarra shows a standing ruler and about 535 glyphs in columns, with two Long Count dates equivalent to 21 May 143 and 13 July 156 CE. Justeson and Kaufman proposed in 1993 a decipherment as an early Mije-Sokean language, reading a narrative of accession, warfare and ritual; Houston and Coe challenged this reading in 2003, and consensus holds that Isthmian script remains undeciphered. Together with Tres Zapotes Stela C (32 BCE) and Tuxtla Statuette (162 CE), it shows Long Count calendrics and a full writing system on Mexico's Gulf coast before Maya Classic monuments. Museo de Antropologia de Xalapa holds it.

sources.title: Justeson, John S. and Kaufman, Terrence, 'A Decipherment of Epi-Olmec Hieroglyphic Writing', Science 259 (1993)
sources.author: Justeson, John S.; Kaufman, Terrence
sources.confirms: Publishes the La Mojarra stela text, its Long Count dates of 143 and 156 CE and a proposed Mije-Sokean decipherment.
sources.qualifies: Decipherment disputed by Houston and Coe (2003); the script is widely regarded as undeciphered.

sources.title: Houston, Stephen and Coe, Michael D., 'Has Isthmian Writing Been Deciphered?', Mexicon 25 (2003)
sources.author: Houston, Stephen; Coe, Michael D.
sources.confirms: Tests the proposed decipherment against the Teotihuacan-style mask text and finds it fails, leaving dates and iconography as secure evidence.

la-mojarra-stela-156.verification_note: Long Count dates are fixed under the GMT correlation; the text's decipherment is contested.
la-mojarra-stela-156.detail: Long Count dates use GMT correlation (584283), accepted by most Mesoamericanists; 156 CE is secure under it. Kaufman and Justeson responded to Houston and Coe in 2004, and debate continues with few new texts to test. Authenticity was questioned briefly after discovery and is accepted. A second carving phase on one side may be later. Text columns run to 21 glyphs each in a script of about 150 known signs, with phonetic and logographic elements. Ruler's costume includes a shark headdress; iconography links him to Olmec-derived traditions at Tres Zapotes and Cerro de las Mesas.

picture.alt: La Mojarra Stela 1 with Isthmian script, Museo de Antropologia de Xalapa
picture.credit: Adrian Hernandez, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

la-mojarra-stela-156.dating_note: Long Count dates are fixed under the GMT correlation; the text's decipherment is contested.

antonine-plague-165.summary: An epidemic reaches Roman armies in Mesopotamia in 165 CE and moves west with Lucius Verus's troops to Rome by 166, recurring until about 180 and again in 189. Galen, who left Rome in 166 and treated cases at Aquileia in 168 to 169, records fever, diarrhoea, black pustules and a crusted rash lasting about two weeks; most modern physicians read his notes as smallpox. Duncan-Jones gathers evidence of falling brick stamps, abandoned quarries, military recruitment problems and Egyptian tax rolls to argue for mortality perhaps near ten percent; Littman estimates seven to ten percent. Inscriptions, including a plaque for soldiers who died of plague, record losses. It is antiquity's first pandemic documented across a connected Eurasian system.

sources.title: Duncan-Jones, R. P., 'The impact of the Antonine plague', Journal of Roman Archaeology 9 (1996)
sources.author: Duncan-Jones, R. P.
sources.confirms: Assembles dated documents, building, mining and census evidence to argue for a severe demographic and economic shock from 165 CE onward.

sources.title: Littman, R. J. and Littman, M. L., 'Galen and the Antonine Plague', American Journal of Philology 94 (1973)
sources.author: Littman, R. J.; Littman, M. L.
sources.confirms: Analyses Galen's clinical descriptions, identifies the disease as smallpox and estimates mortality of seven to ten percent.

sources.title: Harper, Kyle, 'The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of an Empire', Princeton University Press (2017)
sources.author: Harper, Kyle
sources.confirms: Synthesises evidence for the Antonine plague as a smallpox pandemic spread along imperial networks.
sources.qualifies: Mortality estimates remain contested; Harper's high figures are debated by Haldon and others.

antonine-plague-165.verification_note: Mortality estimates range from under two percent to above twenty-five percent; identification as smallpox is probable but unconfirmed by ancient DNA.
antonine-plague-165.detail: Identification as smallpox rests on Galen's descriptions; no ancient DNA has yet confirmed it. Chinese sources record epidemics in Han armies in 161 to 162 and 171 to 185, which some scholars link to one pathogen moving along Eurasian routes. Duncan-Jones's inference of ten percent mortality from documentary gaps has been challenged by Bruun as over-reading. Galen's fullest account appears in Methodus medendi 5.12 and in his commentary on Hippocrates' Epidemics, noting black stools in those who died and dry, scab-like pustules in survivors. Marcus Aurelius died at Vindobona in 180, possibly of this disease.

picture.alt: Memorial plaque commemorating soldiers who died in the Antonine plague
picture.credit: Quinet, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

antonine-plague-165.dating_note: Mortality estimates range from under two percent to above twenty-five percent; identification as smallpox is probable but unconfirmed by ancient DNA.

galen-rome-169.summary: Galen of Pergamon, trained at Alexandria and as gladiator physician, reaches Rome in 162, leaves during the plague in 166, and returns in 169 at Marcus Aurelius's summons to remain until his death around 216. He dissects pigs and Barbary macaques, demonstrates that arteries carry blood and that recurrent laryngeal nerves control voice, ligates ureters to show kidneys produce urine, and writes over three million surviving words. Vivian Nutton shows how Galen's self-presentation distorted later views of ancient medicine, yet his synthesis of humoral theory, anatomy and drug lore becomes the authority in Byzantine, Arabic and Latin medicine until Vesalius and Harvey. He also records the Antonine plague's symptoms first-hand.

sources.title: Nutton, Vivian, 'The Fatal Embrace: Galen and the History of Ancient Medicine', Science in Context 18 (2005)
sources.author: Nutton, Vivian
sources.confirms: Argues Galen's career and views are untypical of ancient practitioners and that humoral theory became universal only after his death; documents his dominance of later medical history.

sources.title: Nutton, Vivian, 'Ancient Medicine', 2nd ed., Routledge (2013)
sources.author: Nutton, Vivian
sources.confirms: Standard account of Galen's life, dates (arrival in Rome 162, return 169, death c. 216), dissections and writings.

galen-rome-169.detail: Galen's death date is given as 199 or 200 in Suda, but Arabic sources and internal evidence put it near 216. His anatomical errors from animal dissection (rete mirabile, five-lobed liver) persisted until sixteenth century. He rejected hospitals as institutions and practised in households, which bears on debates about valetudinaria. His pharmacology, in On Simple Drugs and On Compound Drugs, grades remedies by degree of heat, cold, wetness and dryness, a scheme Arabic physicians formalised. Public anatomical demonstrations in Rome, including a pig whose squeal stopped when he cut a laryngeal nerve, built his reputation among senators and Marcus Aurelius's court.

picture.alt: Galen among physicians in the Vienna Dioscurides manuscript, c. 512 (c. 512 manuscript)
picture.credit: Unknown author, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

sn-185-185.summary: Hou Hanshu's astronomical treatise notes that in Zhongping's second year, on a day in its tenth month (7 December 185), 'a guest star appeared within Nanmen; it was as large as half a mat, multicoloured, and gradually diminished, disappearing in the sixth month of the following year'. Twentieth-century astronomers identified its remnant with RCW 86, a shell about 2,800 parsecs away whose X-ray and infrared observations fit a Type Ia explosion of roughly that age. Chin and Huang read this text as a comet, and readings of its visibility run from eight to twenty months. Such records show systematic sky-watching by Han officials, whose dated accounts of comets, novae and sunspots remain used by modern astronomers.

sources.title: Zhao, Fu-Yuan; Strom, R. G.; Jiang, Shi-Yang, 'The Guest Star of AD185 Must Have Been a Supernova', Chinese Journal of Astronomy and Astrophysics 6 (2006)
sources.author: Zhao, Fu-Yuan; Strom, R. G.; Jiang, Shi-Yang
sources.venue: Chinese Journal of Astronomy and Astrophysics
sources.confirms: Re-examines the Hou Hanshu record, supports the supernova interpretation and the link to RCW 86, and reviews the visibility duration.

sources.title: Chin, Y.-N. and Huang, Y.-L., 'Identification of the guest star of AD 185 as a comet rather than a supernova', Nature 371 (1994)
sources.author: Chin, Y.-N.; Huang, Y.-L.
sources.qualifies: Argues the textual description, including apparent movement, fits a comet rather than a supernova.

sources.title: Williams, Brian J. et al., 'RCW 86: A Type Ia Supernova in a Wind-Blown Bubble', Astrophysical Journal 741 (2011)
sources.author: Williams, Brian J. et al.
sources.confirms: Infrared and X-ray analysis supports RCW 86 as a Type Ia remnant with an age compatible with 185 CE.

sn-185-185.verification_note: Chinese record is secure; astrophysical identification is probable but debated.
sn-185-185.detail: Conversion of that date to 7 December 185 is secure; identification with RCW 86 depends on position near Alpha and Beta Centauri and on remnant age estimates of 1,800 to 2,000 years. Alternative candidates and a comet reading remain in literature, so identification is probable rather than settled. Spitzer and Chandra observations in 2011 found RCW 86 expanding into a low-density cavity, explaining how a Type Ia remnant grew so large in 1,800 years. Han astronomers logged 'guest stars' (kexing) as omens; their catalogue later gave modern astronomers SN 1006, 1054 and 1181 as well.

picture.alt: Supernova remnant RCW 86, candidate remnant of the guest star of 185 CE, NASA composite image
picture.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/UCLA, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

sn-185-185.dating_note: Supernova identification (RCW 86) is widely but not universally accepted; Chin and Huang (1994) read the record as a comet.

hua-tuo-anesthesia-200.summary: Chen Shou's Sanguozhi (c. 290) records physician Hua Tuo (d. c. 208): when illness lay 'where needle and drug could not reach and cutting was required, he had the patient drink mafeisan; in a moment they were as if drunk and dead, knowing nothing, and he opened and removed it'. Bowels were cut, washed and sutured, with recovery in a month. Hua Tuo is also credited with Five Animal exercises and with acupuncture points. Fu's 2002 review treats this account as history's earliest description of surgical anaesthesia, while Chen Yinke and Victor Mair argue it borrows from Indian Buddhist narratives of physician Jivaka, and mafeisan's recipe is lost. The surgery is a documented claim rather than a proven practice.

sources.title: Chen Shou, 'Sanguozhi 29, Biography of Hua Tuo' (c. 290), digitized at Wikisource
sources.author: Chen Shou
sources.confirms: Verbatim: 若病結積在內，針藥所不能及，當須刳割者，便飲其麻沸散，須臾便如醉死無所知，因破取.

sources.title: Fu, Louis, 'Hua Tuo, the Chinese god of surgery', Journal of Medical Biography 10 (2002)
sources.author: Fu, Louis
sources.confirms: Reviews Hua Tuo's biography, the mafeisan account and its reception as the first record of surgical anaesthesia.

sources.title: Mair, Victor H., 'The Biography of Hua-t'o from the History of the Three Kingdoms', in Mair (ed.), 'The Columbia Anthology of Traditional Chinese Literature', Columbia University Press (1994)
sources.author: Mair, Victor H.
sources.qualifies: Translates the biography and, following Chen Yinke, argues parts of the Hua Tuo legend derive from Indian Jivaka tales.

hua-tuo-anesthesia-200.verification_note: Textual accounts exist; the practice of anaesthetised surgery is unverified.
hua-tuo-anesthesia-200.detail: Hua Tuo's dates are uncertain (c. 140 to 208); 200 is approximate. Mafeisan's composition is unknown; later guesses include cannabis (ma) and datura. Hou Hanshu also carries a biography. Scepticism about surgery rests on absence of any later Chinese surgical tradition and on parallels with Buddhist texts, where Jivaka also opens skulls and abdomens. Chen Yinke noted in 1930 that Hua Tuo's name may transcribe Sanskrit agada, 'medicine'. Sanguozhi says Cao Cao executed him for refusing service, and that his medical writings burned with him. His Five Animal exercises (wuqinxi) survive in later qigong tradition.

picture.alt: Hua Tuo memorial hall
picture.credit: Zhou Guanhuai, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

hua-tuo-anesthesia-200.dating_note: Historicity of the surgical accounts is contested (Chen Yinke, Mair); the texts date from c. 290 and 445.

shanghan-lun-200.summary: Zhang Ji (Zhongjing), active in Nanyang around 200 CE, writes in his preface that epidemics killed two thirds of his clan within ten years, seven tenths from 'cold damage'. His treatise classifies febrile disease by six channel stages (taiyang to jueyin) and prescribes over 100 formulas with weights and preparation methods, among them guizhi tang and mahuang tang still in use. Wang Shuhe re-edited it in third century and Song editors split it into Shanghan lun and Jingui yaolue. Paul Unschuld's studies of Chinese medicine place it as China's first work to link diagnosis to prescription systematically, and it remains a core text in East Asian medical training.

sources.title: Unschuld, Paul U., 'Medicine in China: A History of Ideas', 25th anniversary ed., University of California Press (2010)
sources.author: Unschuld, Paul U.
sources.confirms: Discusses Zhang Ji's Shanghan lun around 200 CE, its six-stage classification and formula-based therapy and later editorial history.

sources.title: Goldschmidt, Asaf, 'The Evolution of Chinese Medicine: Song Dynasty, 960-1200', Routledge (2008)
sources.author: Goldschmidt, Asaf
sources.confirms: Traces the Song recovery and canonisation of Zhang Zhongjing's text and its earlier transmission through Wang Shuhe.

sources.title: Mitchell, Craig; Ye, Feng; Wiseman, Nigel, 'Shang Han Lun: On Cold Damage, Translation and Commentaries', Paradigm Publications (1999)
sources.author: Mitchell, Craig; Ye, Feng; Wiseman, Nigel
sources.confirms: Full translation including the preface on clan mortality from epidemics.

shanghan-lun-200.verification_note: Year is approximate within the span given in the summary.
shanghan-lun-200.detail: Zhang Ji's dates (c. 150 to 219) and composition date are inferred from his preface and Han epidemics of 170s to 200s, so 200 is approximate. Some scholars question whether Zhang Ji served as governor of Changsha as later tradition holds. Received text is a Song reconstruction of a third-century edition printed by Imperial Medical Bureau in 1065. Formulas specify drugs by weight in liang and zhu, decoction volumes and dosing schedules, with instructions such as covering a patient to induce sweat after guizhi tang. Japanese Kampo medicine built its pharmacopoeia on these prescriptions, and clinical trials of mahuang tang continue.

picture.alt: Diagram of the textual lineage of Shanghan zabing lun
picture.credit: Minjian Zhongyi Wang, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

tertullian-curiosity-200.summary: In De praescriptione haereticorum, written at Carthage around 200 CE, Tertullian writes: 'What indeed has Athens to do with Jerusalem?' and 'We want no curious disputation after possessing Christ Jesus, no inquisition after enjoying the gospel!' In De spectaculis he condemns theatres and games, and in De idololatria he debates which crafts a Christian may practise, ruling out idol-making and astrology. P. G. Walsh's study of curiositas traces how this Latin word turned from Cicero's neutral inquisitiveness into a vice in Apuleius and Christian fathers. Tertullian's lines are among antiquity's clearest records of a religious case against free inquiry into nature and novelty, which Augustine develops two centuries later.

sources.title: Tertullian, 'De praescriptione haereticorum 7' (c. 200), trans. Peter Holmes, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, digitized at tertullian.org
sources.author: Tertullian
sources.confirms: Chapter 7 verbatim: 'What indeed has Athens to do with Jerusalem?' and 'We want no curious disputation after possessing Christ Jesus, no inquisition after enjoying the gospel!'

sources.title: Walsh, P. G., 'The Rights and Wrongs of Curiosity (Plutarch to Augustine)', Greece and Rome 35 (1988)
sources.author: Walsh, P. G.
sources.confirms: Traces curiositas from Plutarch and Apuleius through Tertullian to Augustine as a moral category condemning idle inquiry.

sources.title: Barnes, Timothy D., 'Tertullian: A Historical and Literary Study', Oxford University Press (1971; rev. 1985)
sources.author: Barnes, Timothy D.
sources.confirms: Dates De praescriptione to c. 203 and establishes Tertullian's Carthaginian context.

tertullian-curiosity-200.verification_note: Year is approximate within the span given in the summary.
tertullian-curiosity-200.detail: Barnes dates De praescriptione to about 203; 200 is approximate. Tertullian elsewhere praises craft and admits Christians work as builders, artisans and soldiers, so his hostility targets speculative philosophy more than technique. In De pallio he celebrates human improvement of nature through agriculture and engineering. His Athens-Jerusalem line became a slogan in later debates about faith and science, often quoted without its context, a polemic against gnostic teachers. Latin text survives in Codex Agobardinus (ninth century) and later copies; Balliol College MS 79, used for imagery, is a fifteenth-century witness.

picture.alt: Page of Tertullian's works in Balliol College MS 79, fifteenth century (fifteenth-century manuscript)
picture.credit: Balliol College, Oxford, MS 79, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

wheelbarrow-china-200.summary: Carved bricks and reliefs from Eastern Han tombs in Sichuan and Shandong, including Shen Fujun's shrine of about 150 CE, depict a man pushing a single-wheeled barrow, and Sanguozhi credits Zhuge Liang with 'wooden oxen' (muniu) used to supply troops on Qinling roads in 231. M. J. T. Lewis's 1994 article in Technology and Culture compares Chinese and Greek evidence and concludes wheelbarrows appear in China by first century CE, with load centred over a large wheel so one person can move several hundred kilograms. Europe has no evidence before about 1200. Chinese barrows carry both goods and passengers for 1,800 years afterward.

sources.title: Lewis, M. J. T., 'The Origins of the Wheelbarrow', Technology and Culture 35 (1994)
sources.author: Lewis, M. J. T.
sources.confirms: Reviews Han tomb images and texts, placing the wheelbarrow in China by the first century CE, and examines contested Greek evidence.

sources.title: Chen Shou, 'Sanguozhi 35, Biography of Zhuge Liang' (c. 290), Chinese Text Project
sources.author: Chen Shou
sources.confirms: Records Zhuge Liang's use of 木牛 (wooden ox) to transport grain in his northern campaigns of 231 and 234.

sources.title: Needham, Joseph and Wang Ling, 'Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 4 part 2: Mechanical Engineering', Cambridge University Press (1965), pp. 258-281
sources.author: Needham, Joseph; Wang Ling
sources.confirms: Collects Han reliefs and later texts on the wheelbarrow and its designs.

wheelbarrow-china-200.verification_note: Han reliefs date to the second century CE; the 'wooden ox' identification is interpretive.
wheelbarrow-china-200.detail: Year 200 is approximate between dated Han reliefs (c. 118 to 150 CE) and wooden oxen of 231. Lewis notes a possible fifth-century BCE Greek building account mentioning a 'one-wheeler' (hypoteros), which he treats as unproven. Identification of wooden oxen as wheelbarrows is a later interpretation of a vague text. Chinese design places its wheel at centre under a frame, so a pusher balances rather than lifts; European barrows put wheels at front and load weight on arms. Later Chinese barrows added sails and carried passengers on both sides of a central wheel, as nineteenth-century photographs from Shanghai show.

picture.alt: Chinese wheelbarrow with a large central wheel, Peking, 1924 photograph
picture.credit: Unknown photographer, 1924 postcard, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

wheelbarrow-china-200.dating_note: Han reliefs date to the second century CE; the 'wooden ox' identification is interpretive.

yue-ware-celadon-200.summary: Potters at Shangyu and nearby sites in northern Zhejiang fire grey stoneware bodies at about 1,200 degrees with lime-rich ash glazes, producing green-glazed vessels in dragon kilns from Eastern Han onward. Kerr and Wood's volume on ceramic technology in Science and Civilisation in China traces this from Shang proto-porcelain through Han ash glazes to Six Dynasties Yue ware. Analysis of Houshan kiln material assigns mature celadon production to late Eastern Han. Yue ware supplies Jin and Southern courts, is exported to Korea and Japan, and leads to Tang 'secret colour' (mise) celadon and porcelain of later dynasties. These kilns set a technical basis for Chinese high-fired ceramics.

sources.title: Kerr, Rose and Wood, Nigel, 'Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 5 part 12: Ceramic Technology', Cambridge University Press (2004); reviewed in Antiquity 80 (2006)
sources.author: Kerr, Rose; Wood, Nigel
sources.confirms: Documents Han high-fired ash-glazed stoneware, dragon kilns and the emergence of Yue celadon in Zhejiang in the Eastern Han.

sources.title: Yan, Lingtong et al., 'Characterization of early Chinese northern celadon with lead glaze from Caocun kiln within Yecheng site', Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports 19 (2018)
sources.author: Yan, Lingtong; Sun, Heyang; Li, Li; Feng, Xiangqian
sources.confirms: States that 'the earliest mature celadon wares were considered to be produced in Yue kiln from Zhejiang during Eastern Han dynasty' and that Han Yue celadon was fired above 1,100 degrees.

yue-ware-celadon-200.verification_note: Mature celadon begins in the late Eastern Han by kiln analysis; exact decade unknown.
yue-ware-celadon-200.detail: Eastern Han to Western Jin production (c. 100 to 300 CE) is a range; 200 is approximate. 'Proto-porcelain' is used for earlier Shang and Zhou glazed stoneware; 'porcelain' in Western usage, white translucent ware, appears only in Sui and Tang. Terminology differences between Chinese and Western scholarship complicate claims of a 'first porcelain'. Dragon kilns at Shangyu, built up slopes to lengths of 10 to 13 metres, reached 1,250 to 1,300 degrees with wood fuel in a reducing atmosphere that turned iron in glaze green. Body analyses show porcelain stone with 2 to 3 percent iron and glazes made from wood ash and clay.

picture.alt: Eastern Han celadon vase from a Yue kiln
picture.credit: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

yue-ware-celadon-200.dating_note: Mature celadon begins in the late Eastern Han by kiln analysis; exact decade unknown.

south-pointing-chariot-235.summary: Fu Xuan's account preserved in Sanguozhi tells how courtiers Gaotang Long and Qin Lang mocked Ma Jun's claim that ancients had a south-pointing chariot. Ma Jun answered: 'Empty argument with words is not as good as trying it and seeing', so Emperor Ming of Wei ordered him to build it 'and the south-pointing chariot was completed'. Jinshu describes such a vehicle: a two-storey carriage drawn by four horses with a wooden immortal 'whose hand always points south however the carriage turns'. Reconstructions use a differential gear train that offsets wheel rotation when turning. It is a mechanical device holding a reference direction without magnetism, an early self-correcting mechanism alongside Hero's automata.

sources.title: Chen Shou, 'Sanguozhi 29' with Pei Songzhi's commentary quoting Fu Xuan on Ma Jun (c. 290/429), digitized at Wikisource
sources.author: Chen Shou; Pei Songzhi
sources.confirms: Verbatim: 言及指南車，二子謂古無指南車 ... 先生曰：虛爭空言，不如試之易效也 ... 詔先生作之，而指南車成.

sources.title: Fang Xuanling et al., 'Jinshu 25, Treatise on Carriages and Dress' (648), digitized at Wikisource
sources.author: Fang Xuanling
sources.confirms: Verbatim: 司南車，一名指南車，駕四馬 ... 刻木為仙人，衣羽衣，立車上，車雖回運而手常南指.

sources.title: Yan, Hong-Sen and Chen, Kuo-Hung, 'A systematic approach for the reconstruction of the south-pointing chariot', Transactions of the Canadian Society for Mechanical Engineering 20 (1996)
sources.author: Hsieh, Wen-Hsiang; Yan, Hong-Sen
sources.venue: Transactions of the Canadian Society for Mechanical Engineering
sources.confirms: Reviews historical records and systematically generates gear-train designs for the south-pointing chariot.

south-pointing-chariot-235.verification_note: Year is approximate within the span given in the summary.
south-pointing-chariot-235.detail: Ma Jun's chariot is dated to Qinglong reign (233 to 237); 235 is approximate. Song shu gives detailed gear counts for a chariot built by Yan Su in 1027, from which modern reconstructions derive; nothing of Ma Jun's version survives. Legends assign such a device to Yellow Emperor and Duke of Zhou, which Ma Jun's opponents rejected. Ma Jun also improved silk looms, reducing 50 or 60 heddles to 12, built a chain pump for palace gardens and a water-driven puppet theatre, as Fu Xuan records. Whether his chariot used true differential gearing or a simpler clutch arrangement cannot be known from texts.

picture.alt: Model of a south-pointing chariot, Science Museum London (modern model)
picture.credit: Andy Dingley, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

cyprian-plague-249.summary: Bishop Cyprian's De mortalitate, written at Carthage about 252, describes a disease with violent diarrhoea, continual vomiting, fever, bleeding from eyes, loss of hearing and sight, and putrefaction of hands and feet. Kyle Harper's 2015 study assembles Dionysius of Alexandria's letters, Eusebius, Zosimus and Historia Augusta to argue for an empire-wide pandemic lasting from 249 to about 270, possibly a viral haemorrhagic fever or pandemic influenza, which struck Rome under Gallus and killed Claudius II in 270. A mass burial with lime at Thebes in Egypt dated to this period may be linked. Harper connects this plague with mid third-century political and military crisis and with Christian charitable responses that Dionysius records.

sources.title: Harper, Kyle, 'Pandemics and passages to late antiquity: rethinking the plague of c.249-270 described by Cyprian', Journal of Roman Archaeology 28 (2015)
sources.author: Harper, Kyle
sources.confirms: Collects the sources, dates the pandemic to c. 249 to 270, analyses Cyprian's symptom description and proposes a viral haemorrhagic fever or influenza.

sources.title: Cyprian of Carthage, 'De mortalitate' (c. 252), trans. Ernest Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, New Advent
sources.author: Cyprian
sources.confirms: Chapter 14 describes bowels loosened, fire in the throat, vomiting, eyes on fire, feet or parts cut off by putrefaction, and loss of hearing or sight.

sources.title: Harper, Kyle, 'The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of an Empire', Princeton University Press (2017)
sources.author: Harper, Kyle
sources.qualifies: Harper's identification of the pathogen and the scale of mortality are debated; other historians see regional epidemics rather than a single pandemic.

cyprian-plague-249.verification_note: Pathogen and total mortality are unknown; Harper's pandemic interpretation is influential but contested.
cyprian-plague-249.detail: Start year 249 follows Harper's reading of Dionysius and Egyptian evidence; some place onset at 251. Pathogen identification is speculative without ancient DNA. Pontius's Life of Cyprian reports Christians nursing sick neighbours in Carthage, an early record of organised care during an epidemic. Dionysius writes that Alexandria's population fell by more than half, comparing census rolls of those aged 14 to 80 to earlier counts of those aged 40 to 70. Cyprian's own text urges Christians not to fear death from this disease, arguing it tests faith equally in believers and pagans.

picture.alt: Cyprian depicted in the Menologion of Basil II, c. 1000 (c. 1000 manuscript)
picture.credit: Menologion of Basil II, Vatican Library, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

cyprian-plague-249.dating_note: Pathogen and total mortality are unknown; Harper's pandemic interpretation is influential but contested.

diophantus-arithmetica-250.summary: Arithmetica, originally thirteen books of which six survive in Greek and four more in Arabic translation, poses about 290 problems seeking rational solutions to determinate and indeterminate equations. Diophantus uses abbreviations for an unknown (an s-like sign), its square (dynamis) and cube, a sign for minus, and rules for moving terms between sides, which Jean Christianidis describes as a method organised around setting up and reducing an equation rather than a collection of tricks. His date is fixed only between Hypsicles (c. 150 BCE), whom he cites, and Theon of Alexandria (c. 350 CE), who cites him; 250 is a conventional midpoint. Hypatia reportedly commented on his work, and Fermat's marginal note on problem II.8 in Bachet's 1621 edition launched his last theorem.

sources.title: Christianidis, Jean, 'The way of Diophantus: Some clarifications on Diophantus' method of solution', Historia Mathematica 34 (2007)
sources.author: Christianidis, Jean
sources.confirms: Analyses Diophantus's solution method as a structured procedure using named unknowns and equation reduction.

sources.title: Christianidis, Jean and Oaks, Jeffrey, 'Practicing algebra in late antiquity: The problem-solving of Diophantus of Alexandria', Historia Mathematica 40 (2013)
sources.author: Christianidis, Jean; Oaks, Jeffrey
sources.confirms: Interprets the Arithmetica as premodern algebra and discusses notation and dating between Hypsicles and Theon.

sources.title: Sesiano, Jacques, 'Books IV to VII of Diophantus' Arithmetica in the Arabic Translation Attributed to Qusta ibn Luqa', Springer (1982)
sources.author: Sesiano, Jacques
sources.confirms: Edits the four Arabic books discovered in 1968, establishing that ten of thirteen books survive.

diophantus-arithmetica-250.verification_note: Diophantus's lifetime is fixed only between c. 150 BCE and c. 350 CE; a mid third-century date is conventional.
diophantus-arithmetica-250.detail: A range of 150 BCE to 350 CE is narrowed by a dedication to one Dionysius, possibly Alexandria's bishop (247 to 264), supporting a third-century date; it remains approximate. A famous epigram giving his age as 84 is of uncertain value. Whether his work counts as algebra is a live historiographical debate (Unguru, Klein, Christianidis). Arabic books IV to VII, found in Mashhad in 1968 and edited by Sesiano, carry Qusta ibn Luqa's ninth-century translation and show more worked verification than Greek books. Diophantus accepts only positive rational solutions and calls a problem with negative answer absurd.

picture.alt: Title page of Bachet's 1621 edition of Diophantus's Arithmetica (1621 printed edition)
picture.credit: Facsimile of Bachet's 1621 edition, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

diophantus-arithmetica-250.dating_note: Diophantus's lifetime is fixed only between c. 150 BCE and c. 350 CE; a mid third-century date is conventional.

hierapolis-sawmill-250.summary: On a sarcophagus of Marcus Aurelius Ammianos in Hierapolis's northern necropolis in Phrygia, a relief carved around 250 CE depicts an undershot water wheel whose axle turns a gear train and a crank; two connecting rods move frame saws back and forth through stone blocks. It is antiquity's only known representation of a crank and connecting-rod mechanism, converting rotary to reciprocating motion. Ammianos's epitaph calls him skilled in machines like Daedalus. Later water-powered stone saws are excavated at Gerasa and Ephesus (sixth century), and Ausonius mentions marble-sawing mills on Moselle tributaries around 370. This relief moved a mechanism once thought medieval back by a millennium.

sources.title: Ritti, Tullia; Grewe, Klaus; Kessener, Paul, 'A relief of a water-powered stone saw mill on a sarcophagus at Hierapolis and its implications', Journal of Roman Archaeology 20 (2007)
sources.author: Ritti, Tullia; Grewe, Klaus; Kessener, Paul
sources.confirms: Publishes the relief, dates the sarcophagus to the third century, and identifies the crank and connecting rod driving two saws from a water wheel.

sources.title: Wilson, Andrew, 'Machines, Power and the Ancient Economy', Journal of Roman Studies 92 (2002)
sources.author: Wilson, Andrew
sources.confirms: Surveys Roman water-powered sawing and other industrial uses of water power.

hierapolis-sawmill-250.verification_note: Year is approximate within the span given in the summary.
hierapolis-sawmill-250.detail: Dating to mid third century rests on letter forms and sarcophagus style; 250 is approximate. Some engineers question whether its carver showed a true crank or a simplified eccentric; Tullia Ritti defends a crank reading from rod attachments and gear depiction. Ausonius's Mosella line 362 refers to saws cutting marble by water. Excavated sawmills at Gerasa (Jordan) and Ephesus, both sixth century, used similar crank drives, and a third-century one is argued at Augusta Raurica. Ammianos may have owned or run such a mill, since Hierapolis quarried travertine and marble for export.

picture.alt: Schematic of the Hierapolis water-powered stone sawmill with crank and connecting rods (modern schematic)
picture.credit: Commons user Lun, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
